item.title: [SCMP] Quad confirmed, Manila envoy signals likely ‘Squad’ talks before Trump-Xi summit
item.description:
The Philippine ambassador to the United States signalled possible meetings of the “Squad” bloc ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila, as Washington confirmed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would hold its first leaders’ summit in more than two years on the sidelines of the regional talks.

An informal defence grouping, the “Squad” forms part of a US-led regional strategy to counter China’s growing influence in the Asia-Pacific region. It comprises the US and three of its treaty allies: the Philippines, Australia and Japan. The Quad, by contrast, includes India in place of the Philippines and is not a formal military alliance.

Speaking exclusively with the South China Morning Post in a recent interview, Jose Manuel Romualdez also voiced hope that Asean would evolve into a Nato-like alliance capable of handling its own security.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippine ambassador to the United States signalled possible meetings of the “Squad” bloc ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila, as Washington confirmed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would hold its first leaders’ summit in more than two years on the sidelines of the regional talks.

An informal defence grouping, the “Squad” forms part of a US-led regional strategy to counter China’s growing influence in the Asia-Pacific region. It comprises the US and three of its treaty allies: the Philippines, Australia and Japan. The Quad, by contrast, includes India in place of the Philippines and is not a formal military alliance.

Speaking exclusively with the South China Morning Post in a recent interview, Jose Manuel Romualdez also voiced hope that Asean would evolve into a Nato-like alliance capable of handling its own security.

The “Squad” and Quad meetings are expected to take place in the Philippines just days before US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month.

“This type of meetings regularly happen, and if it’s an opportunity that is there, I’m sure that they will do it,” Romualdez said when asked about a possible “Squad” defence ministers’ meeting.

On whether the grouping would be raised to the leaders’ level, Romualdez – who is also President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s second cousin – said it would depend on “what kind of an agreement” or meetings that officials “will have on the sidelines of the Asean summit”.

A source familiar with the discussions said the probability of the “Squad” meetings was “very high” and added that since many US allies and partners would be in the Philippines, the “pretence” of US diplomatic commitment could be “cheaply done”.

Before the leaders’ summit from November 16 to 18 in Manila, the Philippine Department of National Defence will host the defence ministers’ meeting and related engagements on October 28 and 29 in Cebu.

Manila’s ambassador to Washington stressed that Marcos had consistently pursued a “multilateral approach” to the Asia-Pacific region, backed by a network of defence agreements with other countries.

“We’re counting now about seven or eight of them, but more importantly, between Japan, Australia, the United States and the Philippines,” he said.

Romualdez confirmed, however, that Marcos would attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen, expressing hope that he could at least have a “possible good conversation” with Xi even if no formal meeting took place.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on Tuesday that the Quad leaders would meet in the Philippine capital next month, marking the group’s first summit in more than two years.

“It’s been agreement now that we’re going to do it; we’re going to do it in Manila, at the Asean conference,” Rubio said in an interview with Indian news channel CNN-News18.

“We don’t have the specific date yet, but that’s going to happen, and we’re very enthusiastic about it.”

The Squad and the Quad were part of the previous Joe Biden administration’s strategy of building a “latticework” of coalitions to counter China’s clout.

The first meeting of “Squad” defence ministers took place on the sidelines of the Shangri-La security dialogue in Singapore in June 2023, followed by a series of interactions.

The Trump administration has continued the dialogue, with the most recent engagement between defence chiefs taking place on the sidelines of the Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, last November.

Military officials of four countries also convened for a defence cooperation council meeting in May in Singapore.

Beyond deepening security ties with regional powers, the Philippine envoy to Washington also floated the idea of an “Asean Nato”, reviving a proposal rejected by the country’s defence secretary, Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, in 2024.

“I’m even hoping that Asean will become like a Nato, that it can take care of its own security,” Romualdez told the SCMP.

He added that “having an integrated security” is more efficient as the Asean countries are “all together” and “live in the same neighbourhood”.

“Then we can make agreements with countries like China as a whole, agreements with the United States,” he said.

“I hope that one day we will be able to have not only our economies integrated, but even our defence and military.”

Teodoro in November 2024 had dismissed the prospect, saying that Asean’s complex “dichotomies and divergence in country interests” would make it challenging to set up a unified military alliance.

The ambassador’s statements come as the Trump administration recalibrates its priorities in the Asia-Pacific, prompting concerns among regional partners over the durability of US security commitments and Washington’s strategy for competing with China.

In June, the US renamed the Indo-Pacific Command as Pacific Command, reversing a change made in 2018. In August, Trump ordered the annual US-South Korean military exercise be cut from 11 days to five.

Washington has redeployed the Japan-based USS George Washington to the Middle East for operations against Iran, leaving no US aircraft carrier permanently stationed in the Indo-Pacific.

The Trump administration has also pressed regional allies and partners to shoulder more of their own defence costs.

Romualdez argued that he saw no sign of US commitments weakening for now, but stressed that Manila had to be “ready for any kind of eventuality”.

“We remain focused on strengthening our armed forces to where we want it to be, so that we would be able to defend ourselves.”

He also ruled out any possible involvement in a Taiwan crisis, saying the Philippines was not part of any security arrangements related to the island and that his country adhered to the one-China policy.

“The only role that Philippines right now has in Taiwan is the fact that we have 250,000 workers. We obviously are concerned about that,” he added, referring to Filipino migrant workers living on the island.

The ambassador’s stance is in sharp contrast to that of defence chief Teodoro, who has rejected Beijing’s warnings over Manila’s engagement with Taiwan.

“We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them,” Teodoro said in September.

Under an expanded defence pact, the Philippines has granted the US military rotational access to strategic sites in northern Luzon, including bases in Cagayan province near Taiwan.

The two countries have also expanded joint military exercises in the northernmost Batanes islands, where Manila is strengthening its own military infrastructure.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the island’s main international partner, the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force and is legally bound to supply it with weapons to defend itself.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Incisive’ final report on Tai Po blaze singles out 4 government bodies
item.description:
An independent committee investigating Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has submitted its findings to the government, with a source saying the “incisive” report has singled out four government bodies for accountability.

It is understood that the 12-chapter report found that among the four government bodies named, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit should bear the greatest responsibility for a lack of oversight of renovation work at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate, which contributed to the heavy death toll from the inferno.

But the insider said on Thursday that the report did not name any bureau secretaries in connection with the blaze that broke out at the Tai Po estate on November 26 last year, killing 168 people.
item.content:encoded:
An independent committee investigating Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has submitted its findings to the government, with a source saying the “incisive” report has singled out four government bodies for accountability.

It is understood that the 12-chapter report found that among the four government bodies named, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit should bear the greatest responsibility for a lack of oversight of renovation work at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate, which contributed to the heavy death toll from the inferno.

But the insider said on Thursday that the report did not name any bureau secretaries in connection with the blaze that broke out at the Tai Po estate on November 26 last year, killing 168 people.

The judge-led panel submitted its final report to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu after holding 30 public sessions and hearing from 80 witnesses, including residents, firefighters, government officials and experts.

“With the evidence and materials received as the factual framework, the committee has completed its inquiry work on the matters set out in its terms of reference, and prepared the report accordingly,” the committee said.

The panel, ordered by Lee, ceased operating following the submission of the report, its website showed.

Lee thanked the committee members for their efforts, saying the panel had provided a comprehensive review of the causes of the fire and recommendations on large-scale building maintenance and renovation projects.

“The government will make comprehensive reforms in areas including the supervision of building maintenance works, building management and the regulation of fire service installations,” he said.

“We will carefully study the committee’s report, actively follow up on its recommendations and shortly announce plans for comprehensive reforms and pursuing accountability.”

The government said it would seek legal advice on how best to publish the report at the “earliest possible juncture” without prejudicing court proceedings. Charges have been laid against seven individuals and two companies for their alleged roles in the tragedy.

A redacted version of the report could be made public next week at the earliest.

The source told the South China Morning Post that the report contained 12 chapters detailing the committee’s findings on the causes of the fire.

He described the report as “incisive”, refuting speculation the tone was mild, but without providing additional details.

The report singled out four government bodies for accountability – the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Independent Checking Unit – as well as some civil servants named during the hearings, the insider said.

The Labour Department was deemed to carry a smaller share of responsibility for failing to act promptly on residents’ complaints about workers smoking at the site.

The source added that the report also included recommendations on construction material standards and measures to combat bid-rigging.

The blaze engulfed seven of the estate’s eight blocks and became Hong Kong’s deadliest fire since 1948.

The committee’s lead counsel, Victor Dawes, identified six “human failures” that led to the tragedy. These included the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding mesh, the widespread installation of combustible polyfoam boards over windows, the deactivation of the fire alarm system and the suspension of the fire hosepipe reel system.

The other failures involved temporary openings in emergency staircases, where fire-rated windows had been replaced with movable boards, and workers’ smoking habits.

At the final hearing, the committee’s legal team presented a 627-page closing statement, blaming the “litany of failures” for the disaster.

The statement said the government bore “unshirkable responsibility” for the tragedy and singled out the four government bodies.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said it was premature to pre-empt the government’s response as the report had not yet been made public.

However, he called on the administration to gauge public sentiment before taking any follow-up actions, adding that he expected Beijing and the government would act to strengthen support for the revamped political system under the “patriots administering Hong Kong” principle.

“I believe the central government and the chief executive will consider the matter from the perspectives of the government’s credibility, governance effectiveness, political stability and the unity of the governing team,” Lau said.

“It has to assure the public that the government is accountable and handles the matter in a fair and impartial manner.”

Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing said the public expected not only civil servants but also ministers to be held accountable. But he noted that with a government transition next July, the administration might decide against a cabinet reshuffle so close to the end of its term.

Lo also suggested that the government publish a report outlining its reform measures to deepen public understanding of its follow-up actions.

The committee counsel’s closing remarks criticised the Fire Services Department for failing to detect that the fire alarm system had been deactivated at the estate and for avoiding its statutory duties.

Following the blaze, the department stepped up inspections of fire services installations and put forward legislative proposals to strengthen regulation of such equipment.

During a check of 1,500 old buildings across Hong Kong, the department found 64 of them had not carried out annual inspections, with malfunctioning fire alarm systems found in 13.

The department extended the checks in April, aiming to inspect 5,000 blocks in two years.

Among its legislative recommendations, the department has proposed amending the Fire Services Ordinance so contractors and technicians would be legally required to obtain prior approval before shutting down fire safety equipment.

Lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai, chairman of the Legislative Council’s security panel, declined to comment on the accountability of the department, arguing that the full picture would only be available after the report was released.

He expressed confidence in the department for “discharging its duty with integrity”.

“The Wang Fuk Court fire was an occasion to remind us that some regulations will have to be updated,” he said. “Many lawmakers agreed that doing so would enhance public safety. I believe when these amendments are submitted for vetting, they will be passed.”

item.title: [SCMP] Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
item.description:
Less than two weeks after Brussels and Beijing struck a surprise deal to avert an escalating trade dispute, their fragile rapprochement has descended into a battle over who blinked first.

In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.

Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
item.content:encoded:
Less than two weeks after Brussels and Beijing struck a surprise deal to avert an escalating trade dispute, their fragile rapprochement has descended into a battle over who blinked first.

In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.

Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.

It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

“I can tell you that the French-German paper you refer to was clearly seen from China as ‘OK, now it’s becoming serious’. For the first time, France and Germany agreed on this,” Pascal Canfin, the ranking member on China in the European Parliament’s trade committee, told reporters on Wednesday.

Canfin was referring to a now-famous joint paper between the EU’s biggest powers, which proposed a kill switch that could kick Chinese companies out of the EU market overnight, which has now become an official policy to be proposed in December.

His comments reflected a new-found confidence in Europe on how to conduct relations with China.

“If you just negotiate without the credible possibility to do something differently, then negotiation is not credible at all. If we have the two legs and one voice, I think we are much stronger than we thought, because China is also dependent on the access to our market,” said Canfin, who will join a delegation of trade MEPs visiting China next week.

In Berlin on Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was “surprised” at the “unanimous support” from EU members at the summit, even as he said Germany did not want a trade war with China.

“The first indication that this could really have an effect on our relations is that obviously the government in Beijing is willing to accept a limited number of car imports to the European Union, which was not the case in the last couple of weeks and months. So we are making progress,” Merz said.

In the run-up to last week’s summit of EU leaders, more than a dozen diplomatic and official sources suggested the bloc had landed on a “two-track” formula of intense dialogue, backed by hard trade action.

The suggestion has been met with fury in Beijing, where official organs have been pushing back strongly against the idea that China could be managed in such a way.

“China’s willingness to make a strategic compromise should not be confused with a willingness to accept an endless series of concessions. Mistaking the former for the latter could turn Beijing’s goodwill into the next source of confrontation,” fumed Brussels Tea House, a newsletter written by Xinhua journalists in the Belgian capital, on Wednesday.

The comments echoed an official commerce ministry statement on Friday, which warned the bloc not to “fantasise” that its pressure had worked. The EU should “harbour no illusions about extracting concessions through pressure, still less underestimate China’s determination and ability to defend its own interests”, the ministry said.

On Wednesday, however, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen doubled down on the strategy, promising further trade restrictions and new instruments to defend European industries against Chinese competition.

“We see jobs lost in our industrial heartlands. So last week, at the European Council, we agreed a clear approach. First, dialogue where it delivers. Second, action where needed. And third, stronger tools to defend our interests,” von der Leyen said, adding that the commission was “already working closely with our chemicals and machinery sectors”, where further quotas were expected.

The deal will cap the import of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 per year from December 1.

The South China Morning Post has been told that quotas will also be applied to South Korea, Japan, Turkey, Britain and Morocco, calculated using last year’s volume of exports plus an additional 15 per cent. The commission would, sources said, be examining these flows for evidence of circumvention by Chinese companies looking to fill out quotas elsewhere.

In her address to the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen spoke of “the removal of certain EU companies from Chinese control lists”.

The SCMP understands this refers to the German company Sindlhauser, an important supplier to ASML which was added to a Chinese blacklist in July and removed in a tit-for-tat delisting. Bloomberg previously reported that, unable to access Chinese inputs, the company was at risk of going bust.

Some are hoping that the Beijing agreement can be the bedrock of something more substantive.

Bernd Lange, who will lead the European Parliament delegation to China next week, called for further agreements “quite soon”, adding that “negotiations forever make no sense”.

“I remember the negotiation on the so-called CAI, the investment agreement, which is deep in the freezer,” Lange told reporters, referring to the Comprehensive Agreement on Investment, frozen by the parliament after a row over human rights sanctions in 2021.

Lange suggested revisiting the investment provisions of the frozen agreement, including whether Brussels and Beijing could ease restrictions on each other’s investors.

Behind the scenes, however, the triumphalism was less apparent. A well-placed official worried that public remarks last week overhyped what negotiators see as a first step, potentially harming the next rounds of negotiations.

Some also wonder if the shift came too late. A deal to cap the import of Chinese hybrid cars is a “pyrrhic victory”, said one senior diplomat, noting that it covered a minute portion of overall trade.

“Look at what is going on in France, [far-right leader Marine] Le Pen could be in next year – I am not sure any of this China hawkishness outlasts [President Emmanuel] Macron in Paris,” they said, with an eye on presidential elections in April 2027, likening the mood in Brussels to a football team celebrating a consolation goal when they are already 6-0 down.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Prabowo’s economic nationalism save Indonesia from potential MSCI downgrade?
item.description:
In the wake of Indonesia’s worst stock-market rout since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has turned to appeals to economic nationalism to shore up confidence, urging citizens to rally behind the country’s battered stock market.

The government has promised reforms in response to warnings from global index provider MSCI that Indonesia could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status.

But analysts say its patriotic appeals will do little to restore investor confidence without concrete steps to improve market transparency and governance, while potentially exposing retail investors to further losses.
item.content:encoded:
In the wake of Indonesia’s worst stock-market rout since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has turned to appeals to economic nationalism to shore up confidence, urging citizens to rally behind the country’s battered stock market.

The government has promised reforms in response to warnings from global index provider MSCI that Indonesia could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status.

But analysts say its patriotic appeals will do little to restore investor confidence without concrete steps to improve market transparency and governance, while potentially exposing retail investors to further losses.

After the Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) plunged 11 per cent on Friday, further sell-offs followed in the ensuing days, prompting a defiant Prabowo to address the market turmoil at a cabinet meeting five days later.

“MSCI wants to scare us, but I say to them: Indonesia fears no one and will not be intimidated!”

Prabowo also claimed Indonesia’s dispute with MSCI was among the “hurdles and obstructions” continuing to harry his administration. “But the nation has the strength, courage and willingness to make the necessary sacrifices.”

The president’s defiance was accompanied by calls from senior figures in his administration and allies in the business community for Indonesians to support the domestic stock market.

Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, deputy speaker of the House of Representatives and a senior leader in the ruling Gerindra party, launched a Buy Indonesia campaign on Tuesday, urging citizens to buy domestic shares to prevent further declines.

“Through collective pan-Indonesia efforts, we can turn our bourse around. Buy Indonesia!” Dasco said on social media, reaffirming his confidence in the resilience of the local economy.

He was among the first officials to visit the Jakarta Stock Exchange on the day of the October 16 crash.

Mufti Nurlatifah, a lecturer in the Department of Communication Science at Yogyakarta’s University of Gadjah Mada, said while Dasco’s public appeal attempted to maintain optimism about Indonesia’s economic future, “it’s hardly enough without giving the public concrete reasons and measurable indicators why they should remain upbeat”.

She said it would be a grave error to conflate citizens’ patriotism with indiscriminate investment in Indonesian stocks.

Indonesian tycoon Jusuf Hamka, recently made one of Prabowo’s presidential advisers, also tried to support the market by announcing on Sunday that he was setting up a consortium to inject 5 trillion rupiah (US$277 million) into the bourse.

“Our blue chips can yield between 8 and 9 per cent annually, higher than term deposits,” he claimed.

Hamka described MSCI’s downgrade threat as a “shakedown” by a foreign force seeking to destabilise Indonesia, and urged local entrepreneurs to “step up and defend our sovereignty by buying up our domestic stocks”.

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of Jakarta-based think tank the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, called the patriotic appeals made by Dasco and Hamka “dangerously misleading”.

“They could put retail investors in jeopardy as stock prices could tank further if and when institutional investors take a hike,” he said.

An MSCI downgrade could remove Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracking emerging markets, potentially prompting funds that follow those benchmarks to reduce their exposure to the country.

To calm market nerves, the Indonesia Stock Exchange met MSCI on Monday and outlined further measures to improve transparency, including identifying affiliated shareholders and excluding highly concentrated stocks from the JCI’s calculation. Authorities have also pledged broader capital-market reforms.

MSCI has said, however, that investors want evidence of the measures being consistently implemented and having a meaningful impact.

MSCI’s consultation on Indonesia’s proposed reclassification remains open until April 30, 2027, with a final decision expected by the end of June that year, giving the government time to demonstrate progress on the reforms.

Bhima argued that the central issue was how the Indonesian stock market was administered, rather than a lack of patriotic support for domestic shares.

“Instead of enacting the necessary reforms in the capital market, the government and its cohorts have opted for a narrative steeped in economic nationalism.”

For Vedi Hadiz, a political sociologist at the University of Melbourne, the market turmoil also reflected tensions arising from Prabowo’s efforts to recentralise political and economic power.

These include the creation of Danantara, a sovereign wealth fund designed to consolidate management of state-owned enterprises, and plans to channel exports of key commodities such as coal and palm oil through a single state-owned company, giving the government greater control over the movement of resources and capital.

“His efforts to change the rules of the game to suit his own political and economic agenda will inevitably cause problems for established business groups who have to adapt to his agenda,” Hadiz said.

Dasco’s Buy Indonesia plea also exposed the tensions emerging from Prabowo’s bid to bring big businesses under tighter political control, Hadiz said. “But an appeal based on economic nationalism glosses over these tensions by suggesting that everyone shares the same interests.”

Hadiz observed that patriotic appeals have featured in previous administrations’ responses to economic turmoil, often with limited results.

He cited former president Joko Widodo’s 2015 appeal to Indonesians to buy local products to counter rupiah depreciation.

In January 1998, amid the rupiah’s collapse, presidential daughter Siti Hardijanti Rukmana launched the Love the Rupiah Movement and tried to set an example by publicly selling US$50,000 of her own money.

Her initiative failed to arrest the currency’s slide, with the rupiah reaching almost 17,000 to the US dollar in June 1998, Bhima noted. “It happened because the appeal was made when the government had lost all public credibility and trust.”

For investors, the concerns extend beyond the immediate MSCI dispute.

Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based family office Four Capital, said he remained “bearish on Indonesia”.

In his assessment, the Indonesian equity market faces a daunting combination of headwinds, including higher global discount rates, a stronger US dollar, expensive oil, weaker purchasing power among the middle class, continued pressure on banks’ asset quality, uncertain commodity margins and the unresolved MSCI issue.

“That is simply not the environment in which I’d want to take large risks,” Ho said.

For Hadiz, however, the stock-market turmoil did not in itself demonstrate that big businesses were resisting Prabowo’s economic agenda, often referred to as Prabowonomics.

“Resistance can take the form of lobbying, holding back investment, demanding concessions or pushing for changes in policy.”

The upheaval nevertheless presents a dilemma for the president.

“Prabowo wants to exercise greater control over the conglomerates, yet still needs their investment and cooperation to make his economic and political agenda work,” Hadiz said.

item.title: [SCMP] Haze forces Malaysian fitness groups to swap outdoor runs for shopping mall laps
item.description:
Runners in Malaysia are swapping their usual routes through parks and city streets for laps around shopping malls, commandeering air-conditioned corridors to keep up their training as a stubborn blanket of haze makes exercising outdoors increasingly hazardous.

The switch comes as smoke from forest and peatland fires continues to foul the air across parts of Southeast Asia, with Malaysia’s capital Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding districts among the hardest-hit areas.

By 9am on Thursday, 15 of Malaysia’s 68 air quality monitoring stations were recording unhealthy pollution levels. Readings reached 163 in Negeri Sembilan, while parts of Kuala Lumpur and neighbouring Selangor remained above 150, according to data from the Department of Environment.
item.content:encoded:
Runners in Malaysia are swapping their usual routes through parks and city streets for laps around shopping malls, commandeering air-conditioned corridors to keep up their training as a stubborn blanket of haze makes exercising outdoors increasingly hazardous.

The switch comes as smoke from forest and peatland fires continues to foul the air across parts of Southeast Asia, with Malaysia’s capital Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding districts among the hardest-hit areas.

By 9am on Thursday, 15 of Malaysia’s 68 air quality monitoring stations were recording unhealthy pollution levels. Readings reached 163 in Negeri Sembilan, while parts of Kuala Lumpur and neighbouring Selangor remained above 150, according to data from the Department of Environment.

At Atria Shopping Gallery in Petaling Jaya, just outside Kuala Lumpur, dozens of runners spent Wednesday evening weaving through the mall’s upper-floor corridors, clocking up laps past shops and escalators in a workout that would ordinarily have taken place on the streets.

The free event, organised by fitness studio The Active Chimp with the mall’s approval, attracted nearly 200 registrations – far exceeding the 50 to 60 participants organisers had anticipated.

“We were actually expecting the first run to attract around 50 to 60 people, but it was actually overwhelming,” The Active Chimp founder Keith Tan said.

Organisers eventually limited participants to around 150, with running coaches setting the pace along a roughly 500-metre circuit and helping participants avoid shoppers.

Tan, 40, came up with the idea after struggling to find somewhere to run without exposing himself to the haze. He approached the mall’s management after noticing how much space was available during quieter hours.

“I was watching, I was teaching classes, and I was like, ‘Oh, the mall’s so empty,’” he recalled. “I was wondering, can we actually run inside the mall when there’s not so many people?”

He pitched the idea to management, arguing that runners needed somewhere to train while the air outside remained hazardous. “It’s hazy and no one can run outside,” he said.

The mall agreed, moving benches to widen the route and providing security personnel to help manage foot traffic. Tan’s coaches also tested the circuit at different times of the day before launching the first organised run.

The fitness entrepreneur, who has worked in the industry for more than a decade, wants the runs to become a regular fixture if the arrangement proves manageable.

“I know the treadmill is a choice, but running on a track is different,” he said. “Personally, it’s my own pain because I wanted to run and I had nowhere to go.”

Retail ‘run’ therapy

Fitness groups across the Klang Valley, which includes Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding cities, have also begun organising indoor mall runs as the haze disrupts outdoor training.

At The Starhill, an upscale shopping centre in Kuala Lumpur’s bustling Bukit Bintang district, the Worst Pace Run Club held its first indoor mall run on Wednesday, promoting the event on social media with a cheeky declaration: “The haze can have the streets, we’ll take the mall!”

Other events advertised this week include a mall run at United Point in Kepong, a session at Sunway Square Mall on Saturday and a 3km (1.9-mile) indoor run at 1 Utama on Sunday, according to running community directory runclubs.my.

These makeshift running tracks follow a similar experiment across the border in Singapore, where the worst haze since 2015 has disrupted outdoor exercise and forced the cancellation of sporting events, including the Great Eastern Women’s Run and the Singapore Half Marathon.

Last Saturday, about 15 runners from X-Run Singapore took over sections of Marina Square shopping centre before opening hours, covering distances of between 9km and 21km with permission from management.

Back in Malaysia, Amirul Hakim, 32, was among those who signed up for the Atria run after missing his usual outdoor routine.

“We haven’t been able to run like we used to for a long time,” he said, explaining that the opportunity to try something new encouraged him to join. “It won’t be the same as running outside because the surface can be slippery … but at least we can have fun and work up a sweat.”

With his office nearby, Amirul said he would consider joining future sessions if the mall allowed them regularly.

No clear skies

Malaysia’s Ministry of Health has urged the public to avoid outdoor exercise when the air pollutant index exceeds 100, warning that fine particles in the haze can penetrate the respiratory system and pose serious health risks. It has recommended N95 masks for those who must venture outside.

The prolonged pollution has also disrupted school activities, with education authorities suspending outdoor sports in affected areas and ordering temporary closures when air quality deteriorates. Under government guidelines, educational institutions must close when the API exceeds 200.

The transboundary haze remains a perennial diplomatic headache in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and land-clearing fires regularly drifts across national borders.

Malaysia and Indonesia were exploring closer cooperation on fire prevention and hotspot monitoring, Deputy Minister of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh told parliament on Wednesday.

“Malaysia and Indonesia will continue to work together through the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution,” he said, outlining plans to strengthen regional prevention and monitoring efforts.

For 50-year-old Steven Ho, who works in Kuala Lumpur’s KL Sentral district, completing an estimated 5km around Atria on Wednesday proved surprisingly challenging due to the air conditioning.

“When we run outside, our body temperature will go up because it’s outside. But here it’s a bit cold,” he said. “I probably need a few more laps to warm up.”

Still, Ho sees great potential in the concept. “Malls that are a bit empty, or floors that are a bit more empty, could open up space for people to run, especially during the haze,” he said.

The coming monsoon season offered another reason to keep the corridors open, Ho added, given how frequently heavy downpours interrupt outdoor running towards the end of the year.

Organiser Tan is already looking beyond the two sessions at Atria, noting that around 180 people had signed up for the next event by the time he spoke to This Week in Asia.

But turning shopping centres into regular running venues will require more than just enthusiastic participants – especially when regular shoppers are going about their day.

“We cannot just accommodate the runners and neglect the shoppers. We have to find a balance,” Tan said. “If safety, traffic and all the benefits can be secured, hopefully it gives the confidence for the mall to actually allow people to run here.”

item.title: [SCMP] China is moving past a GDP-first mindset. Can local officials get with the programme?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities.

When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work.

He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities.

When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work.

He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots.

As China’s economy continues its transition to an era of lower absolute growth figures but greater sophistication, Beijing has expanded its to-do lists for local officials like Xin who are on the front lines of implementing policy.

Once tasked almost solely with stimulating economic growth, these political cadres are now juggling a set of increasingly complex – and sometimes competing – priorities.

To name a few, officials are taking steps to fight corruption, maintain national security, improve public safety, reduce debt, create jobs, nurture China’s home-grown tech and keep the economy growing.

But under the weight of weak domestic consumption and a tepid property market, gross domestic product figures have been fluctuating. Earlier this year, Beijing said it would aim for 4.5 to 5.0 per cent GDP growth for 2026 – the lowest target since 1991.

Caution wins over initiative ... A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, Ankura

While concerns grew about meeting that benchmark after a 4.3 per cent growth rate was reported in the second quarter, a 4.5 per cent rate recorded in the third quarter suggests the lower end of that range remains in sight, pushing the rate up to 4.6 per cent for the first nine months of the year.

All eyes are now on the fifth plenum of the party’s Central Committee, to be held from October 26 to 29. The meeting comes roughly one year before the party’s twice-a-decade national congress, a session expected to feature an extensive personnel reshuffle, including the formation of a new decision-making Politburo.

The plenum is an occasion for Beijing to clarify its policy goals. But analysts said the focus of this edition of the high-stakes gathering might be on the party’s self-improvement and strengthened rule.

Some observers expressed worries that Beijing’s shifting, sometimes contrasting priorities could divert local officials’ attention away from growth.

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China managing director at consulting firm Ankura, said while economic development still mattered, Beijing’s definition of it had changed.

“Growth [is] increasingly judged by its contribution to security and tech self-reliance,” he said.

Local officials, typically risk-averse, would be paying close attention to the party’s signals, Montufar-Helu added.

“Caution wins over initiative,” he said. “A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing.”

Broadening priorities

While the policy juggling act expected of local officials is not a new phenomenon, analysts said more targets are being set.

“Every day, they might have different orders cascade down to them,” said Zhu Jiangnan, an associate professor of politics at the University of Hong Kong. “So what are the real priorities? Those emphasised more by the topmost leaders would become the ones to work on.”

But what localities are told to prioritise today is drastically different from the growth-centric mandate handed down decades ago.

Then, the binding principle was “economic construction”, shaped by China’s paramount leader Deng Xiaoping after he came to power at the end of the 1970s. Successive leaders such as Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao largely adhered to a similar policy.

But Xi Jinping, Communist Party general secretary since 2012 and president since 2013, has broadened what Beijing viewed as critical, analysts said.

First, there was his instruction to “coordinate economic development and security”, enshrined into the party constitution at its 20th national congress in 2022.

At the previous congress in 2017, he coined the term “high-quality development”, introducing another overarching principle to inform decision-making and indicate growth was no longer the only benchmark at play in policy work.

China’s intensifying rivalry with the US has also prompted Beijing to make self-reliance in tech another high-level mandate as it seeks to break the West’s chokehold on advanced products and components, with localities urged to coalesce their resources in this effort.

After Xi visited Shanghai twice this year – trips that were centred around tech – the city’s government gazetted two documents to supercharge basic research and innovation and promote the use of artificial intelligence, observers noted.

To help cadres at all levels tackle the new priorities, Beijing has been pushing to install a “correct” understanding of what constitutes good performance among officials since February, eyeing a strong start to its 15th five-year plan.

The move was seen as a pivot away from focusing on raw GDP growth and “at-all-costs” development as the sole criterion for promotion, placing the debt, fraud and vanity projects that sometimes resulted from this mindset in the crosshairs.

“Nowadays, the focus is on politics and party doctrine,” said the head of a government agency in Zhejiang province who declined to be named. The official, who oversees financing for small and medium-sized enterprises, said she and her colleagues were beginning to make decisions with more caution, weighing the political dimension alongside the economic realm.

“We study political theories and top leaders’ directives and apply them to our work,” she added.

Growth not out of focus

However, this shift in perspective has not left the problems plaguing the economy without a response. When momentum appeared to be waning in the second quarter despite a strong start to the year, Beijing held a succession of meetings, seminars and inspections dedicated to diagnosing and tackling the most pressing issues.

Larry Hu Weijun, chief China economist at Macquarie, said Beijing tended to take a dynamic and adaptable approach.

“Having multiple goals doesn’t mean growth is not important,” he said. “Rather, the importance of growth diminishes once the target is within reach, but rises sharply when the target is under threat.”

Recent actions bear this logic out. Last month, policymakers unveiled a series of measures in quick succession to resuscitate the economy: cutting policy interest rates, offering mortgage interest subsidies for homebuyers and unlocking 550 billion yuan (US$82.18 billion) in local debt quotas to boost investment.

At a meeting of the party’s Politburo in July, Beijing pledged to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending, promptly roll out incremental policies and speed up the transition of growth models for the remainder of the year amid rising volatility in global markets and the second-quarter GDP downturn.

Among these efforts, top economic planner the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Finance and the People’s Bank of China have set up a 100 billion yuan fiscal-financial coordination fund to boost domestic demand.

Policymakers have resisted letting loose a stimulus “flood”, saying their intent has been to focus on countercyclical adjustments and the precise targeting of priority areas, including private and small-scale enterprises, domestic demand and the green energy transition.

Putting officials on notice

However, local officials are frequently reminded on what their priorities are – and how they must deliver. Beijing is unafraid to name and shame as it admonishes deviations in the understanding and implementation of its directives.

One area that has been given extra attention in recent years is public safety, particularly in the wake of several natural disasters. Central authorities have stepped up scrutiny of local governments this year over safety issues and tightened accountability.

Since September, over 400 officials across four regions – Hainan and Jiangsu provinces, as well as the Guangxi Zhuang and Xinjiang Uygur autonomous regions – have been held responsible for safety risks and lapses in local oversight following evaluations by central government inspectors.

Beijing has also taken a closer interest in localities that have been instructed to fire up their economic engines, examining the results of their efforts in detail and doling out penalties for ill-fated or extravagant projects.

In June, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection – the party’s chief anti-corruption organ – named and shamed officials in Jiangxi, Sichuan and Hebei provinces, as well as the Guangxi and Inner Mongolia autonomous regions, for chasing development that increased debt risks and using public funds for projects that did not return a profit.

Businesses get reality check

As local officials work to navigate Beijing’s shifting requirements, they may in turn alter their practices as they deal with businesses, particularly the private and foreign firms operating in the country.

While some firms have acknowledged the need to curb debt and move away from a GDP-first mindset, others have voiced concerns about mixed, even conflicting signals and structural mismatches in policy implementation.

The American Chamber of Commerce in China flagged some of these issues in its annual white paper.

“Central directives prioritising hi-tech self-reliance and domestic national security controls often clash directly with local-level efforts to rebuild foreign business confidence and revive consumer spending,” the chamber wrote in April.

The business advocacy body called on policymakers to create a “proportionate, predictable balance” between national security and economic openness, warning sudden shifts or conflicting signals could lead multinationals to defer long-term investments.

A heavier focus on national security and public safety has been cited by some business figures as complicating their operating environment.

One common complaint, for instance, centres on frequent safety inspections and red tape disrupting firms’ normal operations and adding to their costs. A report published last year in an online content platform run by the Chongqing municipal committee of the Chinese Communist Party noted that some companies were subjected to four or five safety inspections in a single week.

Ankura’s Montufar-Helu said Beijing’s increasing emphasis on security and party discipline has made local officials more risk-averse as they choose which projects and businesses to support with incentives.

“Local governments will steer resources towards the sectors Beijing has flagged as strategic and away from anything that looks risky … Officials will be slower to back projects that could draw scrutiny, including those involving foreign and private companies,” he warned.

“For them, getting things done with local authorities is likely to be harder.”

item.title: [SCMP] Does Singapore’s tougher stance on haze mark an inflection point?
item.description:
Singapore has warned it will go after companies responsible for the forest fires in Indonesia causing the regional haze, but cross-border challenges remain stumbling blocks to solving a problem that has plagued the city state for decades.

Analysts point to long-standing obstacles hampering the country’s decade-old haze legislation, such as complex corporate ownership and opaque transboundary supply chains. To date, no company has been prosecuted under the law.

Beyond legal threats, greater accountability is needed from corporate boards and investors, observers add. The renewed push has reignited tensions over state ownership, with a former Indonesian minister challenging Singapore to take hard action against companies with business links to the city state.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore has warned it will go after companies responsible for the forest fires in Indonesia causing the regional haze, but cross-border challenges remain stumbling blocks to solving a problem that has plagued the city state for decades.

Analysts point to long-standing obstacles hampering the country’s decade-old haze legislation, such as complex corporate ownership and opaque transboundary supply chains. To date, no company has been prosecuted under the law.

Beyond legal threats, greater accountability is needed from corporate boards and investors, observers add. The renewed push has reignited tensions over state ownership, with a former Indonesian minister challenging Singapore to take hard action against companies with business links to the city state.

On Monday, Singapore’s Coordinating Minister for National Security K. Shanmugam told local media the country would use “every legal and regulatory lever” at its disposal to “exert pressure where it matters – including on [companies’] bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors”.

Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister, said the city state would change or introduce laws on an urgent basis to ensure further cooperation.

“Companies cannot claim to be environmentally responsible while refusing to subject themselves to scrutiny. Their claims must be backed by evidence, not just words. They cannot greenwash their behaviour,” he said.

Companies would not be able to simply wait for the haze to clear and return to business as usual, he added. “We will pursue this matter for as long as it takes.”

As of Monday, Singapore sent notices under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) to 10 companies with plantations in South Sumatra and Kalimantan.

Felicia Liu, a senior lecturer in sustainability at the University of York, called the issuance a “significant step”, but said “the real test is whether this translates into meaningful investigations and enforcement where accountability can be established”.

THPA, which came into force in 2014, allows authorities in Singapore to hold companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in the city state even if the activities take place overseas.

It allows the state to require a person to provide documents or information, and can issue preventive notices. Citizens or businesses badly affected by the haze can also hold the haze-linked companies to account under the Act. If found guilty, firms can be fined up to S$100,000 (US$78,245) a day, capped at a total of S$2 million.

But an increasingly complex structural setting and the ambiguity of accountability made it fundamentally difficult for Singapore to take action, said Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School.

“Responsibility attribution is made even more difficult when there are subsidiaries, special-purpose vehicles, nominee ownerships, joint ventures and independent suppliers,” he said.

No company has been fined or sued under the law. In 2015, Singapore issued notices to six companies under THPA and subsequently closed two cases. In response to queries, the National Environment Agency said investigations into four companies – Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau, Sebangun Bumi Andalas Woods Industries and Rimba Hutani Mas – remained ongoing.

Tan-Soo Jie-Sheng, director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, underscored Singapore’s inherent limitations in tackling the haze due to its cross-border nature. “Even within national boundaries, pollution crossing state or provincial borders can be difficult to address,” he said.

Other challenges include identifying forest fires, the companies behind them, and establishing that pollutants from the blazes contributed to the haze in Singapore, he said. “Quantifying the damages attributable to each company introduces further complexity.”

Loh said it was challenging to implement the THPA, acknowledging that it was hard to gather evidence across borders. “It is even more difficult to enforce the law as external parties in other countries cannot control investigations and legal processes in the country where forest-burning occurs,” he said.

Shanmugam said in his press conference that manufacturing giant Asia Pulp and Paper (APP) bought from three of the companies that received notices.

This Week in Asia has contacted APP for comment.

The minister also noted that some of the fires or smoke-source points seemed to be associated with Singapore-listed palm oil producers First Resources and Bumitama Agri, and First Borneo Plantations, and said authorities would be asking more questions of these companies.

Former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi addressed Singapore leaders in a social media post on Tuesday, saying: “Don’t write letters just to make your constituents and voters happy.”

He noted that of the seven companies listed, Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau, SBA Wood Industries and Bangkanesia were “suppliers to conglomerate groups with massive corporate holdings and listings” in Singapore and urged authorities to take action against those with offices in the city state.

“Singapore has no jurisdiction in Indonesia, and you know it. So, if you truly believe you have jurisdiction over these groups, then just charge them. No need to threaten and announce at a press conference. Prosecute their headquarters in Singapore and show us what Singapore is really made of,” Lutfi said.

His remarks struck a nerve among Singaporean social media users, with many accusing him of shirking responsibility and pushing blame to the city state.

Calvin Cheng, a former Singapore nominated member of parliament, fired back on social media that Indonesia was “turning the narrative” onto Singapore. “Indonesia officials use Singapore as the bogeyman whenever something bad happens.”

Loh said the perennial problem was less a policy inadequacy than a failure in business incentive and corporate governance.

“Boards of directors and senior management must play critical roles beyond passive oversight,” he said. “Statements are not enough and they do not absolve the companies from responsibility in the forest burning and haze situation.”

Liu said while Singapore’s individual efforts were not sufficient to solve the systemic crisis, it had an “important opportunity” to lead in corporate environmental accountability.

“The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act alone will not improve accountability in the agroforestry sector overnight,” she said.

“Singapore’s financial sector must also step up on its demands for disclosure and accountability in investment chains to ensure that Singapore, as the region’s financial hub, is not bankrolling haze.”

item.title: [SCMP] For Filipinos, virtual assistant trumps doctor as ‘dream job’. But what’s the reality?
item.description:
When Mark Ifurung left his 18-year career as an IT professional in May, he was happy to ditch his two-hour commutes from his home in Cavite province south of Manila to his office in Makati City.

So for his fresh start, the 40-year-old father of four wanted something that would allow him to work from home. “After being unemployed for five months, I decided to explore freelancing,” he said. “With my background in IT operations and application support, I realised I already have transferable skills that I can offer to clients.”

While job hunting online, he came across information on the “virtual assistant” industry and was lured by the idea of flexibility and attractive pay.
item.content:encoded:
When Mark Ifurung left his 18-year career as an IT professional in May, he was happy to ditch his two-hour commutes from his home in Cavite province south of Manila to his office in Makati City.

So for his fresh start, the 40-year-old father of four wanted something that would allow him to work from home. “After being unemployed for five months, I decided to explore freelancing,” he said. “With my background in IT operations and application support, I realised I already have transferable skills that I can offer to clients.”

While job hunting online, he came across information on the “virtual assistant” industry and was lured by the idea of flexibility and attractive pay.

Ifurung is one of a growing number of Filipinos gravitating to virtual assistant work, a booming sector of the Philippines’ offshore labour industry that has steadily risen post-pandemic.

Virtual assistants provide administrative, technical or creative services to businesses and individuals, often overseas. Unlike traditional office workers, they typically work from home and may serve multiple clients on a freelance basis – handling tasks ranging from scheduling and customer support to social media management and IT services.

VA Masters, a virtual assistant placement agency, estimates there are more than 1 million virtual assistants in the Philippines. Filipinos make up about 38 per cent of the global market, often for clients and companies based in the US, the UK and Australia, according to the agency’s estimates.

A survey based on online job searches from May 2025 to May 2026 by remittance agency Remitly found that the role is now the top “dream job” among Filipinos, overtaking doctors.

“Virtual work in the Philippines is a fast-rising source of employment for Filipinos,” said Verna Dinah Viajar, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines School of Labour and Industrial Relations.

Viajar said virtual assistant work had attracted Filipinos branching out from the business process outsourcing sector, after AI replaced many tasks in IT and communication such as call centres. “With adequate skills in IT communications, many [business process outsourcing] workers have shifted to VAs,” she said.

Work from home, earn abroad

Many virtual assistants in the Philippines are independent contractors who are not tied full time to a particular employer. This allows them to take on several clients at once and increase their income potential.

Erica Marie Ebrona, 29, manages seven clients from her home in Dumaguete City in central Philippines. “I work as a social media and content strategist, handling content planning, captions, strategy and analytics. I have flexible hours, so I can choose when I work as long as I meet deadlines,” she said.

Ebrona started as a virtual assistant in 2023, transitioning from human resources, and earned her first client through a referral.

While her monthly income varies, she earns at least 100,000 pesos (US$1,580) a month – over five times the minimum wage in Metro Manila. Virtual assistant work, she said, “offers flexibility and opportunities to work with international clients”.

Phu Huynh, a labour analyst for the International Labour Organization (ILO), said the strong interest in virtual assistant work “reflects the appeal of relatively accessible remote work that can connect Filipinos directly to international clients and potentially higher earnings without having to migrate abroad”.

A young, digitally connected, and English-speaking workforce made the Philippines an attractive location for outsourced labour – but did not necessarily guarantee decent working conditions, he added.

The industry’s unregulated nature leaves many workers open to abuse, according to experts. Most have no contracts, no social protection benefits, and are vulnerable to health issues due to working in different time zones. This lack of regulation could make some assistants “work like slaves in the cyberworld”, Viajar said.

Their geographical location also means they do not have redress from the head office. “Being in remote work, it is difficult to follow up work grievances, and their isolated work formats … robs them of the opportunity to exercise their rights as workers,” she said.

Most people are drawn to virtual assistant work because of “the prospect of building a better livelihood while remaining connected to their families and communities”, according to Alistair Mercado, CEO and founder of Kasama Connect, a technology platform focused on transparent agreements, payments and accountability for remote work.

But the dream should not stop there, he added. “It should include getting paid reliably, developing expertise and having a meaningful say in the terms of your work.”

To protect independent contractors, “we need to stop treating ‘be careful’ as a worker-protection system”, he said. “Professionals have responsibilities, but clients, platforms, intermediaries and government have responsibilities too.”

AI intervention

Artificial intelligence is another challenge to the industry.

“[The] work is exposed to AI because many routine tasks such as scheduling, data entry, drafting and basic customer support can increasingly be automated through AI technologies,” Huynh said. “However, ILO research suggests AI is more likely to transform many jobs than eliminate them entirely.”

Virtual assistant roles may shift towards more complex tasks requiring judgment, problem solving, managing client relationships and the ability to use AI effectively, he said. “The challenge will be ensuring workers are well equipped with these complementary skills.”

Viajar said that AI has become a necessity for virtual assistants. “AI can easily replace tasks that are repetitive but if the work still requires human cognitive abilities, AI becomes a tool for higher productivity and precision work,” she said.

Virtual assistant Dani Gregorio, 25, does not see AI fully replacing her job just yet.

“I can definitely see why people are worried. We’ve already seen how AI is changing the way different industries operate, and some roles … are being automated or reduced,” she said.

“But I also think we need to look at what AI can actually replace and what it can’t fully replicate … You can automate certain processes, but managing people, building trust, understanding human behaviour, and making decisions that consider the bigger picture require more than simply generating an answer. Emotional intelligence and accountability matter, too.”

Not everyone would have such skills – “and that’s OK”, Gregorio said. “We shouldn’t romanticise one kind of work just because it looks good on social media.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Poster child’: why more Chinese firms have Thailand in their expansion plans
item.description:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks.

Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.
item.content:encoded:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks.

Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.

But the influx has also made Bangkok more mindful of risks, particularly those related to US measures intended to limit Chinese transshipment.

“Thailand is hailed as a new poster child of the ‘China plus one’ strategy of the new era,” said Donald Low, professor of public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

As tech-intensive Chinese manufacturers flock there while the sun sets on export re-routing via Vietnam, the Land of Smiles may gain further ground over its neighbour.

“Thailand has a reasonably mature, sophisticated manufacturing base that is more advanced than Vietnam’s,” Low said.

From Vietnam’s perspective, “manufacturing saturation” and a perception change – aggravated by US trade scrutiny, including punitive tariffs of 40 per cent on Chinese goods found to have been diverted through the country – mean it may have run its course as a popular destination, the scholar added.

Thailand in, Vietnam out?

In 2025, Thailand attracted US$5.33 billion in Chinese investment, compared with Vietnam’s US$2.46 billion, according to data from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce.

Thailand’s location and established industrial infrastructure have allowed China-funded factories to plug straight into supply chains that are being extended from China to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Low said.

“For tech-intensive manufacturing – like electronic components and machinery, electric vehicles [EVs] and solar panels – Thailand has the requisite capabilities to attract investments. BYD, for instance, runs an EV plant there,” he said.

In a success story now touted by Thai officials, the first EV made by BYD in Thailand rolled off the production line in 2024 in Rayong, the location of a US$490 million factory with an annual capacity of 150,000 units and a Thai workforce of 10,000.

On the other hand, BYD’s plan for a similar factory in Vietnam, unveiled in 2024, remains stuck in the slow lane, with construction delayed.

“Even before the US imposed tariffs on transshipped goods, there were already signs Vietnam was ‘saturated’ with manufacturing from China, especially in assembly,” according to Low.

“It was becoming less attractive to assembly manufacturing due to infrastructure bottlenecks and rising labour costs … American levies added to the pressures facing Chinese firms there.”

Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label

Thai trade official

Perception in Vietnam is also becoming less favourable towards Chinese investment. “A growing view is that Vietnamese domestic manufacturers weren’t benefiting from Chinese firms investing there for avoiding US tariffs,” Low said.

“There was little technology transfer, the investments weren’t helping the economy upgrade and worse, they may also squeeze out Vietnamese firms.”

In contrast, Thailand is anticipating a growing influx.

In the first half of 2026, Thai authorities approved 321 mainland China-funded investment projects for government incentives, representing one-quarter of the total. These projects brought in 45.7 billion Thai baht or 9.7 billion Chinese yuan (US$1.4 billion), according to Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI).

Between 2021 and 2025, total investments from mainland China reached 132.5 billion yuan, with an average year-on-year growth of 56 per cent.

Thailand has also entered the top four recipients of Chinese foreign direct investment in Asean, alongside Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia.

Thailand not becoming another Vietnam

Though more Chinese firms are making their way to Thai shores, their motives may still differ substantially, according to a trade official with Thailand BOI’s office in China, adding that some still sought only to divert exports.

“Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label,” she said, declining to be named as she was not authorised to speak to media.

The official said Bangkok’s relatively favourable trade ties with Washington presented an opportunity for companies looking to establish themselves in Thailand – as well as less scrupulous exporters searching for tariff loopholes.

She pointed to Bangkok’s 17 free trade agreements covering 24 partner economies, which would enable “broad export access”, as well as Bangkok and Washington’s reciprocal trade agreement, which included possible zero-duty treatment for certain products.

This stands in contrast with Vietnam’s higher US duty exposure, thanks to stricter transshipment rules and its trade surplus with the US – two times the size of Thailand’s.

Thailand, though also subject to rules of origin verification, experiences “relatively lower US scrutiny”, the official said.

These considerations are likely to have influenced Chinese manufacturers’ plans.

In a December stock exchange filing, Shandong Bailong Chuangyuan Bio-tech, one of China’s largest food ingredient producers, said it had raised 748 million yuan to expand its Thai operations.

“This is a strategic move … The Thai facility will not only boost profitability by leveraging low-cost raw materials and tariff advantages there … It can also circumvent trade barriers,” said the company.

Some analysts warned that a rush by Chinese manufacturers into Thailand could eventually turn the country into another Vietnam, with those seeking a new tariff haven getting squeezed all over again.

“With tools like Section 301 probes, Washington is looking through the map,” said Dan Martin, a Vietnam-based international business adviser with global consultancy Dezan Shira & Associates.

“Other countries like Thailand can also come under scrutiny, just like Vietnam. Exporters should stop hunting for the next loophole.”

But Thailand is not sitting idle, and appears to be heeding lessons from Vietnam’s experience over punitive measures targeting transshipment and “origin fraud”.

Minimal processing or simple relabelling before re-exporting has been under heavy scrutiny by the Thai Department of Foreign Trade, with the department heightening monitoring for products of Chinese origin and formulating watch lists for sectors vulnerable to tariff circumvention, according to Thai media reports.

To avoid US retaliation and access restrictions, and to protect legitimate local producers, Bangkok is collaborating with Washington to inspect suspected supply chains and mandate strict rules of origin certification.

Last year, Thailand’s Anti-Dumping and Subsidy Consideration Committee said it had determined certain Chinese steel pipe imports were slightly altered or transshipped through the country to bypass tariffs, a practice it deemed an evasion of anti-dumping rules.

In February, the US Department of Commerce also determined imported pipes, completed in Thailand but using steel billets from China, circumvented anti-dumping duties.

Thailand still beckons

As Bangkok takes steps to combat re-routing and other tariff avoidance practices, Thai diplomats in China stressed their country still “fully embraces” Chinese investments, adding that Bangkok was committed to helping companies tap Thailand’s potential.

Siwadee Suksawate, commerce consul with the Thai consulate in Guangzhou, said there were immense opportunities for Chinese firms who “invest local and sell local”.

“We have a huge domestic market of 66 million people. In areas like electronics and automotive, especially EVs, we are positioned to attract manufacturers seeking diversification and localisation,” she said.

“Rather than viewing Thailand as [only] for export, more Chinese firms now have long-term commitment and localised production and management.”

Unlike many in Vietnam, prominent Thai voices are continuing to call for infusions of Chinese capital. “Thailand is not wrong to welcome Chinese investment. The capital is real, the factories are being built, and the technology is arriving,” read a May editorial by the Thailand Business News.

“For a developing economy seeking to industrialise rapidly, that is not a relationship to squander.”

New era, new playbook

Underpinning their warmer economic ties after last year’s peak tariff levels, Beijing and Washington have extended their trade truce and pared back tensions, particularly after this year’s summits between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

New Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment

Siwadee Suksawate, Thai commerce consul

The US has agreed to identify US$30 billion worth of “non-sensitive goods” from China, like toys, fireworks and daily necessities, for tariff exemption under the new Board of Trade mechanism. Beijing has agreed in principle to a similar exemption.

Officials and business leaders from Thailand, Vietnam and China said the friendlier atmosphere could reduce the incentive to divert exports.

“This means new Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment,” Suksawate said.

One type of Chinese investment being courted heavily is in hi-tech electronics, she said, adding that Bangkok had optimised tax and other incentives for them, particularly for those setting up shop in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor, a special economic zone close to the Chinese border.

Liu Quanlei, chairman of the Chinese Enterprises Chamber of Commerce in Thailand, observed a similar shift towards local sales.

“Notably, more [Chinese firms] are going local, prioritising sales in Thailand and Asean … This is particularly evident in the tech and digital sector, led by Huawei and ZTE, in the home appliance sector represented by Haier, Midea and TCL, as well as EV makers like BYD and Chery,” Liu said at a business seminar held in September at the 23rd China-Asean Expo in Nanning.

He added some Chinese investors were shipping finished products and components back home, including rice, rubber and non-ferrous metal.

Liu said this demand was expected to bring more positive spillovers to Thailand, Vietnam and other countries in China’s periphery, including Chinese producers based there, in the form of more imports.

Though Thailand has gained a considerable lead on Vietnam, it is not all gloom in Hanoi, even as the momentum wanes for export re-routing.

“Vietnam is no longer a low-cost, low-income economy. It’s naturally looking to upgrade industrial structure and technology capabilities, rather than attract low-end manufacturing,” Low said.

At the China-Asean Expo in September, Vietnamese exhibitors occupied 170 booths spanning 3,000 square metres (32,290 square feet).

While attending the expo, Vietnam’s deputy prime minister Pham Gia Tuc made no reference to export re-routing, but said Hanoi would welcome Chinese trade and investment in artificial intelligence, smart manufacturing and industrial estate development.

Meanwhile, China’s launch of the massive river-to-sea Pinglu Canal in September, a waterway connecting southwest China with the Gulf of Tonkin – and several nearby Vietnamese ports – could again redraw trade in Hanoi’s favour.
