With this work under way, Hui hoped to share the latest developments in Hong Kong’s gold trading ecosystem when the city hosted the London Bullion Market Association Asia Forum in April next year.

Reflecting on this month’s conference in Sorrento, Italy, which he attended, he said industry stakeholders had responded positively to Hong Kong’s plans.

“First of all, they are quite impressed in terms of the timeliness of this project, in a sense that in this world of changing geopolitics,” he said, adding that they were also impressed with the city’s ecosystem approach, its “concrete” plans and “Hong Kong speed”.

Hui said the initiative had progressed rapidly since its announcement in the October 2024 policy address.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s shoppers love Chinese e-commerce. But is the bargain worth it?
item.description:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.
item.content:encoded:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.

“Most items are much cheaper than in the Malaysian market. It’s hard to compare because they come directly from factories or warehouses in China,” said Esha, who works for a competing e-commerce site.

Delivery takes at least two weeks, far longer than many of the app’s local rivals. But that delay has had the opposite effect to the one you might expect.

“With the long wait, it makes more sense to buy almost every week, so the wait feels shorter when parcels keep arriving every week,” Esha said, adding that she still used local platforms for urgent orders.

Many Malaysians are now doing the same. Since the app’s launch in the country last December, social media has been awash with delighted shoppers showing off their hauls, from smartphones to sofas, rolls of toilet paper and even bags of cement.

But surging demand for goods shipped direct from China through the likes of Pinduoduo often comes at the expense of local retailers and manufacturers that struggle to match their Chinese rivals’ deep discounts.

Meanwhile, the millions of parcels flooding into Malaysia and the waste they create are testing the limits of the country’s ability to collect and dispose of it all.

Disappearing margins

Pinduoduo is far from the only e-commerce platform active in Malaysia. Small local businesses, especially in physical retail and manufacturing, have already seen their margins shrink amid intense competition from earlier entrants like Lazada and Shopee.

Still, the app’s arrival has prompted an outcry from local businesses, who complain that direct shipments from far larger competitors in China have unfairly priced them out of their own market.

Shipping direct from China is the strategy that has powered Pinduoduo’s growth since its founding in 2015, giving more established e-commerce players such as Taobao and JD.com a run for their money. Lazada and Taobao are subsidiaries of Alibaba Group, which also owns the South China Morning Post.

Pinduoduo built its empire on a simple premise: allow consumers to pool their purchases into bulk orders directly with factories and wholesalers to get better deals.

“The influx of low-priced products from foreign e-commerce platforms is putting tremendous pressure on Malaysian retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers, particularly micro and small businesses,” said Chin Chee Seong, president of the SME Association of Malaysia, an umbrella body for the country’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Chin said operational costs had shot up by 80 per cent or more this year, citing an SME Association survey in April that found 76 per cent of respondents reported being hit hard by rising fuel and energy costs, with 45 per cent bracing themselves for a cash-flow crunch over the next six months.

“Malaysian SMEs are being squeezed from both sides – rising operating costs and increasingly aggressive price competition. Many simply cannot afford to keep reducing their prices,” he said.

A widespread slump in SME activity would be disastrous for the economy. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for nearly 97 per cent of all registered businesses in Malaysia and employ around 8 million people, roughly half the entire workforce.

“As local shops and businesses lose sales or cease operations, they will reduce hiring and reduce demand for supporting services such as banking, advertising, accounting and other business services,” said Lee Heng Guie, executive director of the Socio-Economic Research Centre, a Malaysian think tank.

“Closed shops result in commercial and retail outlet vacancies, and the landlords may be forced to reduce rents to attract fewer available tenants, reducing property income.”

Retailers of imported consumer goods, from fashion to general merchandise, are likely to be the most immediate and visible casualties. Yet economists warn that the greater danger is that posed to Malaysia’s all-important manufacturing sector.

The rapid shift to buying electronics, apparel, footwear, cosmetics and furniture from overseas sellers could cause local factories to permanently lose their share of the domestic market, said economist Yeah Kim Leng of Sunway University.

“The distinction matters because retail displacement can be transitional as traders pivot to services or niche products, whereas manufacturing capacity, once lost, is far harder to rebuild,” he said.

Trashy dilemma

E-commerce began taking root in Malaysia in the mid-2010s, but demand truly exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when strict movement restrictions forced millions of people to do their shopping online between 2020 and 2022.

That habit has become even more deeply ingrained in the years since. An estimated 900 million parcels were delivered across Malaysia in 2025, according to the latest available government data, a multifold increase from the 52 million a decade earlier.

The appeal for e-commerce players is clear. A February note from equity and market analysts at Kenanga Research forecast that the value of e-commerce merchandise in Malaysia would reach 1.5 trillion ringgit in 2027, up from 1.2 trillion ringgit in 2024 (US$268.9 billion).

But this penchant for hyper-consumption could overwhelm the country’s capacity to deal with the vast amounts of rubbish generated.

Malaysia’s 135 landfills are already close to capacity, handling an average of 39,000 tonnes of solid waste daily, according to government figures from last year. Any increase in e-commerce shipments will almost certainly add to the growing trash pile.

The government has also pointed to a low recycling rate of 37.9 per cent of recoverable materials and poor waste separation practices at household and local council levels.

“The growth of online shopping, driven partly by competitive prices and convenience, has increased the volume of packaging waste,” said Randolph Jeremiah, vice-president of the non-profit Environmental Protection Society Malaysia.

“Although some online platforms, retailers and manufacturers have begun reducing packaging and switching to more recyclable materials, such as paper filling instead of polystyrene, these efforts may not be sufficient to keep pace with rising consumption.”

A raft of government policies has been introduced in an attempt to modernise solid waste management, broaden the use of sustainable plastics and materials, encourage recycling and reduce waste generation.

But grand plans meant little if the problem was not addressed at the source, said Jeremiah, adding that efforts to reduce unnecessary packaging by a handful of platforms, retailers and manufacturers needed to be extended across the entire supply chain.

“At the same time, consumers should make more informed purchasing decisions and practice proper waste separation and recycling,” he added.

Fair play

The overseas e-commerce blitz is not all bad news for Malaysia, however. For some, losing business in one area opens up opportunities in another.

“We had a 40 per cent drop in demand over the past few months for small parcel deliveries because a lot of people can just get their items delivered straight to their homes,” said a local courier operator who asked not to be named.

“But demand has gone up for shipments of bigger items like furniture and kitchenware and even machinery for factories and construction.”

An early investment in warehouse space in Guangzhou, China’s outbound shipping hub, made all the difference for them in securing a steady stream of clients, the operator said, adding: “A lot of our customers nowadays buy direct from factories in China, so having our own warehouse there makes it easy to arrange shipments for them.”

Even entrepreneurs worried about the fallout from direct-to-consumer sales from overseas enjoy the savings as shoppers.

“You must also look at the other side [of the coin]. The consumer is very happy. I’m very happy that I can buy my socks for just 12 ringgit,” said the SME Association’s Chin.

What local businesses wanted was not to stop Pinduoduo and other foreign e-commerce giants selling in Malaysia, he said, but a level playing field.

Under Malaysian law, a 10 per cent sales tax on low-value goods took effect in 2024 to cover imported items worth 500 ringgit or less. But trade groups say many direct overseas shipments slip through untaxed, giving foreign sellers an edge.

Local industries have also warned that directly shipped items such as electronics and toys are not subject to Malaysian safety regulations and may endanger consumers.

“Malaysian businesses should not be disadvantaged simply because they pay local taxes, employ Malaysian workers and comply with our laws and regulations,” Chin said. “We must protect consumer interests without sacrificing Malaysian businesses, jobs and our domestic manufacturing ecosystem.”

When unveiling next year’s budget on October 9, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government would introduce an e-commerce bill at the next parliamentary sitting to close legislative and enforcement loopholes and protect local businesses from unfair competition.

But the government must do more than just draft a new law, said Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

“Malaysian entrepreneurs are not asking for government handouts. They are not asking for competition to be shut down entirely. They only want fairness, so that competition is fair,” he told parliament during the budget debate.

“[Foreign e-commerce sites] need to establish a local presence. Work with local businesses, open offices and hire workers in this country … I am proposing a middle ground, not shutting them down entirely.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong aims for share of HK$350 billion yacht industry as travel scheme launches
item.description:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday.

The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday.

The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address.

Under the scheme, mainland vessels can register through the Marine Department’s Electronic Business System to sail in Hong Kong waters.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the global yacht market was expected to reach HK$350 billion by 2032 and that Hong Kong could capture a slice of the market.

He noted that there were about 6,000 superyachts in the world exceeding 30 metres (98.4 feet). More than 90 of them were in Hong Kong and the government planned to roll out more measures to boost the yacht economy.

“The outline of the national 15th five-year plan clearly calls for developing leisure consumption such as cruises and yachts, and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan also stated that we will actively develop it,” he said.

“Our vision for the yacht economy also reflects the global trend.”

Wong said they are also pushing to build four new yacht clubs at the airport, Lamma Island, Aberdeen and Hung Hom, which would provide more than 1,100 berths.

The new yacht clubs would also have four “very attractive” clubhouses to improve and complete the infrastructure and ecosystem of the city’s yacht economy, he added.

Wong also revealed that three of the five registered vessels were from Shenzhen, one was from Zhuhai and one from Guangzhou’s Nansha.

The five vessels all moored at facilities in Discovery Bay provided by Lantau Yacht Club, which organised the launch ceremony.

Transport minister Chan also said the Marine Department would coordinate with local training institutions to offer online courses for overseas captains, with the aim of turning the city into a hub for superyachts.

Chan said the five yachts had varied itineraries, including sea tours and visits to urban areas, and that many of their passengers had booked hotels for stays of three to four days, reflecting “a new model of high-end tourism consumption”.

Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat said on Thursday that 23 individuals or groups had registered under the new travel scheme as of this week.

Max Teng, secretary general of the Shenzhen Boating Industry Association, was one of the five mainland yacht owners arriving on the first day.

He said he came to Hong Kong specifically for an “ice-breaking journey to witness the historic moment”, and would stay only one night in the city.

Teng was cautious, however, about his willingness to return. “Just the cost this time, not counting fuel, we already spent up to HK$40,000,” he said.

Entry and exit clearance fees were 14,500 yuan, he said, which included a processing fee of 2,000 yuan per trip, port berthing fee of 2,000 yuan per hour and customs declaration fee of 1,000 yuan per vessel.

He praised the smooth application through the official system, although he said some technical details still needed work.

“There are some things that don’t quite match, for example, the shore power interfaces,” he said.

“Freedom of navigation is the most important thing for mainland yacht owners.

“Many mainland businessmen buy boats and register companies in Hong Kong for its international endorsement and tax incentives.”

Teng said that he saw the scheme boosting Hong Kong’s yacht trading and benefiting nearby cities such as Shenzhen.

Another Shenzhen yacht owner, surnamed Sheng, said he had come to Hong Kong with several friends for a three-day free and easy trip, and planned to shop in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui.

“Shenzhen is very close to Hong Kong. Now that the government has made the process more automated and standardised, the more convenient it becomes, the more willing we are to come,” he said.

“If this scheme had come into effect before National Day, we might have stayed a couple more days – during holidays the roads are congested, but the sea is not.”

Sheng added that he would be more interested in sailing his yacht to Victoria Harbour to watch the fireworks during holidays.

Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind the Lantau Yacht Club, welcomed the “long-anticipated” scheme, saying the club had prepared for more mainland yachts coming to Hong Kong since 2019.

“We have special rates for our berths, and we purposely reserve space for people who come in on a transient basis, so we can accommodate yachts, unlike other yacht clubs that usually sell all that space to long-term owners,” he said.

Apart from berthing, the club also offers both long- and short-term service package discounts, including hotel accommodation and golf sessions, which are more cost-effective than a long-term membership.

Mak also noted that 10 mainland yachts had registered for the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show early next month and would start arriving from next week. They represented the largest number in years, up from just two or three previously.

David Norton, commodore of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, said one boat from Zhuhai was set to spend the night at its Causeway Bay headquarters on Friday.

Acknowledging that the club was quite full and could only offer berthing and hospitality on a case-by-case basis, Norton stressed the demand was real.

“There is a big demand in mainland China for participation in water sports, 60 per cent of entries in Hong Kong Race Week at the beginning of the year came from the mainland,” he said, adding he was excited to see if the scheme could bring more mainland entries to water sports events in Hong Kong.

Five designated berthing areas at Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung will provide 115 berths, in addition to those at private yacht clubs.

There are also seven kiosks supplying water to vessels and eight designated bunkering areas, according to the Water Supplies Department and the Marine Department.

While saying the five anchorage areas were well located, Norton noted “there is a lack of facilities” around the areas.

“It’s very hard to get water and find someone to dump some trash or empty the tanks from the toilet,” he said.

He also added that tourists needed an easy way ashore: “They need a landing station, or maybe a water taxi service that will get them on and off the boat. So that’s what’s missing.”

Lawmaker Roy Chu Lap-wai described the registration of five yachts on the first day as “encouraging”.

“In the initial stage, I believe the five yachts that come here will go back and spread the word about how convenient and good Hong Kong is, if everything goes smoothly,” he told a radio programme.

Chu said Hong Kong had many distinctive islands for visiting yachts to explore. He hoped tourists would go island-hopping during the day, then dine and shop in urban areas at night.

“The government also held many successful big events regularly, and they could get more involved in different aspects, so these relatively high-end, big-spending yacht tourists can really spend more money in Hong Kong and contribute to our economy,” he said.

Chu said the city could also develop a “one-day tour” and other services, such as chauffeur-driven cars with professional guides, adding that the Tourism Board could do more to promote these offerings and increase the economic benefits.

item.title: [SCMP] Robin Xing on how China’s ‘two-speed’ economy can solve contrasting problems
item.description:
Robin Xing is chief China economist at Morgan Stanley. A famed economist and Peking University graduate, Xing has a PhD in economics from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and previously worked at Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corp.

In his second Open Questions interview, Xing dissects China’s K-shaped economic divergence and why he remains convinced that the “top half of the K” can offset challenges such as deflation and weak consumption. He also discusses Beijing’s real priorities, the “fallacy of composition” and why helping consumers will sustain and accelerate China’s tech advance.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Robin Xing is chief China economist at Morgan Stanley. A famed economist and Peking University graduate, Xing has a PhD in economics from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and previously worked at Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corp.

In his second Open Questions interview, Xing dissects China’s K-shaped economic divergence and why he remains convinced that the “top half of the K” can offset challenges such as deflation and weak consumption. He also discusses Beijing’s real priorities, the “fallacy of composition” and why helping consumers will sustain and accelerate China’s tech advance.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump have met twice and are expected to meet two more times this year. Will the meetings deliver stability in trade, investment and broader economic ties? Can businesses now proceed with their trade and investment plans with greater clarity and confidence? Is the two-month extension of the tariff truce a disappointment?

The successful meetings this year could help steer the US-China relationship towards managed competition: modestly expanding cooperation in non-sensitive areas such as trade, agriculture and other commercially practical sectors, while important strategic differences – particularly around technology and national security – are likely to persist.

Deep economic interdependence gives both sides an incentive to maintain a floor under the relationship and reduces the potential for broader escalation. That should make bilateral ties more predictable, even as de-risking, localisation and restrictions in sensitive areas continue.

We expect the improvement in clarity and confidence to be concentrated in non-sensitive sectors. Recent progress around the Board of Trade, including reciprocal tariff reductions on around US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods, suggests that both sides are willing to offer incremental stability where national-security concerns are less prominent.

However, in technology, critical minerals and other strategically sensitive areas, we believe the broader direction remains towards localisation and tighter controls.

Amid the slowdown, Beijing has rolled out new measures recently, including mortgage loan subsidies and rate reductions. Are they enough? Has Beijing become more tolerant of the slowdown while remaining convinced of long-term prospects?

China is undergoing a challenging economic transformation, as old growth drivers face diminishing returns. Deflation pressures have persisted, and domestic demand remains weak.

But in the meantime, there is a structural transformation taking place in the country towards what we call the Industrial Revolution 5.0.

This transition will require a lot of spending and capital expenditure. We estimate around US$6 trillion factory upgrade investment in areas like robotics, smart machinery, industrial software, power grids and related infrastructure. In addition, we see another US$6 trillion investment being directed towards strategic new capacity. In total, this represents about US$12 trillion in incremental capex over the next 10 years.

China is now in a two-speed, K-shaped economy. The top half of the K is showing some bright spots

The hope is that this decade-long capex supercycle in advanced manufacturing can help offset the drag from deflation and gradually replace old growth drivers like housing and infrastructure investment.

China is now in a two-speed, K-shaped economy. The top half of the K is showing some bright spots in manufacturing, artificial intelligence and in different emerging sectors.

But you also have a huge bottom half of the K: an “old economy” like housing, consumption, a job-intensive services sector and so on. They are now under a cyclical, very painful adjustment.

Beijing has stepped up targeted easing to cushion the downside. This signals a greater willingness to deploy central fiscal resources directly to support housing demand.

Yet, the overall package remains modest, unlikely to reverse confidence-driven household deleveraging due to a weak job market outlook while the existing mortgage rate is still at 3 per cent. There is still the risk of continued pro-cyclical policy tightening amid structurally lower land sales and elevated local government debt.

We thus expect full-year real GDP growth to remain near the lower end of the 4.5 to 5 per cent target range.

So, what is your take on this two-speed, K-shaped economy?

My view is that the top half of the K will be stronger in the future, leading to the next industrial revolution, contributing to US$12 trillion in new capex, and that’s going to be very powerful in offsetting the drag from old sectors.

Housing investment as a share of GDP will decline to only 3 per cent, and the share for traditional infrastructure will also decline to 4 per cent. Industrial capex right now is 17 per cent of GDP. We think it will increase to close to 20 per cent in 10 years.

That being said, 10 years is a very long horizon. For now, we are seeing deflationary pressure lasting longer than expected.

At the end of last year, some observers assessed that China was gradually reflating, with housing prices stabilising and [consumer price index] and [producer price index] showing signs of improvement. They argued that maybe China was ‘out of the woods’. We disagree. China’s deflationary pressure remains quite prolonged.

Another key issue is the ongoing household deleveraging cycle, which began around 2021, when the housing market peaked. Nearly five years on, households are still deleveraging.

Household debt growth has now turned negative, marking the first absolute contraction on record. This suggests that precautionary savings remain very high, with households prioritising debt repayment while the housing sector continues to adjust.

Even though households have not borrowed much in the past five years, the issue is that asset prices have also been falling. In other words, the denominator is shrinking as well. This creates a typical deflation trap: asset prices decline, sometimes faster than households can pay down debt. Thus, household leverage remains relatively high.

People still feel the need, the urgency, to continue to deleverage. Deleveraging, in turn, is bad for consumption.

In this environment, I think a typical approach should be much more aggressive countercyclical central government borrowing: the central government widens the deficit to support consumers and corporates.

But I think policymakers appear to remain cautious about a much larger demand-side stimulus. They likely view a broad consumption transfer as unsustainable, which will not contribute to long-lasting productivity growth.

Instead, the strategic priority remains firmly anchored on the supply side: self-sufficiency, manufacturing resilience, national energy security and related objectives. These remain the real priorities.

That’s why, in my view, the bottom line for near-term policy is that it will likely defend the growth floor, rather than deliver a meaningful consumption or housing-led reflation package.

Deflationary pressure may persist until the housing market finds a structural bottom and until the productivity benefits from AI are more fully unleashed as part of the transition towards a new industrial revolution. Over time, that could contribute to stronger potential GDP growth – but that will take time.

Various government departments have recently made regulatory moves, including controls on cross-border capital flows and taxing offshore products, that have been seen by some as a signal of tightening. What is your view? How do they compare with the curbs seen in 2021?

There are currently two contrasting narratives. The first is that there is growing discussion and hope for another pivot like September 2024: a larger demand-side stimulus package or a “bazooka,” aimed at reflating consumption and stabilising housing prices.

Many argue that such support is needed because the economy is still in deflation, second-quarter GDP fell short of the target and high-frequency data is tracking at a subdued level.

But on the other side, a lot of corporate leaders and foreign investors are asking a very different question: do recent policy moves signal a return to the 2021 playbook – that is, another round of broad-based regulatory tightening?

My answer is “neither”.

The 2021 tightening cycle was unique. It was a proactive, top-down regulatory reset across multiple sectors, including internet and tech, after-school tutoring, property, gaming, healthcare and others. It also took place against a different macro backdrop: China had been first into the initial Covid-19 shock, and among the first to recover from it.

China’s growth was more robust back then. Against that backdrop, policymakers proactively initiated this broad regulatory reset.

Today, however, I do not think what we are seeing is another policy reset. It looks more like stricter enforcement of existing regulations, because the overarching regulatory framework has already been in place for some time.

In a deflationary environment, the housing market remains under adjustment, which means new project launches and land sales are likely to remain weak. At the same time, subdued nominal GDP growth weighs on corporate revenue growth. The result is growing pressure on government revenues from land and corporate value-added tax.

The macro challenge is the “fallacy of composition”. Each micro-level action may be rational on its own – controlling risk, collecting revenue, closing fiscal gaps or maintaining stability. But if many agencies tighten enforcement at the same time, the aggregate effect can become macro tightening.

That is essentially pro-cyclical tightening. This means when the economy is already under deflationary pressure, policy should arguably be moving in the opposite direction: widening the deficit, supporting households and easing pressure on corporates. Instead, we are now seeing pro-cyclical tightening due to micro-level enforcements.

Pro-cyclical tightening can occur when governments enforce contradictory policies during an economic turndown, which can worsen the slump. What types of enforcement policies are currently in place that may contribute to this effect?

There are three areas of recent enforcement.

First, in housing, the shift from presales towards completed-home sales will slow developers’ asset turnover.

Second, social pension contributions are being tightened. In the past, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) contributed based on the minimum salary; but starting this year, they need to contribute based on a higher real wage.

The third is taxation. Tax authorities are now paying closer attention to higher-income individuals. And lastly, some companies that previously benefited from local tax rebates or preferential treatment are also facing tax clawbacks.

Based on our estimate, the tax and social security contribution measures could create a fiscal and cash-flow drag equivalent to around 1 to 2 per cent of GDP. This may not sound large, but in a deflationary environment, the last thing corporates and households need is an additional burden.

In fact, there has been a de facto fiscal consolidation in the last 12 months, with the augmented fiscal deficit narrowing by 2.5 percentage points of GDP.

The bigger issue is confidence. While this could further weaken private-sector sentiment and capex, more broadly, this kind of micro-level tightening runs counter to the need for more proactive reflationary policy.

In September, Beijing unveiled a capital injection of 360 billion yuan (US$53.7 billion) into state-owned banks and insurers. What is your take?

That was already part of the 2024 plan, which widened the deficit for a few purposes: partly to support consumers through trade-in programmes and partly to stabilise the financial system. So this is not new.

The key issue is the trade-off between state-owned financial sector stability and household balance sheet stability.

If we look at other countries, policy has often supported household deleveraging more directly, for example through aggressive rate cuts. In China, however, policymakers appear to have placed greater emphasis on financial-sector stability. As a result, while rates have been lowered, the reduction in household debt-servicing burdens has been more modest than in many other economies.

The trade-off is that household deleveraging may take longer. Households are trying to pay down debt, but their mortgage burdens have not fallen meaningfully, especially as income growth has also slowed.

So the risk is that the harder households try to deleverage, the more demand weakens – reinforcing a classic deflationary trap.

Over the longer run, China needs to address unbalanced growth and weak consumption, which means shifting from a supply-led growth model to a more consumption-driven one.

We believe more aggressive central government fiscal policy is needed – with a larger deficit aimed at supporting demand and consumption

This can be realised by building a stronger social safety net. Better access to public housing, education, healthcare, pensions and unemployment protection would reduce precautionary savings and help unlock household spending.

If China’s priorities remain as technology self-sufficiency, supply chain resilience, energy security and geopolitics, then fiscal and financial resources available to support consumers will be limited.

That said, there is still a great deal China can do to gradually rebalance the economy, but this will take time and the risks of a deflationary trap may need to become more fully recognised.

We believe more aggressive central government fiscal policy is needed – with a larger deficit aimed at supporting demand and consumption.

US government debt continues to breach successive ceilings, triggering significant sell-offs that have driven up borrowing costs. What are the implications? What lessons should China, as a major holder of US Treasuries, draw from these developments?

If we look at how the US uses government borrowing, the majority is on welfare-related spending, including healthcare. By contrast in China, it’s more on capital formation, capex and investment.

These are two very different approaches. In my view, both economies need some form of rebalancing.

For the US, the priority should probably be gradual fiscal consolidation, reducing the deficit over time while redirecting spending towards reinvestment. For China, given its large manufacturing base and extensive infrastructure, fiscal policy may be more effective if it is directed towards consumption, household welfare and social support.

For investors, the near-term uncertainties are clear. There is still debate over the path of US monetary policy, including where the Fed’s terminal rate will settle, as well as how the US government may respond to pressure on Treasury yields.

But my sense is that most global investors still view corporate America as profitable and innovative. While concerns about US government debt exposure may lead to some hedging, confidence in US assets remains broadly intact.

A key reason is fundamentals: US companies continue to be seen as strong, profitable and innovation-driven, which helps support the broader appeal of American assets.

In this part of the world, many still argue that US government debt is too high and without fiscal consolidation, sovereign credit risks could eventually emerge.

When you speak with global investors, the picture is more nuanced. Many may adjust their exposure to US government debt or demand a higher long-term risk premium on Treasuries. Yet they remain broadly confident in corporate America. Thus, there are almost “two Americas”.

China faces a different challenge. Global investors generally view the central government’s fiscal position and the state-owned financial system as quite robust, largely because China has prioritised financial sector resilience, especially the profitability and stability of state-owned financial institutions.

Few investors are seriously concerned about Chinese sovereign risks, systemic financial risk or China’s long-term national competitiveness.

If anything, China’s industrial strength and supply-chain advantages remain clear. The bigger concern is corporate profitability. Foreign investors are less certain whether Chinese companies can deliver sustainable earnings growth.

This is also a challenge for China to attract more foreign capital and FDI. Yes, China’s supply chain advantages and geopolitical competitiveness are all well recognised, but the key question is whether these strengths can be translated into visible, predictable and sustainable improvements in corporate profitability.

The yuan has been on a steady path upwards, despite Beijing reiterating it has neither the need nor the intention for competitive trade advantages through currency depreciation. What is your take?

There are market voices talking up the possibility of further yuan appreciation, with some even predicting significant strengthening in the next few years. Their argument is largely based on China’s trade surplus. Given the sheer scale of that surplus, they argue that the yuan is likely undervalued.

I am not fully convinced. If we look at other East Asian economies, such as Japan and South Korea, large trade surpluses have not automatically translated into sustained currency appreciation.

A trade surplus is just one side of the story. The other side is the capital account. The key question is what happens to the surplus – is it reinvested domestically or deployed offshore in search of better returns?

In the cases of South Korea and Japan, a sizeable portion of their trade surplus has been reinvested overseas – usually in US assets, like bonds or the stock market because their domestic yields are lower than offshore ones.

China is facing a similar challenge. Yes, China does run a large trade surplus, but persistent deflationary pressure means domestic yields and assets remain relatively unattractive. Government bond yields have been hovering below 2 per cent, while the stock market has recovered from two years ago but is largely muddling through.

Against this backdrop, it’s natural that many exporters, after receiving their export proceeds, may prefer to park their funds offshore and invest in overseas assets instead.

If we look at the broader balance-of-payments picture, it does not clearly support the view that the yuan is undervalued.

What would support a much stronger, sustainable yuan appreciation would be a genuine rebalancing of China’s economy, driven by faster and more effective domestic reflation.

When nominal GDP growth recovers, corporate revenue and profit growth should also improve. In turn, bond yield and equity earnings will likely be higher too, making Chinese assets more attractive, which will provide a more durable foundation for yuan strength.

This year, the yuan may even break 6.7 against the US dollar, but we don’t believe China is actively seeking a significantly stronger currency at this stage.

In our previous interview in March 2025, you highlighted “green shoots” in the tech sector. With China’s AI boom and the rise of new players, from robotics to chipmaking, can green shoots evolve into a new growth driver? Can technology alone sustain – or even accelerate – growth?

I think what we’re seeing now is more than just “green shoots”. In a K-shaped economy, the upper arm of the K is becoming stronger, supported by a profound structural transformation taking place underneath the surface of deflation, something we call the Industrial Revolution 5.0.

Historically, there have been four major industrial revolutions: mechanisation; then electrification; then automation; and fourth, digitalisation, which broadly unfolded from the 1970s through the early 2000s.

Now, China may be among the first economies to move meaningfully into a fifth industrial revolution, one enabled by industrial intelligence and the large-scale deployment of physical AI.

This is not limited to humanoid robots. It is about the broader integration of AI-native operating systems into the physical economy – drones, EVs and robotics in different forms.

Right now, China has 8 million such systems deployed across factories, transport and logistics. That number could rise tenfold to roughly 80 million by 2035. This large-scale deployment of next-generation AI in the real economy could help address China’s labour constraints.

China’s population is ageing and shrinking, but the deployment of physical AI may be sufficient to offset much of the resulting labour shortage. That’s the first key enabler; we call it intelligence.

The second enabler is resilience. Under the 15th five-year plan, China is trying to address all key chokepoints across its domestic technology stack, including areas such as semiconductor equipment, industrial design software and very high-end computer numerical control machines.

China is entering this next industrial revolution from an unmatched starting point

China has historically relied on foreign technology in several of these critical areas, and it is now trying to reduce that dependence with localisation.

Finally, there is leadership. China is moving beyond just exporting finished goods assembled domestically to exporting a full-stack industrial ecosystem, including global standards.

Taken together, intelligence, resilience and leadership suggest that China is entering this next industrial revolution from an unmatched starting point.

China already accounts for 28 per cent of global manufacturing value added and the country covers all of the 666 industrial categories and subcategories defined by the United Nations. That breadth gives China extraordinary scale, depth and flexibility across the industrial system.

China also has a large and expanding base of smart manufacturing capacity, including tens of thousands of smart factories supported by 5G and Internet of Things infrastructure. That’s why it can move away from just a factory country to something broader – an industrial operating system for the world.

In conversations with international investors, China’s industrial story is often too quickly dismissed simply as a narrative of overcapacity, low margins or even trade war-induced decline.

These narratives do not fully capture what is happening. We believe a more important story lies in what’s coming next: China transitioning from being the world’s factory to the world’s industrial operating system.

This could help China address key chokepoints across supply chains. This is also a story about leadership.

A lot of sectors could benefit, such as industrial automation, semiconductor equipment, robotics components, industrial ecosystem software and so on.

If China can accelerate this technology revolution while adopting a more effective approach to economic rebalancing, for example, by using government financial resources to support consumption and welfare, its growth model could become much more sustainable.

Importantly, the capex cycle associated with embodied AI does not have to be value-destructive. It could drive fundamental improvements in productivity, margins and potential GDP growth, creating a more durable foundation for long-term economic expansion.

Through deeper reform and rebalancing, China could also break the deflation trap, which in turn will reinforce its technological progress. Stronger domestic demand is essential because firms need the ability to sell products and services at healthy prices in the home market.

Ultimately, China would benefit from a demand-driven ecosystem, one that gives companies the confidence to invest, hire and spend more on research and development. If policymakers continue to deepen their understanding of this dynamic and deliver the reforms required, China’s Industrial Revolution 5.0 could become not only a technological transformation, but also a more sustainable growth model.

item.title: [SCMP] Huang Qifan, China’s political tumbler, falls after a decade of close corruption calls
item.description:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.
item.content:encoded:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.

Bo and Sun were both members of the Politburo, the pinnacle of the party’s power, and their downfalls were two of the biggest political earthquakes the country has seen in recent decades. Yet Huang survived.

Huang, 74, was also very visible after he left public service in 2018. Rather than retreat to retired obscurity, Huang kept up a busy schedule of interviews and conferences across the country, firing hot takes on China’s economic issues.

So when news of the corruption investigation into Huang finally came on Tuesday, it was a surprise to many – not only because it involved one of China’s most celebrated economic technocrats, but also because it came so long after the political tremors around him appeared to have stopped.

“Subjecting someone like Huang, who had emerged from many previous rounds, to a formal corruption investigation, before the fifth plenum sends a very serious message to the whole party: corrupt officials should not harbour any illusions of escaping detection,” said a Beijing-based political scientist, who declined to be named due to sensitivity of the matter.

“There is no political ‘tumbler’ and no safe landing for corrupt officials in the anti-corruption fight.”

The fifth plenum is a party meeting scheduled for October 26-29 in Beijing at which the organisation’s inner circle will discuss and adopt a landmark document to “deepening party self-governance”.

The event is expected to focus on tackling systemic corruption, tightening internal political oversight, and eliminating organisational loopholes across the bureaucracy and state sectors.

While many anti-corruption investigations into retired senior officials go unnoticed and unannounced, Huang’s unusually heavy speaking schedule made his downfall difficult to hide from the public.

The South China Morning Post understands that Huang was originally scheduled to deliver a keynote speech in Beijing on October 25 and another in Hangzhou the next day.

Before Tuesday’s announcement, word got out that he would miss the Hangzhou event. An employee at AIA Group – the organiser of the October 25 speech in Beijing – said they had not been able to reach Huang or his secretary since Monday.

Huang’s reputation as a tumbler goes back to his relationship with Bo, the charismatic and swashbuckling Politburo member who ran Chongqing from 2007 to 2012.

As Bo rolled out his ideologically charged “singing red songs and smashing the dark forces” campaign, Huang was the administrative and economic brain behind the policies that became known as the “Chongqing model”.

The model combines state-led capitalism, aggressive public-welfare provision, and foreign direct investment with a populist revival of revolutionary Maoist culture and a heavy-handed public security crackdown.

Positioned as an alternative developmental path to China’s coastal, market-driven consensus, the model gained national and international attention as a potential blueprint for addressing rising wealth inequality, regional imbalances and social stratification.

The two men projected an image of an unshakeable governing duo. During the national parliamentary “two sessions” in Beijing in March 2010, Huang famously described his working relationship with Bo as “like a duck to water”. He was also a magnet for reporters at the annual meetings, readily answering questions about the economy and Chongqing.

That alliance faced a critical test in February 2012, when Bo’s estranged police chief, Wang Lijun, fled to the US consulate in Chengdu, triggering one of China’s biggest political scandals in decades.

Following the diplomatic stand-off, Bo was removed from the party’s leadership. He was later sentenced to life in prison on charges of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power.

The aftershocks hit many of Bo’s subordinates in Chongqing, as the municipality’s new leadership headed by caretaker party chief Zhang Dejiang, repeatedly pledged to “eradicate” Bo’s “toxic influence”. Despite the chaos, Huang remained in position.

In November 2012, Sun took over from Zhang, becoming Huang’s new partner and direct supervisor.

Like Bo before his fall, Sun was also seen as a political rising star. He relied on Huang to maintain the city’s administrative machinery and drive double-digit economic growth. Huang, it seemed, had weathered the Bo saga unaffected, and was among six regional officials to be part of President Xi Jinping’s delegation to the United States in 2015.

The political ground shook beneath Chongqing again in 2017, just months after Huang stepped down as the city’s mayor. Sun was rounded up in anti-corruption investigation during a trip to Beijing for a top-level meeting, and ultimately sentenced to life imprisonment on corruption charges.

The southwestern metropolis again pledged to clean up the negative influence of a disgraced party boss and again Huang appeared to sail through the controversy. Huang stayed on in his semi-retired role in the national legislature as vice-chairman of the National People’s Congress Financial and Economic Affairs Committee, finally stepping down in March 2018.

Even after his retirement, Huang, respected as a capable economic manager, remained an influential intellectual heavyweight. Affiliated with prestigious platforms including the China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, the China Finance 40 Forum and Fudan University, he had a towering media profile, offering perspectives on a wide range of economic issues.

In 2021, he warned that the business models of Chinese internet firms would no longer work in the coming decade, slamming them as “taking advantage of weaknesses in human nature to entice purchases”.

In 2022, Huang warned that China’s property market had reached a turning point, questioning whether the country could sustain its decades-long construction boom.

As recently as May this year, he described China’s record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 as “shocking”, urging Beijing to rebalance trade through a combination of gradual yuan appreciation, tariff cuts and improved benefits for workers.

He is known among various lecture organisers as exceptionally proactive and eager to take the podium, and is said to have told organisers that he is willing to talk on any issue.

He is also believed to be in good health for his age, with a fondness for steak and cigars.

His confidence was built on decades of economic policy experience.

Born in Zhuji in Zhejiang province in 1952, Huang rose through Shanghai’s industrial bureaucracy.

Entering the municipal party and government apparatus in 1983, he was deeply involved in the early development and opening of the Pudong New Area.

In October 2001, he was transferred to Chongqing as a vice-mayor, overseeing the city’s industrial policy, state-owned assets, taxation and financial sectors before becoming mayor in January 2010 – a post he held for nearly seven years.

Under his stewardship, Chongqing logged consecutive years of double-digit GDP growth, routinely outpacing the rest of the country.

Huang promoted the Chongqing-Xinjiang-Europe freight railway, and attracted Hewlett-Packard and Foxconn to build an electronics manufacturing hub in the city.

He also pioneered the municipal investment vehicle modelled on Singapore’s state fund Temasek and kept runaway property speculation in check through strict land-supply management and an expansive public rental housing programme.

Huang’s downfall follows a smaller earthquake in Chongqing. Since 2022, the anti-corruption drive has sped up, targeting more and more senior officials across the country.

Chongqing was hit hard, with seven other high-ranking provincial officials coming under investigation since then. The most senior of the seven was then-mayor Hu Henghua, who came under the microscope in March, triggering another shake-up across the administration.

The investigation into Huang comes less than two weeks before the party’s fifth plenum, which brings together the hundreds of full and alternate members of the Central Committee.

The Central Committee’s ranks have been thinned by the anti-corruption campaign, with 34 of its 205 full members under investigation or stripped of their status as deputies to the National People’s Congress.

The Beijing-based political scientist said Chongqing had been the epicentre of China’s most disruptive political tremors over the past two decades and the investigation of Huang nearly a decade after retirement showed Beijing’s resolve to clean up Chongqing’s factional legacy, allowing no perceived seniority to impede its continued organisational housecleaning.

Not all are that surprised by Huang’s fall.

His family’s commercial dealings cast a persistent shadow over his administration. In Chongqing, the extensive business footprint of his son was “an open secret” among political and business circles, according to sources familiar with the situation.

“Many in Chongqing’s government and financial circles know his son very well, as Huang Qifan is widely regarded as the ‘godfather’ of Chongqing’s state-driven financial vehicles, which can mobilise a lot of resources,” said a source who worked with Huang.

The source said the younger Huang quickly immersed himself in China’s capital market deals.

item.title: [SCMP] Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
item.description:
Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping?
item.content:encoded:
Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping?

The summit was necessary. Leader-level meetings are the only guardrail we really have in US-China relations right now. It is very important that these meetings happen.

I’m probably more positive on this than other people because I do think that leader-level meetings in US-China relations are always difficult to put together. And the fact that Trump has done this twice with Xi – once in Beijing and once in Washington – may help regularise such high-level meetings, which we absolutely need to keep the relationship on track right now since we don’t have much else.

I’m not surprised by the negative coverage. The US-China summits are always held to a higher bar when it comes to outcomes of the meeting.

There have been expectations built up over many decades that US-China summits are always a big deal when they happen because they’re very hard to mount, and then they always have to have these long lists of outcomes.

We need to try to normalise these meetings between the US and Chinese leaders if possible. If you have to have a long list of accomplishments all the time, it’s going to be very hard to hold these meetings.

Some argue that the prospect of multiple face-to-face summits this year has put constraints on both sides, especially when it comes to sensitive issues. How could the two sides avoid a repeat of disruptions to bilateral relations, such as the balloon incident in 2023 and the fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022?

What you’re getting at here is exactly the issue of whether we can have constructive strategic stability.

In the US, I believe that constructive strategic stability – to the extent that people who agreed to that were really understanding what the Chinese side was talking about – is really about avoiding these worst-case scenarios. Avoiding conflict, avoiding a crisis that leads potentially to a conflict, et cetera.

The key is for both sides to understand what those issues are that could lead us there. And I do think we have been making progress in this administration on those issues.

President Trump is not new to this. He did this before for four years, and it ended quite badly under Covid-19. But I think whenever I’ve heard him speak about that time, it seems to me that he has thought about it and understands what the dynamic was that led things to get so out of hand and doesn’t want to see that happen again.

I think others in the administration also understand this. I think [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent and [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio definitely understand that this is what they’re trying to accomplish.

You put that strategic stability on top of all of these areas of difference that we have, and it does make it quite difficult to manage. But I do think with those high-level cabinet officials understanding what the boundaries are, there are additional touch points.

Marco Rubio and [Chinese Foreign Minister] Wang Yi have been speaking more than previously. Scott Bessent has a lot of things on his plate, so it may not be as easy for him to engage regularly with his counterpart, but he has been managing to meet [Chinese Vice-Premier] He Lifeng frequently. And you’ve got a number of economic and trade officials under him and under [US Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer who are plugged in together and talking.

I don’t think the crisis will come in the economic sphere. We can work through those questions and not have a crisis. We’ve really been doing this for quite a long time now.

The crises will come in the security area, most likely, and in a way those are harder because the security bureaucracies in both countries aren’t very connected to one another and don’t really have regular dialogue mechanisms.

We’ve always been talking about having some kind of military-to-military mechanisms for communication hotlines. There’s been a little bit of that in this administration and it’s got a bit improved, but it seems always very unstable. So, I think that’s the potential area that has to be guarded against.

President Trump does know where [Beijing’s] red lines are on Taiwan. That has been a learning curve probably for him. But he has a pretty firm view on that issue now, and I feel like Beijing has been reassured that he understands what the mainland’s position is.

It seems to me that the tension over Taiwan has abated, but the one question that Beijing keeps bringing up concerns Taiwan arms sales. I’m hopeful that the US side can find a way to manage that effectively. We’ve managed it in the past and should be able to do it again. And I think Trump will focus on it and try to take care that it gets done in a way that doesn’t cause a crisis.

How do you view the role of this summit in potentially helping address difficulties and challenges ahead in the US-China relationship?

I see US-China bilateral ties as being in a state of fragile stability.

During the summit in Beijing in May and since then, many Chinese colleagues have been excited about the notion that we’ve been able to put a name on the relationship, so we have a framework within which we can know what we’re working towards, which is a constructive relationship of strategic stability.

Looking at this summit, it’s important that they could meet and normalise that, but it’s also important that we be able to see them meeting in the future. We don’t have those kinds of mechanisms set up yet.

In addition to the leader-level meetings, what would be important to maintain this constructive stability is the institutionalisation of the relationship, which we’ve lost over the last 10 years. We need to start building that back to maintain stability.

The summit in September was the start of an institutionalisation of things that were agreed upon in May in Beijing.

For example, the Board of Trade, which was announced in May but really didn’t do much between May and now because of the summits, was actually pressured to meet, set up working groups and talk to one another. There are groups of people under Jamieson Greer and under [Greer’s Chinese counterpart] Li Chenggang who are meeting and talking through these things. You need a lot more connectivity among professionals if you’re going to have stabilisation of this relationship in any way.

The other area maybe that will move forward is AI, which was also announced in May. Scott Bessent announced that there would be an AI dialogue, and maybe that will meet in Shenzhen.

So, we can start to see the institutionalisation of these things. It’s still not nearly enough between the US and China.

I hope we’ll remember how hard it is to get mechanisms restarted because institutionalisation is a big job and it doesn’t happen overnight.

Trump gave Xi a very high-level reception, breaking some traditional protocols, and that triggered a lot of questioning and even criticism in the US. How do you view that?

Trump wants to appear welcoming and hospitable but also strong, so there was a jet flyover during the military review. A lot of this is just Trump’s personal way of thinking about how he wants to stage events. It doesn’t have as much to do with diplomatic protocol.

There were previous occasions when a president went to meet someone at Joint Base Andrews, so it does have some diplomatic precedent.

But I would hesitate to attach a lot of significance to the protocol.

Think of all of the things that they did that are highly unusual for a presidential visit. Walking out to look at the presidential helicopter, going over to see the construction of the White House ballroom. All these things are very much a signature of Trump’s way of handling the visit. I think a lot of people just don’t understand this.

That’s the main criticism: it’s very, very long on symbolism, pageantry, pomp and circumstance, and short on outcomes. This may signal a change in US-China summitry.

We used to try to, in diplomacy, trade diplomatic protocol issues and ceremonial issues, which were very high on the Chinese agenda for a visit, for concerns on the US side, for substantive outcomes.

But it’s no longer the case that we can expect that the Chinese are going to make concessions for only protocolary and ceremonial kinds of considerations. I think that is a change in the relationship that we’re seeing.

Both sides offer high levels of protocol and neither side really gets any trade for that. Maybe we can dispense with the ceremony of a state visit in the future and focus more on substantive issues at regular leader meetings.

Do you think that this summit has laid a proper foundation for Trump and Xi to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in November and Group of 20 (G20) in December? The Chinese side has called 2026 a “big year” for bilateral relations, with the two countries’ leaders having the chance to meet face to face four times. But what about next year? How could the US and China keep up this head-of-state diplomacy?

They will have to make a big effort. This is why I think it is positive that President Trump seems to really value his meetings with President Xi and really wants to continue to communicate with him directly either via face-to-face meetings or other ways.

I hope we’ll take advantage of that because that hasn’t always been the case with US leaders in the past. That is an important advantage that Trump offers in this very difficult time in US-China relations. He’s open to talking to President Xi anytime, I think.

I would like to see if they could connect more on the phone.

Next year they are probably not going to travel as much as they did this year. And that’s another reason the relationship has to be institutionalised in the way that we’ve been talking about. There’s such a thin layer of professional expertise in the government that is plugged in to the other side, and that is probably not going to change too much over the next couple years.

The other thing we have to worry about is that if we institutionalise the relationship under this administration, what’s going to happen in the next administration? I hope the next administration would keep whatever institutionalisation has been started and build on that, not just try to always do their own thing. That’s not going to be a good way for us to proceed with the relationship.

There has been discussion that the Apec gathering in November could open scheduling windows for a US-Russia, China-US-Russia or Trump-Kim Jong-un summit. How do you view the likelihood of these potential bilateral or multilateral meetings taking place?

It definitely raises possibilities for dramatic diplomacy that could certainly appeal to President Trump.

President Trump has already invited [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to come to Miami for the G20 summit, and it’s likely that he’ll attend. It’s creating some ripple effects in Europe because they may or may not be too pleased that he’s coming, but I think that will all be worked out.

President Trump still sees himself as a broker of peace, and so he wants to create these opportunities for dramatic things to happen and big changes in some of the problem areas that we see. Certainly the Russia-Ukraine war is one of them, but North Korea is another one.

We know that he wants to meet again with [North Korean leader] Kim Jong-un, and that has not happened yet. If that could happen in Shenzhen during Apec – several people have mentioned this as a possibility, or that Trump could do it on his way to China – those would be dramatic opportunities.

We were talking earlier about the calendar for next year, and then Trump is getting towards the end of his term. It seems like he might want to do something in this area.

It might make it more attractive for Trump to actually go to Shenzhen and for Xi to come to Miami if there is an opportunity for progress on Ukraine or the North Korea nuclear issue.

It’s very hard to see the preparation going far enough between now and November or December to make dramatic successes out of such a meeting, however. Usually, such things take a lot more preparation, so I would be sceptical on that score. But I have heard a lot of people talking about such possibilities, so perhaps they will materialise.

You mentioned the AI dialogue. The US and China appear to be taking different approaches to developing this technology. There is also debate within the US over whether the development of advanced models should be slowed. Given these international and domestic differences, how do you view the prospects for the bilateral AI dialogue?

I do think it’s going to be extremely difficult.

I participated in US-China discussions on mechanisms to report cyber incidents. The AI dialogue is not exactly the same as that, but in the area that the US is concerned about, I think it’s quite similar and also just as difficult, if not more so.

The US and China have different concerns, and it’s very hard for the two of them to talk to each other because they’re just coming from completely different vantage points.

The Chinese government – and Chinese interlocutors that I’ve talked to reflect this – seems to be quite confident in its ability to control its AI operators and make sure that things that it doesn’t want to have happen in the AI sphere will not happen. Is it overconfident? I am concerned they are not really thinking about the possibilities of loss of control on the Chinese side with AI.

They’re mostly worried about what’s happening on the US side and the possibilities of loss of control, the fact that the US government doesn’t control these private companies, that the companies themselves are reporting a lot of things that are somewhat hair-raising and fear-inducing. The US government seems to be thinking that China is going to have the same concerns it has, whereas it really doesn’t.

And also, the two systems don’t match up in terms of reporting, transparency and other things that you would need to talk about if you were going to try to share best practices or discuss a strategy for keeping incidents from getting out of control.

Trump said that the line for AI safety in the US is the Department of Justice, in other words, the legal system, and that is just not the way the Chinese are going to operate in terms of AI safety.

It’s going to be very hard from an institutional and bureaucratic set-up perspective, this security-to-security bureaucracy mistrust. The Chinese system is just not given to being transparent about these things. Chinese media have focused on various US AI operators who are trying to do the right thing by self-reporting accidents that have happened.

In the Chinese system, these things would not be publicly reported. China has been criticising the US AI labs and taking advantage of this moment to make itself look like a more responsible actor, when I’m not sure that is fully justified.

It’s also very hard to understand how the US and Chinese governments would put together delegations that would look at all similar and have the same kind of expertise. So, I find it a little bit head-scratching as to how this is going to go ahead.

It’s important to get some of these people in the room together and have regular discussions. Maybe they can build up a little bit of personal familiarity that will help us at some point in the future when we hit a real problem. I think that would be an advantage.

Xi has invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China over the next five years. You travelled to China this year and last year to attend events on subnational cooperation between the two countries. What is your read on the state of bilateral local and people-to-people exchanges? Are they still constrained by factors such as visas and flights? There have been recurring calls to reopen the US consulate in Chengdu and the Chinese consulate in Houston. How possible do you think that would be?

This area is still a source of difficulty, even though the two governments have pledged to make improvements.

I noticed that they did mention the number of flights. Certainly, they talked about students. But the question is how to make this happen. There’s still extreme suspicion in local-level, people-to-people exchanges, mostly coming from, to be honest, local-level politicians. There are some organised groups that are also pushing against people-to-people exchange between the US and China.

I don’t see much change in this. I don’t know, if the US midterm elections in November see a huge shift in the Congress, what might happen there. Most of the local anti-China legislation is coming from Republican states, so it depends a little bit on domestic politics.

I don’t know if the Democrats will focus on this as an issue, but in general Democrats have been much more open about people-to-people travel back and forth. I don’t know if they can affect the atmosphere on this issue. It is something to watch.

Certainly, the downturn in Chinese students is noticeable. I work at Yale University, and we’ve got a number of Chinese students who were unable to come for the start of the semester because they didn’t get their visas in time.

Visas are still an issue on both sides. I know people who are having trouble getting visas to go to China, so it’s a two-way thing, and it’s very unfortunate. But it’s really hard to see where a push is going to come from in the US to fix this problem.

We should keep pressuring both sides to make improvements here. And again, the devil’s in the details. These two security bureaucracies have a deep, deep level of mistrust.

Treasury Secretary Bessent said China and the US had agreed to extend the trade truce for two months, until January 10 next year. Why only two months rather than a longer period? What could the two sides achieve during this time frame?

To me, it is a bit surprising that the extension of the Busan trade truce was so minimal. I think two months is about the minimum that they could have agreed.

What that says is they did not want the truce to end because neither side is prepared for what might happen or the consequences of ending that truce. But they couldn’t come up really with any agreement to extend it, so they’ve just basically rolled over the agreement from last year.

Both sides were probably hoping that they would be able to extend the truce and improve it, but apparently that didn’t happen. It’s probable that they didn’t have enough time to do that, because these kinds of negotiations take quite a bit of time and preparation. And you can’t just have a meeting on a Sunday in New York between top officials and expect to hammer these things out in that kind of time frame. So, my suspicion is that they did not manage to agree on any of the improvements in the rollover that they wanted, and they didn’t want to roll over the current truce, which is kind of minimal, for too much of an extended period of time because they still hope to get something better.

Probably the January time frame is not much time to do anything either. But at least if there is a meeting in November, then that gives another forcing function, and there’s also the G20 summit in Miami in December, that’s a lot of connectivity between now and January 10. So, there is a possibility of getting something done there, although it will be difficult.

And then we’ll hit January 10, and the truce will probably roll over one way or another. They won’t want to lose this truce, I don’t think, in January either.

The one factor that probably was pushing on the US side is the midterm elections coming up in early November. I think the US side wanted to get something that would get us past the midterm elections and give some comfortable margin after that to assess where things are going.

Observers in both countries argue that China is becoming more confident and increasingly sees itself as Washington’s equal, while perceptions of continuing US decline are growing globally. The narrative of “the East is rising and the West is declining” continues to surface in public discussions. What do you think about this? Before the September summit, some argued that China was in a stronger position at the negotiating table because of the war on Iran. If that is the case, how long could that last?

I do think China is more confident, reasonably so. And certainly, the US has been losing influence on the international stage for a period of time. In the wake of the war in Iran, that has accelerated, probably.

The question, really, is whether China is making gains from the losses that the US is inflicting on itself. I think China has made some gains, but it is not a slam dunk yet that China has made equal gains to the US’ losses. In other words, I don’t see that China is somehow displacing the US.

The interesting thing to watch is we’ve seen President Xi go to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan and the Brics summit in India, talking in many of his speeches about China being a responsible player, that China stands for a continuation of globalisation, openness and free trade, and I think what people see China doing in practice is somewhat different from that. Or at least they are sceptical that this is what China is standing for and what China is all about.

In fact, a lot of countries, especially in China’s neighbourhood, continue to have concerns about China and are actually threatened by China. And China hasn’t really done much to reassure those countries that they shouldn’t be afraid of China. I think this is the dilemma China has.

It wants to take advantage of this moment when the US is on the back foot, clearly, in Iran and elsewhere, and it has taken some advantage, but it has not managed to really convince people of what its ambitions and intentions are. I think that is going to continue to be a tough balancing act for China.

I hope China will start to show in its actions more what it’s actually thinking about for the long term, and I think that will be important in terms of the narrative too out there in the world.

The US is clearly in a transition period. Domestic politics are at a turning point, and we’re going to have to work through that. So, it’s going to be a period of time. Whether China can take advantage of our domestic transition is really a question for China’s own policy and diplomats to work out.

US allies such as Japan and the Philippines are strengthening their security ties, while tensions with Beijing continue to simmer in the South China Sea, the East China Sea and the waters east of Taiwan. Would this make it more challenging for Beijing and Washington to manage their bilateral relationship?
