The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists.

Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance.

Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since.

“We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.”

By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”.

The zoo’s ample car park now welcomes only a handful of buses at a time. Across from it, a turreted wall built for elaborate performances once staged for Chinese tour groups stands as a chipped and faded monument to the high-water mark of Thai tourism.

Nearly 40 million people visited Thailand in 2019, the final year before the pandemic’s onset and still a Southeast Asian record.

Last year’s total of 32.9 million fell well short of that peak, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to lure travellers back.

The Tourism Authority of Thailand has now trimmed its 2026 forecast to between 30 million and 34 million international visitors, as this year’s US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s 4½-year-old war with Ukraine conspire to drive up oil prices and, with them, international airfares to Southeast Asia.

Years of a strong baht, meanwhile, have nudged budget-conscious international travellers towards cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

Money, geopolitics and changing tastes tell only half the story, however. The rest is down to patience – and Thailand’s is wearing thin.

Misbehaving tourists

Long known as the “land of smiles”, Thailand has for years prided itself on its easy-going approach to hospitality that asks little of guests beyond good manners.

But scroll through Thai social media on any given morning nowadays and the previous night’s transgressions are laid out for all to see: unpaid bills, drunken brawls and arrests for theft or vandalism among them.

Each post gets shared and reshared until the obvious disrespect for a proud local culture starts to sour public opinion on the costs of welcoming millions of strangers every year.

“Thai people are pragmatic. We do like the money [tourism brings],” said Voranai Vanijaka, a prominent political and social commentator. “But at the same time, we are highly nationalistic and we don’t like tourists acting the fool.”

This year alone, tourists have been caught performing sex acts in public, assaulting locals, trespassing on private property and vandalising local landmarks. Recent crackdowns have also revealed dozens of bars and restaurants run by foreigners but masquerading as Thai-owned enterprises.

Other crimes are far more grave. In June, Australian national Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested on suspicion of murdering a teenage Thai girl, stuffing her body into a suitcase and disposing of it in the undergrowth near Pattaya.

Authorities have separately uncovered Chinese and Korean cyberscam operators holed up in luxury villas, an Indian national flaunting firearms on social media and a steady stream of British cannabis mules.

All the while, public attitudes against foreigners have been hardening – a sentiment Voranai said had also been fuelled by global nativist trends, nationalism stirred up by the recent border conflict with Cambodia and grievances over foreign nationals buying up land and businesses.

“There is an anti-foreigner, anti-immigrant feeling sweeping the world; it’s not just in Thailand,” he said, describing a “mood and tone” within which every viral episode of misbehaviour now played out, and a “lower tolerance” for such actions.

The steady drumbeat of bad news pushed Thailand to end its 60-day visa-free stays for tourists from September 15. Days later, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters he thought misbehaving foreigners had “gone too far”.

Not for the first time, Thailand has said it will step back from playing the numbers game to focus on attracting fewer, higher-spending tourists instead.

Officials describe 2027 as “the year of transformation”, aiming to attract wealthier travellers willing to stay a week or two at a time.

A proposed flat fee of 450 baht (US$13.50) on all foreign visitors to fund tourism infrastructure upgrades is also being actively considered.

But this soul-searching over who Thailand wants to welcome, and for how long, comes as hotel bookings during the current low season have disappointed and as travellers appear to be waiting until the last minute to book their stays in the crucial high season that begins in November.

On the upside, Thai tourism authorities are anticipating 200,000 Chinese tourist arrivals during next month’s “golden week” holiday from October 1 to 7, just as a the baht’s recent retreat is offering travellers better value.

Against this uncertain backdrop, Charoon’s crocodile farm has enjoyed something of social media-spurred revival.

In its 1980s heyday, when his father welcomed dignitaries including Singapore’s founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, the business made headlines for encounters with reptiles that visitors elsewhere might only see behind glass.

But as the novelty of live-animal shows began to wear off and tastes changed, the zoo’s weekday crowds thinned to a trickle.

Then, in late August, a TikTok video showing a single visitor sitting alone in the stands at one of the zoo’s elephant shows found an audience all of its own, garnering more than 1 million likes and sending a flood of visitors streaming back through gates.

“I was shocked. I didn’t expect that. I never thought one video could communicate to so many people,” Charoon said.

“People are coming in their thousands. I just hope they keep coming.”

Show respect, or go

Thailand is far from alone in pausing to reconsider its relationship with visitors.

In Indonesia’s Bali, a foreign-led running club accused of barring locals from taking part suspended operations this summer; in Sri Lanka, Buddhist monks held a violent protest outside a newly opened Jewish community centre known as a Chabad house last month, questioning its legality; and in Vietnam, authorities have vowed zero tolerance for foreign misconduct after recent drunken rampages and a deadly shooting linked to foreign nationals.

Social media, as ever, amplifies both the insults delivered and how they are received.

One Phuket business owner, who asked not to be named to protect his livelihood, told This Week in Asia that the types of tourists now visiting Thailand were more entitled, demanding unreasonable discounts and firing off insults at the slightest whiff of not getting their own way.

“I don’t think Thais are xenophobic,” he said. “But my mindset has changed, like a lot of people on Phuket. Customers are customers, but if they’re not nice and don’t respect the culture and the people, we are happy to see them go.”

This change in public sentiment appears to have influenced the government’s decision to halve the 60-day visa free-entry. It has also produced unusually blunt warnings from ministers who normally pull their punches when addressing foreign embassies.

In August, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told the Chinese ambassador to “come out and explain” when sensitive issues arise “instead of speaking only to protect Chinese interests” – remarks that followed a viral confrontation between Chinese passengers and Thai officials at Bangkok’s main airport.

His comments also came amid mounting evidence of Chinese nationals illegally owning land and companies in Thailand, in some cases via officials bribed with as little as 500 baht to issue fraudulent birth certificates conferring land-ownership rights.

A small but vocal protest movement against official corruption and the influence of so-called grey money has since emerged, fronted by veteran conservative agitator Sondhi Limthongkul, who has rallied tens of thousands to take to the streets in the past.

Prime Minister Anutin, who himself rode a wave of nationalist sentiment to victory in February’s election, has responded to the backlash by fast-tracking deportations of foreign criminals and opening a wider investigation into “nominee” arrangements that allow foreign business owners to hide behind Thais.

Chinese, French, British, Indian and Russian nationals have all come under scrutiny, but it has been Israeli nationals – many of them military-aged and arriving in the wake of the war in Gaza – who have attracted the most intense attention, accused of building extensive “nominee”-business networks across southern Thai islands and of operating an illegal cemetery in Chachoengsao province.

“This has gone too far,” Anutin told officials on September 17 in response to the outrage.

“If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that. We have no objection whatsoever,” he said. “But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here.”

Anutin’s point man on the “nominee” scandal, Deputy Interior Minister Polapee Suwunchwee, has since said he is investigating several Chabad houses across the country, warning that any found to have been built unlawfully could be torn down.

Following a meeting with Thailand’s foreign minister earlier this month, Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm told local media that bad behaviour was not unique to citizens of her country, adding that Hebrew-language pre-departure awareness campaigns were being introduced outlining Thai laws and cultural norms.

Nationalist commentators with large online followings have seized upon the anti-Israeli rhetoric, some veering into outright antisemitism.

“There is a risk of this getting out of hand,” Voranai said, referring to growing anti-Israeli “paranoia” stoked by hardline conservatives chasing clicks and the political spotlight.

Yet he doubts the swirling public anger will cost Anutin’s government much in the long run.

“There is no risk to the government at all – except for bad press, which they don’t care about,” Voranai said. “Nor should they, they hold all the power and they can just ride it out.”

Meet the neighbours

Amid the blizzard of bad publicity, some are determined to build bridges between foreigners and their Thai hosts.

John Ho, who was born and raised in Hong Kong but swapped a career in hospitality for a new life in Chiang Mai with his Thai wife a decade ago, this month launched CosmoLocal CNX – a government-backed “pop-up village” offering workshops, talks and communal meals to draw the Thai city’s digital-nomad population into closer contact with their Thai neighbours.

“There’s a transitional period where you’re travelling as a tourist, when you may not care that much about the local culture and language,” Ho said.

“But then, if you want to stay longer and set up a base, it naturally comes to a question of: ‘OK, let’s make friends’. It’s better to learn some Thai, and learn some of the laws around business and work.”

His pop-up, which offers discounted tickets for Thai attendees to keep it accessible, trades on Chiang Mai’s slower pace of life, distinctive northern Lanna culture and small-town feel – qualities that have attracted legions of remote workers since the pandemic.

It is a world away from the raucous party scene of Thailand’s southern islands, where many of the recent cultural clashes have occurred.

“We see the tensions,” Ho said. “But the majority of nomads do care – maybe they need more facilitation to meet the locals. This is the first attempt to do that.”

As for the seemingly endless churn of viral confrontations between Thais and foreigners?

“News cycles are news cycles,” Ho said. “I think a lot of it is out of proportion. Everyone in Thailand welcomes foreigners.”

item.title: [SCMP] Pacing problem: can AI fears overcome US-China race dynamics and force a slowdown?
item.description:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.
item.content:encoded:
When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the sixth part of a series, Chong Ming Lee and Vincent Chow examine what’s behind the call for “pacing” by American AI giants – effectively a slowdown in development – and how the phenomenon is being viewed in China.

After years of rapid development, leading US AI executives are proposing what would have been unthinkable even a year earlier: that it may be time to slow down.

In recent weeks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI chief Sam Altman and SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk have all called for “pacing” the development of frontier artificial intelligence over purported fears that its capabilities were advancing faster than the safeguards designed to control them.

On Wednesday, Amodei pushed further for a slowdown when he addressed the UN Security Council by video link, warning that mismanaged AI posed an existential threat to humanity and urging nations to unite on global safety standards.

These public statements come ahead of a highly anticipated summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York City on the weekend to discuss AI safety, among other issues.

Yet despite converging on the language of restraint, Silicon Valley’s AI leaders remain locked in a high-stakes and costly tech race against each other – and with China – with no clear winner in sight.

These dynamics, both domestically between industry players and globally between the world’s two AI superpowers, make it highly unlikely that a slowdown will happen any time soon, analysts told the South China Morning Post.

“Even the US companies themselves cannot agree on that,” said Victor Shih, a professor at the University of California San Diego and an expert on Chinese elite politics. “So certainly the US and China will not agree on that.”

It has been four years since Washington imposed wide-ranging controls on the export of advanced semiconductor technology to China, citing national security concerns. Yet Chinese AI models from the likes of DeepSeek and Moonshot AI continue to be competitive with their US counterparts in price and capability.

This, in turn, threatens the trillion-dollar valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic as they head towards initial public offerings, as well as challenging US claims of global AI leadership – an explicit priority of US President Donald Trump, who outright dismissed the calls for a slow down in AI development.

“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a hoax,” he wrote on social media last week, raising questions about whether the world can pace AI without the support of one of its most powerful leaders.

The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share

Oskar Galeev, Concordia AI

What is driving calls to slow down?

There have long been concerns about the existential risks of AI. Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, winners of the Turing Award computer science prize and widely regarded as the “Godfathers” of AI, have both warned that the technology could eventually displace all humans, with Hinton saying earlier this month that a 10 per cent chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was not an “unreasonable” estimate.

While such concerns are legitimate, what sets apart the recent statements by industry leaders such as Amodei and Altman was that their AI safety proposals also served commercial and geopolitical ends, said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.

Sun pointed to Amodei’s recent essay “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which the Anthropic founder warned that a swarm of AI agents could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months, potentially causing “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage”.

While the essay laid out why Amodei believes pacing is needed, it also devoted a large part to advocating for tighter restrictions on China’s AI industry. These included US semiconductor chip export controls and a “crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies” in “autocratic” China.

“Amodei explicitly connects pacing with preserving a US lead over China,” Sun said. That made it “difficult” for Chinese policymakers to view the move as “politically neutral”, the Tsinghua fellow added, even if Amodei acknowledged that “[global] pacing will require cooperation with China”.

Reaction in China to Amodei’s essay was dismissive, with many accusing the tech CEO of using the guise of AI safety to shape the rules governing the sector and to entrench Anthropic’s position as an industry leader.

Last week, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, People’s Daily, published a commentary accusing the US of seeking to monopolise frontier AI development, while a DeepSeek engineer invoked Nazi Germany in a blog post that criticised OpenAI and Anthropic for their latest pacing calls.

China was likely to draw a sharp distinction between AI safety and efforts it viewed as “AI containment”, according to Wei Sun, principal analyst for AI at Counterpoint Research. Beijing has recently unveiled new AI initiatives that call for greater AI safety measures and international cooperation on AI governance, including a new “AI Safety Governance Framework” standards document for the industry released last week.

Oskar Galeev, a researcher at Beijing-based AI safety consultancy Concordia AI, said the Chinese government had demonstrated that it increasingly cared about AI safety. But it would still require the US to deal with it on an “equal footing”, he said, rather than as a subordinate being dictated to by a stronger power.

“The more pacing is framed as a way to win geopolitical competition, the harder it becomes to cooperate on the risks both sides share,” he said.

Existential risks, practical realities

Geopolitics aside, even getting the US to pace its own industry would be a challenge, according to UC San Diego’s Shih. While the Anthropic and OpenAI founders have raised alarms about the existential risks of AI, they have also been rebuffed by fellow industry titans including Meta Platforms’ Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who dismissed such worries as “complete nonsense” at an event last week.

Huang dismissed such “doomerism” while on a New York Times podcast on Wednesday , arguing that fearmongering only slowed down industry adoption.

There are questions over how a pacing mechanism would be enforced given high levels of mistrust between US AI companies.

As Karen Hao chronicled in her award-winning 2025 book Empire of AI, Altman and Musk helped found OpenAI in 2015 because they did not trust Google to develop AI safely. Six years later, Amodei and other former OpenAI executives and researchers left to start Anthropic after losing trust in Altman to develop AI safely.

Musk, founder of Grok model developer SpaceXAI – formerly xAI – took Altman to court earlier this year after having long accused the OpenAI CEO of prioritising profits over AI safety.

Qian Zilan, a research scholar at the independent AI governance think tank GovAI, said US AI leaders claimed that they wanted to build safe AI but did not trust others to do the same. This created pressure to continue building powerful AI systems, driven by fears that slowing down would cede ground to a rival who would deploy a system with far fewer safeguards.

Further intensifying these dynamics are the massive investments being made by US and Chinese companies in underlying AI infrastructure, such as chips and data centres, with the pace of spending not slowing down.

According to a Morgan Stanley report published earlier this month, capital expenditure by Chinese AI hyperscalers was forecast to jump 121 per cent year on year in 2026 to 995 billion yuan (US$142 billion), outpacing the 41 per cent growth among US peers.

China has long been a laggard in terms of AI investment, but recent successes, including DeepSeek’s breakthrough moment in January 2025 and growing policy support from Beijing, have spiked investment levels.

Still, even as the gap narrowed, China was set to spend only around 17 per cent as much as the US on AI infrastructure over the five years to 2030, Morgan Stanley estimated. Given that China’s AI spending was a much smaller share of its economy than the US, it would not likely slow down its investment momentum, Lu Ting, managing director and chief China economist at Nomura Securities, said at a Fortune event in Guangzhou last week.

“I think the key question in China is whether it can obtain chips, how many chips it can get, and how many Nvidia chips it can buy,” he said.

With China not showing signs of slowing down, the US want to maintain its pace over fears of China fully catching up, said Shan Hui, chief China economist at Goldman Sachs, at the same event. “The next 12 to 18 months will not slow down, and may even accelerate, especially in terms of AI infrastructure,” she said.

Adding to investor frenzy is the rush from both leading American and Chinese AI companies to go public. Despite its high-profile safety warnings, Anthropic itself was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, Axios reported earlier this month, citing multiple sources.

In China, Kimi developer Moonshot AI has reportedly been valued at US$50 billion in an ongoing funding round and confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, people with knowledge of the matter told SCMP earlier this month.

Meanwhile, GLM developer Z.ai, which is listed in Hong Kong, announced plans earlier this month to raise an additional US$5 billion through a combination of new shares and convertible bonds, just two months after raising US$4 billion in a share placement.

According to Tsinghua’s Sun, the new influx of capital and unprecedented investor interest made a collective slowdown difficult. “If one frontier company deliberately slows the development of its most capable models while its competitors continue to move ahead, it risks losing market share, capital, talent and technological leadership,” he said, adding that this also applies to countries.

Genuine safety fears

While there were legitimate concerns about the feasibility of pacing AI development, recent incidents involving AI agents demonstrating unprecedented cyber hacking capabilities had “captured the attention of both policymakers and the public”, said Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have in recent months released details about how their models hacked into other companies’ internal systems through “agentic swarms” that went undetected for weeks.

Besides industry warnings, calls for greater safeguards have also intensified among US and European politicians after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role at Anthropic earlier this month and accused the companies of “gambling with our lives” with their plans to accelerate AI development.

Central to their plans was recursive self-improvement (RSI), Coxon warned, which involved automating the AI research and development process itself with the use of AI – a controversial practice that some experts say could lead to humans losing control of AI entirely.

Still, both American and Chinese AI industry leaders have in recent months described RSI as imminent. Given the AI hacking incidents, calls for restraint from industry should not be dismissed as “regulatory theatre,” said Counterpoint Research’s Sun, as the arguments for AI safety had become “much more concrete.”

According to Singer, AI’s growing threat to both US and Chinese interests and humanity as a whole could ultimately be what overrides geopolitical and commercial incentives to continue racing ahead.

“At this stage, voluntary pacing isn’t just feasible, it’s pragmatic [in] the face of serious risks,” Singer said. “Regardless of whether a model is developed in San Francisco or Shanghai, they can create risks that transcend borders.”

Even in its attacks on Amodei and Washington’s hawkish tech policy towards China, the People’s Daily commentary nonetheless called on Washington to work with Beijing to “manage risks through dialogue and communication” and “promote AI to benefit mankind”.

Wang Shengyu, a research assistant at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Centre for China Analysis, said China’s dominant national security apparatus may be more sympathetic to calls for a slow down given the risks of AI expanding from cyberattacks to bioweapon development.

Last week, China’s top intelligence official Chen Yixin called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology in an article published in a journal run by the country’s Cyberspace Administration.

“Once the benefits and risks of frontier AI become concrete enough to create real policy trade-offs, the final judgment is likely to rest with President Xi [whether to slow down AI development]”, Wang said.

As the Xi-Trump meeting nears, experts cautioned against expecting a sweeping agreement on AI, saying any breakthrough would focus on narrower areas where US and Chinese interests overlapped.

A good deliverable from the summit would be for the two sides to agree to have more AI dialogue in future, while finding out what the common concerns over AI risks were, said Tsinghua’s Sun.

There are early signs that this may be possible. Following Sunday’s meeting, US Treasury Secretary Bessent said that the US and China had discussed a “US-China AI dialogue” mechanism and further meetings to discuss AI-related issues.

He added that the US side would “want a shared vision of common goals and threats” with China, including a proposed “notification mechanism” between the two countries.

“Just like any cross-border activity, moving from opaque to more transparency between the No 1 and No 2 AI powers in the world is very important,” Bessent said.

item.title: [SCMP] As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
item.description:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.
item.content:encoded:
When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips.

However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud.

By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said.

That critical lifeline could be on the verge of collapsing.

Washington is reportedly moving to expand its tech blockade from physical hardware to cloud networks. As the US Congress weighs legislation to restrict foreign remote access and executive agencies review cloud-leasing loopholes, China’s AI sector faces its most severe choke point since the chip bans began.

The impending US crackdown threatens to reshape the global AI ecosystem, challenging Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia’s international revenues and forcing Beijing into an acceleration of its domestic chip push.

The cloud escape hatch

Developing AI infrastructure across borders has long been common practice among Chinese developers looking to bypass hardware bans while avoiding US regulatory hurdles, according to observers.

“For a long time, Chinese AI companies have circumvented chip export bans by leasing overseas data centres,” said Arisa Liu, chief director and research fellow at Taiwan Industry Economics Services, a unit of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research. “[This] has indeed contributed a significant amount of overseas market demand to Nvidia.”

To make good use of these remote servers, some Chinese teams have taken extraordinary measures to overcome technical bottlenecks. Chinese engineers personally carried hard drives storing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to train an AI model at a local data centre, saving months of digital transfer time, The Wall Street Journal reported last year.

Driven by the global AI boom, demand for high-performance computing power has sent global cloud rental rates soaring.

Leading AI infrastructure provider Nebius Group raised rental prices on certain Nvidia chips by roughly 30 per cent in June, with a further 21 per cent increase to come into effect on October 1. Hyperscaler rates for Nvidia’s A100 processors rose to US$3.75 per hour in late August, up from US$3.71 a month earlier, according to tracking firm Silicon Data.

To maintain secrecy and navigate cross-border payments, some Chinese teams have even executed cloud-leasing transactions via blockchain-based smart contracts and paid in cryptocurrency to keep both parties hidden behind anonymous digital wallets, the Journal reported in 2024.

However, the regulatory net in Washington is rapidly closing.

The administration of US President Donald Trump was reviewing remote access arrangements and was working on policies to curb it, according to reports by Bloomberg and The Information. In January, the US House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which, if signed into law, would expand American export controls to remote cloud computing access.

“If the US passes and implements relevant legislation that extends restrictions from physical chips to cloud leasing, Nvidia’s overall sales growth momentum will inevitably be curtailed to some extent,” Liu said.

Legal experts noted that current compliance remained a grey area. Currently, there are “no regulations or similar provisions in place to restrict or prohibit” such remote access, said Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners.

The only measure that came close to banning the practice was the “AI Diffusion Rule”, said Hong, who focuses on trade compliance. The regulation, which requires US cloud service providers to exercise caution when providing cloud services for Chinese AI models, was introduced by the Biden administration in January 2025 but rescinded by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) after Trump came to power.

The Remote Access Security Act “was introduced for a similar purpose”, Hong said. However, once it goes into effect, “the businesses of cloud service giants such as Oracle and Amazon.com will be significantly impacted, which is bound to provoke a strong backlash”.

Even if the US did not enact legislation to regulate cloud services, the BIS could “theoretically impose penalties on data centres and even model developers that use illegally smuggled chips” on the grounds of “General Prohibition 10”, which penalises transactions conducted with knowledge that a violation has occurred, Hong explained.

“Hi-tech companies should avoid becoming entangled in such legal liabilities at all times,” he added.

Southeast Asia’s data centre boom

If Washington closes the cloud computing loophole, the immediate shock waves will hit Southeast Asia, one of the world’s fastest-growing data centre hubs.

Local data centre capacity in the region was projected to expand at 35 per cent each year from 2023 through 2028, outpacing the global average of 15 per cent, according to market intelligence platform Speeda.

Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – Tencent Holdings and TikTok owner ByteDance, have spent years building out regional infrastructure to serve the Chinese market.

Asian hyperscalers preferred the region for several reasons, including “competitive development costs across construction, equipment and human capital; and lower operating costs”, according to Vivian Wong, lead analyst for APAC at DC Byte, a market consultancy in the data centre industry.

If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market

Alex Cordovil, Dell’Oro Group

“If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market … Southeast Asia is the natural first step for that expansion, given proximity, existing business ties, land and power availability,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, a market research firm in the telecommunications, security and data centre industries.

Beyond local demands, the region has attracted international workloads, “including from Chinese internet and cloud companies”, Cordovil said. “Export controls are part of that picture: certain accelerator architectures are only available outside mainland China, so workloads that depend on them naturally gravitate to locations where that supply is accessible.”

The region also offers competitive energy economics.

In Southeast Asia, electricity prices average US$118 per megawatt hour (MWh), with the lowest in Indonesia at US$60 per MWh, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy focusing on the energy, chemicals, renewables, metals and mining.

While higher than China’s average industrial rates - between 600 yuan (US$89) and 700 yuan per MWh, and half that in energy-rich regions like Inner Mongolia and Guizhou – Southeast Asia remains cheaper than US hubs like northern Virginia and Silicon Valley, where prices range between US$70 and US$120 per MWh. In comparison, European centres like Germany and Ireland see prices ranging between €150 (US$174) and €250 per MWh, according to state-backed media China Energy News.

Should remote access become a constraint for certain customers in Southeast Asia, it would “likely create a transient imbalance between supply and demand in the region”, he said, adding that the imbalance was expected to be “short lived” as demand was deep.

Wong held a similar view, saying that “any released capacity is likely to be taken up relatively quickly by other customers”.

The domestic bottleneck

For Chinese AI firms, losing overseas cloud access will lay bare a troubling reality: despite heavy state investment, domestic hardware is not yet fully equipped to handle frontier model training at scale.

Despite China’s push for self-sufficiency in chips, the country’s most advanced AI models are still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP previously reported.

The AI development life cycle involves training and inference – the use of a trained model to generate new content. Systems such as DeepSeek-V4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have been successfully adapted to Chinese hardware for inference work only.

For now, the most advanced Nvidia chips remain unavailable in China, including the B200, B300, H100 and H800. Chinese firms either use Nvidia chips they have in inventory or gain access through cloud computing.

The H200, the latest of Nvidia’s Hopper-series chips but a generation behind the Blackwell family, was approved for import by both Washington and Beijing but is only available in small quantities.

ByteDance and Tencent Holdings each received about 10,000 H200s and a few other Chinese customers obtained shipments of a similar size, the Financial Times reported in August.

“There is a massive gap between this quantity and the actual demand of such top-tier tech giants, which often consume tens of thousands or even over 100,000 advanced [graphics processing units],” said Liu of the Taiwan institution.

Nvidia in late August reported that shipments of H200s to China accounted for less than 1 per cent of its US$89 billion data-centre revenue in the quarter that ended July 26. However, it said it did not expect any data-centre computing revenue from China in the following quarter.

Liu added that even though Nvidia’s income might be temporarily curtailed if the US imposed the ban on remote access, “this shortfall may be partially offset by massive orders from other international tech giants” given strong AI demand globally.

Accelerating self-reliance

If the US bans Chinese companies from renting Nvidia-powered data centres overseas, it may lead to higher domestic rental rates, the Shenzhen-based data centre broker noted. For now, rates for B300 chips outside China are two to three times higher than local prices, not including differences in electricity costs.

Even if there were no restriction on renting overseas data centres, replacing Nvidia with domestic chips was “the main trend”, said a semiconductor designer at one of China’s biggest chipmakers, who requested anonymity.

“Who knows if Nvidia processors have back doors,” the person said. Nvidia has repeatedly said that there are no back doors, kill switches or spyware in its products.

Some Chinese teams have started using local chips for AI training. In June, Meituan released LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that it said was fully trained and run on a 50,000-card domestic computing power cluster, without naming the supplier.

Huawei Technologies’ rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year.

The semiconductor design engineer said the best domestic AI chip currently was the Ascend 950 from Huawei Technologies, not only for its performance but for the whole ecosystem from architecture to networks. Huawei announced last week that the next-generation Ascend 960DT, designed for model training, will be ready in the first quarter of 2027, nine months ahead of schedule.

However, transferring training workloads from Nvidia to domestic chips is a steep engineering bottleneck. The hurdles included the software ecosystem, as Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) platform has long been the industry standard for AI development, the SCMP reported in August.

Migrating existing workflows to Huawei’s Ascend chips could add at least 50 per cent to training time and cost, according to researcher James Wang.

Still, China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade. The supply of advanced-node wafers made using 7-nanometre processes and below was projected to grow at 46 per cent annually between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a recent report.

That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035 from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank.

As Washington moves to extend its tech blockade from hardware shipments to virtual server networks, Chinese AI developers may soon lose their refuge in the cloud. What remains to be seen is whether the squeeze will stall China’s frontier AI ambitions or simply accelerate its push towards technological self-sufficiency.

item.title: [SCMP] China has gained pace in the space race by recovering rockets – but can it relaunch one?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.

US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.

Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.

US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.

Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.

Last month, Chinese private aerospace company LandSpace landed the booster of its Zhuque-3 rocket on deployable landing legs at a site in the northwestern province of Gansu, marking the country’s first successful ground-based controlled recovery using landing legs, an approach that closely resembles that of SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

The significance of landing a launched rocket goes beyond the spectacle of bringing a booster back intact, according to industry experts.

Rocket reuse was “essential for achieving low-cost, frequent and sustainable [launches] … and providing new opportunities for large-scale commercial space exploration”, a team from three major Chinese aerospace research institutions said in a paper published in March.

LandSpace said the first stage represented “about 70 per cent” of a rocket’s cost, with reuse able to spread that expense over multiple missions, underscoring the cost advantages of reusing first-stage boosters.

Some Chinese launch services can cost around US$20,000 per kilogram (about US$9,070 a pound) of payload, compared with roughly US$2,700 to US$3,000 for SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9, according to a report published by the Mercator Institute for China Studies in February.

The large gap helps explain why rocket makers are racing to develop vehicles that can be recovered and reused.

The Chinese paper from March said there were several different approaches to bringing a rocket back, including recovery using parachutes or wings to slow the vehicle for a safer arrival.

Other approaches include landing leg recovery, with the booster using its engines to control its descent before touching down vertically on deployable landing legs.

While China still lags behind the US in landing leg recovery, it is also betting on a different approach to booster recovery: an offshore net-capture system that uses a recovery vessel to catch the descending booster.

In July, it successfully retrieved part of a Long March-10B reusable rocket following its maiden launch by using a unique sea-based net-capture system for the first time.

Compared with the landing leg recovery approach, net-capture had relatively less demanding requirements for the booster’s final landing-point accuracy, avoided the need to install heavy landing-support structures on the rocket and allowed the offshore recovery platform to be deployed flexibly, Wang Long, the founder of space technology consultancy Nihao Taikong, was quoted as saying in a report by Shenzhen-based Securities Times in July.

Hao Jinjie, an engineer at China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, told state broadcaster CGTN the net-capture method was “like dropping a pen from the 100th floor into a pencil holder, while keeping its speed and orientation under control”.

China’s pursuit of reusable rockets draws on both its state aerospace groups and its ability to mobilise the private sector behind national priorities through the deployment of industrial policy.

Galactic Energy’s kerosene-fuelled Pallas-1 reached orbit earlier this month, with a recovery attempt deliberately deferred to later missions. The rocket is designed to carry up to 7 tonnes to a low-Earth orbit, intended for use on the first stage of at least 25 flights.

ISpace flew the same low-altitude methane demonstrator twice in 2023, though its orbital SQX-3 has yet to launch. Space Pioneer, Orienspace, Deep Blue Aerospace and Space Epoch also have reusable rockets at various stages of testing or development.

To make reusability economically viable, a booster needs to be able to re-enter space and survive repeated launches. Dai Zheng, chief commander of the Zhuque-3 missions at LandSpace, said those were areas in which China had little experience.

China had no established technical framework covering rocket reuse standards, inspection procedures or rules governing component replacement, Dai told state broadcaster CCTV in an interview last month.

“China has just solved the question of whether a rocket can come back,” he said, adding that there was “no system yet for determining whether a recovered rocket can fly again”.

In a research report published last month, analysts at Jinyuan Securities emphasised that a reusable rocket required a complete post-recovery processing cycle, including safely draining and disposing of residual propellant, isolating potential hazards and conducting non-destructive inspections of the vehicle’s structure, welds and propellant tanks.

Other necessary steps involved assessing the remaining life of engines after repeated thermal and pressure cycles, replacing worn components such as seals and valves, and carrying out system-wide functional tests before another flight.

LandSpace has said it plans to reuse the Zhuque-3 booster recovered last month in a space mission in the next six months, while the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology has said it aims to conduct a reuse flight of the first-stage Long March-10B by the end of this year.

Success in those endeavours would mark a crucial shift for China from demonstrating that it can recover a booster to proving that it can fly one again – essential to realising its commercial space ambitions.

A decade ago, a central government white paper called for research into low-cost launch vehicles and reusable transport systems capable of travelling between Earth and space.

Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency

Xu Ying, GalaxySpace

What began as a research objective has moved through engineering trials and become a national industrial push. China’s latest five-year plan made building the country into a “space power” a priority, and specifically mentioned the development of reusable launch technology, including a reusable heavy-lift launcher for deep-space programmes.

Every serious ambition China has in space – from constellations of broadband satellites to orbiting computing networks and missions to the moon – will depend on reusable launch systems.

“Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency,” said Xu Ying, general manager of public affairs at satellite manufacturer GalaxySpace. Only then, she added, could “space infrastructure” be deployed at scale and become commercially viable.

China’s two flagship broadband projects show the size of the task. China Satellite Net plans for its Guowang constellation to have 12,992 satellites, with roughly 1,300 scheduled to be in orbit by 2029 and the full network deployed by 2035.

Shanghai-based SpaceSail’s Qianfan network is aiming for more than 15,000 by 2030, but the two Chinese companies combined have less than 500 satellites in orbit at present – around 4 per cent of Starlink’s orbiting fleet of more than 11,000.

LandSpace launched 10 Qianfan satellites into orbit on Tuesday, marking the first deployment for a large-scale satellite internet constellation by a private Chinese rocket company. Another eight were launched on Wednesday.

SpaceSail aims to expand the Qianfan constellation to 324 satellites by the end of the year – up from 256 at present – leaving a narrow window of just over three months to launch 68 more.

A space industry researcher based in Xian, capital of northwestern China’s Shaanxi province, said some experts were optimistic that China would be able to make steady progress in the reusable rocket race.

He said that while SpaceX – founded in 2002 – had a head start in many aspects of the commercial space sector, Chinese companies were making progress. However, he added, China’s industry might encounter difficulties due to a comparative lack of experience in advanced rocket engines, as “no one from outside China would teach you how to design them”.

Engines accounted for more than 50 per cent of the total cost of a rocket, Wang Zijing, an analyst at Soochow Securities, wrote in a research note issued this month.

Jinyuan Securities said engine life and repeated ignition were among the biggest technical challenges in the reuse of boosters.

A reusable booster must restart its engines during ascent, re-entry and landing and operate reliably across a wide range of thrust levels, meaning that key components including its turbopumps, combustion chamber, nozzle and valves must be able to withstand repeated thermal and pressure cycles as well as vibration loads.

No Chinese rocket engine has yet made a second orbital flight. Meanwhile, a SpaceX Falcon 9 booster was sent into space for the 37th time last month.

“Reusable technology remains a new field that requires continued learning,” Lou Luliang, the chief designer of the Long March-10B, told Beijing-based China Aerospace News in a report published in July. “The thermal and mechanical conditions during an actual return, component damage and the patterns of reuse cannot all be fully understood through ground testing alone”.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s rocket boom has made Hainan a space hub. Can launches fuel wider growth?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.

Long known for its coconuts, its namesake chicken and generations of emigrants who left for Southeast Asia in search of a living, Wenchang has been thrust onto the frontier of national development. Beijing’s space ambitions have turned the city into a showcase for rocket launches – and given Hainan a catalyst to reshape an economy long reliant on tourism and consumer services.

Today, the island province is working to build a more diversified and sustainable growth model and, together with its ambition to host a premier free-trade port, is embracing a hi-tech future increasingly centred on the space economy.

From coconuts to rockets: Hainan’s economic reboot

“Commercial space flight could give Hainan a clearer manufacturing focus while complementing its traditional strengths in tourism and consumer services,” said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government.

Home to more than 10 million people and comparable in size to Belgium, Hainan now boasts a growing industrial cluster known as Wenchang International Aerospace City. At its centre are two state-owned rocket launch facilities: one serving national programmes and another handling commercial missions.

The Wenchang Space Launch Site staged its first launch in 2016 and focuses mainly on lunar exploration and human space flight. Just a few miles away sits the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, China’s first dedicated commercial launch platform.

Since its inaugural mission in November 2024, the commercial site has completed 21 launches and has sent 221 satellites into orbit, according to Xu Xikai, deputy head of the development department at Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch, the site’s operator.

Two more general-purpose liquid-fuel launch pads were also under construction and could host their maiden missions by the end of this year, Xu noted. Longer-term plans envision as many as eight large coastal launch pads, together with tracking facilities and systems for recovering rockets at sea.

We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains

Xu Xikai, Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch

Wenchang’s coastal geography gives it a major advantage. Massive rockets can be delivered directly by sea, bypassing the road, tunnel and bridge constraints faced by inland facilities. And at about 19 degrees north latitude, rockets gain an extra momentum boost from the Earth’s rotation, reducing fuel requirements or allowing heavier payloads, Xu explained.

“For large-diameter, heavy-lift rockets in the future, coastal launch sites will increasingly have an advantage,” he said.

Geography, however, is also one of Hainan’s economic weaknesses. The island has historically lacked a heavy industrial base, meaning much of the specialised hardware and construction materials required for space manufacturing must be shipped in.

Inside Wenchang’s manufacturing ambitions

The challenge for Hainan is transforming launch sites into the nucleus of a wider industrial ecosystem – and early signs are encouraging.

Wenchang International Aerospace City recorded a surge in revenue amid an “unprecedented” pace of rocket launches, according to a June report by Nanhai Net, a state-run news portal operated by the Hainan Daily Press Group.

The aerospace park’s revenue jumped 85 per cent in 2025 to 23.53 billion yuan (US$3.5 billion), while manufacturing output from its rocket supply chain more than doubled to over 8 billion yuan, the report stated.

Under a provincial action plan from 2025 to 2027, Hainan also aims to raise annual operating revenue at Wenchang’s aerospace cluster to 10 billion yuan by 2027, while building an integrated supply chain spanning rockets, satellites and data services.

The expansion comes as Beijing presses ahead with reforms to open the island further and develop new sources of growth – though competition is intensifying. Two other commercial launch sites have already begun operating in Gansu and Shandong provinces, while at least four more are under development nationwide.

To stay ahead, Hainan’s strategy is to push further up the industrial chain. Its action plan prioritises a “super factory” next to the launch pads, designed to produce up to 1,000 satellites annually. The location would allow freshly assembled satellites to move straight from production line to launch pad with very little transit time, the Star Market Daily, a Shanghai-based financial news outlet focused on technology and capital markets, reported in December.

Described by local authorities as Asia’s largest satellite-manufacturing facility, the industrial complex is also expected to support China’s Qianfan low-Earth-orbit constellation. A planned special bonded zone for satellite data would further leverage Hainan’s free-trade policies to attract data from overseas, according to the report.

“We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains,” said Xu of Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch.

The infrastructure buildout is already reshaping launch activity. After more than two years of development, the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site has moved from experimental testing to routine operations. It handled more than 30 per cent of China’s commercial satellite launches in 2025 and successfully carried out the country’s first offshore rocket booster recovery.

Business beyond the launch pad

Putting a rocket into orbit, however, is only one part of the emerging space economy. Ye Shiyang, a Wenchang native who chairs the company behind the Aerospace Supercomputing Centre in Wenchang International Aerospace City, argued Hainan must capture a larger share of the value generated after a rocket launches.

“Over the past few years, we have connected the entire chain – from collecting and receiving satellite data to storing, processing, applying and trading it,” Ye said.

Completed in 2023, the supercomputing centre occupies about 40,000 square metres (about 431,000 square feet), with about 22,400 square metres of floor space. A guide at the centre said it offered peak computing power of 100 petaflops – a measure of processing capacity – and was designed to accommodate about 2,000 server racks.

Meanwhile, three of the centre’s remote-sensing satellites operate as part of Jilin-1, which is described by its developer as the world’s largest commercial sub-metre Earth-observation constellation. The centre has also built 13 ground stations, according to a guide there.

The practical applications could be numerous. Satellite images processed in Wenchang can distinguish food crops from cash crops, identify fallow land and monitor crop growth, assess pest outbreaks and track the effects of typhoons. Such imaging tools can also help to detect water pollution, illegal logging and unauthorised land use.

These services, Ye argued, could generate steady demand from agricultural, environmental and land-management authorities, giving Hainan a revenue stream that is less dependent on the schedule of rocket launches.

The aerospace city is also developing a space tourism business. The Jixing Meteorite Museum, for instance, displays more than 400 specimens gathered from around the world, while exhibitions introduce visitors to satellite data and supercomputing.

“We are developing space tourism in response to market demand,” Ye said. “Visitors should not only watch a launch or see a rocket or satellite. They should also understand the industry and technology behind them.”

In 2025, tourism, modern services, hi-tech industries and tropical agriculture – Hainan’s four pillar sectors – accounted for 65.9 per cent of the province’s gross domestic product, according to the provincial government.

“The Wenchang launch site has already become a tourist attraction, and this could give Hainan an economic model built around tourism, consumer services and aerospace manufacturing – and give its manufacturing sector a much clearer direction,” said Peng of the Guangdong Society of Reform.

For a Wenchang native surnamed Xie, the transformation has been drastic. Growing up in a village in Longlou town, he once walked barefoot along unpaved red-earth tracks. Today, working as a taxi driver, he has watched the sprawling aerospace complex reshape the place he calls home.

As the launch site and surrounding projects expanded, local families were relocated and farmland acquired. While some households received hundreds of thousands of yuan in compensation, Xie noted how traditional livelihoods were quickly fading, leaving coconut processing as one of the few legacy industries remaining.

“Farmers around here barely farm any more,” he said.

In Longlou, the coconut palms still remain – quiet reminders of a past that existed before the rockets arrived, even as a new economy takes shape around them.

item.title: [SCMP] Wu Shicun on why Beijing will not rule out Scarborough Shoal construction
item.description:
Wu Shicun is the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies and chairman of the Huayang Centre for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance. In this interview, the first in a series about the South China Sea dispute, he discusses ways Beijing can respond to rival claimants.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

With Manila intensifying its “transparency” campaign, how does China view the current situation and what challenges does it face?
item.content:encoded:
Wu Shicun is the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies and chairman of the Huayang Centre for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance. In this interview, the first in a series about the South China Sea dispute, he discusses ways Beijing can respond to rival claimants.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

With Manila intensifying its “transparency” campaign, how does China view the current situation and what challenges does it face?

Manila’s so-called “assertive transparency” initiative operates on its own distinct logic and playbook. [The initiative includes documenting and publicising what Manila calls Chinese grey-zone tactics, such as blockades and the use of water cannons.]

Since 2023, the Philippines has deliberately intruded into the waters around Renai Jiao [the Chinese name for the disputed Second Thomas Shoal], deliberately provoking China into intercepting its vessels or deploying water cannons.

On-board media outlets then package these confrontation scenes into short, viral videos and disseminate them globally. These clips manufacture an international perception that “China is the bully in the South China Sea and the Philippines is the victim”. This is the core mechanism behind their public relations strategy.

Behind this are Philippine domestic political considerations, aimed at securing more budget and equipment support from the Philippine Congress for its coastguard.

In contrast, Beijing’s energy has been primarily concentrated on rule-making. For instance, in promoting consultations for a Code of Conduct in the South China Sea (COC), negotiations have been grinding steadily forward for over a decade since 2013.

Concurrently, working group meetings on the implementation of the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea [DOC] recently convened for their 56th session in Vietnam. These institutional frameworks are where China invests the bulk of its diplomatic capital.

Regarding narrative construction, there was a period when China was in a passive position, especially during the 2023 Second Thomas Shoal stand-off and later when the Philippines intruded on Sabina Shoal and spread false information such as “China intends to occupy the feature”.

But as we gradually recognised the Philippines’ tactics and the Western media backing behind the scenes, we began to adjust our counter-strategy, sometimes proactively clarifying to the international community Manila’s false narratives and exposing their deliberate methods of smearing China.

This is exactly why Beijing is now proposing to proactively construct a new South China Sea narrative. This shift is a direct lesson learned from countering the Philippines’ playbook.

Our strategy has undergone a profound paradigm shift; it is expected to become even more proactive in the future. Because as a responsible major power, China must always tell the truth.

Meanwhile, extra-regional countries such as the United States and Japan use the Philippines’ narrative as an excuse to intervene in South China Sea affairs, thereby binding their military apparatus to the Philippines.

The United States wants to use its military bases and supply them with weapons. Japan, through signing the reciprocal access agreement with the Philippines, has lowered the threshold for Japan’s Ground, Maritime, and Air Self-Defence Forces to enter Philippine bases; Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and other countries have also signed visiting forces agreements similar to the reciprocal access agreement with the Philippines.

Recently, Japan also participated in the US-Philippine Balikatan military exercises. In this year’s exercise involving seven countries, Japan sent more than 1,400 personnel, three warships and helicopters for the first time, and conducted live-fire drills with a surface-to-ship missile system during the exercise. This was also the first time Japan used a show of force overseas after World War II.

Even many middle powers are seeking to cash in on the friction and seek geopolitical benefits, relying on the Philippines to stir up trouble. The combination of various factors has enabled the assertive transparency initiative to achieve its expected PR goals for a period of time.

However, today the international community – other Southeast Asian countries – has gradually seen through these tactics, and the initiative’s influence is gradually weakening. The global public is no longer so easily buying into its fact-distorting hype.

With deepening defence ties between Japan and the Philippines, and strengthened Vietnam-Philippine maritime cooperation, what challenges does Beijing’s bilateral strategy of engaging in direct talks with claimant countries face and how should China respond?

This is indeed a new development. Other rival claimants are attempting to join forces to counter China on certain issues. At the same time, they have been lukewarm towards China’s initiatives that are designed to foster regional peace, stability and environmental protection while delivering tangible benefits to littoral states.

Some coastal nations are quietly conducting exclusive economic zone delimitations, which effectively encroach upon China’s rights and claims in the South China Sea, with some even crossing over into waters under Chinese jurisdiction.

Our policy remains consistent: resolving disputes through peaceful means, bilateral consultations and negotiations. Yet, we’re seeing increasingly frequent contact between Vietnam and the Philippines recently.

Beyond state visits, they have privately hammered out internal agreements to tighten maritime cooperation, explore the possibility of bilateral maritime delimitation, conduct joint law enforcement and share intelligence. Manila has even gone so far as to encourage Vietnamese fishermen to operate in the waters surrounding Huangyan Island [Scarborough Shoal], an attempt to pile pressure onto China’s maritime law enforcement.

Data shows that a considerable number of Vietnamese fishing vessels have appeared in waters around Huangyan Island. Video footage captured during our annual Sansha and South China Sea patrols reveals a substantial presence of boats flying the Vietnamese flag.

Considering the straight-line distance from Vietnam to these waters is nearly 1,000km (600 miles), such long-range cross-sea fishing operations are economically unsustainable for ordinary fishermen.

Without government subsidies and escort protection provided by the Vietnamese and Philippine coastguard authorities, these fishermen are likely to return empty-handed. Therefore, there is undeniably state backing and financial aid behind this.

There is clear growing coordination between rival claimants and with extra-regional countries, and Beijing is fully aware of it. However, I do not believe this poses a substantial threat to China’s rights and claims.

If they ever choose to make these delimitation agreements public – agreements that bypass China and violate our sovereign rights – Beijing simply will not recognise them, and it has a comprehensive suite of countermeasures at its disposal.

These countries are well aware of this reality, which explains why they prefer to quietly put delimitation on hold. Take the delimitation between Vietnam and Indonesia as an example. Although both sides signed a delimitation agreement, the boundary maps and geographical coordinates that should customarily be submitted to the UN Secretary General have yet to be provided.

Could you elaborate on what specific measures Beijing might take?

No matter how other countries attempt to draw these maritime lines, if an action infringes upon China’s interests, we will not only refuse to recognise it but will simply carry on with business as usual.

Take the attempts by Japan and the Philippines to delimit boundaries in the waters east of Taiwan – even if they draw their lines, China will absolutely never recognise them. Such behaviour will ultimately prove counterproductive for them, instead prompting China to further strengthen maritime law enforcement operations and enhance its actual presence in relevant waters.

I don’t believe these countries have thought this through properly. The era when China had its hands tied is gone. If they are trying to play petty games, they have completely miscalculated.

Why does Beijing treat Vietnam and the Philippines differently in the South China Sea dispute and how should it balance maritime tensions with Hanoi against the commitment to building a community with a shared future?

A US scholar previously asked me whether China was applying a “double standard” to Hanoi and Manila.

I told him plainly that when it comes to infringements in the South China Sea, China has no double standards. China has red lines whenever its rights and claims are violated – it’s simply the handling methods that differ.

The Philippines relies heavily on hyping things up through “megaphone diplomacy”, playing the victim card to court international sympathy. Manila deliberately provokes China’s rights and claims, anticipating that China will step in to carry out law enforcement and use water cannons. In its pursuit of so-called transparency, Manila behaves rather like a child who screams the moment you barely touch them.

As for Vietnam’s island-building, China’s opposition has been consistent and clear. We have repeatedly lodged diplomatic representations through both state-to-state and party-to-party channels, demanding that Hanoi halt such constructions.

These activities violate the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea, disrupting regional peace and stability while complicating the situation and escalating tensions. Its actions also do nothing to help the ongoing negotiations for the Code of Conduct in the South China Sea.

Data published by the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI) confirms Vietnam’s actions. For example, Vietnam has been carrying out reclamation work across 18 islands and reefs [in the Paracel Islands].

Hanoi’s dredging across the archipelago has pushed its total artificial land mass past 11 sq km (4 square miles), putting its reclamation scale on a trajectory to rival or even exceed what China built between 2013 and 2015.

It is the tactics deployed by Beijing that differ, purely because Hanoi and Manila employ entirely different methods. Vietnam operates quietly.

Moreover, China does not wish for these island-building activities to derail the broader Sino-Vietnamese relationship, as the disputes do not represent the entirety of our bilateral ties. We are keen to avoid a situation where poor management or mishandling of maritime friction damages our bilateral relations or harms China’s ties with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Crucially, there is a deep-seated consensus between our two ruling parties, encapsulated in the “16-character guideline” [friendly neighbourliness, comprehensive cooperation, durable stability and looking towards the future] and the “Four Goods” spirit [being good neighbours, good comrades, good partners and good friends]. This is the big picture of Sino-Vietnamese relations.

How effective has China’s island-building been in protecting its maritime interests over the past decade and does Beijing still hold its “Big Triangle” strategic advantage – the highly fortified outposts at Fiery Cross, Mischief, and Subi Reefs – in the Spratly Islands, given Vietnam’s accelerated reclamation activities?

Whether China’s strategic edge remains intact largely depends on Vietnam’s subsequent moves once its island-building projects are wrapped up. Although Hanoi has pledged to deploy only civilian facilities, it remains to be seen whether they will actually walk the talk.

Vietnam occupies a considerable number of features, most notably Barque Canada Reef, which boasts the largest reclaimed footprint and is highly capable of supporting an airstrip.

According to data published by the AMTI, some experts estimate that Vietnam could eventually possess six to seven runways and 15 harbours across the Nansha [Spratly] Islands.

If these facilities are geared towards military purposes, might they be opened up for shared use with the US or Japan down the line? After all, Vietnam’s military and security cooperation with Washington and Tokyo has deepened significantly and intelligence-sharing is already under way.

Should they begin to pose a security threat to our civilian facilities, fishermen and garrisoned troops on those reefs, Beijing will certainly roll out appropriate countermeasures.

However, taking a broader view, this will not, in the short term, exert a disruptive or game-changing impact on China’s current capacity to safeguard its rights, law enforcement or project its maritime power.

You’ve said island-building could continue if necessary. Where would be the most critical location for reclamation, Scarborough Shoal or Antelope Reef? Why has China chosen this moment to dredge Antelope Reef after refraining from large-scale reclamation for the past decade?

Whether to build on Huangyan Island depends on several factors. Firstly, will intrusions into the territorial sea baseline around Huangyan Island that China announced in 2024 become the norm, as well as challenges from the Philippines and other external forces in future?

If parties enter territorial waters or fly through airspace without declaration and permission, China will certainly take countermeasures. Therefore, this potential security threat is an important precondition.

Secondly, the Philippines has consistently claimed that its fishermen enjoy “traditional fishing rights” in Huangyan Island’s lagoon – something China absolutely does not recognise.

If the other party frequently engages in such infringements and damages the marine environment in Huangyan Island’s waters, it will place enormous pressure on China’s rights protection and law enforcement.

Currently, Chinese coastguard vessels face very long voyages and substantial logistical costs for resupplying and travelling between Huangyan Island and home ports.

If future challenges make our maritime law enforcement difficult to manage, then in future we cannot rule out constructing some fixed facilities on Huangyan Island to meet the supply needs of law enforcement vessels and other transport vessels or provide humanitarian medical assistance.

Looking ahead, in the waters east of the Huangyan Island, joint patrols by non-regional actors such as the United States, Australia and even Japan – alongside the Philippine Coast Guard and Navy – are likely to become increasingly frequent.

In the absence of mutually observed rules of engagement, the probability of maritime collisions will only rise. Should an incident result in casualties, could the United States intervene? That possibility exists.

China will not proactively engage in further land reclamation or island-building. However, the possibility of constructing certain fixed facilities to meet the requirements of defending our legitimate rights remains on the table. If Beijing ultimately takes this step, it is because external forces have left us with no choice.

Is China’s dredging at Antelope Reef in the Paracel Islands a direct response to Vietnam’s island-building in the Spratly Islands? Or are there other calculations at play?

Some have tried to frame this as a tit-for-tat scenario – suggesting that because Vietnam is reclaiming land in the Spratlys, China is doing the same in the Paracels – but that is simply not the case. These are two completely unrelated matters. China has never recognised any dispute with Vietnam over the Paracel Islands.

China’s actions in the Paracel Islands are primarily because it still faces rights infringements and illegal fishing from some neighbouring countries, and even provocations by foreign military and police vessels. For instance, the recent entry of a Dutch frigate into the territorial waters of the Paracel Islands proves that our control in that area still has vulnerabilities.

As for Antelope Reef, Beijing’s activities are predominantly for civilian purposes, aimed at protecting and restoring the marine environment. This does not correlate whatsoever with Vietnam’s construction work in the Spratly Islands.
