It’s a very obscure regional dish that I’ve never tried and most British people have never tried. But an English woman wrote a blog post about it that went viral in China, so it’s now almost certainly better known in China than it is at home.

I would say that a lot of Chinese people who have not had the chance to travel abroad make these huge generalisations about Western food that are just as silly as those some Westerners make about all Chinese food.

I’ve also found it very surprising that a lot of Chinese people have told me over the years that they think Western food is healthier because there’s this sort of tradition of scientific nutrition where you’re told how many calories and how much protein and that sort of thing.

But I find that very strange because it seems to me that people in China, certainly the older generation, have a knowledge of healthy eating that is incredibly deep and incredibly useful, whereas I think a lot of Westerners are actually quite confused about how to eat healthily.

There is also this idea that Chinese food can be quite oily and Western food is not. But again, I think that’s really strange because if you think about traditional Chinese food, it involves a lot of soups and steamed dishes and boiled dishes, and traditional Chinese home cooking does not use a lot of oil.

I think it’s quite sad to see that people in China are now making a lot of the same mistakes that we’ve already made in the West of cooking less and eating less fresh food. It is one of the unfortunate side effects of modernisation and industrialisation, isn’t it?

What do you think of Westernised Chinese food, such as the fast food restaurants popular in the US, like Panda Express?

You have to remember that Chinese food is not just the food of the country of China. It’s also the food of a huge Chinese diaspora.

So Chinese food is already part of global culture and it’s a presence in every city practically all over the world. Not only Chinese people living in the West want to eat Chinese food.

Chinese food doesn’t have to be one thing. I think people are always inventing and adapting and borrowing ideas from each other. For example, I recently wrote an article about Shanghainese Western food, which is a bit like Hong Kong-style Western food.

So in China you have versions of Western food that are completely separate from what Westerners actually want to eat. They are adapted to Chinese tastes, and I think in the West you also have Chinese food that’s not designed for Chinese people. It’s made for Westerners. I don’t have a problem with that. I think it’s fun to be inventive.

The only problem is when people start to judge Chinese food by Panda Express and think that it represents the cuisine of a very large and sophisticated gastronomic nation.

We just have to be a bit careful about judging it.

In many Chinese cities, the highly rated and expensive restaurants tend to be Japanese. This seems to be the case in other major cities around the world. Why is Japanese food more likely to be considered fine dining than Chinese food?

I think the status of food is always about money.

Japan got rich before China in the late 20th century, so its food acquired high status at a time when China was quite closed to the outside world and was not rich and did not have high status.

It’s the same within China with regional cuisines. For example, when there were many rich merchants from Anhui, Anhui food was considered one of the “eight major cuisines”. But when I was a student in Sichuan in the 1990s, all of the expensive restaurants were Cantonese because places like Hong Kong and Shenzhen got rich first.

What’s interesting now is that China is getting richer and more powerful, so I think the status of China and Chinese culture is rising. The problem at the moment is that we don’t have enough chefs in the UK. We have very tight immigration rules in Britain and it’s almost impossible these days for chefs to come here and work.

If we had more free movement of chefs, Chinese food here in Britain would become more ambitious and more expensive.

It’s even more important to find ways to communicate with each other, and it’s also incredibly important to try and understand each other

Fuchsia Dunlop

Do you face any challenges in defending Chinese food in the West?

The whole environment is becoming more complicated because of geopolitical tensions. Obviously the relationship between the West and China has become more complicated.

But I think in that context it’s even more important to find ways to communicate with each other, and it’s also incredibly important to try and understand each other.

So, for example, it’s fantastic that China is now more open to foreign tourists, because foreigners will go to China and actually see something of the country, meet people and have a real experience.

At the same time, the first encounters most foreigners have with Chinese culture often involve Chinese food, and it’s an area that’s not so politically contentious, a space where you can actually learn a lot about China and have a fantastic experience of China without being so complicated.

Have there been any obstacles to cultural exchange between China and Britain over the years? Could Chinese food serve as a bridge?

The real difference is that, as I’ve described, in the 1990s, when I started doing this work, the food was all Cantonese, now it’s very regional.

So we have restaurants in London that serve Sichuan food, as well as dishes from Chongqing, Hunan, and the northeast. We have some quite wonderful Shanghai supper clubs. Although we only see a small proportion of Chinese food because China is huge, already people can see that Chinese food is not one thing, that it’s very diverse.

And we now even have more northern food, so handmade noodles and breads, like Xian street food, that can just show different sides of Chinese food culture.

Some people say that if the Chinese ate less meat it would help slow down global warming. This is very controversial in China because meat is an integral part of Chinese cuisine. What are your views?

The truth is that we should all be eating less meat if we want to tackle climate change. The situation in China is that most people didn’t eat much meat until the 1990s. And now, with the reform and opening up that followed, everyone wants to eat more meat – more like the extravagant way we eat in the West.

So objectively it is a huge problem that you have over a billion people suddenly eating more meat. But I can understand the Chinese view that it’s really unfair.

Climate change is a global problem. It would be great if Chinese people were more aware of the role that eating meat plays in climate change, but people in the West also have to change their diets and eat less meat.

And I think traditional Chinese cuisine is a fantastic resource and inspiration for that. Because in traditional Chinese cuisine there are so many ways of using a little bit of meat to make vegetarian ingredients taste fantastic – like mapo tofu and dry-fried green beans.

There are all these dishes where you have a little bit of meat and lots of vegetables that are really delicious. We can learn a lot from traditional Chinese food about how to eat less meat.

But the main thing is that it is unfair for Westerners to put the whole burden on Chinese consumers without looking at their own behaviour.

How have Chinese eating habits changed over the decades? How much of the change is political?

The first thing is that so many young people don’t really cook. The older generation, when I lived in Chengdu, were really excellent cooks. Not only did they cook daily meals, they also made pickles, sausages and other preserves. You can really see how these skills are now being lost.

It’s also quite interesting to see how Chinese people are eating more industrialised and prepared food.

At the same time in Britain, there’s a book that came out two years ago about ultra-processed foods, looking at the harmful effects of eating too much processed food, and I see China making the same mistakes we’ve made, and it’s a real shame.

China has a fantastic food culture, which is a huge resource for how to eat healthily and deliciously.

So it’s sad to see that younger people are losing touch with that and I hope that as people in China become more health conscious, which they are, and as they become more aware of the environmental impact of how we eat, which I hope will become more widespread, then they will be able to see their own culture as an invaluable resource for eating more healthily and sustainably.

But I think it is more about economic changes. When I lived in Chengdu in the 1990s, there was very little manufactured food. There were no supermarkets and everyone went to fresh markets to buy vegetables and fish.

And now there’s a huge expansion of food production and factory farming in China. There’s mass production of meat and also of ready meals, as you mentioned, and even restaurants are serving food that’s pre-prepared.

It’s all driven by the same technology and economics as in the West, and also the whole sort of takeaway food system, the fact that you can order anything at home that you don’t have to cook.

Which dish do you think best represents Chinese cuisine?

If I had to choose one, I would probably choose mapo tofu.

The reason is that it’s a really good example of a recipe that uses a little bit of meat and very delicious fermented bean spices to give an amazing flavour to a plant food. For me, it’s a really good example of how Chinese food offers ways to eat healthily and sustainably but without sacrificing pleasure, because this dish is utterly delicious.

Do you have any ongoing projects?

At the moment I’m writing another cookbook, and it’s not just about one region. It’s more of a simple homestyle Chinese cookbook, a bit like my previous book Every Grain of Rice.

So it’s designed to give readers the tools of some traditional Chinese techniques to cook wonderful food at home, not always with Chinese ingredients, but to cook food that’s really delicious and quite healthy and exciting.

item.title: [SCMP] 80 years on from WWII, China’s interests lie in peaceful Asia-Pacific: Rana Mitter
item.description:
Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture. He is S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on the politics of modern China. He was also director of Oxford’s China Centre.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As China prepares to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, what are your thoughts on the role of the conflict in shaping contemporary China?
item.content:encoded:
Rana Mitter is a leading historian whose research focuses on the impact of Japan’s invasion of China during the second world war on the development of Chinese politics, society and culture. He is S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School and previously taught at Oxford University on the politics of modern China. He was also director of Oxford’s China Centre.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

As China prepares to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II, what are your thoughts on the role of the conflict in shaping contemporary China?

World War II is one of the most important factors in the shaping of modern China, but it’s often underestimated, both in China and the West.

This was the greatest political and economic trauma of the 20th century. The invasion of China by Japan led to many millions of deaths. Many Chinese became refugees within their own country.

The infrastructure and the communications built in the 1920s and 1930s were largely smashed into pieces, so that was a huge influence in terms of having to start again after the war.

The war made it more likely that China would have a revolution rather than just reform after it ended, because economic and social conditions became so devastatingly bad that it opened up space for the Chinese Communist Party to really develop the revolution in the countryside.

Beyond that, many aspects of modern China that we think of as part of the revolution actually emerged during the war – such as the system of work units for example, that existed for a long time in socialist China under Mao Zedong and even beyond.

The role of women became more prominent in Chinese life during the war years. Many younger women also became involved in national defence, health and nutrition, trying to make society after the war better for families and more stable.

During the 1920s and 1930s, China was heavily split between rival military leaders. At the end of the war, China was much closer to becoming unified as a country, as many of those warlords were eliminated during the wartime period.

Although it would finally be the 1949 revolution under Mao that provided a solid unification of the country, the process began in the wartime years.

World War II continues to be very important in terms of remembering a time when different factions and parties, nationalists, communists and others came together against an outside enemy and were able to find a sense of national purpose.

How could Beijing use the 80th World War II anniversary commemoration as an opportunity to improve people-to-people exchanges with the West?

The problem is that China still isn’t very good at seizing diplomatic opportunities because it tends to fall back on language that is mainly about China’s complaints, rather than about opportunities that could really open up.

The opportunities tend to be expressed in very broad, positive but vague terms, and the complaints tend to be very specific. And the problem is, it’s quite hard to get people on your side if you don’t actually engage in a dialogue that seems as if both sides are genuinely talking to each other.

An example is cutting down the EU-China summit from two days to one. Beijing also insisted that the Europeans should come to Beijing, when actually it was China’s turn to come to Europe.

So Europeans have done these things – they’re diplomatic people. They say OK, but it’s not the easiest start in terms of suggesting that China is opening up a new conversation, where China is willing to actually be expansive and creative in its thinking.

So maybe a sort of reset of Chinese diplomacy is an opportunity to do that. So far, there aren’t many signs of that. China has, in the past couple of years, withdrawn from the famous Wolf Warrior diplomacy, but it hasn’t yet worked out what sits in its place.

Do you think Chinese officials understand how their diplomacy is viewed from an outside perspective?

Very smart Chinese diplomats are aware that China has a PR problem. Just because people now find the US much less predictable doesn’t mean that they think China is a safe bet.

So, finding ways to essentially define China – not just in words, but in actions and in patterns of behaviour – as a reliable partner, that’s the really key challenge for Chinese diplomacy in the next few years.

The language is sometimes there – not always, but sometimes – but the actions involve a lot of quite difficult and long-term effort. And so far, if that’s happening, it’s only at a very early stage of that process.

A lot of Chinese diplomats, publicly and privately, have said they thought the previous Wolf Warrior effort was a mistake, asking what comes next and how China actually takes advantage of the changing world order.

That will involve more than just hoping that people will feel alienated from America and automatically seek out China. They won’t. Well, that will not be enough on its own.

World War II ended in the Pacific theatre with two atomic bombs dropped on Japan. Now, 80 years later, Britain and France have announced joint cooperation on nuclear weapons and the US has once again deployed nuclear forces in the UK. What does this say about the future of nuclear weapons?

Nuclear non-proliferation is definitely much weaker than it has been. Many of the Cold War-era treaties between the Soviet Union and the US seem to be essentially falling away. Britain and France are primarily concerned with their own major security vulnerability as the future American position on Russia remains uncertain.

A lot of different actors are looking at new threats in the world and trying to work out whether their current nuclear stance is sustainable. Ukraine gave up nuclear weapons in 1994, which made it vulnerable to the Russian invasion. Many countries will be looking at Ukraine’s experience and trying to avoid that.

The US has engaged directly with Russia to end the Ukraine war but those warmer ties now seem to have cooled off. What is your view of the changing dynamic between them?

Right now, the person who is probably having to think most carefully about changing the US position is Russian President Vladimir Putin.

For much of the first part of the year, the Donald Trump administration tried to find ways to bring Moscow back into the negotiations about Ukraine.

But in the past few weeks, it’s become clear that President Trump thinks Putin has no intention of coming to a peace agreement. It’s possible that he may take a much more confrontational attitude with Russia.

The world was very surprised when Trump actually made the decision to bomb Iran. His general doctrine is that getting into wars is a bad idea, but when he considers it necessary he is prepared to use force – and that’s something Putin might now have to think about.

How could this changing dynamic in Russia-US ties affect China?

Maybe several months ago, there were some people in Washington who thought that it might be possible to detach Russia from China in a “reverse Nixon”, or “reverse Kissinger” play, but that is not a very widely held idea any more, for two reasons.

First, people realise that there is a very close relationship between Russia and China. This was made clear by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi when meeting his European Union counterparts. For the first time, it was much more explicit that China would not wish to see Russia lose.

The other factor is the American idea that they could detach Russia from China and bring it close to the US has fallen away. People have seen that Putin has not changed his policy towards Ukraine at all and is bombing it more fiercely than before.

We’re likely to see a scenario in which the US tries to neutralise Russia as much as possible while still looking for a negotiation on Ukraine, but essentially there probably will be more concentration on pushing back against China alone.

What conditions could bring about the end of the war?

We don’t know what conditions it will take to come to an end, but we do know that, at least in the past few weeks, President Trump has reauthorised the supply of weaponry to Ukraine to fight back against Russia, which at one point he was holding back on.

Now it’s clear that weaponry is going to Ukraine and the war may last longer than would have seemed the case just a few weeks ago, when it seemed Ukraine might run out of ammunition.

The question becomes whether Russia can maintain its all-out war-based economy and conscription of soldiers, while keeping inflation – which is very, very high – under control.

The longer the Ukraine war continues, the less likely it is that Russia can do that, and the more weapons that are supplied by the Americans, along with the Europeans, the longer the Ukrainians can keep fighting.

Under former president Joe Biden, Washington and other Western capitals formed a united stance on a wide range of China-related issues. How will Trump’s presidency change that alliance on China?

Europeans are looking to negotiate on their own issues with the US, such as tariffs. The question of China has been put a bit on the back shelf but essentially, the issue is that China provides useful supply chains.

There is also a problem, in particular for Europe, of whether it can draw on China’s markets but not be overwhelmed by Chinese exports, particularly in areas like autos and electric batteries. Those problems are not really changed by the relationship with the US.

The EU has a whole variety of fundamental issues it needs to solve – about how it creates a new industrial model, where it cooperates with China and where it needs to restrict its market.

And in some ways, it’s learning from China, because China has heavily restricted its own market in some areas, such as online service provision. So the Europeans will also pick and choose where they feel vulnerable, opening up in certain areas and closing in others.

The Trump administration is still figuring out its policy on China. There are different strands of thinking that you can see from the outside, but how important they are in relation to each other, and how they will balance out in the end, is still unclear.

For instance, there are some traditional hawks, such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio and others, who take a view on China that in some ways would not have been that different from Republicans seven or 10 years ago.

But you also have the whole technology world – Silicon Valley and beyond. A lot of them are still very interested in making sure that the relationship with China is smooth.

Apple is one of the most profitable and innovative companies in the United States, but huge amounts of its production and connection still take place in China. Of course, some production has moved to India, but China is still really important to a company like Apple.

There has been a growing interest in moving more production and intellectual property back to the US but there’s no sense yet that this is a complete disconnection from China, and that points in a different direction from the hawks.

Then there is the question of what Trump himself thinks. It’s interesting to look at the tariff policy, because tariffs have been put on China but also on other countries, including traditional US allies.

Also, when Trump says “I like to talk to my good friend Xi Jinping. We can talk about things” – what does he want to talk about? Not clear.

Compared with other presidents, Trump seems to really like personal diplomacy. In other words, he believes that his personal relationships with leaders are the important thing.

Speaking of leadership diplomacy, what conditions do you think will be needed for Trump and Xi to meet?

I think a meeting between the two leaders is quite likely. Trump is announcing that the deal has been done with China. He would only want to go to China if the deal is kind of there, so he can mark it in a big ceremony and have a prominent meeting with Xi.

I don’t think he would want to go to China to negotiate. We’re moving into a phase where the US wants to get most of its tariff deals done within the next couple of months.

During his first term, Trump had a very grand welcoming ceremony provided by Xi in Beijing. I think he would like to do that again – a big, grand meeting that Trump will think of as a historic event, that showcases he’s able to do negotiations and deals with China in a way that other presidents haven’t been able to do. I think he would want to push quite hard in that direction. That’s my guess.

Are the two presidents likely to get along?

I think that’s perfectly possible. You might remember that when Trump invited Xi to Mar-a-Lago, he said that he gave Xi a big piece of chocolate cake. He never talked about giving chocolate cake to German chancellor Angela Merkel.

That’s a sign that he feels there’s some sort of ability to speak leader to leader in that sense. Xi has said less about Trump, but he hasn’t said any very publicly hostile things personally about him.

Will it stop competition? No. Will it stop conflict? Maybe. In some areas – I would single out technology – I think the US and China are going to be increasingly in competition and there will be less sharing of intellectual property or scientific development.

That would mean other countries could benefit from both, or they may have to choose a side. This will not change because of a meeting.

But can the two leaders talk about lowering the temperature and avoiding misunderstandings that could lead to military confrontation? That might be more possible.

Turning to China’s security environment, how might Beijing’s relations with its neighbours change, given the uncertainties of Washington’s policies during the Trump administration?

My guess is that China will be assessing how solid and secure American security guarantees are in Asia. There’s some evidence that the United States might want to maintain and maybe deepen its relationship with standing allies Japan, Australia and South Korea.

We know that Trump is interested in the Korean peninsula. In his first term, he wanted to do personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. But even when South Korea is going through political change and a lot of turmoil, there’s no sense that I’ve seen that the United States is stepping back from its relationship.

I would say that if you are looking from Beijing, the conclusion to draw at the moment is that things will change much less in Asia than in Europe.

Supposing American security guarantees, naval presence and alliances were withdrawn from Asia – the first thing that would be likely to happen is that Japan and South Korea would think hard about getting their own nuclear weapons. They have the capacity, science and the technology. They could do it, but they won’t do it at the moment.

in a strange way, Beijing’s best bet for keeping the region relatively nuclear-free is to encourage the Americans to stay. And most of its neighbours would share that analysis.

They want the Chinese market, but they also want American security. They don’t want either one to disappear. I think that’s what makes the calculation different in Asia and that will affect the way that China and the US deal with other countries in the region.

What about the South China Sea?

The South China Sea is probably one of the most potentially dangerous flashpoints, along with Taiwan.

The South China Sea has more of a chance of running out of control because it’s not just between two or three entities – seven or eight are involved. The US is not so directly involved in that.

But I would say that China is missing a big soft power opportunity, which it could take up at a time of uncertainty about American security intentions, of being able to provide reassurance to regional neighbours like the Philippines.

If China is not looking to increase its maritime and territorial claims, it could create a much better basis of trust in the region. But right now there’s much more military activity from China, not just near the Philippines but also off the coast of Australia, and that’s heightening tensions in the region.

How is the importance of Taiwan to Beijing shaping the security environment?

One of the most interesting things is that after repeatedly trying to take the island, Mao Zedong basically said to then-US president Richard Nixon, when they met in Beijing in 1972, that the Taiwan problem could be left to the side for 100 years.

That’s a reminder that actually the Taiwan question has not been a constant one at the forefront of China’s relationship with the world.

Right now, there are a whole variety of reasons that China needs to think about its changing place in the world. It has an opportunity to influence the world order at a time when the United States is changing its role.

It also has significant economic problems at home, in terms of creating new forms of employment, dealing with the way technology has changed labour markets, and stimulating domestic consumption, which the party has repeatedly said is a really important domestic priority.

In that context, you could say that with all those important problems, Taiwan doesn’t appear as a major solution or issue that will help to resolve any of them.

If you look at Chinese policy priorities, it’s very clear that the single most important task for the government is the economy.

China needs the Asia-Pacific region to be economically productive to get its economy going again. That means the attention has to be on the domestic economy and how it relates to a peaceful, calm Asia that does not have any sort of confrontation.

In five to 10 years, if current trends continue, the Asia-Pacific region could be even more of a driver of the global economy than it is now. It can become the most economically dynamic region in the world, with lots of foreign direct investment and expansion.

However, for that vision of Asia to emerge, the region needs to stay peaceful and stable and absolutely avoid wars. Any regional confrontations could put that economic future in danger and that would be very bad for China and its neighbours.

Alongside the nationalism that comes with the promise of building a powerful China, there is also a revival of traditional Chinese culture in both society and the official narrative. How do you think this will shape China’s governance and foreign policy?

This is one of the most interesting and important elements of what’s going on in thought and ideology in China today.

First of all, there is a real interest in what some people call traditional thought, or pre-modern thought, which includes the Confucian tradition but also lots of other areas, such as Taoism.

The Chinese government has been sponsoring publication of China’s canon of official writings, with the parts that suit contemporary politics tending to be stressed.

For instance, Confucian thinking does have an interest in proper hierarchy and this is something that is obviously very attractive to the Communist Party, because it wants people, essentially, to be stable and ordered.

But there are other ideas – such as individual self-development or self-cultivation, which could lead more to the idea that people should have individual rights – that are less popular with the party.

China’s political culture since 1949 has been heavily shaped by the Marxism and Leninism that underpins the Chinese Communist Party.

Many of the ideas are still there and you can hear them in the language of Xi and other top leaders. Even while they are praising traditional Chinese culture and wisdom, they are also pointing out that Marxism and Leninism still have significance.

How are these two things compatible? Actually, it’s not easy.

There was a TV show broadcast in Hunan province that got a lot of criticism on Chinese social media. It was called When Marx Met Confucius and was a way of trying to talk about the difficulties in combining these ideas.

There is actually quite an interesting and difficult tension in the way that these two thought systems operate in China today, but I think that they are both very much part of the debate.

How has the Chinese intellectual landscape changed in the past 10 years? Do you share the view that it can be summarised as a rise in nationalism, Sinification of ideas and declining critical voices? What other trends are you seeing and what are their effects?

In some ways, China’s intellectual sphere has narrowed, at least in public, but in other important ways, it has expanded.

The narrowing is real, and probably the biggest obstacle that China places in its own path to developing new ideas at home and being able to exert influence abroad. It’s difficult to persuade the wider world that you’re a force for new thinking if new thinking at home is heavily restricted.

In terms of subjects, including history, most people would say that the room for publication and discussion is much more limited than it was 10, 15 or 20 years ago. Many aspects of modern history are harder to research and write about in China today than in the past.

The most productive recent time intellectually in China was the late 1990s and early 2000s, when there was the most capacity to be able to speak more freely. That time will need to come again as China comes to grips with its new role in the world. It’s not possible to have a very narrowed intellectual sphere and a very wide influence.

But there are some areas where I think things are broader, and I’m particularly thinking about social media and the way it has expanded and grown so significantly in China in the past decade.

Lots of ideas actually are discussed at a popular level, even when there’s censorship a lot of ideas still get out there – not about top-level politics as that’s too sensitive to permit – but if you think about things like concerns about economic change, people’s concerns about their own financial situation, ideas about the position of women, society, feminism, those are quite visible in Chinese social media.

That is not the same thing as two or three scholars sitting in a think tank writing some big paper, but in terms of understanding social trends and how they are shaping China today, social media has been very valuable to reflect those changes.

How has the China studies community been affected by the changes of recent years? What will the subject look like, with a growing percentage of scholars outside the country unable to conduct interviews and on-the-ground research in China?

You have put your finger on one of the most problematic issues – the number of students studying Chinese languages and doing higher-level research in the West on China is going down significantly. It was never very high, but it was going up, and now the numbers are shrinking.

One reason is the sense that doing serious research in China – particularly for social scientists but also for researchers who need to use archives and libraries – is much more difficult than it used to be.

What real China researchers need is to be able to travel and set up their own agendas, to be able to do interviews at the local level that enable them to understand how local government works, or to collect large amounts of data that enables them to see how effective or ineffective particular policies are.

This is the work of real social science, and it involves transparency and openness on data and a willingness to welcome the gathering of data, rather than assuming that it has to be banned for security reasons.

So, although more scholars are coming back to China, opening up more capacity to be able to do real research in China is the next barrier that needs to be overcome.

There are a lot of brilliant Chinese students in many countries in the West who are doing significant social science and humanities research. But their Western equivalents who study China can’t do that kind of work in China, so it becomes very unbalanced.

What about your own experience with the Asia studies and Chinese history students you taught at Oxford and now Harvard?

When it comes to postgraduate students doing PhDs, a significant number are Chinese. We do still have some Westerners, but the problem is that they have to be enthusiastic about China, willing to learn its language and culture, and then be able to find a meaningful project to research.

It’s harder now to assure students that they can find a pathway to doing really good social science research inside China, so a lot of students just leave China out. If people say China is a very difficult place to do research and South Korea is easy, maybe people just decide they want to learn Korean instead.

The sense among Western researchers that it’s hard to do serious research in China has transmitted to students finding it difficult to find a career path if they do study China. I think that’s a great shame.

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan’s innovative Nakagin Capsule Tower is finding new life
item.description:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.
item.content:encoded:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.

Nakagin’s scattered course would have pleased its avant-garde architect Kisho Kurokawa (1934-2007), who conceived the design to emancipate what he called Homo movens (mobile humans). Many fans still demonstrate their unbridled enthusiasm for the building by donning zany get-ups inspired by its form – often described as a stack of front-loading washing machines.

In my mind’s eye, however, Nakagin had always been a colony of barnacles. That analogy borrows from the free movement of these crustaceans before anchoring themselves in place. But unfortunately, it was the unexpected immobility of Kurokawa’s capsules during their first phase of life that ultimately thwarted his vision that they be modular, interchangeable and recyclable.

That idea of impermanent permanence remains irresistible, however – at least in Japan. Which was one reason Metabolism captured the imagination of many during the country’s buoyant post-war expansion, making its name and ethos heard at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. Adaptable buildings and cities – with renewable nodes fed by circulation systems – sparked interest. Adding excitement was the promise of Expo ’70, whose theme was “progress and harmony for mankind”.

At that landmark event in Osaka, futuristic pavilions, including several by Kurokawa, allowed the forward-thinking to see for themselves the biomimetic potential of a movement whose proponents included other eminent architects, Kenzo Tange and Fumihiko Maki among them.

Nakagin, however, earned the kind of cult status accorded few other buildings in Japan. One reason was the charisma of Kurokawa, also a media personality and, towards the end of his career, a politician. His building was among the few examples of Metabolist architecture ever realised.

In late 2022, Ikko Yokoyama visited a warehouse in Chiba, near Tokyo, where salvaged Nakagin capsules, resembling pet Cyclops, awaited adoption. As lead curator of design and architecture at M+, she was there to see one of 23 pods that had been saved by the Nakagin Capsule Tower Preservation and Restoration Project, founded by former resident Tatsuyuki Maeda.

Hong Kong’s museum of contemporary visual culture was prepared for this inevitable moment, according to Yokoyama. Debate had raged for years about whether to preserve Nakagin whole, with Kurokawa himself shifting from yes to no. Ultimately, land value outweighed legacy, says Dytham, who had tried without success to persuade developers and hospitality groups to turn Nakagin into a boutique hotel. “It wasn’t sustainable to keep it there,” he says.

The decision to tear it down was made despite its uniqueness. Unlike anything the West had produced – except, perhaps, in the minds of Britain’s Archigram group of architects – Nakagin consisted of capsules “plugged” into the building’s towers, or cores, one 11 storeys high, the other two floors taller. Tight spaces between each pod impeded access and meant that repairs were difficult because “you couldn’t get in”, says Dytham. Worse, owners were unwilling to pay the high cost of detaching their capsules for upkeep every 25 years, as Kurokawa had warned they must. Decay set in, leaks appeared and damage from Japan’s frequent earthquakes saw the building’s exterior netted for safety. Additionally, the presence of asbestos complicated matters.

But M+’s capsule speaks volumes about their enduring appeal. A806 now stands beside another of the museum’s inspired acquisitions, Kiyotomo (1988), the sushi bar designed by Shiro Kuramata. Unlike that 656 sq ft restaurant – which was disassembled in Japan, shipped to Hong Kong and later put together again by the original contractors and an M+ team of restorers – Kurokawa’s capsule was purchased fully reconditioned.

The 2.78 metre x 2.69 metre x 4.21 metre capsule in the East Galleries is one of six standard units, complete with their famous round window at one end accommodating a circular blind that folds open like a hand fan. Also included within the 121.9 sq ft space are mod cons and a dinky unit bath, those tiny waterproof rooms sold as a single product in Japan.

“Like organ donation”, as Yokoyama puts it, parts for the capsule were harvested from others in the building because none of the pods survived with all of its original fittings intact. Kiyotomo’s neighbour now also boasts a new blue carpet and mattress, in addition to a fold-down desk, television and reel-to-reel tape deck, among other integrated features. Combine the service and payload modules of a spaceship and you get the idea.

Of the capsules plucked to safety by Maeda’s group, 14 have been sold to companies and museums, including M+ and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which purchased Kurokawa’s prized personal unit. Of the nine remaining, he says, four are to stay in Japan while five will head abroad.

Some have already been turned into display modules and mobile units and, next year, hotel-room conversions are expected, which should come as no surprise: in 1979, Kurokawa’s ideas also gave birth to the world’s first capsule hotel. New Japan Umeda continues to offer budget accommodation in Osaka.

Maeda’s is not the only group intent on giving the (in) famous corner building a second life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project is named after the pod that another ex-resident helped restore several years before the building came down. This group, which owns seven units, has even more ambitious, albeit firmly parochial, aims.

“We plan to reconstruct a mini-tower using several capsules we own,” the group reveals via core member, architect Akiko Ishimaru.

“We aim to keep the reconstructed ones for 50 years [100 years after their completion] by continuing to use them ourselves. We want to utilise the capsules that were born in Japan and rebuild them in Japan.”

Crowdfunding has helped pay for the work so far. “The cost of asbestos control and investigation during the survey and dismantling, transportation and storage of seven capsules, storage of original parts, printing of a book with records, restoration of the interior of capsule A606, crowdfunding gifts [such as the aforementioned book], and fees consumed most of the total 8,673,000 yen [HK$443,000],” the group says.

Ishimaru’s efforts to keep Nakagin from history’s scrapheap underscores the passion in the project. But that’s not to say she fully enjoyed her year living in the building (and seven more working in two other capsules).

“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] Inside scorching Pakistani factories making clothes for global fashion brands
item.description:
Machines whirred around Siddiqui as her vision blurred and her heart hammered. The garment factory on the outskirts of Karachi was sweltering. The room was packed with sweating fellow workers and huge industrial equipment that radiated heat. The air felt thick with the humidity of this summer’s monsoon.

Siddiqui, who asked to be identified only by surname, felt like she was suffocating. Concerned colleagues called over her supervisor. “The supervisor said, ‘Just complete this work,’” the 28-year-old said. “Suddenly darkness came before my eyes.”

Exhausted by the heat, she collapsed.
item.content:encoded:
Machines whirred around Siddiqui as her vision blurred and her heart hammered. The garment factory on the outskirts of Karachi was sweltering. The room was packed with sweating fellow workers and huge industrial equipment that radiated heat. The air felt thick with the humidity of this summer’s monsoon.

Siddiqui, who asked to be identified only by surname, felt like she was suffocating. Concerned colleagues called over her supervisor. “The supervisor said, ‘Just complete this work,’” the 28-year-old said. “Suddenly darkness came before my eyes.”

Exhausted by the heat, she collapsed.

Extreme heat – intensified by climate change – is creating dangerous conditions for factory workers in Pakistan.

From blue jeans to homeware, these factories produce goods for global companies that have pledged to protect workers’ safety. But experts and labour rights advocates say those promises remain unfulfilled, as temperatures rise and workers pay the price with their health and safety.

Of the more than a dozen workers interviewed in Karachi, all described scorching workplaces, absent heat protocols and negative health effects, including fainting. They spoke on the condition that their identities be protected out of fear of retaliation by their employers.

All but one said they lost wages when heat-related illness forced them to miss work. Ten of the workers made goods for global brands sold in the United States and Europe.

For workers like Siddiqui, extreme heat – temperatures at or above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) combined with high humidity – is not just a workplace hazard. Living with her six children in a small room with no air conditioning on the outskirts of Karachi, temperatures routinely exceed 37.8 degrees during heatwaves.

Inside the garment factory where she stitches clothes for Spanish brands like Zara and Mango, it is even hotter. Huge machines churn heat into the air. There are fans, but they’re often broken or small. Windows are slitlike and set high, or even closed to deter theft, further trapping the heat, workers said.

“Smoke, heat, you face it,” said a 34-year-old male factory worker.

Silent killer

Extreme heat is a silent killer. It can show few outward symptoms while causing severe internal damage and worsening conditions, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes and asthma. Studies have linked it to dehydration, heatstroke, organ failure and death.

“The longer you work in the heat, the less that you’re protected from it and the health risks rise,” said Andreas Flouris, the founder of FAME Lab, which researches heat’s impact on health.

The number of people exposed to extreme heat is growing exponentially due to climate change. Heat stress is a leading cause of weather-related deaths, according to the World Health Organization. Studies by World Weather Attribution say that climate change has also drastically increased the frequency, intensity and risks of extreme heatwaves in Pakistan.

Workers interviewed described temporary muscle paralysis, swollen limbs, blood pressure swings, breathing problems, blurred vision and exhaustion that peaked in the hottest months. One worker showed scaly skin rashes on her arms from routine chemical exposure, saying how the pain intensified during summer.

All said they had seen colleagues faint from the heat. Several said they had fainted themselves, some multiple times. Those who fainted were often offered only a short break or sugary drink before being told to resume work.

They said complaining to supervisors led to no changes. Only one worker had paid sick leave. The rest said that missed hours – even from fainting on the job or from heat-related illnesses – meant slashed wages.

Siddiqui wept on the floor of her home as she described fainting and being sent to the hospital. As she earned 15,000 rupees (US$54) a month, the hospital visit cost, which her employer refused to pay, left her unable to buy food for her children.

“Sometimes they eat one meal, sometimes they don’t eat a meal,” she said, adding that the younger children sometimes cry from hunger. “The older ones have gotten used to it.”

There are simple, scalable and economically feasible measures factories can take to protect their workers from extreme heat, including accurately measuring temperature and humidity inside workplaces, providing cold drinking water and allowing workers breaks, according to Flouris.

Other solutions include installing barriers to block radiant heat from machinery, installing quality ventilation and cooling systems and painting rooftops white to deflect sunlight. “We’re talking about some very simple strategies,” he said.

Simple solutions, none taken

Factory workers said that almost none of these measures were taken in their workplaces. Several said their factories’ metal roofs made the summer heat unbearable, yet they received no extra water or breaks.

All the workers said there were no heat sensors installed. Only one worker said a ventilation system was installed at their workplace, but that it was turned on only when auditors visited the factory for inspection. The workers said water was provided by their employers, but that it was rarely cold and they were not sure if it was clean. “Sometimes it smells like dead rats,” the 34-year-old male worker said.

Pakistan has national and provincial laws as well as constitutional protections meant to shield workers from such conditions, according to Farhan Haider, a programme manager at the Pakistan Institute of Labour Education and Research in Karachi.

Some companies supplied by the factories, including Inditex – Zara’s parent company – and Mango have signed legally binding agreements to protect workers or have their own company safety pledges.

The most concrete is the International Accord for Health and Safety in the Textile and Garment Industry, which in 2025 announced it would treat heat as a workplace safety risk and develop heat stress protocols, which are under review but not yet in effect.

Representatives from the Pakistan Accord, a country-specific safety programme that operates as an extension of the broader International Accord, did not reply to a request for interview or comment.

Brands had a responsibility to ensure their suppliers are held accountable for worker safety, including extreme heat, said Cara Schulte, a researcher at Climate Rights International who published a report last year about worker conditions in Pakistan.

Inditex said in an email the company was strengthening efforts to address heat stress in its supply chain through updated factory audits, guidance and training for suppliers and collaboration with industry initiatives. Mango called worker health and safety a “non-negotiable priority”, citing its supplier code of conduct, which was “strengthened this year to explicitly address extreme temperatures and heat stress.”

A government spokeswoman for Sindh province, where Karachi is located, acknowledged implementation remained an issue. “The government is making efforts to enforce these regulations, but given the province’s vast size and the presence of numerous industrial zones, complaints are inevitable,” said Sadia Javed, who is also a member of the provincial assembly.

For workers like Siddiqui, complaints remain ignored as temperatures continue to rise. “If you feel too unwell, [supervisors] say, ‘This is an everyday problem. Women cry and complain a lot, but the work still must be done,’” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] US troops in South Korea must be ready for missions beyond peninsula, commander says
item.description:
The commander of the US Eighth Army in South Korea said his troops must be ready for deployment outside the Korean peninsula if ordered, arguing that it would be “irresponsible” to focus “myopically” on threats there.

Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert said that while his command’s focus was on fulfilling US commitments under its mutual defence treaty with Seoul, the Eighth Army’s location did not limit the missions it could undertake.

It would be “irresponsible to focus myopically” on threats on the Korean peninsula alone, he told the South China Morning Post by email, or to “suggest that we cannot do other things simply because we are in Korea”.
item.content:encoded:
The commander of the US Eighth Army in South Korea said his troops must be ready for deployment outside the Korean peninsula if ordered, arguing that it would be “irresponsible” to focus “myopically” on threats there.

Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert said that while his command’s focus was on fulfilling US commitments under its mutual defence treaty with Seoul, the Eighth Army’s location did not limit the missions it could undertake.

It would be “irresponsible to focus myopically” on threats on the Korean peninsula alone, he told the South China Morning Post by email, or to “suggest that we cannot do other things simply because we are in Korea”.

Describing the Eighth Army as part of a “global force” that trains for “readiness so that we can deploy where needed by our national command authority,” Hilbert cited the Eighth Army’s participation in multinational exercises across the Asia-Pacific as an example of its activities beyond the peninsula.

“We view readiness as largely threat-agnostic. If we have a trained, ready force capable of executing the Army’s assigned missions, we can apply that force against whatever threat is required,” said Hilbert.

“So, we train every day with our Korean allies against our principal threat, while also ensuring we remain available and ready for whatever the nation may require.”

Hilbert’s comments reflect the Trump administration’s push to place greater responsibility on allies for their own defence while increasing the strategic flexibility of United States Forces Korea (USFK), allowing American troops to be deployed beyond the Korean peninsula for contingencies elsewhere in the Asia-Pacific.

Headquartered at Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek, south of Seoul, the Eighth Army commands US ground forces in South Korea. It is the only US Army stationed on the Asian continent in the Asia-Pacific region and the sole permanently forward-deployed American field army.

As part of the roughly 28,500-strong USFK, the Eighth Army has traditionally focused on deterring North Korean threats rather than preparing for contingencies elsewhere, such as in the Taiwan Strait. But the Trump administration has signalled a shift towards a broader regional role.

The national defence strategy, published in January, instructed that Washington aim for “strong denial defence along the first island chain,” while calling for Seoul to take “primary responsibility” for deterring Pyongyang with “critical but more limited US support”, noting that the “shift in the balance of responsibility is consistent with America’s interest in updating US force posture on the Korean peninsula”.

The first island chain refers to a string of islands and archipelagos running from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines and the South China Sea. The Korean peninsula falls within this line.

During a press briefing in August last year, General Xavier Brunson, commander of USFK, said that “strategic flexibility” will be at the centre of the “alliance modernisation” between Seoul and Washington in responding to the “threat” that nuclear-armed China, Russia and North Korea pose to a “free and open Indo-Pacific”.

A more reciprocal US-South Korea alliance

Lami Kim, Korea chair in advanced technologies, national security and defence at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, said that the nature of the alliance is shifting towards a “more reciprocal partnership,” instead of Washington’s primarily “one-directional” responsibility to defend Seoul.

“Both countries are expected to contribute to each other’s security and South Korea assumes greater responsibility for its own defence,” said Kim.

“I think this is a natural evolution that reflects South Korea’s significantly enhanced military capabilities – a far cry from its position in the 1950s, when the alliance was first established.”

Troy Stangarone, a visiting senior fellow at the Korea Economic Institute of America, said that the broader trend in US-South Korea defence ties has been towards Seoul taking on a larger role, while growing its domestic defence industrial base, and the US seeking “greater flexibility” to utilise US forces for other contingencies.

“The United States has already moved forces and equipment off the Korean peninsula to support US operations, both in the recent Iran war and the Iraq war in 2003. I would expect it to continue to do so as conditions require,” said Stangarone.

Seoul’s enhanced military capabilities were reflected in its weapons’ recent integration and partnership with the US military. In August, the US Army awarded a contract worth up to US$260 million to South Korea’s Hanwha to deliver prototypes of its K9 Mobile Howitzer for its new Mobile Tactical Cannon programme – a first case of a South Korean weapons system acquired by the US military.

US defence contractor General Atomics also showcased a scale model of the Mojave short take-off and landing (STOL) drone at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition last week. The drone was co-developed and co-produced with Hanwha Aerospace under a partnership agreement signed last year.

Keeping US forces supplied in the Pacific

Speaking at a panel discussion during the AUSA Annual Meeting, Brunson said the US Army is trying to “change” the “depot mindset” of maintaining US weapons and equipment by travelling back and forth between the continental US and the Asia-Pacific region, which often consumes several days and weeks for those systems to be delivered.

He said partnering with South Korea, which he described as having “an absolutely premier industrial base”, can achieve “admirable endurance” and keep US forces with an “enviable posture” within the first island chain.

“What’s going to be important in the future, in particular in a fight in the Pacific, is our ability to endure, whether that be able to protect the things that we’ve placed forward, or whether that be the ability to stay there because we can sustain ourselves inside the first island chain from Korea,” said Brunson.

Brunson’s remarks follow Hilbert’s earlier proposal at the Land Forces Pacific symposium in Hawaii in May, where he said partnering with South Korea’s advanced manufacturing base would reduce the need to cross the Pacific and increase “strategic flexibility” for the US Joint Forces.

Kim said that as the alliance becomes “increasingly reciprocal”, it is becoming more difficult for Seoul to expect Washington to “maintain its security commitments without making meaningful contributions in return”.

“South Korea would likely provide logistical support to US forces in the event of a regional contingency,” said Kim.

“If the conflict became prolonged, South Korea’s defence industrial base could also play an important role in replenishing American weapons stockpiles and sustaining US military operations.”

Stangarone said that South Korea, as a logistics hub, plays a “critical role”, as it is the only US ally in the region with the defence industrial base capable of supporting US forces in the case of a contingency.

“Despite periodic calls for South Korea to commit forces to any contingency in the region, it has long been clear that its primary role is a supporting role providing needed munitions and armaments,” said Stangarone.

“South Korea shares interests and capabilities with the United States in the Indo-Pacific. While deterring North Korea needs to remain the priority, Seoul can and should play a larger role in US strategy in the region in recognition of its own growing capabilities.”

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asian families tying house move to top schools spur privilege worries
item.description:
Singapore’s recent parliamentary debate over primary school admissions has put a familiar parental strategy in the city state under the spotlight – parents moving house to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools.

Speaking with This Week in Asia, property agents say some families in Singapore have been approaching them with the intention of buying or renting particular residences at least two years before their children’s primary school admission.

Living close to a sought-after school does not guarantee entry, however, as a family might still face balloting for a particular school if it is oversubscribed.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore’s recent parliamentary debate over primary school admissions has put a familiar parental strategy in the city state under the spotlight – parents moving house to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools.

Speaking with This Week in Asia, property agents say some families in Singapore have been approaching them with the intention of buying or renting particular residences at least two years before their children’s primary school admission.

Living close to a sought-after school does not guarantee entry, however, as a family might still face balloting for a particular school if it is oversubscribed.

The debate comes as Singapore prepares to widen admission to 12 schools in predominantly private-housing neighbourhoods, in a bid to encourage greater social mixing.

Beyond Singapore, the school admissions systems in Malaysia and Indonesia also factor residential addresses, albeit with different criteria taking into account socio-economic conditions.

Planning years ahead

Joyce Foo, a property agent in Singapore, said some families accepted living in smaller homes to improve their children’s school admission chances. She recalled one family who moved from a five-room to a four-room public housing flat to be nearer their preferred school, with a parent also volunteering there.

When advising her clients, she would consider past balloting results, housing budgets and potential sale of the properties they are eyeing 10 years later.

“They want to make that move, but they also don’t want to lose money,” she said.

Those calculations now need to be considered alongside recent changes to Singapore’s school admission framework. From next year, for registration of children starting Primary 1 in 2028, most schools will reserve 60 places, up from 40, for Phase 2C, which does not factor in school ties.

At the 12 schools located in neighbourhoods dominated by private houses, Phase 2C places will be split equally between applicants living within 2km and those farther away. Priority admission for children of primary school alumni remains.

Foo said some alumni parents were now considering renting, rather than buying near their former schools, or looking at alternatives with better prospects of success.

“Many parents come to inquire because they want to have that certainty that their kid will be placed.”

However, she had not seen a surge in customer inquiries following the announcement. Based on her 13 years’ experience in Singapore’s property market, Foo said the data she had analysed showed that sales demand and rental premiums were not necessarily correlated with properties within 1km of popular schools.

Jason Tan, an associate professor at Singapore’s National Institute of Education, said the admissions framework encouraged parents to strategise because certain conditions depended on what they could do, including alumni connections, volunteer work and residential addresses.

“Most of the criteria have nothing to do with the individual child,” Tan said.

Giving priority to children living near schools made sense because of their young age, Tan said. But better-off families have a clear advantage as they can choose whether to move closer to a preferred school, according to Tan.

Family income matters

In Malaysia’s Klang Valley, senior sales manager Neo Wee Liem and his wife also linked preferred school admission for their son to house-hunting criteria as they wanted their eldest child to have a grounding in Mandarin.

After returning from Singapore and renting in Petaling Jaya, the Neos shortlisted three Chinese-medium primary schools, taking into account their housing budget, living space and transport convenience, before making a final decision.

“We were not really picky on which Chinese school it was,” Neo said.

In Malaysia, Chinese- and Tamil-medium primary schools sit within the national education system alongside Malay-medium primary schools. Private and international schools are also options for parents who can afford them.

Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim, an education advocate who is a co-founder of Malaysia’s Parent Action Group for Education, said such housing calculations were a source of concern.

“When families contemplate paying additional rent, changing their living arrangements or reorganising their daily lives just to secure a school place, it raises questions about the fairness and accessibility of the system.

Shakira Teh Sharifuddin, a PhD candidate at University College London’s Institute of Education and an economist at a public policy body, said the priorities of families varied across locations, income groups and educational stages.

What parents living in more urban areas look for in schools for their children differed from their peers living in rural communities or less-developed districts, such as Chinese education, she said.

For some Malay families, whether from urban or rural areas, they do not need to buy a house near top secondary schools or selective boarding schools to secure a place, according to Shakira.

Nonetheless, the financial position of different families would still play a role in determining their attitude towards school selection, she said.

“Lower-income and more rural families could find themselves basically just taking what the system gives to them, because there are fewer options.”

Falsifying residential addresses

In Indonesia, families also make housing decisions based on preferred schools for their children.

In a 2019 CNN Indonesia report, a father rented a house in East Jakarta and changed his residence details so his child could apply to a secondary school under Indonesia’s old zoning policy.

Last year, Indonesia revised its school admission policy under which a family’s residence address is a key consideration. Local governments have the flexibility to designate housing areas for school admission.

At least 70 per cent of public primary-school places are allocated based on a family’s residential address. At least 15 per cent are set aside for students from low-income families and those with disabilities.

Ubaid Matraji, the national coordinator of the Indonesian Education Monitoring Network (JPPI) watchdog group, said such a principle of school admission was fair, but varying degrees of school quality continued to be a major concern for families.

“On paper, this system is fairer because everyone has the same opportunity to attend the school nearest to home. But it becomes a problem because the quality of schools is not the same,” he said.

Some parents used their work or business address, “rented” addresses of relatives or falsified residence documents to improve their children’s chances of getting into popular schools, Ubaid added.

His comments indicate that the problem has not disappeared even with Jakarta’s latest school admission policy. Explaining its rationale for the reforms last year, Indonesia’s education ministry identified false housing addresses as one of the key problems under the old system.

Under the national framework, local governments can work with private schools to accept pupils when the capacity of public schools is insufficient and provide financial help for those from lower-income families.

Ubaid, however, said the authorities should ensure that there were enough public-school places for children seeking admission.

As for families who have missed out on public-school places, private schools are not a feasible option because of higher costs, such as registration and development fees, according to Ubaid.

For Noor Azimah, whether it is in Malaysia, Indonesia or elsewhere, school access should not be determined by the ability of families to pay for houses.

“A child’s educational opportunity should not become a property-market privilege,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Will Xi, Trump, Putin meet at Apec? First, they must agree on an agenda
item.description:
While US President Donald Trump has said he is open to sitting down with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit, it remains far from certain that the three leaders will actually meet in a few weeks.

Observers said much would depend on whether the countries could agree on an agenda, with one expert describing this as a “critical lever”.

Russia was set to gain most if the trilateral meeting took place, experts said, as the summit would be a potent symbol that the country’s international isolation was ending and of its great-power status. While Trump would get to show he could deal with the other powers, this could unsettle US allies.
item.content:encoded:
While US President Donald Trump has said he is open to sitting down with Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the Apec summit, it remains far from certain that the three leaders will actually meet in a few weeks.

Observers said much would depend on whether the countries could agree on an agenda, with one expert describing this as a “critical lever”.

Russia was set to gain most if the trilateral meeting took place, experts said, as the summit would be a potent symbol that the country’s international isolation was ending and of its great-power status. While Trump would get to show he could deal with the other powers, this could unsettle US allies.

Speculation has been building over whether the three leaders, who are all expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, will hold an unprecedented sit-down on the sidelines.

Putin earlier said he was “all for” a trilateral meeting but added that the agenda had to be clear. “[A trilateral meeting is] certainly possible. To a large extent, this will depend on China as the host of the event,” he said.

On Monday, Trump also signalled he was open to such talks. But he said it would be “not so much for Ukraine” and that such a meeting would have to be “based on denuclearisation”, an issue Beijing has long resisted negotiating.

His comments followed a Wall Street Journal report on Monday that said Putin floated the three-way talks as a way to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.

The South China Morning Post understands that Chinese officials have privately welcomed the idea of three-way talks, but have not pushed aggressively for them. There has also been little substantive discussion of an agenda or preparations.

When asked on both Monday and Tuesday to comment on the possibility of a trilateral meeting, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she had no information to provide.

Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University, said the agenda would set the tone for any summit and determine its success.

“The agenda is the critical lever for whether a meeting can actually take place,” Wang said.

“If the three parties harbour conflicting private agendas or if their proposed topics are fundamentally misaligned, the meeting is highly unlikely to happen.

“Only when the agenda focuses on areas of consensus while steering clear of ‘red lines’ … can a dialogue become a viable possibility.”

Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute, a Washington think tank, agreed, arguing that the three countries had “overlapping interests” but did not share a “common strategic vision”.

He added that while the nuclear issue offered the most obvious potential starting point, Ukraine, trade, Taiwan and the broader international order would inevitably enter any conversation.

Hemant Adlakha of Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi said that “without a clearly agreed-upon agenda, the possibility of the trilateral [talks] happening in Shenzhen is rather remote”.

He suggested that, in the absence of a formal meeting, the three leaders might instead opt for a more informal encounter, perhaps a “stroll together or a cup of tea”.

Lyle Goldstein of Defence Priorities, a Washington think tank, said the agenda might determine whether the potential gathering was “short and symbolic or alternatively lengthy or substantive”. He argued that Trump’s meetings with Xi and Putin had been “helpful overall in cooling world tensions”.

Wang said Beijing would be keen to discuss issues that were global, constructive and mutually beneficial, such as the risks inherent in major-power relations, the global economic recovery, food and energy security and climate change.

But Beijing would resist any pressure to align with a particular bloc as well as “unfair proposals” such as “forcing China into US-Russia nuclear arms control negotiations”.

“[China is] open to discussing mutually beneficial cooperation, but issues concerning [its] sovereign rights are off the table, and any demand to ‘take sides’ is a non-starter,” he added.

Beijing has long refused to join trilateral arms control talks with Washington and Moscow, arguing that its nuclear arsenal does not match up to those of the US and Russia. China is thought to have hundreds of warheads, while the Russian and American stockpiles are in the thousands.

Cui Hongjian, head of European Union studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said the thaw in Washington’s ties with both Beijing and Moscow had laid some groundwork for a meeting, but that stability would need to be maintained for talks to go ahead.

He pointed to uncertainty over the Ukraine war, which he said was weighing on the US-Russia relationship, and to the trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.

“To bring about a three-way meeting, I think an important precondition is that each of the bilateral relationships stays stable, with no major reversals or changes,” he said.

Cui said the political will of the three sides would also be decisive. The Trump administration, in particular, would first need to weigh how a meeting fitted its domestic politics, including the looming midterm elections, before committing fully to talks on the agenda, he said.

Sergey Radchenko, a Chinese and Russian foreign policy specialist at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, said a meeting of the three powers would give Russia a chance to “separate the US from its European allies” and hand the Kremlin political leverage while bolstering its status as a great power.

He expected Ukraine to be on the agenda if a meeting took place, with Russia pushing for an end to the war. He also said China’s presence could open the door to talks on security guarantees that would bind Beijing to any settlement.

But he doubted that Xi “will necessarily be enthused by the idea of such a summit”.

“He and Putin have previously cooperated in trilateral formats. However, this is a proposition of a completely different order, and perhaps it is a format that Xi will find difficult to handle,” he said.
