Simon offered a more granular reading of the three leaders’ incentives. Trump, he said, would see the meeting as “an opportunity to demonstrate his ability to deal directly with the world’s other two major powers, without being constrained by traditional alliances”.

For Putin, simply sitting at the table would be a diplomatic victory, ending Russia’s isolation and giving him a platform to discuss Ukraine, whereas Xi is likely to be the most cautious, according to the Quincy Institute’s Simon.

“Xi would welcome the recognition of China as an indispensable global power, but would be cautious about becoming part of an arrangement that legitimises American and Russian spheres of influence at China’s expense,” he said.

Cui suggested that if the meeting went ahead next month, it would send a positive signal that the three major powers shared a desire to promote global stability and development.

Beijing, as host, would stand to gain by showing its sense of international responsibility, he said.

“Objectively speaking, this meeting offers China primarily symbolic value, with substantive gains playing a secondary role,” Wang added.

“Symbolically, this is where its greatest value lies. It reaffirms China’s status as a global hub, demonstrating that no major international issue can be advanced without China’s participation. It underscores China’s role as a core force for balancing relations between major powers and stabilising the international order.”

But such a meeting could unsettle US allies, including European countries and Japan, according to Wang. He said a trilateral dialogue would deepen “strategic anxiety” in Europe and Japan since both had long shaped their foreign policies around the US’ stance in great-power rivalries.

If such talks became regular, he said, it would mark the end of a “global order defined by bloc-based confrontation” and could potentially leave US allies such as Europe and Japan in “a state of strategic disorientation, compelling them to re-evaluate their own positions on the global stage”.

However, Goldstein argued that seeing the trilateral as “bad news” for Japan and Europe amounted to a “zero-sum worldview”, and that having such meetings regularly could inspire other sets of three-way talks, including between Europe, Russia and the US or alternatively China, Japan and the US.

Also, Adlakha said, the trilateral meeting might “severely” test China’s efforts to maintain a careful balance between supporting Putin and preserving ties with Europe.

But Wang played down expectations, suggesting that a meeting would at most produce a crisis communication channel to prevent strategic miscalculation, a basic consensus on global issues and clearer “red lines” for each side.

“Any expectation that such a meeting could resolve the Russia-Ukraine conflict or fundamentally reshape the global order is entirely unrealistic,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] As Indonesia faces MSCI downgrade threat, officials vow reforms to ease fears
item.description:
As the threat of a reclassification by MSCI that could relegate Indonesia to an investment hinterland looms, the country’s financial regulators and stock exchange officials have vowed to address systemic concerns, including removing stocks with concentrated ownership.

The global index provider announced on Friday it was launching a formal consultation to decide whether to downgrade Southeast Asia’s largest economy from “emerging market” to “stand-alone” status, similar to countries such as Argentina, Zimbabwe, Ukraine and Russia.

MSCI cited persistent concerns over Indonesia’s market dysfunction, including opaque ownership structures, highly concentrated shareholdings and coordinated trading practices. Its final decision is expected by June 30 next year.
item.content:encoded:
As the threat of a reclassification by MSCI that could relegate Indonesia to an investment hinterland looms, the country’s financial regulators and stock exchange officials have vowed to address systemic concerns, including removing stocks with concentrated ownership.

The global index provider announced on Friday it was launching a formal consultation to decide whether to downgrade Southeast Asia’s largest economy from “emerging market” to “stand-alone” status, similar to countries such as Argentina, Zimbabwe, Ukraine and Russia.

MSCI cited persistent concerns over Indonesia’s market dysfunction, including opaque ownership structures, highly concentrated shareholdings and coordinated trading practices. Its final decision is expected by June 30 next year.

On Monday, officials from the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) held an online meeting with MSCI representatives, where they laid out measures to reform the country’s problematic stock market.

“First, we will include a description of whether 1 per cent shareholders are affiliated or unaffiliated [with the company] when publishing the names. Second, to provide a more credible and integrated price index, we will remove all high shareholding concentration [HSC] shares from the Jakarta Composite Index,” IDX CEO Jeffrey Hendrik told reporters.

“We hope these two initiatives will provide greater transparency and greater market data integrity.”

HSC refers to a market situation in which a huge percentage of a company’s shares – in some cases above 95 per cent – are owned by a small number of shareholders, with a very small free float available for public trading.

According to Hendrik, HSC shares currently account for 18 per cent of JCI’s total weighting. Such shares had been excluded from Hong Kong’s benchmark Hang Seng Index, he added.

Hendrik said the new measures followed previous steps taken by the Indonesian bourse to improve transparency, such as setting 15 per cent as the minimum requirement of free float, or the proportion of a company’s shares readily available for the general public to buy and sell, and expanding the number of investor categories from nine to 39, among others.

The JCI plunged 3.64 per cent at the close of trading on Monday to a six-year low at 4,996.60. After MSCI issued its warning, the benchmark index plunged 11.6 per cent on Friday, making it one of the world’s worst performers and wiping out around US$85 billion in market capitalisation. On Tuesday, the index rose 5.65 per cent to close at 5,278.

A downgrade to stand-alone market status could trigger US$5.6 billion in passive fund outflows, with another US$2.7 billion fleeing if FTSE Russell – a leading global provider of benchmarks – were to take similar action, Goldman Sachs warned in a note on Sunday, as quoted by CNBC.

As of Sunday, the proportion of foreign ownership of Indonesian stocks was 25 per cent, down from 27 per cent in January, while the value of foreign holdings had dropped to US$130 billion from US$250 billion in January, the investment bank said.

Over the weekend, the Financial Services Authority (OJK) in Indonesia and IDX sought to steady the nervous market by declaring a fine of 2.1 trillion rupiah (US$116.4 million) on three firms alleged to have manipulated trading of their shares.

Two of the firms, Barito Renewables Energy and Petrindo Jaya Kreasi, belonged to a group owned by conglomerate Prajogo Pangestu, while another, Dian Swastatika Sentosa, is part of the Sinar Mas conglomerate.

More fixes needed

While economists welcomed the measures by IDX, they said regulators still needed to impose firm law enforcement to help Indonesia avoid reclassification by MSCI.

“The key to adjusting the perception of Indonesia needs to come from strict enforcement of IDX and OJK rules and regulations and the imposition of sanctions, including significant fines and even imprisonment. This is criminal behaviour after all,” said Angus Mackintosh, an Asean specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore.

“Forthright statements from the top are required to ensure that actions are taken to their logical conclusion, even if those market abusers are closely connected to the government.”

Bhima Yudhistira, executive director at Jakarta-based think tank Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios), said that the disclosure of 1 per cent shareholders “must be accompanied by an investigation into their ultimate beneficial ownership, as many companies use the names of other companies, or nominees, as their shareholders”.

The market was also rattled by an effort by state wealth fund and investment agency Danantara to acquire shares of the IDX, which would “ultimately lead to a decline in the independence of the stock exchange”, Bhima added.

The IDX is currently undergoing a demutualisation process, which will see it become a limited liability company owned by shareholders. IDX is currently owned by its members, including 90 securities companies.

Dipo Ramli, an economist with the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia, said that IDX was still facing “a decline in market confidence,” which could “indirectly influence” the assessment of the Indonesian economy by rating agencies.

Earlier this year, Fitch and Moody’s downgraded Indonesia’s rating outlook from stable to negative due to concerns relating to economic governance by President Prabowo Subianto’s administration.

Martyn Terpilowski, a British investor in Indonesia, said that “foreigners are unlikely to buy” the charm offensive by regulators to lure them back into the market.

“What you find in Indonesia, a lot of the deals are off-market transactions. That’s because the actual real price of the stock is heavily inflated and the insiders know that,” Terpilowski said. “It’s just not a transparent market that people can invest into.”

He also questioned the authorities’ promise to make the market more open to investors.

“It’s a difficult one because the economy will be hurt if US$40 billion flows out of the economy. The question is, if they open the floodgates to allow a better system, will that hurt the oligarchs more?” Terpilowski said.

“The problem you’ve got in Indonesia is pretty similar to the United States now, as the business leaders are all very close to the government leaders.”

Wider economic crisis?

Bhima argued that the current pressure on the Indonesian bourse could lead to an economic crisis similar to one in the late 1990s.

“There’s a disconnect between the government’s claims of economic success and the actual state of economic fundamentals. There is damaged governance in the stock exchange, as well as the declining independence of Bank Indonesia,” Bhima said.

“This could lead to a financial crisis, similar to the 1998 model, due to distrust over policy credibility. The issues are already intertwined between the [government] fiscal and financial sectors.”

Mackintosh, however, said the wider economic crisis would not occur as long as regulators continued overhauling the local stock market and making it transparent.

“IDX and OJK need to show their teeth in dealing with these problems and sanction those companies which are connected to share manipulation activity and market abuse. The brokers involved should also be sanctioned, heavily fined and disbarred from trading,” Mackintosh said.

“There is a good deal of scepticism around the move by the MSCI in that it has impacted the whole stock market, bringing about a significant correction and destruction across the board, when the vast majority of companies maintain high-quality governance standards.”

item.title: [SCMP] From fishing boats to Michelin stars: Vietnam’s CoCo Dining turns the humble into haute cuisine

item.content:encoded:
“You know the phrase ‘fish out of water’? Well, that’s me in the city,” chef Vo Thanh Vuong laughs. “Now, I’m back on the water.”

It’s just past dawn; we’re on a fishing boat off the coast of Vung Tau, roughly 100km (62 miles) southeast of Vietnam’s largest city, Ho Chi Minh. Vung Tau is the port that supplies Ho Chi Minh City’s best restaurants, but by the fleet’s clock, it’s already late; most of the other vessels have already unloaded their catch. Vuong is showing me how to hold a fishing rod. His hands seem to know the motion better than his mind does.

Vuong grew up in Phan Thiet, about 160km (100 miles) north along the coast, where his family’s livelihood depended on what the South China Sea had to offer. Vung Tau is where his family’s boat went down in 2000, when he was 11 years old, 40km (25 miles) off its coast. Losing the watercraft cost them dearly, and suddenly, every pair of hands mattered – including his. Vuong was fishing full-time until he was 20, long enough to know the fishing life was not for him.

So, he left for Ho Chi Minh City, also known as Saigon.

Now, almost two decades later, he is back on the water – not because he has to be, but because he wants to be.

By mid-morning, we have caught almost nothing. Vuong shrugs. He tells me this is what most trips are like: long stretches of nothing punctuated by work. Because “the sea gave you very little entertainment, you learned to be comfortable with silence”.

Back on shore, we head to a local fish market in Vung Tau to pick up something for lunch. Everything is laid out at knee-height. Vuong moves through the displays like he’s reading a familiar book. He picks up a big fish with one hand and turns it over. He doesn’t wince or fidget the way many people do when handling something slippery and cold. He checks the gills, the eyes, the firmness and sets it back down – or keeps it, and moves on.

“When an ingredient is truly good, you don’t need to do much to it. Sometimes, the best thing a cook can do is step out of the way.”

In Vung Tau, he cooks a meal from the catch of the day. “Do you want to see the fisherman or the chef cook today,” he asks. He explains that the fisherman cooks fast, because at sea, speed is survival: you cook to eat and move on. But the chef cooks slower, because he has learned to enjoy the process – the prepping, the seasoning, the tasting, the small adjustments.

We tell him we want both. He laughs and gets to work.

His preparation is simple, and he hums as he cooks – the way he did as the youngest boy in his family, with two brothers and a sister. Several gas stoves are burning at once. He chops the garnishes with precision and seasons the braising liquid, gauging measurements by eye.

He steams a mix of flower crabs and three-spot swimming crabs with beer. He sets a hotpot going with tamarind, pineapple and tomato, and portions the cobia into chunks. He treats the oriental trumpeter whiting like a ceviche: sliced thin, cured in lime juice for 15 minutes, then tossed with a home-made sweet-spicy sauce, raw onion and herbs – the way he used to make it on the boats.

On those trips, food was whatever the sea and the hold allowed. Rice and instant noodles were the foundation, and they carried mam (fermented-seafood paste), nuoc mam (fish sauce), dried fish and squid, pickled vegetables, eggs and water. A good meal might be muc com – baby squid with its roe – with sour fish soup and pickles. “We would spend the whole day catching fish for other people,” he recalls. “At night, we’d sit together and argue about which fish was best for ourselves.”

Some nights, the swells were heavy enough that seawater splashed into their rice bowls; the rice would turn salty, but they would look at each other, laugh and keep eating. “You didn’t complain,” he says. “You were hungry, and you were at sea.”

And the night the power died and the charcoal got too wet to burn, they ate a freshly caught grouper raw on deck – bled, sliced thin, with wild lime and sea salt, similar to what he prepares for us.

He serves the food the way he always does: everyone else first, himself last. It’s what he calls a staff meal, the food he makes for his team at CoCo Dining – his one-Michelin-star Vietnamese restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City, opened in 2021 – after service.

What he has prepared for us today is not, by his own admission, the food that made his name – that food was French. When Vuong left fishing behind and enrolled in culinary school in Ho Chi Minh City, he didn’t go in with a plan. He had no kitchen training and no technique. He also had no language for what he was learning.

What he did have was nine years at sea. At the time, that felt like something to hide. “I didn’t want to expose my past,” he says, recalling his inexperience. “I had self-esteem issues.”

Vuong didn’t finish Grade 6 and, later, quit culinary school. He became a chef by observing the people around him, figuring things out along the way. He spent eight years training under French-Cambodian culinarian Sakal Phoeung and learned to cook in the French tradition.

In Vietnam, that still carries a particular weight: post-colonisation, French cuisine remains the benchmark for fine dining. For a Vietnamese chef with no pedigree, no formal training and a past aboard fishing boats, French haute cuisine was how Vuong proved he belonged.

“I simply didn’t see [Vietnamese cuisine] as something I needed to learn,” he recalls. “It was everyday food, so I didn’t think about it as a cuisine I could build a career around.”

So, Vuong learned to cook French, well enough to find success with it. For years, that was his identity in the kitchen. It even won him the first prize on the televised cooking competition Top Chef Vietnam in 2019. From 2021 to 2023, he was changing the menu at CoCo Dining twice a year, working mainly with modern gastronomy and fermentation. Eventually, he felt like he was running out of ideas.

One night, towards the end of 2023, he and Daniel Dang Hung Minh – CoCo Dining’s managing director – were drinking together, unwinding after another week of trying to solve a menu that wouldn’t come together. Vuong started cooking just for the two of them, preparing the kind of Vietnamese drinking food he would naturally make for himself. After tasting it, Dang said: “This tastes much more like you; this is where you’re strongest. Why don’t you just be honest with your cooking?”

Vuong resisted. He thought, “No, this can’t be the direction of a fine-dining restaurant.” He had spent years learning modern techniques and developing himself as a chef. Going back to familiar food almost felt like going backwards.

But what Dang had said stayed with him, so Vuong started experimenting secretly at home. “Maybe I had been trying too hard to become the chef I thought I was supposed to be,” he says, “instead of being honest about the chef I actually was.”

In 2024, CoCo Dining served a menu called Ra Khoi – meaning “to set sail” – but for Vuong, it signified “a return to the source”, as the first tasting menu he designed after deciding to lean into his fishing heritage. His first version of the menu pulled together fragments of memories: the mam muc (fermented-squid paste) he used to eat on the boat became stuffed baby squid with fermented-squid sauce. A wind-dried prawn reminded him of how his family preserved seafood, so he worked with tiger prawn. A simple crab salad became blue crab with mustard greens.

Never before had Vuong put his childhood on a plate on purpose. Last year, the restaurant earned its Michelin star. It turns out, the fisherman and the chef could coexist after all.

“I wasn’t sitting there thinking to myself, ‘I’m going to make a menu about my childhood.’ I was just following one memory into another, and suddenly, there was a menu,” he says.

Back in Ho Chi Minh City, Vuong brings out his oldest jar of mam chao (fermented fish) from the fermentation room at CoCo Dining. A whiff of it brings us back to the market of Vung Tau. The fermented fish is threadfin bream, sun-dried for five days in Phan Thiet by his family, who have been fishing and making mam for generations. At the restaurant, he and his team mix it with a starter made from sticky rice, layer it in a jar and seal it tightly. Usually, it’s ready after a month, but he lets his develop for at least two. “We learned not to waste anything,” he says. “Even the fish that wasn’t going to be sold had a purpose.”

Vuong believes his role is to bring the ingredients to life again: “In a museum, you put an artefact behind glass to stop it from changing. In my kitchen, the things I want to preserve are alive: they ferment, they age, they dry and they continue to change.”

It’s what makes his “archive” different from a museum’s. Recipes can be written down and “collected” and remain the same for generations, but his fermentations live and breathe. “You can’t treat each batch exactly the same,” he says. “You have to observe it, smell it, taste it and understand how it is developing.”

At CoCo Dining, Vuong balances the deep umami of his fermented seafood with ginger and other aromatics. In his signature dish, baby squid is stuffed with squid trimmings and pork, then glazed with a sauce made from squid ink and a spoonful of the mam muc. If diners are curious, he brings out a jar so they can taste the fermented-squid paste as it is.

“For me, that’s the heart of my ‘Living Archive’. If you put something in a box and never touch it, eventually, it becomes history. If you cook it, share it and pass it to someone else, it continues to live,” he explains.

His menu, Luu Tich (“Living Archive”), arrives at a moment when what deserves to be preserved and presented as part of Vietnamese culinary heritage is under debate. Vietnam is bidding to become the next global gastronomy hub, with a pitch built on “luxury” through authenticity rather than European-style fine dining. Vuong is cautious about the language. He has spent too long on the other side of the word “authentic” to trust it easily.

Real necessity informed those techniques, he says. “Coming from a fishing boat off Phan Thiet, the word ‘luxury’ felt very far from my life. But there was a lot of knowledge in those practices.”

“Vietnam doesn’t need to borrow someone else’s definition of luxury”

Vo Thanh Vuong

For him, that knowledge of salt, patience and time is its own form of wealth. “Vietnam doesn’t need to borrow someone else’s definition of luxury,” Vuong says. He thinks that luxury today can be the time and attention we give to something that was once simply part of daily life, “not taking something humble and making it expensive just because we put it on a fine-dining plate”.

But that doesn’t mean he cooks the same way his grandmother did. In Vuong’s eyes, French technique is merely another set of tools – just as sorting and scaling fish is part of a fisherman’s toolkit. Both, he says, come from the same place: trying to understand an ingredient and bring out the best in it.

But does that make a dish less Vietnamese?

“If authenticity means following a recipe strictly without any changes, maybe some will feel that what we do is not authentic enough,” he says. “I’m not trying to recreate the past exactly. A dish doesn’t become inauthentic because it evolves. It becomes inauthentic only when you lose sight of where it came from.”

If he were to curate a museum piece for people 100 years from now to understand where he came from, he would choose a thung leu, the wooden barrel used to make fish sauce in Phan Thiet. His grandfather used to make fish sauce at home, and the whole area of Phan Thiet, Vuong remembers, smelled like fish sauce. “Now, Phan Thiet is much more modern; that smell has mostly disappeared,” he says. “Not many households make fish sauce at home any more, so something that was once part of everyday life has become much less visible.”

In the museum, the label for the exhibit would read: “Thung Leu, Phan Thiet, Vietnam – a wooden vessel for making nuoc mam. For one boy from the coast, it was simply part of home. Inside it are fish, salt and time. Around it is the knowledge of generations who learned how to live with the sea.”

item.title: [SCMP] Kurt Campbell on US deterrence, the Quad, Aukus and Taiwan after Xi-Trump summit
item.description:
Kurt Campbell is a veteran US diplomat and strategist who has played a leading role in shaping Washington’s approach to China and the Indo-Pacific for more than a decade.

He served as the White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs from 2021 to 2024 and as US deputy secretary of state from 2024 to 2025. Previously, he served as assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs from 2009 to 2013 and was a key architect of the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia”.

Often described as the Biden administration’s “Asia tsar”, Campbell also helped develop the Quad and the “small yard, high fence” approach to technology competition.
item.content:encoded:
Kurt Campbell is a veteran US diplomat and strategist who has played a leading role in shaping Washington’s approach to China and the Indo-Pacific for more than a decade.

He served as the White House coordinator for Indo-Pacific affairs from 2021 to 2024 and as US deputy secretary of state from 2024 to 2025. Previously, he served as assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs from 2009 to 2013 and was a key architect of the Obama administration’s “pivot to Asia”.

Often described as the Biden administration’s “Asia tsar”, Campbell also helped develop the Quad and the “small yard, high fence” approach to technology competition.

A former US Navy officer, Harvard professor and co-founder of the Centre for a New American Security, he is now chairman and co-founder of The Asia Group, a Washington-based strategic advisory firm.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

You once argued that America’s enduring advantage over China was “allied scale” rather than unilateral dominance. But China’s strategy today looks different from the one Washington confronted in 2021. China now presents itself as a champion of sovereignty, non-interference and a more “multipolar” order while expanding its diplomatic and security presence. Is this a genuine strategic shift or a new form of competition expressed in different language? What is the realistic objective of US policy towards China today?

I think it is the determination of both leaders to take steps to stabilise a complex dynamic relationship between the two countries.

Both leaders understand that at the current moment, it is in the best interests of both countries to get along strategically. There are a variety of reasons for that. Some of them rest in a desire to improve competitive advantage. And some are motivated by a desire to genuinely work together.

My own sense is that the US is most effective as a global power when it works constructively with its allies and partners. President [Donald] Trump has taken more time and put more focus on building a stronger relationship with China than he has on working with some of his allies and partners. I very much support efforts to stabilise US-China relations. But I would like to see President Trump make more effort to stabilise relations with other partners. For instance, what we’re seeing in relations with Canada is quite shocking, suggesting that Canada is no longer one of the closest friends and partners to the US.

I find the fact that Canada is seeking to join the EU quite troubling. My general argument would be that US technology strategy, US efforts to sustain the global order are best achieved not just by trying to stabilise the US-China relationship, but by also seeking to maintain a strong posture with allies and partners.

So what is the realistic objective for US policy towards China?

There are a number of things that are necessary for US-China relations as we head into the next critical phase. I personally believe that the path to true cooperation between the United States and China on AI is very complicated, especially since President Trump said he seeks a dialogue with China but insists on dominance.

That message is a complicated one for Chinese friends to hear. It probably is a disincentive to seek true collaboration, because it suggests that the terms are implicitly or explicitly negative for China. What I think is important going forward is that both countries understand clearly the risks of frontier work, especially when researchers on both sides are increasingly voicing concerns about AI that we don’t fully understand or comprehend.

It is important that both the United States and China recognise that racing for advantage in a technological space that holds such potential risk – as well as promise – raises concerns. I would commend the work that the two countries have taken to date to at least find a degree of common ground for a continuing dialogue. But I will also say that this issue is developing rapidly, and both sides are going to need to adapt their position to establish a true dialogue around potential areas of collaboration, on safety reporting and mutual engagement.

The question for many of us is what is the appropriate metaphor when we think about AI. Is it nuclear weapons? Is it Covid? Is it climate change? Are there other experiences historically that we can utilise and apply to this new technology in the US-China context?

I think the one thing that is unique here is the role of the labs. These are not just technological capacities. They are the most powerful economic and commercial players of modern times. They are absolutely dominant. So they will want a voice in any deliberation between the United States and China. We don’t have as many experiences in the past in which it’s not just government to government, but the most powerful commercial and technological voices as well.

So are you particularly concerned about AI competition between China and the US?

In the larger context, I am worried about AI writ large. I believe that the politics of AI in the United States are becoming increasingly complicated. There is a bipartisan anxiety about data centres and their development. You’re seeing many states now questioning the buildout of these large entities. There are questions about capital use. There is an incredible level of investment in AI that has taken investment from other areas. In fact, many believe that to the extent that we have economic growth in the United States currently, it is largely because of the investment in AI. But I think more directly, it is undeniable when the most senior people in various companies are calling for government intervention and restraint that alerts us that there is a problem here.

Every week there is a new story of an AI entity that has escaped captivity and gone on an excursion, often creating havoc. There are also stories of engineers choosing to resign from these prestigious posts because they are worried not just about an incident but the status of humankind. Many very senior people have worried about human extinction.

It seems to me that if that is a truly serious matter and debated among engineers and designers of AI, it is incumbent on us to reflect, to think about guardrails, to consider safety and to understand that there are existential issues here that in many respects transcend simple competition.

Let’s talk about Taiwan and Japan. Does strategic ambiguity remain the best policy or have China’s military capabilities and pressure campaigns made greater clarity necessary?

I still believe that one of the great success stories of US-China relations – this is rarely discussed – is the complex maintenance of peace and stability between the two countries with respect to Taiwan.

There have been lots of tensions and disappointments, but the truth is the status quo has served the interests of the people of Taiwan. I would argue the framework that the United States and China have maintained for decades is being increasingly tested by military and political developments. But I still believe that this framework is in the best interests of all concerned. And so it is often said that we have a degree of strategic ambiguity but tactical clarity; I think that it is important for the United States to underscore our determination to maintain peace and stability.

But it is also the case that a dialogue over Taiwan is handled carefully between the two leaders. It’s undeniable that this issue has come up and that it is being actively discussed.

If Beijing imposed a quarantine or blockade without launching a conventional attack, would that trigger a US response?

I’m out of government now. I’m not really in the business of offering views on particular scenarios. My own sense is that the more we discuss openly potential scenarios, the less it might be stabilising to the situation. If anything, they tend to draw sharp contours in a complex environment. And, in many respects, create even greater distrust.

My own sense is that the United States should maintain a strong unofficial relationship with Taiwan, recognise how critical this issue is in a larger US-China relationship and manage this with care and dexterity.

Despite the ups and downs, history reflects that it is possible to take the necessary steps to maintain peace and stability. And I fully expect that this can continue.

On Taiwan, what is the strategic cost of treating arms sales to Taiwan as negotiable within the broader US-China relationship? Is there any practical form of Taiwan-related cooperation that Washington and Beijing could undertake? What would a credible cross-strait dialogue look like if Beijing continues to reject engagement with Taiwan’s current government?

The strategic risk of treating arms sales to Taiwan as negotiable is that it can inject doubt into the credibility that has helped preserve cross-strait stability for decades. While there are deep differences over Taiwan, both Washington and Beijing have a common interest in crisis management, military-to-military communications and reducing the risk of unintended escalation.

Given the tensions between China and Japan, what responsibility does Washington have to ensure that the US-Japan alliance remains a mechanism for deterrence rather than escalation? Is Japan primarily becoming a frontline deterrent, an industrial and technological partner or a military coequal?

I would simply say that Japan is an important partner of the United States. It has a relatively small military and its defence investments are quite modest. I believe that one of the most critical paths of diplomacy in Asia is to make sure that lines of communication between Beijing and Tokyo are open.

My own sense is that the Japanese would prefer to have a more open dialogue with Beijing. I think one of the issues occasionally challenging is that the historical issues still animate Beijing’s thinking about Japan.

One of the things that I’ve noted is the effectiveness of Chinese diplomacy generally, their ability to reach out to countries in which they have a complex history. In particular, what we’ve seen is renewed diplomacy between China and India. I think it would be in China’s interests to open up more lines of communication with Tokyo. I do not believe that Japan is somehow an American cat’s paw. The people of Japan are deeply peace-loving. Efforts to revise the constitution or to move Japan in a more assertive direction have actually met with substantial domestic opposition.

I think some of the military modernisation in Japan is indeed modest. It is designed to reflect increasing challenges in the Indo-Pacific. And remember, those do not come exclusively in the US or in the Japan-China relationship.

What Japan is confronting is an increasingly hostile North Korea that is well armed and has nuclear capabilities. So Japan is seeking to play a larger role in Asia. I support that. But at the same time, I do believe there have been periods in the past where the lines of communication between Tokyo and Beijing have been much stronger. I do know that the Japanese are troubled by how difficult it has been to establish communication with Beijing. And I think just as President Trump and President Xi [Jinping] have found some common purpose and would meet in a complex time, I think President Xi and Prime Minister [Sanae] Takaichi can find the political courage to sit down as well.

China increasingly portrays this sort of alliance – whether it’s with Japan, or trilateral cooperation with South Korea and Japan, or quadrilateral with India, Australia and Japan – as an instrument of containment. Given China’s thinking, how should Washington support their expanded security role while assuring China that these alliances are defensive?

The US seeking closer relations between Japan and South Korea has more to do with their own histories than it does with China. I would simply remind Chinese friends that not every development in Asia is about China: South Korea and Japan have profound historical tensions, but they are close allies of the United States. It is only natural that the United States would seek the two countries to coordinate more closely. Each country has its own unique relationship with China. It is also the case that closer coordination among the three could have a stabilising impact across the Indo-Pacific. The Quad has not met at the leader level under President Trump, but its first incarnation in the early 2000s was a result of the tragedy that struck Indonesia and Malaysia. The terrible tsunami.

I myself had been actively engaged in the Quad. Much of what the Quad was involved with in its most recent incarnation was Covid vaccine development and South Pacific issues related to education and training.

I would say that the Quad was primarily about delivering well-being to underserved groups and creating more capacity. I don’t believe that any country in the Quad would support the institution becoming an alliance aimed at any one country. I see it mostly as developing common approaches to complex societal and security problems. These are four maritime democracies and each again has its own set of relationships.

With Beijing, more recently, we are seeing India and China edging closer to a more substantial dialogue. I think the Quad can exist with a range of diplomatic formations in Asia. As much as anything, it helps anchor the United States in the Indo-Pacific, which is in the strategic interests of Washington.

Should the Quad become more institutionalised? Or would that make it less flexible and more threatening to China? How vulnerable is it to domestic political changes in these four member states?

I cannot speak to what’s expected next in the Trump administration, but there has been no discussion recently of reconvening the Quad at the leader level. I think without that, it’s difficult to sustain active forward momentum. I do not know what President Trump’s ambitions are for the Quad besides the foreign ministry meetings and a variety of other assessments. But I think at this juncture, there is no push or intention towards institutionalisation. If anything, the focus continues to be on areas which are primarily about the well-being, for instance, of Pacific island nations. One of the areas of cooperation in the past, for instance, was on dealing with illegal fishing in the Pacific, which is an issue that Pacific island nations care deeply about and do not have the capacity to address.

So I do not see the institution emerging as a direct vehicle for somehow containing China. And I just think that framework is outmoded. China is a great, powerful country with deep interests across the world. It’s not possible to contain China and the most recent work towards this coming summit between the United States and China brings that point home. China is a country that needs to be engaged actively. It is not possible to think about China in the context of containment.

Would a reduced US-China rivalry lessen the importance of security partnerships such as the Quad, Aukus and other minilateral groupings? If so, what implications would that have for the balance of power, deterrence and Indo-Pacific stability?

Partnerships like the Quad and Aukus are valuable because countries across the Indo-Pacific recognise that many of the region’s challenges, from maritime security and technological change to supply chain resilience and disaster response, require closer cooperation. The value of these partnerships does not depend on the status of the US-China relationship.

Even in a period of more stable US-China relations, these partnerships would continue to play a critical role in strengthening deterrence, building collective capacity and fostering a regional balance that supports peace and prosperity. In many respects, the greatest contribution of a grouping like the Quad is the creation of habits of cooperation, strategic trust and practical capabilities.

What would the durable regional security architecture look like if it included China rather than being organised against China? Is it possible to have such a thing?

We’ve had a number of efforts at regional security or regional dialogue, such as the East Asia Summit, the Asean Regional Forum, which have been established for decades.

One of the challenges has been the uneven participation of the United States. We don’t attend all of the meetings. In fact, I think you’ve seen, particularly in the Trump administration, an ambivalence about regional institutions. We’ve long sought to create capacities for more dialogue and cooperation among Indo-Pacific actors. We’ve seen that at Apec. We’ve seen that at the Asean Regional Forum and in the East Asia Summit. I would go as far as to say that, by some measurements, nine of the 20 members in G20 are Indo-Pacific nations. In many respects that institutional innovation was designed to reflect the increasing importance, not just of China but of other rising nations in the Indo-Pacific.

I would like to see the United States more actively engaged in that multilateral diplomacy. I do not think it is a secret that the United States is less interested and focused on that diplomacy and seeks, in many respects, to act unilaterally without constraints with other countries. I do not believe that is in America’s strategic interests. I think investing in regional architecture is important and a critical dimension of our national power.

What’s your take on the US changing the name of INDOPACOM to USPACOM?

It was Trump’s first administration that originally changed it to Indo-Pacific. And now they’re changing it back. I don’t know if that is a desire to return to an earlier period framework. At first, the Indo-Pacific framework was adopted by Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, and that framework was accepted by parts of the Trump administration. When President [Joe] Biden came to power, the Japanese asked for that framework to be continued. We supported that. I do not know if this is a request from President Xi to President Trump, or whether this is a rethinking by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. There are too many things that have happened in terms of Pentagon policy to speculate about why they move in one direction or another.

How can Washington reassure its Asian allies and Southeast Asian countries that its partnerships do not force them to choose between the US and China? Is the current alliance-centred strategy sufficiently attentive to Asean priorities?

The most important dimension here is for the United States to invest actively in regional institutions and bilateral engagements. Most of the frameworks of engagement that we have seen most recently have been around highly difficult trade relations with a variety of countries in Southeast Asia. I increasingly hear from a variety of Southeast Asian countries that they are adopting policies that allow them to maintain a degree of flexibility in engagement with both Washington and Beijing.

The most effective US policy does not demand countries to make some sort of overt choice between the two.

And there is a deep recognition that commercial and political ties between Beijing and Southeast Asia are only natural, as is the United States maintaining close ties in Southeast Asia. These are not zero-sum relationships. They can be mutually beneficial.

What do you think is Hong Kong’s role in Sino-US relations? And how should the city move forward?

It’s a complex city. It’s undeniable. It is, in many respects, a financial launching point for China’s relations with the world. It still has some characteristics of its past, but it is increasingly a Chinese city that has an extraordinarily critical and important role in the global economy.

And as far as I can tell, it appears to continue to play a very dynamic role in the global financial economy. And it is continuing to be a meeting place between East and West and the financial centre of activities across the Indo-Pacific. There are other capitals that are emerging in that equation: Singapore, Tokyo and the like. But Hong Kong continues to play a vital role.

item.title: [SCMP] Dire straits: why Filipino sailors continue to brave troubled Middle East waters
item.description:
Filipino seafarer Jay was on lookout duty aboard a vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz one evening in August when drones swarmed overhead, darting past his ship and two others it was following.

Within seconds, an explosion rang out from the tanker ahead.

“That was traumatic for me when I saw that the tanker ahead of our vessel had been hit,” said Jay, whose real name has been withheld to protect him from possible employer retribution.
item.content:encoded:
Filipino seafarer Jay was on lookout duty aboard a vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz one evening in August when drones swarmed overhead, darting past his ship and two others it was following.

Within seconds, an explosion rang out from the tanker ahead.

“That was traumatic for me when I saw that the tanker ahead of our vessel had been hit,” said Jay, whose real name has been withheld to protect him from possible employer retribution.

The 29-year-old and his fellow crew members made it through the strait unscathed, but the experience stayed with him. “We never talked about what happened; it was done. We would move on and proceed to the next voyage,” he said.

For sailors like Jay, however, the danger does not end when a voyage is over. As conflict threatens the Strait of Hormuz and other maritime chokepoints in the Gulf region, these Filipino workers face a difficult choice: risk sailing through dangerous waters or refuse a voyage and potentially jeopardise their livelihoods.

The Philippines is the world’s leading supplier of seafarers, with over 468,000 Filipino seafarers deployed last year, according to data from the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW).

In March 2024, DMW issued a memorandum setting out the right of Filipino seafarers to refuse to sail through high-risk areas, particularly the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden and surrounding waters, following an increase in piracy, hijackings and armed attacks on civilian ships.

Under the rules, Filipino seafarers who refused to sail through these areas are entitled to protections including repatriation help and two months’ basic wages. Recruitment and placement agencies also cannot bar them from future contracts or employment.

The memorandum was issued after Houthi rebels attacked a commercial vessel in the Red Sea that month, killing two Filipino seafarers and injuring three others.

Nearly 1,500 Filipino seafarers had exercised that right over the past three years, according to the DMW. In September, 10 Filipinos who refused to sail through the Strait of Hormuz returned safely to the Philippines.

Since the Iran war began on February 22, five Filipinos had died and one remained missing, Secretary of Migrant Workers Hans Cacdac confirmed in September.

Protection problem

Manila generally assesses potential threats to overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) and issues corresponding alert levels, according to Arnold de Vera, director of the workers and employees programme at the University of the Philippines Law Centre. “The worst cases justify a ban on deployment and, for those already there, mandatory repatriation,” he said.

However, much of their protection still depends on the recruitment agencies and foreign employers that hire them.

“Our system of regulatory protection for OFWs relies heavily on the statutory provision imposing a solidary liability between the foreign employer and the local recruitment and placement agency. By making them solidarily liable, the local agency can be made to answer to the liabilities attributable to the foreign employer,” de Vera said.

Many seafarers are also covered by collective bargaining agreements negotiated by unions and shipowners, which provide another layer of protection, according to de Vera.

Implementation remains a challenge, though, particularly when disputes end up in litigation. The division of responsibility for worker safety can leave seafarers in situations where exercising their right to refuse becomes complicated.

After Jay’s ship docked in Al Jubail, Saudi Arabia, he decided to exercise his right to refuse to sail, knowing that he would again have to transit the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, both designated high-risk areas. “I sent an email to my company informing them that I would exercise my right to refuse. I also emailed the DMW and other concerned groups,” he said.

However, he and his fellow crew members were not allowed off the vessel. “It is very hard to be poor. My company said that it had filed for financial losses because its other ships had been attacked. We asked our company to increase our compensation if we would not be sent home but they failed to meet our demand … we continued to sail even after we exercised our right to refuse.”

In September, the family of a Filipino seafarer killed aboard an oil tanker attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz claimed that he had not been informed in advance that the vessel would transit the strait.

The DMW said that same month it was examining compliance with regulations. This Week in Asia also contacted the department for comment.

Jay said his employer had failed to address the psychological toll of the experience, focusing instead on completing the voyage. “They don’t even care about the mental health of their crew that has experienced this trauma. What they told us is [there will be] no crew change and [to] deliver the cargo,” he added.

He feared that his agency might not rehire him when his contract ended because his email to the DMW had included the name of his vessel and its route.

Family obligations

The prospect of losing future work was also a factor for Filipino seafarer Ronald Allan Ruiz, who transited the Strait of Hormuz despite the risks. “In the Red Sea, what we deal with is the pirates, the Somalis … the conflict between Iran and the US, and the nearby tensions, that is what changed things,” Ruiz said.

He and his fellow Filipino crew members had agreed to the voyage because of their families’ financial needs back home. They were also offered incentives for transiting high-risk areas, he said. “Even though you have the right to refuse to sail, [the financial need] doesn’t go away for our colleagues either. Maybe the office won’t rehire you – because, of course, the company deals with a big business.”

Although Ruiz felt his recruitment agency and employer had treated him fairly, he remained concerned about the uncertainty he might face if he returned home.

“There’s also what we call ‘if the price is right’. So sometimes even when you’re afraid, you also think about your family,” he said. “If you go home, they might not rehire you right away, you could be without work for a long time.”

Advocacy groups say escalating tensions have become a serious concern for seafarers and their families.

“Every ship attacked puts more seafarers at risk. Their families send them off to work, not to face the deadly consequences of wars fought for the interests of powerful countries. How many more lives must be put in danger before our government takes a clear stand?” said Edwin Dela Cruz, president of the International Seafarers Action Centre.

Yet for seafarers such as Ruiz, the need to provide for their families means the risks can be difficult to avoid.

“Every Filipino here is here because of the job, because of the money. So [even if] deep down, we don’t want to sail through danger … sometimes people have a lot of financial obligations, or we just tell ourselves bahala na [come what may].”

item.title: [SCMP] Calls grow for India to lure tech talent home as US tightens job curbs
item.description:
After completing a master’s degree in data science at Pace University in New York in May last year, Tarun returned to India in October, saying frequent changes in US visa rules and employer sponsorship requirements had made it difficult for him to find a job in the world’s largest economy.

Tarun, who is from the southern Indian city of Tirupati, felt returning home was a more prudent move than pursuing a job in the US indefinitely.

“I got a job within one month here [Bengaluru] with an American engineering company,” he said, without giving further details about his job. “At the end of the day, my decision is about my happiness. I am close to my friends and family.”
item.content:encoded:
After completing a master’s degree in data science at Pace University in New York in May last year, Tarun returned to India in October, saying frequent changes in US visa rules and employer sponsorship requirements had made it difficult for him to find a job in the world’s largest economy.

Tarun, who is from the southern Indian city of Tirupati, felt returning home was a more prudent move than pursuing a job in the US indefinitely.

“I got a job within one month here [Bengaluru] with an American engineering company,” he said, without giving further details about his job. “At the end of the day, my decision is about my happiness. I am close to my friends and family.”

Tarun’s experience mirrors a debate over whether growing uncertainty surrounding US immigration rules could spur more Indian professionals to return home, with prominent figures in India’s tech industry weighing in on the issue.

In a viral social media post, Sridhar Vembu, co-founder and chief scientist of Chennai-headquartered cloud software company Zoho Corporation, urged Indian professionals in the US to return, arguing that India could turn the increasingly hostile climate in Washington towards foreign talent into a valuable opportunity to grow its technological capabilities.

“Indians have made a major contribution to America’s technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us. Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work,” Vembu wrote on October 9.

“Let this be the birth pains of a bold new future. Come back, let’s build India,” he said.

Indians have made a major contribution to America's technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us.

Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work.

Let this be the birth pains of a bold…

— Sridhar Vembu (@svembu) October 9, 2026

The US is home to the world’s largest Indian diaspora, estimated at between 5.8 million and 6.1 million people as January, many of whom hold senior positions at global technology companies.

Former Indian education minister Dharmendra Pradhan has backed Vembu’s call to contribute to India’s tech growth, emphasising the need to strengthen local capabilities and foster innovation.

“With confidence in our talent and a commitment to building indigenous capabilities, we can help shape the future of technology,” he wrote on social media.

The posts have raised expectations of Indian tech talent to accelerate innovation in India.

“It would be great if the government took more initiative to support professionals because there are a lot of highly talented Indians who are in the US. Many of them are struggling with visa pressures,” said Tarun.

On October 8, the US administration suspended the Permanent Labour Certification programme, a key step for foreign professionals to work in the US and potentially obtain permanent residency under an employer-sponsored process, affecting Indian companies such as Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, as well as US giants including Microsoft and Adobe.

Speaking on the move on the same day, US Vice-President J.D. Vance accused major companies of fraudulently bringing in lower-paid foreign workers whom he described as “indentured servants” instead of employing Americans.

India’s Ministry of External Affairs slammed his remarks as “deeply offensive” the following day.

“We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem,” it said in a statement.

Vance later clarified that his remarks were criticism of American companies and the visa system rather than of workers.

Indian professionals said that his remarks showed a lack of respect towards them.

“A professional is not ‘cheaper’ because they were born in India, China, Brazil or anywhere else. Their salary may be different. Their immigration status may be different. But their education, experience, expertise, ambition and dignity are not cheaper,” Dhananjay Ramakrishnappa, a manager of operations at Bengaluru-based software firm Flexara, said in a social media post, which also mentioned that he had previously worked in the US for 13 years.

“What worries me even more is the fear that many immigrants now feel about simply travelling home to see their families,” he said.

He said that a US-based family friend did not travel to India to attend her mother’s last rites because she feared that she would not be able to come back.

Washington’s curbs against foreign professionals could tighten further as it is reportedly examining a proposal to levy a US$70,000 fee on international students seeking post-graduation work authorisation.

Ramakrishnappa, who returned to India in 2017 after working in senior US-based executive roles with Microsoft, told This Week in Asia that Indian-origin professionals who had spent a decade or two working in the US tech sector could become successful entrepreneurs in India.

Subbu K., head of technology at New York-based start-up Trust Guard AI, however, said he was torn between whether to stay in the US or return to India. His daughter, who is studying in a US high school, might not be keen to head home, he added.

“I would love to do that [return to India] because it gives me the best of both worlds,” said Subbu, who still holds an Indian passport after spending over two decades working in the US tech sector.

Nonetheless, tech professionals and analysts say India has to take steps to lure more tech talent home.

Subbu worried about red tape in India, citing how a friend of his spent around eight months to get clearance from Indian regulators to start a business, compared with as fast as within a day in the US.

Vivek Mishra, deputy director of the strategic studies programme at the Observer Research Foundation, said the significant salary gap between what Indian tech professionals could earn in the US and India could be a deterrent.

“There has to be a calculated outreach to these people. Otherwise it will be just a slogan,” he said.

Uday Chandra, professor of political science at India’s Ashoka University, said appealing to Indian talent to return home based on “innate patriotism” alone would not work.

“Ultimately, highly skilled professionals will go wherever their talents are valued and they can pursue their ambitions. India will need to compete for such talent,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Sydney opens US$4 billion second airport with few flights
item.description:
After more than half a century of political procrastination, environmental protests and funding shortfalls, Sydney finally has a second airport. But the new A$5.6 billion (US$4 billion) site’s commercial prospects are already in question.

Western Sydney International, 50km (31 miles) inland from the city centre, will handle its first passenger flight on Sunday – a Jetstar service to the Gold Coast. But the facility has attracted only a handful of airlines and has half a dozen or fewer scheduled flights a day for the next 12 months, according to aviation data company Cirium.

Australia’s biggest aviation infrastructure development in decades is opening just as the global travel industry endures its toughest period since the pandemic. Around the world, airlines are sounding the alarm on rising fuel costs and fares as the Iran war drags on. Many, including dominant Australian carrier Qantas, are cutting back on domestic capacity rather than laying on more flights.
item.content:encoded:
After more than half a century of political procrastination, environmental protests and funding shortfalls, Sydney finally has a second airport. But the new A$5.6 billion (US$4 billion) site’s commercial prospects are already in question.

Western Sydney International, 50km (31 miles) inland from the city centre, will handle its first passenger flight on Sunday – a Jetstar service to the Gold Coast. But the facility has attracted only a handful of airlines and has half a dozen or fewer scheduled flights a day for the next 12 months, according to aviation data company Cirium.

Australia’s biggest aviation infrastructure development in decades is opening just as the global travel industry endures its toughest period since the pandemic. Around the world, airlines are sounding the alarm on rising fuel costs and fares as the Iran war drags on. Many, including dominant Australian carrier Qantas, are cutting back on domestic capacity rather than laying on more flights.

Airlines are also struggling to get their hands on new jets, leaving few spare aircraft to send to start-ups like Western Sydney International where passenger demand is unproven.

Compounding the government-owned airport’s challenges, a planned rail link would not open until 2027 at the earliest, while a shuttle bus to the centre of Sydney costs A$55 and takes about one hour. That means Sydney Kingsford Smith, 20 minutes by taxi or train from the central business district and Australia’s primary gateway, remains a more practical option for most people.

“The main airport is much more convenient to almost all travellers,” said David Levinson, a professor of transport at the University of Sydney. Western Sydney International’s passenger forecasts look “a bit optimistic,” he said.

Named for pioneering Australian aviator Nancy Bird Walton, the new airport expects to handle 8.4 million passengers a year by the end of the decade, and almost 20 million annually by 2045, according to its master plan. Both figures are fractions of the numbers handled by the city’s main airport.

Western Sydney International is built on old farmland at Badgerys Creek. The government settled on the site in 2014, ending a debate about the need and location for a second airport that stretches back to 1946. Construction started in 2018 and the airport opened for cargo flights in July.

The surrounding population is key to the facility’s commercial fate. By 2030, half of Sydney’s 6.1 million people will live in the city’s west, according to the airport’s master plan. Some 40 per cent of Greater Western Sydney’s population was born overseas, which should generate demand for flights to countries such as India, China and Vietnam, the document says.

Yet Qantas plans to operate little more than one domestic flight a day, on average, from March next year, according to Cirium data through September 2027. Virgin Australia, the country’s second-largest carrier, has no flights scheduled. The new airport’s main customer is Jetstar, the leisure-focused, low-cost carrier owned by Qantas.

“We are looking closely at the Western Sydney opportunity and assessing whether it would fit into a network and schedule that best serves the needs of our customers,” Virgin Australia said in a statement.

Qantas referred to a speech by Chief Executive Officer Vanessa Hudson in June, when she described Western Sydney as “such an important market”, specifically highlighting its relevance to Jetstar. “We expect demand will grow, and when we see that, we’ll put more frequency in,” she said at the time.

Other airlines that will use the new airport are Air New Zealand, VietJet, Fiji Airways and Singapore Airlines.

In an interview, Western Sydney International Chief Executive Officer Simon Hickey said more airlines would use the airport in time, and talks were taking place with several other carriers. “Right now, I’m really happy with where we’re sitting,” he said.

But Hickey also needs the local population to give the airport a chance, which would help him persuade other carriers that there’s demand to capture. “It’s use it or lose it,” he said. “That will mean that we continue to grow and other airlines will come and join the pack.”

To be sure, long-term appetite for air travel is relentless. Worldwide passenger demand was expected to more than double by 2050, according to the International Air Transport Association.

And while it may be off to a slow start, Western Sydney International has some advantages over Sydney’s main airport. Most importantly, it has no overnight curfew like at Kingsford Smith, allowing international airlines to schedule departures that connect with other flights at their own hubs. The new airport expects to handle 82 million passengers a year by 2063 and ultimately become Sydney’s primary air-travel hub.

It takes time for a new airport to establish itself, said Stephen Beckett, CEO of Airlines for Australia & New Zealand, which represents Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand and Virgin Australia.

“Some airlines will sit back and make their own commercial assessments based on passenger demand,” he said.

For now, Western Sydney International is already drawing unfavourable comparisons with airports elsewhere that ultimately failed to live up to expectations.

Levinson, the transport professor at the University of Sydney, compared Western Sydney International to Mirabel Airport outside Montreal. Mirabel opened in 1975 in time for the Montreal Olympics but handled its last commercial passenger flight in 2004. The airport now operates chiefly as a freight hub.

Right now, Western Sydney International is trying to serve a market that does not yet exist, Levinson said. The new airport’s opening is “early, given actual demand,” he said.

There was a risk Sydney’s secondary airport would end up with a similar status as Avalon Airport, which is more than 50km outside Melbourne, according to Peter Forsyth, an aviation economics consultant who’s a former professor at Monash University. Avalon, where Jetstar has operated flights since 2004, has never broken through as a genuine alternative airport to Melbourne’s main airport, he said.

Growth at Sydney’s new airport would be a slow burn, said Forsyth. “There is a market there,” he said. “But exactly how big it is, I don’t know.”

item.title: [SCMP] India needs more fighter jets. It cannot build them fast enough
item.description:
India has a soaring ambition to modernise its air force, built around a fleet of domestically developed fighter jets. Yet production of these aircraft has been hampered by engine delays and other bottlenecks that defence analysts say could limit its ability to fight future air wars.

On October 11 at an airbase in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh strapped into a Tejas jet for the last time. It was his final fighter sortie before retiring later this month and he flew it in an Indian-built jet to show support for the country’s domestic defence industry.

A week earlier, he had warned that the Indian Air Force (IAF) faced a critical shortage of fighter squadrons. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year,” Singh said on October 3, noting that “between 36 and 40 aircraft” would need to be produced annually to meet India’s target of having 42 fighter squadrons in service.
item.content:encoded:
India has a soaring ambition to modernise its air force, built around a fleet of domestically developed fighter jets. Yet production of these aircraft has been hampered by engine delays and other bottlenecks that defence analysts say could limit its ability to fight future air wars.

On October 11 at an airbase in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh strapped into a Tejas jet for the last time. It was his final fighter sortie before retiring later this month and he flew it in an Indian-built jet to show support for the country’s domestic defence industry.

A week earlier, he had warned that the Indian Air Force (IAF) faced a critical shortage of fighter squadrons. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year,” Singh said on October 3, noting that “between 36 and 40 aircraft” would need to be produced annually to meet India’s target of having 42 fighter squadrons in service.

“Actually, we need even more than that,” he said.

The Tejas programme, which dates back to the 1980s, has become emblematic of India’s drive to build up its domestic defence industry. A Mark 1A variant of the light combat aircraft was unveiled last year and a Mark 2 is still under development.

Induction of the Mark 1A is only now about to begin, 2½ years late, after the F404 engines needed from US manufacturer GE Aerospace arrived late and the various radar, weapons and software systems took longer to integrate than planned.

Vice-Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said in late September that induction was expected to begin within one or two months, following a protracted development cycle and exhaustive operational evaluations of the aircraft’s avionics suite.

GE Aerospace, the Tejas programme’s only engine supplier, recently stepped up deliveries to principal manufacturer Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), shipping three F404-IN20 engines in August and another four engines in September. That makes 14 engines delivered so far, against the 20 that are due to arrive by the end of this year.

State-run HAL aims to produce 24 Tejas fighters annually. The IAF has already ordered 83 Mark 1As, wants to add 97 more and is also actively considering the Mark 2 variant.

Projections indicate at least 350 – and potentially more than 400 – Tejas will eventually be built, with the aircraft expected to form the backbone of India’s air force in future.

However, “repeated delays in certification, weapons/radar integration and engine supply show that indigenisation still needs execution, not just policy”, said Gurcharan Singh Bedi, a retired IAF air marshal.

“Having acquired the capability to produce the aircraft, we are then just talking of scale, which can be boosted. But it will take a very strong focus by the government and a very hard commitment by HAL or whosoever produces these aircraft.”

Fleet depletion

India’s air force badly needs replacements for the ageing aircraft that are leaving active service.

The IAF officially retired the last of its Cold War-era Soviet-designed MiG-21 jets in September last year – 36 in total – with another six squadrons of Anglo-French Sepecat Jaguar ground-attack fighters due to be phased out between 2028 and 2031.

To keep the remainder of its Jaguar fleet flying, India is buying nine of the aircraft that Britain’s Royal Air Force retired in 2007 to use for spare parts.

Three MiG-29 squadrons and three squadrons of the French-designed Mirage 2000 are set to also be retired through the mid-to-late 2030s.

Each IAF squadron contains about 18 active aircraft, plus three or four in reserve.

Bedi agreed with outgoing air force chief Singh’s assessment that roughly two new squadrons per year would be needed simply to maintain the number of aircraft India had in service.

HAL’s target of 24 Tejas fighters a year would fall short of that goal, but a second programme could help close the gap, he said.

In February, India cleared the purchase of 114 Rafales from France, under a government-to-government deal as part of its Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft programme.

Taken together, Bedi said this would bring annual deliveries close to the 32 or 36 aircraft required.

Final talks on price and production arrangements for the Rafales are still pending, though local media reports indicate manufacturer Dassault Aviation has agreed to 50-60 per cent “Make in India” content for the aircraft, as well as technology transfers and the integration of Indian weapons and systems.

Bedi said a “genuine acceleration” of India’s fighter jet production would depend on HAL meeting or beating its target of 24 combat aircraft per year, the timely delivery of multi-role fighters from France and retirements not outpacing inductions.

“The chief has spelled out the requirement, but it’s difficult to meet in the near future,” he said of Singh’s assessment. “At the same time, I believe anything is possible.”

‘The real constraint’

Several new aircraft are on the way. The first flight of the Tejas Mark 2 is expected between June and September 2027, with initial induction planned for 2030-31 if development stays on track.

India also wants to have a prototype of its fifth-generation stealth fighter, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), airborne for a test flight by September 2028.

Bids to develop and produce the AMCA prototype have come in from India’s Tata Advanced Systems and domestic consortiums led by Larsen & Toubro and Bharat Forge, while France’s Safran is competing with a partnership formed by India’s Reliance and Britain’s Rolls-Royce to supply AMCA’s engine.

Sanjay Iyer, a retired Indian Army brigadier, said these overlapping programmes were likely to hit another bottleneck: the fact that they had to draw from the same pool of test pilots, certification staff and integration engineers.

“That is the real constraint, not shop-floor space,” he said. “And even if every Tejas [production] line ran flat out, you would still fall short of 36 to 40 a year.”

Iyer argued that India’s aircraft production problems could best be tackled through increased domestic engine manufacturing, design discipline and boosting private industry’s role.

Much time was lost on the Mark 1A’s development because of design changes, he said, adding that private companies – some of which already made fuselages and wings for HAL – should also be allowed to assemble aircraft.

“As long as one American supplier decides when your fighters fly, your output figures are really their output figures,” Iyer said regarding the Tejas’ GE engine. “And geopolitical considerations matter too. The US is not beyond twisting India’s arm if its other interests are affected.”

Holding buffer stocks of engines could serve as a costly stopgap solution, he added, further calling the opening of AMCA development and manufacturing to domestic private industry a “good sign”.

item.title: [SCMP] The China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
item.description:
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.

But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.

A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
item.content:encoded:
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.

But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.

A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.

“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.

Arora’s experience, together with broader economic data, illustrates the challenge facing countries seeking to diversify their supply chains: shifting production out of China does not necessarily mean reducing reliance on Chinese industry. A recent report by investment bank Morgan Stanley examined this pattern, arguing the country had strengthened its role in global supply chains despite trade tensions.

“China has continued to deepen its presence in global supply chains by capturing value-added content in global imports and increasing exports to [emerging markets],” the bank’s analysts, including chief Asia economist Chetan Ahya and chief China economist Robin Xing, wrote in the note, published earlier this month.

The world’s second-largest economy was “well-positioned” to deepen that presence, the analysts argued, citing its focus on high-growth sectors, integrated supply chains, a financial system aligned with strategic goals and a large pool of skilled workers.

The upstream advantage

The challenge facing the likes of India and Vietnam is whether they can develop the industrial expertise and networks required to make more inputs at home. But a closer look at the data suggests that as manufacturing expands in these economies, Chinese supplies remain essential.

These developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China

Morgan Stanley analysts

“While India has made significant headway in electronics manufacturing, it still imports a large part of its intermediate and capital goods from China,” the Morgan Stanley analysts wrote, noting that 52 per cent of India’s imported Chinese content went into domestic investments.

Looking beyond where products are finally assembled, they tracked “value-added content” – the value contributed by a country through the goods and services used along the chain. A product assembled in Vietnam, for instance, may still contain Chinese parts or rely on Chinese machinery.

Using this measure, the analysts found that China’s share of value-added content in global imports rose from 12.6 per cent in 2017 to 14.3 per cent in 2024. The report also found that Chinese inputs are playing a growing role in Asian economies often touted as manufacturing rivals.

In Vietnam, 55 per cent of imported Chinese content is channelled towards exports, according to the analysts. “We also find that Chinese value-added content has not just increased in the rest of Asia’s exports to the US, but also to non-US markets as well,” they wrote.

“Overall, these developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China.”

Arora’s experience illustrates how difficult mainland China’s manufacturing ecosystem is to replace. Taiwan’s higher-end products, he said, were less suited to the low-cost goods his Indian customers needed while Vietnam offered fewer options.

“Only China has that ecosystem,” he said.

Nevertheless, Arora said he believed India was making headway. He cited the expansion of home-grown electronics giant Dixon Technologies into television and phone assembly, as well as the growing ability of Indian firms to design and develop circuit boards and prototypes that once required trips to Shenzhen.
