“Instead they focus on things like religious infrastructure. There are cases of violence against minorities. When anyone speaks against them, it is labelled as treason or sedition.”

When Modi came to power, he promised the creation of millions of jobs ⁠each year. Yet, despite India’s strong economic growth since then, unemployment remains at slightly above 5 per cent, according to government data.

A Reuters poll last year said that data masks the severity of joblessness, especially among the youth. Unemployment among the 367 million people in the country aged 15-29 stood at 9.9 per cent in 2025, according to the data.

Research by Azim Premji University’s State of Working India 2026 report found unemployment among graduates aged 15-25 was nearly 40 per cent, while about one in five graduates aged 25-29 remained ‌jobless.

In May, unrest erupted across the country when the government invalidated examinations for ‌national medical colleges, a pathway to jobs for the poor and the middle class, after test papers were leaked.

Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in Delhi, said repeated examination paper leaks had deepened a sense among young Indians that the system was denying them opportunities even after years of study.

“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.

While national elections are not due for almost three years, the country’s biggest state, Uttar Pradesh, goes to the polls early next year, which could provide a test of Modi’s popularity.

Analysts however remain cautious about the outcome.

The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago, said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond EVs and perception, how China is gaining ground in Central Asia
item.description:
In Kazakhstan’s futuristic capital Astana, car dealer Auyez Kabdygali is planning a big change to his business as he switches from importing European cars to Chinese electric vehicles.

Kabdygali says there is increasing demand for Chinese EVs both from locals and Russian customers due to their competitive price and quality. His grandfather is among the converts – he has an order in for a BYD Han, the carmaker’s flagship model, and plans to collect it from a terminal on the border with China and drive it hundreds of kilometres home.

The 33-year-old car dealer is among a growing number of Kazakhs who hold positive views of China. It is a sentiment driven not just by its EVs, but the economic pay-offs from China’s expanding footprint in Kazakhstan and its posture as a cooperative, non-interfering partner.
item.content:encoded:
In Kazakhstan’s futuristic capital Astana, car dealer Auyez Kabdygali is planning a big change to his business as he switches from importing European cars to Chinese electric vehicles.

Kabdygali says there is increasing demand for Chinese EVs both from locals and Russian customers due to their competitive price and quality. His grandfather is among the converts – he has an order in for a BYD Han, the carmaker’s flagship model, and plans to collect it from a terminal on the border with China and drive it hundreds of kilometres home.

The 33-year-old car dealer is among a growing number of Kazakhs who hold positive views of China. It is a sentiment driven not just by its EVs, but the economic pay-offs from China’s expanding footprint in Kazakhstan and its posture as a cooperative, non-interfering partner.

Strolling through Astana – a city of more than 1.3 million people – feels much like walking through the most developed major cities in northern China. Its modern architectural landmarks loom over Soviet-era blocks, while a newly opened Chinese-built light rail train runs along the city’s central axis.

China’s footprint can be seen across the city, from the high-rise Beijing Tower to the Chinese consumer goods and cosmetics lining the shelves in stores.

This shift is taking place as the broader Central Asian region has become a more crowded arena for diplomacy, with Beijing and Washington – along with Tokyo and Seoul – all competing for strategic influence.

But observers note that while Beijing has made economic inroads, there is still scepticism towards China in the region and unease over its rivalry with the United States, and Astana is among the capitals trying to balance relations with the two powers.

‘Friendly market’

Astana car dealer Kabdygali welcomes investment from China, a country he views as a friendly neighbour with more cultural similarities to Kazakhstan than the US.

China for him represents economic support – and enormous market potential.

“[Nearly] all the products we’re buying are Chinese products … so you can say that they are really helping everyday life here,” he said. “China is helping us to maintain the economy.”

Kabdygali’s positive views have also been shaped by visits to the country and Chinese friends he made while studying English in Malaysia.

His brother went to Shanghai for a university course in 2007, and Kabdygali regularly visited him during the two years he was there. The whole family later travelled to China’s southern tropical island Hainan for a holiday, and in 2012 they went to Beijing to consult a traditional Chinese medicine practitioner about some health issues.

Today, the young businessman drives a BYD, pays with Alipay at his local coffee shop, and regularly tunes in to a Chinese gaming streamer on YouTube.

Kabdygali is not worried about the country becoming overreliant on China. He said trade with China was “necessary” and the whole world was buying from the country. But he added that he hoped Kazakhstan could export more food and manufactured goods to China to balance the trade deficit.

He also shrugged off concerns over the intensifying US-China competition in Kazakhstan and the region.

“China is more of a friendly market. They focus on their own economy and just want to make good products, whereas the US manipulates things. They invade countries and make things worse,” he said.

“If there are no competitors, if there was no US, China would become the US.”

Central Asian view

After Beijing launched its global infrastructure scheme – the Belt and Road Initiative – in Kazakhstan in 2013 there was a dip in favourable attitudes towards China in both Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, according to a study in the journal Post-Soviet Affairs in August.

But public sentiment in the two countries has turned more positive since 2021, driven largely by the tangible economic benefits of Chinese investment.

More than 49,000 people were surveyed for the study across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan between 2017 and 2023.

Jessica Neafie, the paper’s co-author and assistant professor at Kazakhstan’s Nazarbayev University, said that in the early years of the belt and road strategy, the unprecedented exposure to China and a large influx of visible investments in Central Asia triggered a backlash.

She said it fuelled a “mix of concern for foreign investment and its effect on local identity and nationalism”.

The study pointed to the heightened anti-Beijing sentiment that led to a Chinese firm in 2020 scrapping a US$280 million logistics centre project in Kyrgyzstan after hundreds of residents took to the streets in protest.

Neafie said public sentiment had improved since then as tangible economic results were seen and China’s regional image improved.

“A lot of people saw their concerns not come to fruition, but rather see again more jobs, infrastructure and benefits,” she said. “So the ways that they’re exposed to China don’t end up in all cases harming them.”

Neafie said respondents to the survey cited Beijing’s policy of non-interference as the top reason they viewed China favourably.

But while there was some improvement, the study found that concerns over Chinese debt and land acquisition had persisted and that continued to have an impact on perceptions of China.

Geopolitical anxieties – particularly fears that closer economic ties with China might jeopardise relations with Russia – remain one of the main drivers of negative sentiment.

“Confidence in the economic benefits of Chinese engagement can coexist with – and in many cases outweigh – anxieties about debt, land and geopolitical realignment, but it does not erase them,” according to the paper.

But Neafie noted that younger people – with more access to social media and more exchanges with Chinese – tended to view China more objectively. She said anxiety over geopolitics was largely found among the older generations who lived through the Sino-Soviet tensions of the 1970s, when Central Asia was part of the Soviet Union.

China in Astana

In Astana, the light rail is now the fastest route from the airport to downtown. At the brand new airport station there are turnstiles that support facial recognition technology.

The train runs along an elevated track every five minutes, as it whizzes past the city’s gleaming skyscrapers, monuments and landmark buildings.

Corruption allegations had stalled the project but it eventually began operations in May, more than a decade after it was first proposed.

Built with Chinese technology, standards and equipment it is Central Asia’s first urban light rail and the region’s first fully driverless train system. A second phase of the project to expand the network is now under way, with Chinese-run construction sites visible across Astana.

Back in 2013, Astana was the first to sign up to Beijing’s belt and road programme. China has since then ramped up investment across Kazakhstan and wider Central Asia, targeting small and medium-sized projects as a strategy to expand its influence in the region.

Infrastructure is not the only sign of the growing Chinese presence in Astana. In the city’s shopping malls, Chinese powerhouses draw steady crowds – from drinks chain Mixue to variety chain store Miniso, consumer tech giant Xiaomi and sportswear brand Li-Ning – while Chinese beauty brands such as Shanghai Song have been embraced by local cosmetics stores.

Yichang beer is a bestseller in liquor stores but it is actually brewed in Kazakhstan with rice to mimic the crisp Chinese-style beers. Its producer started exporting the beer to China in 2024, creating a buzz on social media.

On the roads of the capital there are more Chinese EVs, alongside established brands such as Kia and Hyundai from South Korea and Toyota from Japan.

In the first four months of 2026, car dealers in Kazakhstan sold some 2,122 electric and hybrid vehicles, according to official data. Of those, more than 2,000 – or over 97 per cent – came from Chinese carmakers, including BYD, Li Auto, Geely Galaxy, Zeekr and Rox.

A taxi driver in Astana who gave only his first name, Abylai, was driving a BYD and planned to upgrade to the new Han sedan. “It’s a good car for the price,” he said. “Almost all my friends drive Chinese cars such as BYD and Changan.”

Kabdygali, the car dealer, said his customers were drawn to the cost-efficiency of Chinese EVs and modern features such as infotainment systems, while concerns about quality had eased over time – mainly due to word of mouth.

Geopolitical ambitions

Several major powers – including Japan, South Korea and Turkey – have been vying for more influence in Central Asia in recent years, competing for critical mineral resources, trade routes and infrastructure contracts.

Beijing has opted for a different path as it seeks smaller projects to quickly establish ties and build enduring influence, according to Neafie from Nazarbayev University.

She said China had the capacity and risk tolerance to finance smaller, high-risk projects, which competitors like Japan or South Korea could not easily afford if they failed or underdelivered.

“It’s not just altruism. These things lead to better economic outcomes … [and] have a long-term effect on relationships and public diplomacy,” she said, adding that in the long run these middle-level projects could “make a huge amount of difference”.

Accelerated by the fallout from the war in Ukraine, cooperation between China and Central Asian countries has evolved into an institutionalised partnership, expanding beyond energy to include public health and digital technology.

Zhu Yongbiao, director of the Centre for Afghanistan Studies at Lanzhou University, said that compared to the US approach, China’s investment in the region was more practical and comprehensive.

“Whether it’s cutting-edge tech and flagship products – like electric vehicles, solar power, the digital economy, AI and TikTok – or everyday goods like socks and screws, China has it all,” he said.

“Crucially, it can deliver tailored products and solutions suited to the diverse needs of different Central Asian countries, an advantage the US simply lacks.”

Central Asia has shifted from being a security partner to a cornerstone of US regional strategy as Western economies seek to de-risk supply chains from China and Russia, with the Donald Trump administration focusing its attention on Kazakhstan – drawn by its critical mineral reserves.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio began a five-day trip to India and Uzbekistan on Saturday. In Samarkand, the top US diplomat will lead a delegation of more than 200 business leaders and take part in a series of bilateral engagements with senior officials from all five Central Asian nations – Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan.

But intensifying US-China rivalry in the region may not be a bad thing, according to observers.

Zhu said Beijing and Washington actually had opportunities to cooperate in Central Asia on environmental protection, energy market access and regional security surrounding Afghanistan.

And in Kazakhstan the geopolitical pressure is minimal, according to Neafie. She said China and the US were both focused on economic engagement rather than military or security influence, and in a country that is developing fast that economic competition might even be welcomed.

item.title: [SCMP] Is China’s Shenzhen ready to host Xi, Trump and Putin during Apec summit?
item.description:
In Shenzhen, drones are banned, shiny new hotels have opened their doors and taxi drivers are carrying devices that can translate nearly 150 languages.

Since President Xi Jinping announced last year that China’s southern tech hub would host Apec meetings in November, the city has done all it can to get ready under the watchful eyes of the local, provincial and national authorities.

While every Apec summit draws the world’s attention, this year’s edition is considered to be especially high-stakes as Xi, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are all expected to attend. Last year, Putin did not join the summit in South Korea.
item.content:encoded:
In Shenzhen, drones are banned, shiny new hotels have opened their doors and taxi drivers are carrying devices that can translate nearly 150 languages.

Since President Xi Jinping announced last year that China’s southern tech hub would host Apec meetings in November, the city has done all it can to get ready under the watchful eyes of the local, provincial and national authorities.

While every Apec summit draws the world’s attention, this year’s edition is considered to be especially high-stakes as Xi, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are all expected to attend. Last year, Putin did not join the summit in South Korea.

In the past few weeks alone, Guangdong’s provincial Communist Party chief Huang Kunming has inspected Shenzhen twice to make sure preparations are going as planned.

“Shenzhen must, on one hand, maintain focus on details to comprehensively plug any gaps, optimise and refine service guarantees, and go all out to ensure the conference is held safely, smoothly and successfully. On the other hand, it must take the hosting of the Apec meeting as a new starting point to accelerate the expansion of high-level opening up,” he said last week.

Compared with Shanghai and Beijing, which hosted Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summits in 2001 and 2014, respectively, Shenzhen is less internationally known. However, analysts say the city could benefit from the event in the long term.

When Xi made the announcement, he noted that Shenzhen had “transformed from a backward fishing village into a modern international metropolis in just a few decades”.

“Together with surrounding areas, it forms the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area, which can be considered a growth pole of the world economy,” he added.

This narrative emphasised Shenzhen’s alignment with the meeting’s agenda, said Zhang Jingjia, an economist at the Apec Study Centre at Nankai University. China has made “openness, innovation and cooperation” priorities for the summit, and Shenzhen was a living example of that, she said.

When Beijing and Shanghai held the meetings, they focused on diplomacy and international finance, said Han Yonghui, executive dean of the Guangdong Institute for International Strategies. But Shenzhen’s tech companies, manufacturing system, ports and border crossings could show how the digital economy can function in real-world scenarios, he added.

Hosting an inter-governmental meeting would test a city’s organisational abilities, Han said. It required proper venues, hotels, ports, railways, telecommunication networks and security, as well as diplomatic coordination, multilingual services, volunteers and community support, he added.

The city has made security its top priority. Since July, local police have imposed a strict no-fly zone covering the city centre and stepped up random checks of subway passengers.

A statement from the provincial public security bureau said at the time that hidden conflicts and risks should be detected, while street crimes – including thefts and robberies – needed to be “completely eradicated”.

“Ensuring Apec safety is a major political responsibility for police around the province,” the statement said. “We need to plan early … and act with a heavy fist.”

Special teams have also been equipped to patrol the region. Shenzhen police have formed a low-altitude drone unit to patrol more than 600 routes and reach any point in the city centre within three minutes, authorities said.

This week, the government also called for residents to take leave or work from home to reduce traffic during the summit.

The venue for the summit – the Shenzhen International Exchange Centre in Futian district – was built especially for the event. In July, it hosted the Apec Forestry Ministerial Meeting, which Zhang described as a “test run” for the leaders’ meetings.

Shenzhen previously hosted major exhibitions, including the China Hi-Tech Fair, the International Cultural Industry Fair and the China International Optoelectronic Exposition, which showed that the city had the capacity to host large-scale meetings, said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government.

According to the Shenzhen authorities, the city has focused on upgrading its airport, crossings and railway, including this week’s opening of the revamped Huanggang Port that connects the city to Hong Kong.

Language is also a concern. More bilingual signs have been erected in the airport and bus stops, while taxi drivers have been issued with translation devices able to handle 146 languages.

Downtown Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei – the world’s largest electronics marketplace – was offering language training sessions to vendors, and multilingual volunteers were stationed in community service centres across the city, a report on the local government website said in August.

According to media reports, parks, gyms and commercial centres have also been renovated. More than 1,500 training sessions were organised for officials, business owners, delivery riders, residents and volunteers on languages, diplomatic etiquette, business English and public service.

“In addition, Shenzhen’s tech enterprises and industrial achievements are themselves content that can be showcased to all parties during the meeting, which is a feature other cities are unlikely to have,” Zhang said.

Shenzhen could benefit from hosting this meeting, just like Beijing and Shanghai did, analysts said. After hosting Apec, Beijing’s suburban Huairou district developed a whole industry around international exhibitions and hosted several more global summits, Zhang added, while Shanghai saw greater development in tourism and commerce.

Shenzhen’s residents are mostly happy to see parks revamped and other infrastructure improved, but are also looking forward to the return of normality.

A local doctor said she and her colleagues were placed on call for the duration of the summit to handle potential emergencies, and all leave was prohibited. But she said she “welcomes and supports” the city hosting a meeting of such importance for the first time.

“For ordinary people, what’s most useful isn’t the buzz during the meetings, but the public services and environment that stay,” Zhang said.

She added that the new exhibition centre could host public events, while the summit would raise the city’s international profile and foster global cooperation – ultimately driving investment and job growth.

item.title: [SCMP] Pakistan risks deeper instability as political feud threatens counterterrorism efforts
item.description:
Pakistan’s counterterrorism campaign against Taliban insurgents risks being undermined by public resentment, following the dismissal of the opposition-led administration of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province.

According to a statement issued by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s office after an emergency cabinet meeting last Sunday, the decision to impose temporary federal rule was necessitated by the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

The KP provincial administration, led by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, had refused to support intensified military operations against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants, despite surging levels of violence over the last few years.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan’s counterterrorism campaign against Taliban insurgents risks being undermined by public resentment, following the dismissal of the opposition-led administration of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province.

According to a statement issued by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s office after an emergency cabinet meeting last Sunday, the decision to impose temporary federal rule was necessitated by the “provincial government’s deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism”.

The KP provincial administration, led by the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, had refused to support intensified military operations against Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants, despite surging levels of violence over the last few years.

Instead, the KP provincial assembly has passed several resolutions questioning the efficacy of counterterrorism operations and threatening to block them, while the PTI-led administration rallied resistance by tribal elders in the most afflicted districts bordering Afghanistan.

According to Abdul Basit, an expert on militancy and senior associate fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Singapore’s Nanyang University of Technology, this partisan politicking led to a breakdown in counterterrorism coordination between the federal and KP governments.

This deprived the counterterrorism campaign of the “extremely, extremely critical” unanimity needed to effectively combat the rampant TTP, Basit said.

Instead, the resulting “blame game” over security failures in KP made national counterterrorism policy “controversial and politicised”.

Basit said this left the federal government with “no other way” than to impose an emergency in KP, where the monthly TTP casualty toll had climbed to an “alarming” 270 to 300 people.

“This year is the most volatile year since Pakistan started fighting terrorism” after the September 11 attack on the US by al-Qaeda, he said.

Underlying the KP administration’s intransigence was the PTI’s feud with the civil-military hybrid government in Islamabad over the imprisonment of the party’s leader and former prime minister Imran Khan, after his conviction on corruption-related and other charges.

Khan’s journey from political obscurity to high office, followed by imprisonment on controversial charges, is typical of Pakistani power politics.

For decades, the country’s powerful military – which has directly ruled Pakistan for roughly half of its 79-year history – has propped up lawmakers and parties, only for relations to sour and defiant politicians to be jailed, sidelined or exiled.

Khan and the PTI rose to power in 2018 with the support of the military and judiciary, a year after Sharif’s elder brother Nawaz Sharif was removed as prime minister by the Supreme Court on flimsy grounds in a ruling that has since been overturned upon review.

Khan’s government fell in April 2022 after the military withdrew support over its mismanagement of Pakistan’s economy, which left the country on the brink of a Sri Lanka-like default on international payments.

Later that year, the head of the military’s Inter-Services Intelligence agency held an unprecedented press conference to announce it would remain politically neutral in the future.

However, tensions between Khan and the generals reached boiling point in May 2023, when his arrest by security forces sparked rioting and mob attacks against military installations – some of it facilitated by serving and retired military officers, to the government’s horror.

Despite a multitude of hurdles erected by federal authorities during the February 2024 general election, the PTI emerged as the single largest party, mostly due to the loyalty of voters in KP, which the party had governed since 2013.

The PTI’s loss of authority there has deprived the party of its remaining leverage in the corridors of power.

Ominously, public resentment against the politically dominant military and its counterterrorism operations may be the last card it has to play, analysts say.

PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan called the sacking of the KP government “an extremely alarming and grave political mistake”.

In a social media post last Sunday, he said the province’s people would “never accept such actions against their rights”, adding that “peace cannot be established, nor stability brought, by ignoring this mandate, weakening provincial autonomy and creating conflict between the federation and the province”.

Farwa Aamer, director of South Asia initiatives at the New York-based Asia Society Policy Institute, said Pakistan’s internal divisions “make the situation more vulnerable”.

Political instability had been “one of the contributors to the fragile security situation” the country had experienced over the past 20 years, Aamer said.

A harmonious political situation would enable a more effective and focused security policy to tackle insurgencies in KP and western Balochistan provinces by the TTP and ethno-nationalists, respectively.

“That is what the global investors also seek when they look into, say, investing in the country’s mineral sector,” Aamer said.

The economic fallout from the tussle over counterterrorism policy was one of the reasons Sharif cited to justify imposing emergency rule in KP last Sunday.

“I will not allow them [the PTI] to destabilise the economy,” Sharif told his cabinet.

But the “genuine security crisis” was unlikely to be solved by greater central government involvement in KP, said Elizabeth Threlkeld, a former US diplomat who served in Peshawar, the provincial administrative centre.

The PTI remained “widely popular” in KP and efforts to further limit the party’s political space “can backfire” at a time when the population was already under significant pressure from militant attacks and security operations, said Threlkeld, who is now director of the South Asia programme at the Stimson Centre think tank in Washington.

Warning that “it is all but impossible to undertake effective counter-militancy operations without the cooperation of the affected population”, she said the dismissal of the KP administration “risks generating further resentments and driving centre-provincial tensions at a critical moment”.

The inability of the government and opposition to reach a consensus on security policy “is especially concerning”, Threlkeld said.

The political controversy complicated counterterrorism policy by amplifying concerns about the disruptive impact of military operations on the lives of residents in affected areas, Basit said.

During past operations in the last two decades, residents have been forced to evacuate for months at a time with relatively little help from authorities, and many returned to find their homes and livelihoods destroyed.

Basit feared “non-kinetic” aspects of counterterrorism policy key to its lasting success – political ownership and good governance, alongside the rehabilitation of conflict-affected areas – could remain “unfulfilled” unless Islamabad convincingly responded to the KP public’s criticism of past military operations and scepticism about the efficacy of new ones.

“These are questions that the [Pakistani] state needs to answer clearly,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Shunned in the West, Ye hands Indonesia a rare mega-tour coup
item.description:
Taylor Swift and Lady Gaga each chose Singapore as their only Southeast Asian stop on recent world tours. Fellow American singer Olivia Rodrigo played Thailand and the Philippines, but likewise skipped Indonesia.

Next weekend, however, Jakarta is finally getting the big international headline act it has been craving – in the form of Ye.

The controversial American rapper, formerly known as Kanye West, is set to play Indonesia’s capital next Saturday, marking the only Southeast Asian appearance on his current tour.
item.content:encoded:
Taylor Swift and Lady Gaga each chose Singapore as their only Southeast Asian stop on recent world tours. Fellow American singer Olivia Rodrigo played Thailand and the Philippines, but likewise skipped Indonesia.

Next weekend, however, Jakarta is finally getting the big international headline act it has been craving – in the form of Ye.

The controversial American rapper, formerly known as Kanye West, is set to play Indonesia’s capital next Saturday, marking the only Southeast Asian appearance on his current tour.

The promoter, Raw Vision Collective, expects 15,000 international visitors to attend. In the first 24 hours of ticket sales going live, foreign buyers from 73 countries made up 52.8 per cent of purchases, according to marketing and communications lead Karen Tjahja.

“For the first time in Indonesia’s concert history, international attendees are expected to exceed more than 5 to 9 per cent of concertgoers,” Tjahja told This Week in Asia.

But the choice of Ye, who has faced travel restrictions and had concerts cancelled over his controversial remarks, has prompted questions about whether he is the right act to put Indonesia back on the international music map.

Capital gains

Raw Vision Collective says it invited Ye “less as competition” with neighbouring countries and “more as an opportunity to strengthen Southeast Asia’s live-entertainment ecosystem”.

It points to a large domestic audience, a vibrant creative scene and Jakarta’s Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, which can hold about 77,000 concertgoers.

Officials have thrown their weight behind the performance. At a press conference held by Raw Vision Collective last month, Indonesia’s Tourism Minister Widiyanti Putri Wardhana noted the potential for concerts by major overseas acts to generate benefits across various economic sectors, from accommodation and transport to food.

Jakarta Governor Pramono Anung also pledged the city’s full support for the concert, calling it an opportunity to showcase Indonesia’s capital to the world.

“We believe Jakarta can build on its own strengths,” Tjahja said, adding that successful productions elsewhere in the region had helped “establish Southeast Asia as a stronger destination for global tours”.

“We hope that with the success of this concert, this will just be the beginning of Indonesia positively being back on the global stage.”

Singapore serves as an example. The city state “has shown how major concerts can attract regional visitors and drive tourism”, Tjahja said.

Yet Singapore’s success has often come at the expense of its neighbours. Swift played six nights in the city state and nowhere else in the region in 2024. A year later, Lady Gaga also played four exclusive nights.

Permits and piety

Musicians who know the scene well say paperwork is part of Indonesia’s problem.

Herry Sutresna, also known by his stage name Morgue Vanguard and the founder of Indonesian hip-hop group Homicide, told This Week in Asia that Indonesia could attract foreign talent but was a harder sell than Singapore or Australia, partly because of its famously unwieldy bureaucracy.

“It’s not really about convincing the artists themselves, but rather the difficulty of organising concerts locally regarding permits, costs and all the other red tape involved,” he said.

Still, plenty of foreign performers have played Indonesia in the past. Hikmawan “Indra” Saefullah, who played guitar in the Indonesian indie band Alone at Last from 2002 to 2013, listed Deep Purple, Mick Jagger, Sepultura, Metallica and Green Day, as well as multi-day live music events such as the Java Jazz Festival and Hammersonic.

Lady Gaga was meant to play Jakarta in 2012, with all 52,000 tickets already sold for a concert when several organisations, including the Islamic Defenders Front, objected to the singer’s dance moves and outfits, calling her “a devil worshipper”.

Police subsequently refused to issue an event permit, saying they could not guarantee safety, and the show was ultimately scrapped.

Sutresna said such mass protest campaigns were relatively rare, however, pointing instead to routine logistical and bureaucratic issues as the cause of most event disruptions in Indonesia.

Purely business?

Ye is “a special case” because of his past controversies, according to Saefullah.

The rapper has been widely condemned in recent years for making antisemitic remarks that cost him major sponsorships and performance opportunities.

Last year, he released a song titled “Heil Hitler”, which several streaming platforms banned, after previously expressing admiration for the Nazi dictator in interviews, publicly denying the existence of the Holocaust and saying he identified as a Nazi himself.

Planned Ye concerts in Poland, France, Switzerland and India have been cancelled this year, with venues variously citing security and legal concerns. He was also slated to headline a festival in Britain this summer before the entire event was aborted after he was barred from entering the country.

In January, he took out a full-page advertisement in The Wall Street Journal, explicitly apologising to black and Jewish people, opening up about a previously undiagnosed brain injury and detailing his treatment for bipolar disorder.

Saefullah said Ye had a strong fan base in Indonesia, where rap had long been popular in “inspiring the growth of the hip-hop subculture within the local music scene” – but he still saw opportunism in Ye’s Jakarta booking.

“Regarding him performing only in Jakarta, I see it as a purely business-driven decision,” he said. “Raw Vision Collective capitalised on the situation Ye and his team were facing, with tour dates being cancelled elsewhere.”

Tjahja said the promoter understood “the concerns surrounding Ye’s past public statements” but was “not in a position to comment on an artist’s personal views or ideology”. This Week in Asia has asked Ye’s management for comment.

Yohanes Sulaiman, a lecturer in international relations at Jenderal Achmad Yani University, said Ye’s past remarks were unlikely to be much of an issue in Indonesia, given its tense relationship with Israel, with which it has no formal diplomatic ties.

A number of Indonesian public figures had made antisemitic remarks over the years without consequence, he added.

“In Indonesia, he will probably have a lot of cheerleaders,” Sutresna said. “Unless he suddenly swings in another direction, like supporting [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu … That would be a different story.”

item.title: [SCMP] Dino-mite treasures: inside Singapore’s ‘Fort Knox’ storing playthings of ultra-rich
item.description:
Stored in a climate-controlled environment within what is commonly known as the “Fort Knox of Singapore” rests the skull of a triceratops which once roamed the Earth 66 million years ago.

The jagged edges of its frill and horns are largely intact, and according to its owner, Chaw Wei Yang, 26, it is one of the most complete triceratops skull fossils ever found.

Chaw, who runs Fine Art Storage Services (FASS) located inside Le Freeport, formerly known as Singapore Freeport, along with his partners, acquired the option to the fossil while it was still in the ground in Montana, United States. It was dug up just a few months ago.
item.content:encoded:
Stored in a climate-controlled environment within what is commonly known as the “Fort Knox of Singapore” rests the skull of a triceratops which once roamed the Earth 66 million years ago.

The jagged edges of its frill and horns are largely intact, and according to its owner, Chaw Wei Yang, 26, it is one of the most complete triceratops skull fossils ever found.

Chaw, who runs Fine Art Storage Services (FASS) located inside Le Freeport, formerly known as Singapore Freeport, along with his partners, acquired the option to the fossil while it was still in the ground in Montana, United States. It was dug up just a few months ago.

“I love dinosaurs, and I’m not the only one. It’s a very universal thing – we grew up with dinosaurs, and that kind of segues to why I got into collecting them because for dinosaurs, the appeal is universal. For art, it can be very subjective,” Chaw said. He did not disclose how much he paid for the option and excavation.

In July, a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton called Gus from South Dakota became the world’s most expensive fossil sold at auction, after fetching a record US$50.13 million. At 11.6 metres (38 feet) in length with a skull measuring 137cm (54 inches), Gus is one of the largest T. rexes ever found, according to Sotheby’s.

Natural history artefacts such as fossils and meteorites are becoming increasingly popular among the latest generation of fine art collectors as the lines between the art world and palaeontology blur, according to Art News in May.

The childhood fascination with dinosaurs appeared to be colliding with a new generation of wealth, the outlet reported, quoting experts as saying that the buyers are younger collectors who grew up during the explosion of dinosaur culture in the 1980s and 1990s, when Jurassic Park and natural history museums made it into popular culture.

Chaw’s own fascination began as a child when his mother bought him a mosasaurus tooth from the Singapore Science Centre. “Something unique about this generation is that we grew up with a lot of pop culture and media, and the world has become so connected so people start to find different communities that resonate with them,” he said. “Dinosaurs just speak to the inner child in all of us.”

He is aware of the naysayers who point out that these fossils should be left to be studied by scientists and displayed in museums but argue that there is a symbiotic relationship between private collectors who fund excavations and lovers of palaeontology.

“It’s in the best interest of both parties. For the individuals who dig it up, if they find something unique, special or scientifically significant, they will work with museums and universities to get it studied,” Chaw said. “Obviously, there may be people who are a little bit more money centric, but most of the people that I’ve met and work with, they are all passionate people first.”

Chaw has contacted museums to loan them his fossil but most major institutions already house triceratops fossils in their permanent collections.

Quiet luxury

The triceratops fossil was on display at the FASS space over the course of Formula One week in Singapore alongside meteorites, megalodon teeth and fluorides that are millions of years old.

In the lead-up to last Sunday’s race, high net worth individuals flocked to the city state to attend meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions such as the Milken Institute Asia Summit and Token2049.

It was the perfect time for FASS to show off its one stop service of storing, shipping, insuring and installing fine art and collectibles tax-free. Chaw was unwilling to disclose the exact value of the pieces that FASS handles, but said that it extended into the billions of dollars.

Because of the high value of items in storage, its rooms are humidity- and temperature-controlled and fitted with gas suspension systems instead of water sprinklers in the event of a fire.

Singapore’s appeal as a politically stable safe haven was another draw, he said. “When you’re storing such important or meaningful things, to a collector, you just want to have the best. You want it to be safe, and you want everything to be stored in the best conditions. It’s basically for peace of mind.”

Following a S$3 billion (US$2.3 billion) money-laundering case involving 10 foreign nationals in 2023, Singapore tightened its asset recovery strategy. This included introducing laws that allowed authorities to petition courts to sell seized assets even before conviction, such as fine art, antiques, investment-grade wine, vessels, exotic livestock like fish and reptiles, and racehorses.

Some of the confiscated items from the 2023 case – including jewellery, designer bags and watches – were stored inside a bulletproof, maximum-security vault at Le Freeport before their auction this year.

FASS also connects collectors wanting to acquire pieces from each other. But the laws had little impact on sales since strict know-your-client checks were already performed before the unravelling of the case in 2023, Chaw said.

“There’s very high-profile people that we’ve turned down before, just because they don’t pass the … checks,” he said. “We’re in Singapore and what people appreciate about us is that we are by the law.”

For a select few, FASS puts on private exhibitions, displaying their best pieces, some of which are on sale. Saying that discretion was a priority for his clients, Chaw was unable to disclose the identities of the ultra-high-net-worth individuals and celebrities he hosted this year or how much was transacted during the week.

“We bring out the best in class. This year was more natural history focused, last year was maybe more art focused, maybe next year we could do wine and watches. We try to bring in something unique and significant every year,” Chaw said.

This year, his triceratops was a highlight of the exhibition. And while he admitted there was interest in the fossil over the week, he has no intention of parting with the object of his inner child’s desires just yet.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s second Asean summit presence comes at a price for region
item.description:
US President Donald Trump is expected to drive hard bargains on tariffs and critical minerals in his return to the Asean summit in Manila next month, with Washington seeking greater economic and strategic concessions while remaining hawkish on China.

The Philippines confirmed on Wednesday that Trump would fly in for the summit from November 16 to 18, before attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen that same week.

Trump’s second consecutive appearance at the forum signals continued US engagement despite his preference for one-on-one deals, analysts say. The timing of the trip ahead of an expected meeting with counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen is also seen as a chance for the US to reassure regional partners of its commitment.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump is expected to drive hard bargains on tariffs and critical minerals in his return to the Asean summit in Manila next month, with Washington seeking greater economic and strategic concessions while remaining hawkish on China.

The Philippines confirmed on Wednesday that Trump would fly in for the summit from November 16 to 18, before attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen that same week.

Trump’s second consecutive appearance at the forum signals continued US engagement despite his preference for one-on-one deals, analysts say. The timing of the trip ahead of an expected meeting with counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen is also seen as a chance for the US to reassure regional partners of its commitment.

But they warn that renewed US tariff pressure and demands for closer alignment could push the Association of Southeast Asian Nations members into competing bilateral deals that would undermine economic ties with both superpowers.

“His attendance at two consecutive Asean summits is significant, given his preference for bilateral engagement and transactional diplomacy over multilateral institutions. The fact that the Philippines is a close treaty ally of the US also makes a difference, particularly given their strong defence cooperation and shared security interests in the South China Sea,” said Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

Lin added that Trump’s visit was a positive sign that Southeast Asia remained important to Washington.

“As an ally, President Trump is here to strengthen the Philippines’ position on many issues that confront both countries in Southeast Asia and the wider Indo-Pacific,” said Julio Amador, CEO of Amador Research Services and visiting fellow at Perry World House. “While it is tempting to look at the Apec summit as the main goal, I believe that the East Asia summit, which figures a lot in security issues, is more vital to the visit.”

Security concerns

Analysts said that a large part of Trump’s agenda in attending the Asean summit would deal with trade and economic security.

“A big part of it is to show that the US is still vital to the security of the region, and shoring up its alliances and partnerships and putting forward a case for economic security,” Amador said.

He added that as US foreign policy primarily focused on alliance and security, the visit was also likely to affirm the economic aspect, particularly the Luzon Economic Corridor – a connectivity project that could inject as much as US$100 billion into the Philippine economy – as a crucial part of bilateral ties.

“The administration has made it clear that economic security is now closely linked to national security,” Lin said. “Beyond securing better market access for American products, Washington will likely be looking for concrete commitments on supply-chain security, critical minerals, technology cooperation, AI and greater investment in the US.”

The order of Trump’s stops is “telling”, according to Asean observer Vu Lam. “As chair and treaty ally, Manila has pledged to conclude a legally binding code of conduct in the South China Sea by the end of its chairmanship. Visiting an ally just before Beijing offers reassurance and some leverage,” the Australia-based researcher said.

Collins Chong, a foreign affairs and security analyst at Universiti Malaya, said that Trump’s visit was a calculated move to sustain the momentum of his diplomatic engagement with the region after his trip to Malaysia last year.

“Trump recognises that personal diplomacy and direct engagement with regional leaders remain indispensable tools in preserving American influence, especially at a time when China continues to expand its … presence across Southeast Asia,” Chong said.

Total US-Asean trade in goods and services reached US$686 billion in 2025, reflecting the region’s growing importance. “Asean is now an increasingly important geopolitical and geoeconomic battleground, encompassing critical minerals, semiconductors, energy security, advanced manufacturing, maritime connectivity and diversified supply chains,” he said.

As such, Washington cannot allow Beijing to become the “overwhelmingly dominant economic and strategic reference point” for Asean. “The challenge is not simply to contain China’s military rise, but to prevent Beijing from accumulating structural influence over the industries, infrastructure, technologies and maritime routes, eventually gaining strength to challenge the US in key areas,” Chong said.

“Trump is seeking to translate American market access, security commitments and technological advantages into greater strategic returns, while ensuring that China cannot turn Southeast Asia into an uncontested platform for its expanding regional power.”

Tariff talks

Following a new wave of US tariffs under alleged forced labour practices in its Section 301 investigations in July, levies will continue to be the focus, according to the experts.

“The main difference is that we are moving from the initial tariff shock to a more established pattern of bilateral bargaining,” Lin said. “The pressure on Southeast Asian economies remains, but it is becoming more targeted and tied to specific regulatory and economic-security commitments.”

This could push members into making separate bilateral deals, she added. “Ultimately, Asean cannot prevent its members from pursuing bilateral deals, but it should ensure that these arrangements do not undermine regional economic integration or weaken Asean’s collective position.”

Lam said such agreements were likely, pointing to developments last year, when Thailand agreed to remove tariffs on nearly all US goods and Vietnam gave preferential access to almost all US exports.

“Expect commitments on intellectual property, purchases of US goods and tighter rules on Chinese transshipment too. In return, they hope for lower tariffs and fewer future US trade actions, but nothing is guaranteed. Their concessions are long term, while US tariff relief can be withdrawn at any time,” Lam said.

Trump’s hard bargains in matters such as export controls, supply-chain security, technology governance and trade practices involving third countries could increasingly involve geopolitical considerations, Lin said. “We saw how similar provisions in the earlier agreements with Malaysia and Cambodia became politically sensitive because of China’s concerns about ‘poison pill’ clauses.”

Asean countries faced a difficult balancing act as “they want more predictable access to the US market, but they also need to preserve their economic relationships with China and avoid commitments that could constrain their strategic autonomy”.

item.title: [SCMP] Tsui Ao-lung’s journey from airport worker to Hong Kong fashion champion
item.description:
Tsui Ao-lung did not walk a conventional path to becoming Hong Kong’s newest fashion-design champion. He has no formal training in garment design and he spent three years away from the industry altogether, earning an income moving cargo at the Hong Kong International Airport and waiting restaurant tables to pay off debts from a T-shirt brand he had co-founded. When he finally returned to the craft last year, it was almost by accident: a stylist had asked him to create stage outfits for a concert, so he taught himself how to design for the stage.

It was a circuitous route that led him, on September 5, to claim the top prize at the Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest 2026 (YDC), a highlight of the annual Centrestage showcase, itself a flagship event of the third Hong Kong Fashion Fest, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. Competing against nine other finalists under the theme “You”, the 29-year-old took home the HK$60,000 cash prize, champion title and an overseas internship opportunity sponsored by knitwear manufacturing firm Fang Brothers Knitting.

His winning collection, “The Tide”, draws its name and mood from “Kuang Chao”, a 1970s Cantopop hit by Hong Kong singer Susanna Kwan Kuk-ying. Tsui used the song as a springboard to dive into the journey of a woman’s life across four seasons, capturing her highs, lows and the experience of existence in four hand-stitched pieces.
item.content:encoded:
Tsui Ao-lung did not walk a conventional path to becoming Hong Kong’s newest fashion-design champion. He has no formal training in garment design and he spent three years away from the industry altogether, earning an income moving cargo at the Hong Kong International Airport and waiting restaurant tables to pay off debts from a T-shirt brand he had co-founded. When he finally returned to the craft last year, it was almost by accident: a stylist had asked him to create stage outfits for a concert, so he taught himself how to design for the stage.

It was a circuitous route that led him, on September 5, to claim the top prize at the Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest 2026 (YDC), a highlight of the annual Centrestage showcase, itself a flagship event of the third Hong Kong Fashion Fest, organised by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. Competing against nine other finalists under the theme “You”, the 29-year-old took home the HK$60,000 cash prize, champion title and an overseas internship opportunity sponsored by knitwear manufacturing firm Fang Brothers Knitting.

His winning collection, “The Tide”, draws its name and mood from “Kuang Chao”, a 1970s Cantopop hit by Hong Kong singer Susanna Kwan Kuk-ying. Tsui used the song as a springboard to dive into the journey of a woman’s life across four seasons, capturing her highs, lows and the experience of existence in four hand-stitched pieces.

However, what the judges and the audience could not have anticipated, when the designer’s creations strutted down the catwalk, is that Tsui had let his exacting nature take the wheel, scrapping and overhauling entire looks in the days before the show, with the final touches to his pieces added right before he had to present them. A real-life Project Runway – Hong Kong edition, that is.

We talk to Tsui about winning the competition, his three years away from design, his ambition to eventually launch his own brand again and how he thinks he can work 18 hours a day without ever feeling tired.

What motivated you to enter YDC this year?

It was to tell stories, to express things I wanted to say. I think YDC is a great opportunity. It has a good platform and a complete system that lets people from all walks of life see your work. I never thought of taking part before, because I wanted to try and rely on myself, to strive on my own. But then, at a certain point, I thought, “Since the opportunity is there, why not give it a shot?”

How did it feel to win the contest?

I felt happy, very happy, but also relieved. So many people were screaming. I worked long shifts leading up to the finale. After that, I slept for hours.

What was your biggest challenge?

I used to do casual wear – simple clothes. YDC was my first time doing fittings, organising so many outfits, shoes and so on – I felt like I couldn’t handle it all. When I finished the four designs, I was very unsatisfied. So, I kept tweaking them, completely redoing some of the looks from scratch, and I ended up remaking the pieces I wasn’t happy with after the fittings, working on them up to the last minute before I had to leave for the show.

What was your workspace like?

I actually went back and forth to Guangzhou to make the clothes. A lot of suppliers are concentrated there, so if I needed materials or components, I could buy them straight away. Because I don’t have my own studio, I worked out of a shared “central sample room” – a space used by several shops. I didn’t have a fixed area on the premises, so whenever a space opened up, I’d drag my dress dummy and tools over there to work. Most of the time, I’d wait until late at night, after everyone else had left and the lights were off, so I could spread all my stuff out and sew in peace, staying until 4am or 5am. It took a lot of patience, and I kept pricking my fingers, but that’s how I got it done. Many friends were helping me. I didn’t ask them to, and I never shared what I was making with anyone. But in the last two weeks, they came to the fittings and helped me. I am so grateful.

How did you arrive at the core theme for your winning collection?

I often refer to music and films to capture a mood or feeling. For “The Tide”, the theme came from a Cantopop song called “Kuang Chao”. I came across it and was inspired to take that mood and expand on it. Since the song is about ups and downs, I thought about leaning into a woman’s perspective to explore the cycles of her life, moving through spring, summer, autumn and winter. I also wanted to connect it to the city – you’ll find elements of Hong Kong hidden in the clothes. Whether it’s a person or a place, there will always be moments of glory, but also moments of decline. It’s just as the lyrics go, “It’s them; it is also you and me”.

What was the most important quality you wanted to showcase?

For me, it’s all about the handiwork and hand-stitched details – they really make up the core of the whole collection. Having that focus on craftsmanship gives the collection a natural, cohesive feel.

What first got you into making clothes?

It was a total accident. After secondary school, a friend – my former business partner – had a group of friends who were really passionate about making clothes and starting brands, so I tagged along to join the fun. Back then, our mindset was purely about having a good time and experimenting together. “You make one for me to wear, I make one for you to wear” – that kind of thing. Slowly, everyone else stopped making clothes and abandoned dressmaking. I’m the only one left.

You spent three years away from designing. What was that period like?

During those three years, I actually prepared a lot; I mapped out plans for the next five seasons. I specifically avoided taking on design work because I’m uncompromising – I didn’t want to enter a system of creating commercial filler to make money. I waited tables and moved goods at the airport to make ends meet. Ironically, even while trying hard to avoid seeing them, I’d still spot people wearing clothes from my previous brand on their way to work. I really want to start a brand again, but I know one thing: you have to be ready before you do it. Once you come out, you have to be confident, professional, strong. You can’t just do it half-heartedly.

Describe your creative process.

First, I think of a story. When we actually start making the clothes, we often look at the fabric first and then build on the basic concept, step by step. I write a narrative, and then build the storyline, block by block, although whether it turns out the way I originally intended is a different matter.

How does Hong Kong shape your designs?

I watch a lot of concerts; they often inspire my work. For example, the second look in my collection, the cheongsam – nobody guessed that the inspiration came from one of Eason Chan Yick-shun’s concerts, where he happened to be wearing a belt styled like a corset. I pull inspiration from plenty of other concert looks, too, though I never copy them directly; I just use them as a starting point.

What kind of designer do you want to be?

I’m open to pretty much anything. My advantage, or maybe my flaw, is that I can see the positives in any style, so I don’t mind doing whatever type. But I’m more drawn to pieces with character. I’ll mostly stick to a story-driven line. I want to tell a story naturally, with relevant clothing elements to package it, while keeping my own touch.

What’s your ideal way of working?

I hope it’s one where I don’t have to rest, because I don’t like being inactive. I did YDC and worked 18-hour days – eating just one late-night meal a day – and had absolutely no problem with it. I didn’t feel tired. I can work straight through the night. It’s not just passion – my body’s simply wired that way. It’s like an engine: once it starts, it runs non-stop. Once I start working, I can’t stop.

item.title: [SCMP] Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
item.description:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.
item.content:encoded:
One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world.

The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour.

In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year.

But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces.

While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon.

That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies.

Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers.

“Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS).

“But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.”

The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together.

Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another

Seth Goldstein, Morningstar

Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics.

While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation.

“Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein.

The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said.

Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders.

The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”.

“This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter.

Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject.

Can Tesla do without China?

At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025.

Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale.

Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers.

Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line.

Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced. It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain.

China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS.

“Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said.

“That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.”

Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added.

Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account.

Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May.

Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors.

And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies.

The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised

Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney

Between Washington and Beijing

Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor.

Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May.

Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus.

The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June.

But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”.

Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations.

How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang.

“The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.”

She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.”

Tesla lays the first bricks

Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China.

It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry.

Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said.

CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market.

Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience.

“A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm.

Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said.

SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology.

Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments.

However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake.

While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said.

Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’

However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”.

“So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.”

Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call.

A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator.

Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US.

“There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research.

Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said.

Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added.

These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026.

Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11.

“The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said.

Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO.

“China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

item.title: [SCMP] A rural city, once known for livestock, now provides China’s AI computing fuel
item.description:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, Ulanqab – a city several hundred kilometres northwest of Beijing whose Mongolian name means “red cliff pass” – was known for its windswept pastureland, where cattle grazed and potatoes thrived under long hours of sunlight.

Its economy hinged on the weather, driven by the cool, strong breezes sweeping through the Yinshan mountain range.

Today, giant wind turbines stand next to livestock across those sloping grasslands.

As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, the same climate that has sustained Ulanqab’s pastoral economy is turning this Inner Mongolian city into one of China’s most coveted industrial assets.

Earlier this month, Chinese renewable energy company Envision Group brought its Galaxy Campus online in Ulanqab. The AI computing facility has, at its heart, a 120,000-square-metre AI data centre, roughly the area of 20 standard football pitches, according to a company statement.

Designed to accommodate up to one million AI accelerators, the campus has a planned power capacity of over two gigawatts, a scale that would make it one of the world’s largest AI computing facilities.

For comparison, Colossus 2, the massive US-based AI data centre run by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, has a projected 1.5-gigawatt IT power capacity, according to a ranking by consultancy Epoch AI.

Envision selected the Ulanqab location because it could pair computing infrastructure directly with renewable power, with the Galaxy Campus partly powered by Envision wind farms, according to the firm.

Ulanqab accounts for about one-tenth of China’s total wind resources and one-third of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s, according to China’s Xinhua news agency.

“Much of that wind once simply blew past, wasted,” said Yang Wenlong, a project director at Envision Group. “Now it can be turned into electricity for computing, and then into tokens.”

About 67 per cent of Ulanqab’s energy was powered by green electricity, including solar power, Yang noted.

A decade-long pivot

Ulanqab’s shift from raising cattle and potato harvesting to the AI frontier has followed a decade-long path.

In 2013, Huawei Technologies began working with the Ulanqab municipal government to expand its data centre presence there. Five years later, US tech giant Apple announced plans to host its iCloud service on data centres in the city, the same year Chinese cloud platform UCloud began building its own facility in Ulanqab.

Short video giant Kuaishou initiated construction of a data centre in 2020, and completed the first phase of a centre designed for 300,000 servers several years later.

Traditional data centre operators VNET, Centrin Data and Chindata have since added green, AI-focused computing projects in Ulanqab, and Hangzhou-based AI model start-up DeepSeek was reportedly set to add one gigawatt of computing capacity in the city earlier this year.

As of June, Ulanqab had signed 89 data centre deals, 86 of which were AI computing projects, according to local government figures.

The city has a combined 12.5 gigawatts of capacity under development or planned, three times the 4.2 gigawatts projected for Johor, the southern state of Malaysia that has emerged as one of the largest data centre sites in the Asia-Pacific region, according to recent research by investment bank Goldman Sachs.
