“We are no longer selling computing power; we are selling tokens,” said Liu Huansuo, deputy director of Ulanqab’s big data management bureau, referring to the industry’s preferred measure for the units of text processed by AI models.

China’s appetite for those tokens has exploded in recent years. Daily consumption rose from about 100 billion at the beginning of 2024 to 100 trillion by the end of 2025, before exceeding 140 trillion in March 2026, according to government data.

This surge in token demand is driving a greater need for the electricity and computing infrastructure required to produce them. For Ulanqab, the wind blowing across the grasslands is no longer merely an energy resource – it helps to power an AI query.

And every AI token comes with a cost.

The power economy

“Every one million tokens generated requires two to three kilowatt-hours of electricity,” said Luo Xiyong of data centre operator Zhonglian Data.

In Ulanqab, data centre operators have access to some of China’s cheapest power.

Rates vary by supply arrangement, but some operators have secured electricity for about 0.35 yuan (US$0.05) per kilowatt-hour, less than half the roughly 0.70 yuan charged in eastern provinces. Electricity can account for 60 to 70 per cent of a data centre’s operating costs, making even modest savings significant.

At full utilisation, a one-gigawatt AI computing centre might consume as much as 8.76 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity a year. Cutting the electricity cost by just 0.1 yuan per kilowatt-hour might reduce a centre’s annual power bill by about 876 million yuan.

For China’s burgeoning AI industry, which is still searching for viable ways to monetise its models, cheap power is no marginal advantage – it is a central part of the business model.

But it is only half the equation. The electricity consumed by computing equipment ultimately becomes heat that has to be removed.

That is how Ulanqab’s cold, dry climate provides another advantage. With an annual average temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius, the city can use outside air as a natural cooling resource for much of the year, reducing reliance on energy-intensive mechanical systems and leaving more electricity available for computing.

Power usage effectiveness (PUE) measures the ratio between a data centre’s total electricity consumption and the electricity delivered to its servers. A PUE of 1.0 means every watt goes directly to computing, while a higher figure indicates more power is consumed by supporting systems such as cooling and power conversion.

Leading data-centre clusters in the region have a PUE below 1.15, against a national average of close to 1.5, meaning that more of each watt reaches its chips.

A difference of only a few cents can translate into hundreds of millions of yuan in savings at gigawatt scale. Those efficiencies matter because the amount of electricity consumed by computing has been rapidly rising.

China’s data centres consumed about 170 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.6 per cent of national power use, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA).

By 2030, annual consumption by the sector was expected to reach about 800 billion kilowatt-hours, nearly five times 2025 levels, and account for roughly 6 per cent of national electricity use, according to Wang Hongzhi, director of the NEA.

A coordinated system

The race to secure electricity for AI infrastructure is not unique to China. In the US, the rapid expansion of AI data centres has raised concerns about whether existing power grids can keep pace with demand, with some projects facing delays because of a bottleneck in securing enough electricity.

This is in contrast to Ulanqab, where AI giants and tech behemoths are betting that its wind and solar power, combined with a cooler climate, can provide a cheaper and more sustainable foundation for the next generation of AI infrastructure.

For China, the challenge is not only generating enough electricity, but also ensuring that electricity supply and computing capacity grow in tandem.

In 2026, China’s Government Work Report called for the coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply for the first time, reflecting Beijing’s push to better align its rapidly expanding AI infrastructure with the country’s power system.

The concept, known as “computing-power and electricity coordination”, aimed to bring together electricity generation, grid capacity, energy storage and computing resources so that renewable power could be used more efficiently to support growing AI demand.

Jiang Yi, spokesman for the National Development and Reform Commission, described the new power grid as providing stable, clean electricity, the computing network as the “brain” directing intelligent power-grid scheduling and renewable energy consumption, and the communications network as the “highway” supporting cross-regional computing.

That vision goes beyond simply building more data centres. It requires linking electricity, computing and communications infrastructure into a more coordinated, national system.

For Ulanqab, that could make its advantages more valuable. Its wind farms provide renewable electricity, data centres then convert that power into computing capacity, and a national network could help deliver that capacity to users far beyond Inner Mongolia.

But China’s computing boom has created another challenge: not all that capacity is being used.

While demand for AI computing is surging in some of the country’s biggest technology centres, large amounts of capacity elsewhere remain underused, leaving servers, power infrastructure and expensive data centre facilities running below their potential.

Data from the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT) puts the gap in stark terms. In 2025, China’s intelligent-computing centres had about 3.8 billion card-hours of intelligent-computing capacity available, but only about 1.4 billion card-hours were actually used, putting utilisation at just 36.8 per cent.

CAICT has called for closer coordination between computing supply and demand, including better scheduling of computing resources and more precise matching between users and available capacity.

The mismatch reflects the geography of China’s computing buildout. Regions such as Ulanqab have attracted data centres because of cheap electricity, abundant land and favourable climates, while much of the demand for AI computing remains concentrated in China’s eastern cities and affluent regions, where technology companies and users are based.

Moving up the value chain

For Ulanqab, the next challenge is therefore not simply building more servers, but making sure those servers are connected to real demand.

The city is now seeking to move up the AI value chain. Under a three-year action plan for 2026-28, Ulanqab plans to expand computing capacity to more than 200,000 petaflops – a measurement of computing capacity – by 2026 and develop a platform for trading and settling AI tokens.

The plan calls for Ulanqab to evolve from a data centre hub into a broader computing and AI services centre, focusing on green computing for large AI model training and inference, while encouraging investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware, AI software and talent.

The aim is to capture more value from its renewable power: not simply selling electricity or computing capacity, but turning that power into AI computing and ultimately into the tokens generated by AI models.

For a user sitting thousands of kilometres away, an AI query may take only seconds to answer.

Behind that response, however, is a chain of infrastructure stretching back to places such as Ulanqab: servers drawing electricity, cooling systems removing heat and wind turbines turning the movement of air across the grasslands into power.

The next time someone asks a chatbot a question, part of the answer may begin with the wind passing through the grasslands of Inner Mongolia – transformed first into electricity, then computing power and finally into the words that appear on a screen.

item.title: [SCMP] Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
item.description:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.
item.content:encoded:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.

Rather than operating via a single entity, this public capital flows through a layered matrix of national funds, local investment vehicles, state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately managed funds. It is a system that converts top-down policy priorities into private-market bets, with an alternative perspective on what can be considered a return on investment.

Last year, state-affiliated investors supplied more than 90 per cent of the committed capital tracked in China’s private-equity market, a surge from just under 79 per cent in 2021, according to domestic data provider Zerone.

This mandate comes directly from the top. At a high-level national science and technology gathering in Beijing on July 8, President Xi Jinping urged financial capital firms to “invest early, invest small, invest for the long term and invest in hard technology”.

How this capital is deployed could determine whether China will succeed in its ambitions to become a self-reliant tech superpower – or suffocate its economy under the weight of state-engineered overcapacity.

How the money moves

“2018 was roughly the turning point for us,” said Shen Qinhua, founding partner of Puhua Capital, a Hangzhou-based investment firm with about 40 billion yuan (US$5.91 billion) under management. Puhua aimed to raise between 7 billion and 8 billion yuan in 2026, with state-affiliated investors expected to account for about 90 per cent of the total, he said.

According to Shen, it was around eight years ago that traditional private-business owners in eastern Zhejiang province started to pull back their investments in Puhua, as they realised that venture funds’ long holding periods had failed to match their liquidity expectations.

China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage

– Zhou Kaibing, Hangzhou Venture Capital Association

Around the same time, dollar funds began retreating amid escalating US-China tensions. More recently, restrictions on investment in sensitive technologies from both sides have deepened the financial divide, while Beijing’s aggressive push into strategic technologies has drawn a diverse array of state investors.

This state support arrives in vastly different forms and at distinct stages of a company’s life cycle.

For CXMT, which is headed for a blockbuster public market debut in Shanghai next week, a combination of national, provincial and municipal investors supplied the massive capital, credit support and project construction resources required to build a capital-intensive memory chipmaker from scratch. Industrial and private investors came later.

It is one of the clearest examples of the “Hefei model”, under which the provincial capital of central China’s Anhui uses state investment vehicles to back strategic industries, absorb early risk and anchor companies locally before bringing in market capital.

By contrast, state funds entered Unitree Robotics much later in the game. That financing came after the robot maker had already proven its technological and commercial viability, timing that aligned with Beijing’s elevation of robotics to a strategic priority.

Unicorn artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek, initially funded entirely by private wealth, only recently drew backing from the national AI fund after emerging as a powerful symbol of China’s challenge to US tech supremacy.

Hong Kong-listed Zhipu, whose market cap at the market close on Friday was HK$585.95 billion (US$74.72 billion), attracted a cluster of local government funds when it neared its initial public offering in January, as cities vied for a stake to secure a share in the booming AI sector – or remain economically relevant.

One main delivery mechanism for state capital is the fund-of-funds model.

Puhua Capital, for instance, has twice been selected to manage sub-funds backed by the National SME Development Fund, which is financed by central and local fiscal capital alongside smaller state and institutional investors.

In this set-up, the national fund typically provides a 30 per cent anchor commitment. Puhua would raise another 30 per cent to 40 per cent from provincial, municipal or district-level state vehicles, before securing the remaining balance and deciding where to base the fund.

Puhua would retain its day-to-day investment autonomy, but operate under strict oversight. An appointed observer, separate from the investment committee, could join deal discussions from an early stage and veto proposed investments.

Furthermore, at least 70 per cent of the capital must be deployed into “522” companies – businesses with no more than 200 million yuan in annual sales, 200 million yuan in assets and 500 employees. Performance metrics and related-party transactions would be regularly audited.

“The requirements are higher,” Shen said, “but so is the support for policy direction and industrial coordination.”

In this way, a fund-of-funds brings in broader outside capital while steering it to policy priorities. Meanwhile, the National Venture Capital Guidance Fund, launched late last year, operates further upstream, channelling central fiscal money through regional funds into hundreds of professionally managed sub-funds focused strictly on early-stage technologies.

Some point towards specific industries. For example, the “Big Fund” – China’s flagship semiconductor investor – concentrates capital into this fiercely competitive arena, taking equity stakes directly and backing specialist funds across the chip supply chain.

Others can be deployed through local platforms that take stakes or finance construction, as in Hefei, as well as via investments and acquisitions by state-owned companies.

Who bears the risk?

Capital is pouring into strategic industries through funds with longer lifespans as exit routes expand. Platforms like Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market and the Hong Kong stock exchange now allow these companies to go public sooner, enabling broader retail investors to share in the potential gains.

“A loop is gradually taking shape, directing more capital towards hard tech companies,” said Mi Lei, founder of CAS Star, a venture-capital firm spun out of an institute under the state-run Chinese Academy of Sciences. The firm’s early bets on China’s photonics sector have begun to see tangible returns amid the AI boom.

However, state investors and private funds do not always share the same scorecard. While a market fund is judged mostly on financial returns, local governments must also account for the number of factories built, jobs created and taxes generated – competing goals that can weaken financial discipline and fuel intercity rivalries.

This local tournament has made China’s industrial policy unusually entrepreneurial – and competitive. Beijing signals the strategic direction, while cities fiercely contest fund structures, industrial estates, credit support and real-world applications.

In the nascent stages of an industry, this rivalry can foster healthy development, or what Shen described as “a hundred flowers blooming”. But it can also lead to severe overcrowding, driven by local governments’ fear of missing out on the next big macroeconomic wave.

The solar panel and electric vehicle (EV) sectors offer stark cautionary tales for today’s policy darlings, such as AI, semiconductors and embodied intelligence.

Expanding production capacity can benefit a single city seeking to boost its local economy, but when dozens of cities replicate the strategy simultaneously, the result is crippling overcapacity and collapsing profit margins on a nationwide basis.

“China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage,” said Zhou Kaibing, chairman of the Hangzhou Venture Capital Association. He noted that some companies with little initial appetite for scaling up began to aggressively add capacity after winning government support.

The structural risks of this approach were highlighted by state broadcaster CCTV in April through the downfall of Neta, a once-prominent EV brand owned by Hozon Auto.

Local governments in Tongxiang in Zhejiang province, Yichun in central Jiangxi province, and Nanning in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region all took equity stakes in Hozon, providing factories, land, subsidies and financing to secure production bases within their regions – even as the carmaker remained deeply unprofitable.

As its products lost ground in a brutally competitive domestic market, the company fell into court-supervised restructuring in 2025. The failure has put billions of yuan in state-backed equity, subsidies and fixed industrial assets at risk.

This raises an uncomfortable question for policy architects: are these losses an acceptable cost of doing business in a nascent industry, or do they represent a fundamental failure of discipline in public investment?

Zhou argued that to mitigate these risks, governments should avoid trying to act as talent scouts themselves. Instead, they should delegate capital management to professional fund managers, who are better equipped to pick market winners and diversify risk.

The state investment system excels at moving money, but it is still learning how – and where – to take risks, he said.

Course correction

Beijing, however, is very much aware of these structural vulnerabilities.

At the same science and technology gathering in Beijing, Xi issued a pointed warning, saying that regions must adapt policy to local conditions rather than blindly chase hot sectors or engage in wasteful, copycat development and “involution-style” competition.

The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure. You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return

– Mi Lei, CAS Star

Policymakers are now attempting a delicate balancing act: mobilising unprecedented capital for technology while imposing rigorous discipline on how it is deployed.

In recent years, this policy response has been rolled out in stages. The State Council’s 2024 policy document, which introduced 17 guidelines on promoting high-quality venture capital, served as the sector’s broadest overhaul since 2016.

It encouraged “patient capital” with a more long-term outlook, shifting the evaluation metrics from a deal-by-deal basis to that of a fund’s full life cycle, while protecting managers from liability for honest failures and broadening exit strategies beyond initial public offerings.

By 2025, new rules shifted the focus directly onto government fund management. This guidance curbed overlapping funds and duplicate local investments, demanded more professional management and called for a greater tolerance for legitimate, due-diligence-backed investment losses.

This year, the State Council’s guidance for investment approval extended the course correction to the factories, industrial estates and public liabilities that often accompany state-backed investments. It also tightened its oversight of fixed-asset projects, enabling it to halt disorderly capacity expansion while introducing lifetime responsibility for officials whose unlawful investment decisions cause serious economic consequences.

“The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure,” said CAS Star’s Mi. “You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return.”

The ultimate test for the equity investment model with Chinese characteristics is whether its bureaucracy can not only learn to accept the inevitable losers that are inherent to venture capital, but also retain the discipline required to cut their losses after failed bets.

item.title: [SCMP] Apple’s biggest-ever leak happened in India. Will firms rethink their China relocations?
item.description:
When Apple set its sights on India as its next promising market, CEO Tim Cook planned to take a leaf out of the company’s China playbook – a retail and manufacturing strategy that had paid hefty dividends to the US tech giant.

“We are, in essence, taking what we learned in China years ago and how we scale to China and bringing that to bear,” Cook told investors in February 2023. The company had just seen record quarterly sales in the Indian market, and was just weeks ahead of the opening of Apple’s first stores in the country. “India is a hugely exciting market for us.”

At the time, Cook’s optimism in India also carried a degree of pragmatism. To navigate the rising trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies and avoid US tariffs on China-made goods – both the duties already in place and those likely to be imposed in the future – Apple had bet on India to become its next manufacturing hub.
item.content:encoded:
When Apple set its sights on India as its next promising market, CEO Tim Cook planned to take a leaf out of the company’s China playbook – a retail and manufacturing strategy that had paid hefty dividends to the US tech giant.

“We are, in essence, taking what we learned in China years ago and how we scale to China and bringing that to bear,” Cook told investors in February 2023. The company had just seen record quarterly sales in the Indian market, and was just weeks ahead of the opening of Apple’s first stores in the country. “India is a hugely exciting market for us.”

At the time, Cook’s optimism in India also carried a degree of pragmatism. To navigate the rising trade tensions between the world’s two largest economies and avoid US tariffs on China-made goods – both the duties already in place and those likely to be imposed in the future – Apple had bet on India to become its next manufacturing hub.

India began to deliver. In 2022, the country produced around 6 per cent of all iPhones, but by 2026, that figure was expected to surpass 25 per cent, according to data from Counterpoint Research.

However, this year Cook’s vision faced a sobering reality check. In June, a massive cyberattack by hacking group World Leaks hit Tata Electronics, Apple’s Bengaluru-based partner for iPhone parts and assembly, leaking more than 200,000 files on the dark web. Analysts called the leak the biggest in the company’s history.

“India has proven it can scale production; now it must prove it can scale trust,” said Christopher Tang, a professor specialising in global supply chain management at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).

While India managed to ramp up labour-intensive assembly, attract major suppliers such as Foxconn and Tata, and leveraged government incentives, the incident revealed that the ecosystem still needed to catch up in three vital areas: information governance, supplier discipline, and cyber-operational integration, Tang noted.

“India can become a major global manufacturing hub,” Tang said. “But overtaking China as the world’s premier factory is a much higher bar.”

The breach may slow Apple’s willingness to transfer its most sensitive product data

Christopher Tang, UCLA

Made in India?

The files from the Tata leak included Apple’s component and supplier lists, as well as photos of the firm’s unreleased iPhone 18 Pro, exposing sensitive details of the chips on its main circuit board as well as hundreds of parts, according to Reuters.

Apple, Tata and the Indian authorities were reportedly investigating the incident. Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment.

“This leak is significant because Apple’s secret sauce that creates its competitive advantage depends not only on Apple’s own systems but also on every node in its manufacturing network,” Tang said.

“The breach may slow Apple’s willingness to transfer its most sensitive product data or highest-complexity product ramps too quickly to newer hubs,” he added.

This year’s leak was only the most recent test of India’s fast-expanding manufacturing capabilities. In 2024, Tata suffered a fire that led to a production halt at its facilities in Tamil Nadu, a state in the country’s south.

Despite the fallout, analysts said they did not expect the breach to diminish the importance of India in Apple’s ongoing efforts to diversify its global manufacturing.

“The current situation will be very much of a remediation-and-move-on situation, rather than an existential threat to Tata’s partnership with Apple,” said Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research.

“Ultimately, we believe this doesn’t halt India’s momentum, but it will surely lead to an industry-wide re-evaluation” of the information technology infrastructure of electronic manufacturers, Pathak said.

Still, the breach cast a shadow over Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s “Make in India” initiative to transform India into a global manufacturing and innovation hub, challenging China’s dominance as the “world’s factory”.

The expansion of Apple’s manufacturing network in India helped drive the country’s broader industrial upgrade. In recent years, the US tech giant’s major suppliers, including Foxconn and Tata, have scaled up operations heavily across the country from Tamil Nadu to neighbouring state Karnataka.

Foxconn, also known as Hon Hai Precision Industry, injected another US$1.5 billion into its India unit last year.

However, Apple’s aggressive expansion plans in India also faced pressure from its home country. US President Donald Trump said publicly last May that he had asked Cook to stop building plants in India and step up production in America.

Beyond Apple, India has also attracted South Korea’s Samsung and Chinese handset makers including Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo to build production bases there.

India has surged to become the world’s second-largest mobile phone maker by volume, with 99.2 per cent of its locally sold handsets produced inside the country, according to official data.

Just last week, New Delhi unveiled a new US$6.5 billion initiative, the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme, to incentivise smartphone brands that produce their devices locally and source domestic components. The initiative targets US$460 billion in domestic mobile phone production over the next five years, with a significant increase in exports.

Hedging or diversifying?

India has been gaining an increasingly significant role in Apple’s supply chain. Last year, Cook revealed that most of the iPhones sold in the US were produced in India. In the meantime, almost all iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and AirPods products sold in the US market were made in Vietnam.

China, on the other hand, would continue to manufacture the vast majority of products sold in the rest of the world, according to Cook.

Apple’s geographic diversification efforts, known as the “China plus one” strategy, sought to shift away from total reliance on the Chinese manufacturing powerhouse amid geopolitical tensions and a supply bottleneck.

The diversification efforts accelerated during the Covid-19 pandemic, when virus control protocols in China dragged some of Apple’s product shipments to a halt at one point.

“For Apple, ‘China plus one’ is primarily a hedge against geopolitical risk, rather than a decision driven purely by commercial efficiency,” said Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.

“This incident will not reverse its strategy, but it reminds Apple that diversification is not a simple copy-and-paste of the China playbook,” Sun said.

When talking about China’s manufacturing advantages, observers have usually focused on China’s low cost, efficiency and sheer scale, while underestimating its suppliers’ ‘soft power’ in commercial confidentiality, rapid response and systemic risk control, he added.

“Supply chain security is, in itself, a core manufacturing capability,” Sun said.

While Apple has previously faced product leaks in the form of unauthorised photos and smuggled parts from factory floors – including facilities in China – the scale of the recent cyber breach was unprecedented, according to analysts.

Every added node is an added point of vulnerability

Sun Chenghao, Tsinghua University

Sun noted that a leak of this magnitude was highly unlikely to hit long-established Chinese Apple suppliers, although the possibility could not be wholly dismissed.

“The key is not just firewalls; it’s the organisational discipline, tiered authorisation, physical isolation, supplier compliance auditing and a culture of secrecy forged over decades of collaboration,” Sun said.

A global supply chain alert

Analysts noted that the strategy, adopted to mitigate geopolitical risks, inadvertently exposed the supply chain to other risks.

“The more fragmented a supply chain becomes, the more a company must share blueprints, test data, supplier lists, quality standards and internal workflows across more touch points,” Sun said.

“Every added node is an added point of vulnerability.”

A source within Apple’s supply chain noted that cyberattacks are a universal threat, which is increasingly prevalent after the explosion of artificial intelligence technology.

“It’s not just Tata; all suppliers have been under attack in some way,” said the person, who asked to remain anonymous due to the sensitivity of the matter. “What happened to Tata sounded an alert across the supply chain globally.”

While India faces immediate scrutiny, experts stressed that cybersecurity required an ongoing arms race extending beyond any single company or region.

“No country or supplier ecosystem is immune,” UCLA’s Tang said.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s shoppers love Chinese e-commerce. Its factories pay the price
item.description:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.
item.content:encoded:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.

“Most items are much cheaper than in the Malaysian market. It’s hard to compare because they come directly from factories or warehouses in China,” said Esha, who works for a competing e-commerce site.

Delivery takes at least two weeks, far longer than many of the app’s local rivals. But that delay has had the opposite effect to the one you might expect.

“With the long wait, it makes more sense to buy almost every week, so the wait feels shorter when parcels keep arriving every week,” Esha said, adding that she still used local platforms for urgent orders.

Many Malaysians are now doing the same. Since the app’s launch in the country last December, social media has been awash with delighted shoppers showing off their hauls, from smartphones to sofas, rolls of toilet paper and even bags of cement.

But surging demand for goods shipped direct from China through the likes of Pinduoduo often comes at the expense of local retailers and manufacturers that struggle to match their Chinese rivals’ deep discounts.

Meanwhile, the millions of parcels flooding into Malaysia and the waste they create are testing the limits of the country’s ability to collect and dispose of it all.

Disappearing margins

Pinduoduo is far from the only e-commerce platform active in Malaysia. Small local businesses, especially in physical retail and manufacturing, have already seen their margins shrink amid intense competition from earlier entrants like Lazada and Shopee.

Still, the app’s arrival has prompted an outcry from local businesses, who complain that direct shipments from far larger competitors in China have unfairly priced them out of their own market.

Shipping direct from China is the strategy that has powered Pinduoduo’s growth since its founding in 2015, giving more established e-commerce players such as Taobao and JD.com a run for their money. Lazada and Taobao are subsidiaries of Alibaba Group, which also owns the South China Morning Post.

Pinduoduo built its empire on a simple premise: allow consumers to pool their purchases into bulk orders directly with factories and wholesalers to get better deals.

“The influx of low-priced products from foreign e-commerce platforms is putting tremendous pressure on Malaysian retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers, particularly micro and small businesses,” said Chin Chee Seong, president of the SME Association of Malaysia, an umbrella body for the country’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Chin said operational costs had shot up by 80 per cent or more this year, citing an SME Association survey in April that found 76 per cent of respondents reported being hit hard by rising fuel and energy costs, with 45 per cent bracing themselves for a cash-flow crunch over the next six months.

“Malaysian SMEs are being squeezed from both sides – rising operating costs and increasingly aggressive price competition. Many simply cannot afford to keep reducing their prices,” he said.

A widespread slump in SME activity would be disastrous for the economy. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for nearly 97 per cent of all registered businesses in Malaysia and employ around 8 million people, roughly half the entire workforce.

“As local shops and businesses lose sales or cease operations, they will reduce hiring and reduce demand for supporting services such as banking, advertising, accounting and other business services,” said Lee Heng Guie, executive director of the Socio-Economic Research Centre, a Malaysian think tank.

“Closed shops result in commercial and retail outlet vacancies, and the landlords may be forced to reduce rents to attract fewer available tenants, reducing property income.”

Retailers of imported consumer goods, from fashion to general merchandise, are likely to be the most immediate and visible casualties. Yet economists warn that the greater danger is that posed to Malaysia’s all-important manufacturing sector.

The rapid shift to buying electronics, apparel, footwear, cosmetics and furniture from overseas sellers could cause local factories to permanently lose their share of the domestic market, said economist Yeah Kim Leng of Sunway University.

“The distinction matters because retail displacement can be transitional as traders pivot to services or niche products, whereas manufacturing capacity, once lost, is far harder to rebuild,” he said.

Trashy dilemma

E-commerce began taking root in Malaysia in the mid-2010s, but demand truly exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when strict movement restrictions forced millions of people to do their shopping online between 2020 and 2022.

That habit has become even more deeply ingrained in the years since. An estimated 900 million parcels were delivered across Malaysia in 2025, according to the latest available government data, a multifold increase from the 52 million a decade earlier.

The appeal for e-commerce players is clear. A February note from equity and market analysts at Kenanga Research forecast that the value of e-commerce merchandise in Malaysia would reach 1.5 trillion ringgit in 2027, up from 1.2 trillion ringgit in 2024 (US$268.9 billion).

But this penchant for hyper-consumption could overwhelm the country’s capacity to deal with the vast amounts of rubbish generated.

Malaysia’s 135 landfills are already close to capacity, handling an average of 39,000 tonnes of solid waste daily, according to government figures from last year. Any increase in e-commerce shipments will almost certainly add to the growing trash pile.

The government has also pointed to a low recycling rate of 37.9 per cent of recoverable materials and poor waste separation practices at household and local council levels.

“The growth of online shopping, driven partly by competitive prices and convenience, has increased the volume of packaging waste,” said Randolph Jeremiah, vice-president of the non-profit Environmental Protection Society Malaysia.

“Although some online platforms, retailers and manufacturers have begun reducing packaging and switching to more recyclable materials, such as paper filling instead of polystyrene, these efforts may not be sufficient to keep pace with rising consumption.”

A raft of government policies has been introduced in an attempt to modernise solid waste management, broaden the use of sustainable plastics and materials, encourage recycling and reduce waste generation.

But grand plans meant little if the problem was not addressed at the source, said Jeremiah, adding that efforts to reduce unnecessary packaging by a handful of platforms, retailers and manufacturers needed to be extended across the entire supply chain.

“At the same time, consumers should make more informed purchasing decisions and practice proper waste separation and recycling,” he added.

Fair play

The overseas e-commerce blitz is not all bad news for Malaysia, however. For some, losing business in one area opens up opportunities in another.

“We had a 40 per cent drop in demand over the past few months for small parcel deliveries because a lot of people can just get their items delivered straight to their homes,” said a local courier operator who asked not to be named.

“But demand has gone up for shipments of bigger items like furniture and kitchenware and even machinery for factories and construction.”

An early investment in warehouse space in Guangzhou, China’s outbound shipping hub, made all the difference for them in securing a steady stream of clients, the operator said, adding: “A lot of our customers nowadays buy direct from factories in China, so having our own warehouse there makes it easy to arrange shipments for them.”

Even entrepreneurs worried about the fallout from direct-to-consumer sales from overseas enjoy the savings as shoppers.

“You must also look at the other side [of the coin]. The consumer is very happy. I’m very happy that I can buy my socks for just 12 ringgit,” said the SME Association’s Chin.

What local businesses wanted was not to stop Pinduoduo and other foreign e-commerce giants selling in Malaysia, he said, but a level playing field.

Under Malaysian law, a 10 per cent sales tax on low-value goods took effect in 2024 to cover imported items worth 500 ringgit or less. But trade groups say many direct overseas shipments slip through untaxed, giving foreign sellers an edge.

Local industries have also warned that directly shipped items such as electronics and toys are not subject to Malaysian safety regulations and may endanger consumers.

“Malaysian businesses should not be disadvantaged simply because they pay local taxes, employ Malaysian workers and comply with our laws and regulations,” Chin said. “We must protect consumer interests without sacrificing Malaysian businesses, jobs and our domestic manufacturing ecosystem.”

When unveiling next year’s budget on October 9, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government would introduce an e-commerce bill at the next parliamentary sitting to close legislative and enforcement loopholes and protect local businesses from unfair competition.

But the government must do more than just draft a new law, said Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

“Malaysian entrepreneurs are not asking for government handouts. They are not asking for competition to be shut down entirely. They only want fairness, so that competition is fair,” he told parliament during the budget debate.

“[Foreign e-commerce sites] need to establish a local presence. Work with local businesses, open offices and hire workers in this country … I am proposing a middle ground, not shutting them down entirely.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘A pack of lies’: Abby Choi’s mother rejects claims Kwong family repaid her debts
item.description:
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”.

Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment.

Wrapping up her five-day testimony in the High Court, Cheung also rejected the defence’s suggestion that she was so addicted to mahjong that Choi had to pledge a property she received as a wedding gift to secure a HK$4 million mortgage to repay her mother’s debts.
item.content:encoded:
The mother of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung has denied in court that she was repeatedly in debt because of gambling, calling her former son-in-law’s claim that he had financially supported her “a pack of lies”.

Cheung Yin-fa accused Alex Kwong Kong-chi on Monday of acting unscrupulously by demanding the return of HK$150,000 in shopping expenses she owed him, while failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million he had received from Choi for investment.

Wrapping up her five-day testimony in the High Court, Cheung also rejected the defence’s suggestion that she was so addicted to mahjong that Choi had to pledge a property she received as a wedding gift to secure a HK$4 million mortgage to repay her mother’s debts.

Cheung appeared emotional as she responded to the defence’s contention that Kwong, who said he had run a restaurant in mainland China and worked as a parallel betting agent in Macau, had helped repay her debts and supported her over the years.

“This Kwong family of brutes repaid my debts? Impossible,” she said. “How can he tell such a lie? Is he human? It’s all a pack of lies.”

She also denied ever receiving HK$7.5 million from Kwong through a luxury watch company, saying the money was simply a return of funds she had given him via a currency exchange shop.

Kwong, 31, is accused of conspiring with his father and elder brother to murder his ex-wife after parts of the 28-year-old’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were found at a flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Village in February 2023.

He is standing trial on a joint murder charge alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35.

Kwong Kau, a retired police sergeant, has pleaded not guilty to preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body, while his two sons pleaded guilty to that charge before the trial.

Prosecutors argue the family feud stemmed from the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin. The father, the property’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the luxury home and enlisted his two sons to help kill her so that he could keep it.

Under cross-examination, Alex Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, said his client did not oppose the sale and had been asked by Choi to persuade his father to sign a power of attorney allowing her to negotiate with prospective buyers.

Cheung reiterated that the entire Kwong family had been reluctant to sell the flat until she threatened legal action.

Raffell cited a series of text conversations that he said showed Alex Kwong had previously given his former mother-in-law more than HK$500,000.

Cheung rejected that interpretation, saying she owed Kwong only HK$150,000 for shopping expenses. She added that he had given her daughter HK$370,000 in profit from the sale of a car that his ex-wife had bought.

On her gambling habits, Cheung acknowledged that she occasionally visited mahjong parlours with friends and gambled up to HK$100,000 for “entertainment”, but stressed she had never run up debts so severe that debt collectors harassed her family.

Raffell suggested that Choi helped her mother clear her debts by taking out a second mortgage of up to HK$4 million from a high-rise property at the Manhattan Hill residential estate in Lai Chi Kok, which she received from the father of her partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, as a wedding gift.

The counsel noted that the white Toyota Alphard that Cheung had been using to travel to court in the present case was splashed with red paint in February this year, which he said was indicative of her financial difficulties.

Messaging records showed that Cheung complained to Detective Constable Ko Yan-ki, the chief investigating officer of the murder case, that she had been harassed by a woman she met in a mahjong parlour in Mong Kok over a monetary dispute she thought had been resolved seven years ago.

Raffell also highlighted text exchanges between Cheung and Choi, in which the witness acknowledged she would occasionally play mahjong “till daybreak” and that what she owed her daughter “cannot even be repaid in this life”.

Cheung dismissed Alex Kwong’s contention as smearing and stressed she did not have any outstanding debt. She also denied that her gratitude towards Choi was because she had repaid her gambling debts, saying she was simply thankful for her daughter’s support.

Raffell suggested that Alex Kwong had co-owned a restaurant in Guangzhou and knew an agent who sold Richard Mille watches in Macau.

Cheung admitted she had no direct knowledge of her former son-in-law’s income, apart from what Choi had told her about his failure to contribute to the support of their two children.

Separately, Raffell argued that his client had been angry with Cheung for calling police after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023, despite knowing that he was wanted over his role in a HK$6.3 million theft case after jumping bail in 2015.

Cheung said she was unaware that authorities were still pursuing her former in-law. She reiterated that she believed the matter had been “settled” by Kwong Kau years before Choi’s killing.

During re-examination, prosecutor on fiat Charlotte Draycott SC sought to counter the defence’s suggestion that Cheung’s family was not as wealthy as she had claimed. She asked Cheung to explain the jewellery and luxury items she had worn or brought to court during her week-long testimony.

They included a luxury watch set with diamonds and rubies, a pair of bracelets, a diamond necklace and a pair of earrings.

Cheung said the valuables – excluding the watch, which was a gift from Choi – were worth at least HK$1 million.

She added that the handbag she carried to court on Monday was worth about HK$50,000, while another Hermes Birkin bag she had previously brought to court had been bought by Alex Kwong for more than HK$100,000 using her money.

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese brokers work to crack the final code: win clients on global stage
item.description:
China’s investment banks spent decades trying to emulate Goldman Sachs, the Wall Street powerhouse that became a benchmark for the country’s financial ambitions and whose alumni included senior US policymakers like former Treasury secretary Henry Paulson.

Today, Beijing’s goal has evolved beyond building a Chinese version of Goldman.

At the Central Financial Work Conference in 2023, President Xi Jinping called for cultivating first-class investment institutions as part of China’s ambition to become a financial superpower with distinct Chinese characteristics.
item.content:encoded:
China’s investment banks spent decades trying to emulate Goldman Sachs, the Wall Street powerhouse that became a benchmark for the country’s financial ambitions and whose alumni included senior US policymakers like former Treasury secretary Henry Paulson.

Today, Beijing’s goal has evolved beyond building a Chinese version of Goldman.

At the Central Financial Work Conference in 2023, President Xi Jinping called for cultivating first-class investment institutions as part of China’s ambition to become a financial superpower with distinct Chinese characteristics.

Many analysts and industry players believe the foundations are already in place. China now operates the world’s second-largest capital market after the US, while direct financing through stocks and bonds for the first time surpassed bank lending in 2025, ushering in a golden era for securities firms, they said.

The next challenge lies beyond mainland China. As Hong Kong’s role in China’s capital markets expands and mainland companies invest more aggressively overseas, Chinese brokerages are increasingly pushing into international markets.

“Overseas business, particularly in Hong Kong, is one of the key growth drivers for Chinese securities companies as they expand beyond their home market,” said Franco Lam, a director at Fitch Ratings.

From apprentice to contender

Compared with Wall Street and the City of London, China’s capital markets have a relatively short history.

When China International Capital Corporation (CICC) was established in 1995 as the country’s first Sino-foreign joint-venture investment bank, its ambitions were global from the outset. Yet its bankers had little experience to draw on.

Fang Fenglei, one of CICC’s founding executives, in an article published in 2018 in China Securities Journal, recalled how Morgan Stanley, one of the venture’s founding shareholders, arranged study visits for him to New York and London to learn the operations of Western financial markets, as part of what he described as a journey to “learn from the West”.

The learning curve was steep. Paulson said in his book, Dealing with China, that Goldman Sachs bankers gave CICC executives and Chinese officials what amounted to a crash course in taking companies public as they prepared China Mobile’s predecessor for its Hong Kong and New York listing in 1997.

The deal raised US$4.2 billion, offering an early glimpse of how quickly the gap between Chinese and Western investment banks could narrow.

At the time, the relationship between Chinese and foreign investment banks was heavily tilted in favour of Wall Street, whose firms brought technical expertise and access to international institutional investors that Chinese brokerages lacked.

Over the following two decades, Chinese securities firms moved beyond simply learning the mechanics of international investment banking to acquiring the networks and capabilities needed to compete overseas.

A first-class investment bank should not merely be large, but should have a voice in global capital allocation and asset pricing while attracting top financial talent

Wu Qing, China Securities Regulatory Commission

Citic Securities took a major step in 2013 by acquiring brokerage CLSA from French bank Credit Agricole, gaining an established research, sales and trading platform spanning major global financial centres. More than a decade later, the group is increasingly adopting the Citic Securities International, or CSI, identity across its global operations as it gradually phases out the CLSA brand.

Industry veterans liken the transition to one from apprentice to competitor.

Wang Junhong, deputy CEO of Guotai Junan International, where he has worked since 2012, said Chinese brokerages spent their early overseas years as “apprentices”, often playing secondary roles on deals led by foreign banks.

But as Chinese bankers accumulated experience and recruited internationally trained talent, they progressed from taking part in underwriting syndicates to leading them, Wang said.

“You go from being a participant in the underwriting syndicate to becoming the lead underwriter,” Wang said in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post. “The apprentice graduates. You become capable of standing on your own, and in some businesses you may even do better.”

Today, Chinese investment banks were “at least on an equal footing” with their Western rivals in much of Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market, and led in some areas, Wang said.

The rise of Chinese companies had also changed the equation, he said. As mainland businesses grew larger and more familiar to global investors, Chinese brokerages’ understanding of their home market became increasingly valuable. At the same time, the growth of mainland institutional investors and private wealth had created a much deeper pool of Chinese capital to support offshore transactions, Wang added.

Beijing’s push for global champions

Beijing is giving new momentum to a decades-old ambition as it pursues its broader goal of becoming a financial superpower.

China’s securities regulator has set a goal of having two to three investment banks and financial institutions with international competitiveness and market leadership by 2035.

Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), said in December that a first-class investment bank should “not merely be large”, but should have a voice in global capital allocation and asset pricing while attracting top financial talent.

The renewed policy push has been accompanied by a wave of fresh capital. At least nine mainland Chinese securities firms had announced or completed plans to inject a combined 51.7 billion yuan (US$7.7 billion) into their Hong Kong operations as of the end of August, according to a calculation by the SCMP.

Among the largest commitments, Citic Securities raised 16 billion yuan to support its international business, while Guotai Haitong Securities and Huatai Securities announced plans to inject 9 billion yuan and up to HK$9 billion (US$1.1 billion), respectively, into their offshore units to support overseas expansion.

By the end of 2025, 34 Chinese securities firms had established 36 international subsidiaries with combined assets of HK$1.94 trillion, up nearly 32 per cent from a year earlier, according to data from the Securities Association of China.

But Wang said the industry’s recent capital injections should not be viewed simply as compliance with Beijing’s policy directives.

“When you have a good business foundation and want to do more business, you need more capital to support it,” he said, describing much of the fundraising as “proactive” expansion rather than a sign of weak overseas operations.

The timing has also been favourable. A revival in Hong Kong’s IPO market and growing demand from mainland clients for offshore diversification had created new growth opportunities, especially as the recovery in mainland capital market activity remained gradual, Fitch’s Lam said.

Hong Kong: the proving ground

For most Chinese securities firms, internationalisation has started in the same place: Hong Kong.

Wang described the city as both a “bridgehead” and a “core hub” for the industry’s overseas expansion. Its proximity to the mainland, bilingual business environment, and status as the principal offshore financing centre for mainland companies made it the natural first stop, he added.

Hong Kong also provided Chinese investment banks with a market where their biggest competitive advantage – deep knowledge of Chinese companies and investors – mattered most. Mainland companies now accounted for about 78 per cent of Hong Kong’s stock market capitalisation and 90 per cent of trading turnover, according to Fitch Ratings.

While mainland markets had stabilised in the first half of 2026, profitability growth across the securities sector could moderate in the second half because of a high comparison base and softer market sentiment, according to Fitch.

IPO activity on the mainland also remained below levels seen in 2022 and 2023, Lam said. Hong Kong, by contrast, offered access to mainland clients through cross-border links, a broader range of investment products, a diverse international institutional-investor base and global market reach, he said. Changes to listing rules had also enhanced the city’s appeal as a listing venue, Lam added.

Those advantages have translated into stronger balance sheets and a growing pipeline of capital-market business.

Citic Securities generated 15.86 billion yuan in revenue outside mainland China in the first half of 2026, up 45.5 per cent from a year earlier, while net profit at its international arm more than doubled to US$829 million, according to its interim report.

CICC’s overseas revenue rose 45 per cent to 9.19 billion yuan over the same period, accounting for about 35 per cent of its total revenue.

Hong Kong subsidiaries of Chinese securities firms accounted for 50.6 per cent of IPO business among the city’s top 30 brokers in the first eight months of 2026, up from 35.3 per cent in 2022, according to Fitch data. The share held by foreign securities firms fell to 26.5 per cent from 29.3 per cent over the same period.

Chinese brokerages were also seeking to diversify beyond the more volatile investment banking and trading businesses by expanding wealth and asset management operations, while cross-border investment schemes were creating additional opportunities over the medium term, Lam said.

“If you see more opportunities coming ahead, definitely they want to put more capital into areas where there is more growth potential,” he added.

Their success in Hong Kong also points to the next challenge: whether advantages built around Chinese companies, Chinese capital and a China-linked financial centre can be replicated in markets where those advantages are less pronounced.

There is still a long way to go. The 2.0 version has yet to arrive

Chen Zhiwu, University of Hong Kong

Charting a new path

The next experiment is already under way. Chinese securities firms are extending their reach beyond their traditional Hong Kong base, with Southeast Asia and the Middle East emerging as key growth markets.

China Securities established a regional office in the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) in late September to pursue opportunities in equity and debt capital markets, investment banking, asset management and institutional business.

CICC opened its own DIFC branch a year earlier, positioning Dubai as a gateway between China and the Gulf region.

Southeast Asia has become another testing ground. China Galaxy Securities has built one of the industry’s broadest regional networks, spanning Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

However, the expansion abroad has also exposed firms to the risks of operating beyond familiar markets.

Everbright Securities’ investment in European sports-rights agency MP & Silva and Haitong International’s heavy losses during the offshore bond market downturn offered costly lessons. Haitong International lost a combined US$1.7 billion in 2022 and 2023 after defaults swept through the high-yield debt market, where it had become a major player.

Winning local trust

“There is still a long way to go. The 2.0 version has yet to arrive,” said Chen Zhiwu, a finance professor at the University of Hong Kong, referring to the next stage of internationalisation in which Chinese securities firms build substantial businesses among local, non-Chinese clients.

“Internationalisation is not just about setting up an office in New York or London. That is relatively easy,” Chen said.

The harder test, he said, was whether a company in Europe, Southeast Asia or Latin America, presented with a choice between a local bank, a Wall Street institution and a Chinese broker, would choose the Chinese firm to lead its IPO or advise on an acquisition.

The same question applied to wealth management: would a wealthy local family be willing to “entrust millions of dollars to a Chinese institution”? Chen asked. “It means that you can make them feel you are one of us or you can be one of us.”

Guotai Junan’s experience in Vietnam illustrates the challenge. Its local brokerage, acquired in 2019, ranked about 40th among roughly 80 securities firms in the country and was aiming to break into the top tier over the longer term, according to Guotai Junan’s Wang.

“We want to accelerate our growth, and given our client base, capital scale and market expertise, we could become much bigger very quickly. But there are still some constraints,” Wang said.

The veteran banker, who also chairs Guotai Junan’s operations in Vietnam and Macau, said an outsized presence by Chinese companies could stir local sensitivities in some overseas markets such as Vietnam.

“If a Chinese company became one of the dominant players, they might feel some pressure,” he said.

For Wang, Chinese investment banks would only become “truly global” when they could occupy a position in London or New York similar to the one Goldman Sachs and other global banks enjoyed in Hong Kong, and when their client base was no longer predominantly Chinese.

“Ultimately, you need to serve local companies with global presence,” he said. “Can you serve an American company like Apple? Can you serve Google?”

If that was the case, Wang said, “then I think you could say you have truly become global”.

item.title: [SCMP] From Hong Kong to Guangdong, exploring the rich tapestry of Cantonese culinary traditions
item.description:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.
item.content:encoded:
The term “Chinese cuisine” is an almost pointless label, encompassing as it does styles of cooking as diverse as Sichuan, Dongbei and Zhejiang, to name but a few. If thinking about a monolithic Chinese cuisine is inappropriate, does the same hold true for Guangdong’s Cantonese cuisine?

Consider chicken. A classic Hong Kong-style preparation might see white-cut chicken cooked in a simmering aromatic stock so the meat is gently poached and the skin adopts a gelatinous layer.

Further up the Pearl River Delta in Shunde (Shun Tak in Cantonese), the entire bird is deboned without tearing the skin and steamed together with ham and mushrooms.

From Guangdong’s northern coast, the traditional Chiu Chow or Chaoshan dish of poached saltwater chicken sees the meat steeped in a heavily seasoned salt brine or master stock, cooled and served at room temperature with a pounded garlic vinegar dip.

Hakka culinary heritage, founded in the hills of the province’s interior, takes an entirely different approach, wrapping the chicken tightly in paper and burying it completely in a pot of blazing hot, coarse sea salt.

Four distinct takes, four very different culinary approaches. Yet all of these dishes developed in the historic Guangdong province, an area roughly a third the size of France or Spain. Despite their common origin, should these different culinary traditions all be considered Cantonese?

Yes and no, says Silas Li, chef at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983. “I look at this almost like a family tree,” he says. “Technically, they represent distinct cultural traditions, but practically – and especially here in Hong Kong – they live under the same big roof.”

Historically, geography is a key determinant of a cuisine’s evolution. Li calls it the “true mother of recipe development”.

Shunde, sitting within the fertile Pearl River Delta surrounded by streams and fish ponds, supported a cuisine based on freshwater fish, mud carp, milk-yielding water buffalo, and tender river vegetables. For Li, this is the “cradle of classical Cantonese cooking”, the place where the region’s core standards for knife skills, slow-braising, seafood precision, and controlling the wok were established.

Elsewhere, along Guangdong’s Chaoshan coast, Chiu Chow communities had direct access to the ocean, inspiring a cuisine centred on deep-sea catches, saltwater poaching, and marine preserves, such as home-made fish sauces.

Hakka communities, however, were historically migratory and lived up in landlocked, rugged hills that offered no easy access to the coast or rivers. Consequently, they relied on calorie-dense pork, preserved salted vegetables and heavy salt-baking.

In Hong Kong, however, the different traditions have lived together for so long that the lines have naturally blurred.

“For me, Shun Tak is Cantonese core, while Chiu Chow and Hakka are sibling traditions that make our local food scene so much richer,” says Li, who draws inspiration for modern and classic dishes from all three culinary traditions at his restaurant in Happy Valley.

Chef and restaurateur Du Jianqing from Puning in Chaoshan is behind Shanghai’s two-Michelin-starred Amazing Chinese Cuisine and Selection by Du.

Du says he prefers not to view the question of whether Chiu Chow is part of Cantonese cuisine as a “battle over belonging”. Instead, he casts a wider, more inclusive net, thinking of both traditions as integral parts of the cuisine of Lingnan, a geographical area below the Nanling mountains that encompasses Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan, Hong Kong, Macau and northern Vietnam, once occupied by the ancient Baiyue people.

“From the perspective of Chinese culinary culture, Lingnan cuisine has always been a rich and open system. Cantonese (Guangfu), Chiu Chow and Hakka cuisines together form the essential components of Lingnan culinary culture,” he says.

Cantonese and Chiu Chow cooking both place great emphasis on seasonality, ingredient quality, natural flavours and a high level of craftsmanship. But for Du, the main defining feature of Chiu Chow cuisine is not a specific classic dish or set of dishes, but an obsessive pursuit of xian, or freshness/umami.

“This freshness is not just about flavour, but an overall respect for seasonality, origin, firepower, knife skills, and the state of the ingredients. People in Chaoshan often talk about ‘eating fresh’ (shi xian), which means savouring the best possible state of today, this season and this exact moment,” he says.

If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience

Silas Li, Hong Kong Cuisine 1983

Chef Huang Jinghui, better known as Chef Fei, was born and raised in Chaoshan. He runs a small empire of celebrated restaurants, all of which specialise in Cantonese and Chiu Chow dishes.

Chef Fei also highlights how porous boundaries between culinary traditions can be. “I see Chiu Chow cuisine and Cantonese cuisine as deeply interconnected culinary traditions, rather than two that need to be clearly separated,” he says.

He points to the considerable overlap in ingredients, techniques and culinary traditions – from delicacies such as abalone, sea cucumber and fish maw to Chiu Chow-style braised dishes, Cantonese barbecue and traditional slow-cooked soups, each with its own expression across the two cuisines.

However, he says that at the same time, Chiu Chow cuisine has its own distinctive regional character and culinary traditions.

“For me, rather than focusing too much on how Chiu Chow cuisine should be categorised, what matters more is the flavour, craftsmanship and traditions it represents, and the richness and diversity it brings to the dining experience,” he says.

While Du and Chef Fei are less fussy about a fluid, inclusive view of Cantonese cooking, Li at Hong Kong Cuisine 1983 argues that maintaining distinct categories remains essential for the dining experience itself.

“If you just lump everything under ‘Cantonese’, you lose the story, and in fine dining, the story and the heritage are half of what the guest is paying to experience,” he says. “If we just call it generic Chinese food, it dilutes the respect these ancient subcultures deserve.”

While he finds diners from the communities whose cuisine he cooks to be his toughest critics, Li notes that the average local guest has become far more sophisticated.

“The modern Hong Kong diner – and even international guests – is way more educated now,” Li says. “They aren’t just looking for a vague ‘Chinese meal’; they want provenance, they ask about techniques, and they appreciate the subtle regional nuances.”

At Yan Garden in Beijing – a restaurant conceptualised by Chef Fei and led day-to-day by executive Chinese chef Peter Chen at the Mandarin Oriental Qianmen – Chen sees this curiosity playing out among broader audiences. He notes that around 10 to 15 per cent of guests are international, while the remainder are local Chinese consumers, with the dining experience itself serving as an educational bridge.

“Dishes such as our traditional marinated specialities, seafood preparations and seasonal Chiu Chow delicacies often spark conversations about the cuisine’s heritage and techniques,” Chen says.

Du observes a similar dynamic at Selection by Du in Shanghai. “Guests from Europe and the Americas tend to view us as ‘Chinese cuisine’, hoping to discover Chinese food through this meal,” he says. “Guests from Southeast Asia, Hong Kong and Macau – owing to the deep Chiu Chow or Nanyang cultural roots in their home regions – more easily recognise the delicate nature and emphasis on original flavours in Chiu Chow cuisine.”

This evolving awareness reflects a broader transformation across Chinese gastronomy. Over the last 10 years, Du notes that diners’ knowledge has expanded rapidly, moving regional cooking into a dynamic new phase.

“More regional cuisines are establishing their own brand identities – Yunnan, Guizhou, Jiangxi, Taizhou, Shunde and Zhejiang cuisines are all receiving increasing attention,” he says. “This does not mean Cantonese cuisine’s influence is waning, but rather that Chinese dining as a whole is becoming richer and more specialised.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong touts distinct features to set it apart from London in global gold hub push
item.description:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.

In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system.

Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect Asian liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management.
item.content:encoded:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.

In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system.

Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect Asian liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management.

“We are confident achieving [this] because in the Asia time zone we see Hong Kong as uniquely positioned to do that,” he said.

In the wide-ranging interview, Hui also discussed the city’s efforts to promote the international use of the yuan, the development of China’s digital currency, the e-CNY, and next week’s Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong.

Asked whether the Saudi Central Bank’s recent departure from mBridge had dealt a blow to the project, Hui said it would press ahead. The China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform is seen as an alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system.

The Saudi Central Bank, a key participant, confirmed last month that it had left the project after completing what it described as a limited proof-of-concept trial in May last year.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Hong Kong is a founding member and co-developer of mBridge.

The city is also accelerating the development of its gold trading ecosystem as a key part of its first five-year plan, which runs to 2030. The initiative is intended to support the development of mainland China’s gold economy, which combines the world’s largest domestic gold production and consumption markets.

Hui said government ownership and backing, integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement and cooperation with Shanghai would distinguish Hong Kong’s offering. The cross-border cooperation would allow eligible gold stored in the city to be used to settle trades in both markets.

Asked about competition with Singapore as a regional gold trading hub, Hui said Hong Kong was focused on improving its own performance.

“What Hong Kong tries to do is always to compete against ourselves because fundamentally we have to focus on areas that are within our control,” he said.

He expressed confidence in Hong Kong’s competitive advantages.

“What sets a global commodities market from the other markets is that it is really a market that is not just about financials but also close to the real economy,” he said.

“It has to be about also storage, about logistics, and also, at the same time, about trading, of course. And also when it comes to disputes, there could also be some legal issues.

“So actually, it’s a whole value chain in terms of the potential composition of this industry association to be set up before the end of this year.”

Hui added that following a trial in July, the integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement service was due to launch officially in the first quarter of next year.

“The clearing system now in the UK is run by the London Bullion Market Association, which is an industry association,” he said. “But the clearing house in Hong Kong is owned and run by the government. So I think this government backing sets us apart in terms of credibility.

“Another thing that is different between Hong Kong and London in that context is the fact that our current system will not just do physical delivery but also money settlement.”

Hui said 11 banks were already taking part in the payment settlement arrangements and others had expressed strong interest in joining, adding that the city would discuss cooperation on delivery standards with the London association.

Hui, who chairs the board overseeing the clearing facility, said a representative of the Shanghai Bourse served as deputy chair. Under the cross-border delivery connect arrangement, physical gold stored in certified Hong Kong vaults can be used to settle contracts traded in the local market and on Shanghai’s international board.

“If there is gold that is going to satisfy both the settlement in the Hong Kong contract and the Shanghai contract, they can use the vaults in Hong Kong, catering for both the Hong Kong market and the Shanghai market to do that,” he said. “It is an area that is uniquely Hong Kong.”

He added that the government was aiming to increase Hong Kong’s gold storage capacity to more than 2,000 tonnes within three years, with half at the airport and the remainder expected to come from the private sector.

Some gold refineries have also been established in the city.

Asked how Hong Kong could help the mainland gain greater influence over gold pricing, Hui said this would come once the city had attracted enough market participants and built sufficient liquidity.

“I see pricing more as an outcome, in the sense that once we build up a sufficient liquidity, at the same time a quantum of gold here, so it will eventually come,” he said, stressing the importance of building a critical mass of market participants.

On products, Hui highlighted the relaunch of a US dollar-denominated gold futures contract and said details of a yuan-denominated contract would be announced before the end of this year.

With this work under way, Hui hoped to share the latest developments in Hong Kong’s gold trading ecosystem when the city hosted the London Bullion Market Association Global Precious Metals Conference in April next year.

Reflecting on this month’s conference in Sorrento, Italy, which he attended, he said industry stakeholders had responded positively to Hong Kong’s plans.

“First of all, they are quite impressed in terms of the timeliness of this project, in a sense that in this world of changing geopolitics,” he said, adding that they were also impressed with the city’s ecosystem approach, its “concrete plans” and “Hong Kong speed”.

Hui said the initiative had progressed rapidly since its announcement in the October 2024 policy address.

item.title: [SCMP] Japan taps foreign tech to plug defence gaps as China’s power grows. Will it pay off?
item.description:
