Japan is increasingly turning to foreign companies to accelerate its military modernisation, drawing on overseas technology, expertise and production capacity to plug defence gaps that could prove critical in a potential regional conflict involving China.

The push has gathered momentum over the past week, with Tokyo confirming a contract for Ukrainian interceptor drones and a multinational fighter consortium preparing to expand its design operations in Japan.

French defence giant Thales is also reportedly planning what could become Japan’s first foreign-run military maintenance facility, initially serving the Maritime Self-Defence Force.
item.content:encoded:
Japan is increasingly turning to foreign companies to accelerate its military modernisation, drawing on overseas technology, expertise and production capacity to plug defence gaps that could prove critical in a potential regional conflict involving China.

The push has gathered momentum over the past week, with Tokyo confirming a contract for Ukrainian interceptor drones and a multinational fighter consortium preparing to expand its design operations in Japan.

French defence giant Thales is also reportedly planning what could become Japan’s first foreign-run military maintenance facility, initially serving the Maritime Self-Defence Force.

Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi confirmed last Friday that Japan had signed a contract to acquire interceptor drones from Ukrainian start-up SkyFall.

The company’s combat-tested P1-SUN family is designed to intercept unmanned aerial systems, including reconnaissance and attack drones, but Tokyo has not disclosed which model it ordered.

The acquisition follows Japan’s fast-track mass-procurement contract for the Terra B1 interceptor from Japanese company Terra Drone, which has also invested in two Ukrainian drone manufacturers to tap into their military technology and combat experience.

Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics and a former Japanese defence ministry official, described Tokyo’s approach as a “two-phase” strategy of acquiring foreign systems to address urgent capability gaps while simultaneously developing domestic alternatives over the longer term.

Some overlap between the two was acceptable to avoid capability gaps during the transition.

He identified weaknesses in one-way attack drones and AI-enabled operational support systems, saying Japanese manufacturers had technical expertise but lacked know-how gained from “real-world battlefield experience”.

Beyond drones, Edgewing, a joint venture of Japanese, British and Italian defence companies, plans to open a design and development centre in Japan next year for a next-generation fighter programme.

According to Japanese news service Nikkei, the Aichi prefecture facility could eventually employ around 1,000 people.

Taken together, these developments point to a broader shift in Japan’s approach to military modernisation.

Tokyo has long acquired foreign-made weapon systems, mainly from the United States, but in recent years it has also sought partners elsewhere for advanced technology, joint development, production and maintenance.

Tokyo has acknowledged the limits of domestic industry.

Its 2026 defence white paper highlights pressures on the country’s defence-industrial base, including limited production volumes and companies withdrawing from the sector.

It advocates international research and development, licensed production and advanced foreign technology, while Japan’s Defence Buildup Programme calls for shorter development timelines to field urgently needed equipment faster.

Underpinning this shift is Tokyo’s stark assessment of regional security, with the white paper labelling Beijing’s growing military power and activities as Tokyo’s “greatest strategic challenge”.

Experts say closer cooperation with foreign defence companies could help Japan gain combat-tested technologies more quickly, share the costs and expertise required to develop advanced weapons, and expand its production and maintenance capabilities – potentially strengthening its ability to counter the People’s Liberation Army.

In a study released in July, Celine Pajon, head of Japan and Indo-Pacific research at the French Institute of International Relations, argued that foreign partnerships could ease Japan’s rising development costs, production constraints and dependence on US technology.

Her study linked a stronger domestic defence industry to Japan’s “strategic autonomy” and identified European countries as promising partners for joint development and technology-sharing.

Defence expert Yoshihiro Inaba, the Japan correspondent for the Naval News website, highlighted gaps in uncrewed weapons, low-cost missiles and AI capable of “processing vast amounts of information”.

Companies such as Anduril, Palantir and General Atomics were among those supporting Japan’s efforts to address those shortfalls.

In its fiscal 2027 defence budget request, Tokyo proposed developing and acquiring low-cost stand-off missiles.

Inaba argued that importing such weapons could help Japan fast-track its long-range strike capabilities while developing domestic alternatives, without requiring major changes to Self-Defence Forces equipment.

He pointed to China’s growing “quantitative advantage” over Japan, including its fleet of “highly capable but expensive surface combatants”.

Japan could therefore improve its ability to counter these vessels by combining its existing domestically produced missiles with “a larger inventory of lower-cost cruise missiles”, supported by the surveillance and command-and-control systems needed to identify and target them, he said.

Still, even if larger stocks of inexpensive weapons helped Japan to counter Chinese warships, sustaining their use throughout a prolonged conflict would pose a separate challenge.

Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, cautioned that the bigger test was whether Tokyo could “produce, maintain and replace” military equipment on the scale needed during a prolonged conflict.

She noted that China’s much larger defence-industrial base gave it a capacity for expansion that Japan “cannot readily match”. While foreign partnerships could help address specific shortcomings, they would not eliminate the fundamental imbalance between the two countries.

Matsuoka also warned that Japan’s military preparations could reinforce Beijing’s perception that Tokyo and its partners were “preparing for confrontation”, deepening mutual mistrust.

Beyond these geopolitical risks, Japan would still face major industrial challenges. Foreign partnerships could accelerate technology transfers, Matsuoka said, but producing weapons “reliably at scale” required skilled workers, qualified suppliers and secure access to components and materials.

Reliance on foreign export approvals, software support and critical components could leave Japan vulnerable during a conflict with China, Matsuoka warned.

Japan could also struggle to sustain operations if it acquired systems it “cannot repair, modify or replenish independently”.

Ogi also cautioned that foreign defence companies’ growing presence in Japan did not necessarily reflect Tokyo’s military requirements. Such moves were “primarily motivated by the commercial interests of foreign companies”, he argued, as they anticipated further increases in Japanese defence spending.

For Japan, the challenge will be turning foreign technology and expertise into military capabilities quickly enough to address some of China’s advantages, while ensuring those systems can be maintained, produced and replenished if a longer conflict disrupts overseas supply chains.

“Foreign cooperation does not eliminate dependence; it redistributes it,” Matsuoka said.

item.title: [SCMP] India’s proposed social media ban for under-18s wins parents’ backing
item.description:
Digangana Mukherjee, a mother of a six-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, has banned television at her home in the Indian city of Mysore because she does not want her children to become addicted to watching content on screen.

A year ago, when her son’s school started using a smart classroom board that streamed online content, she and her husband decided to enrol him in a school where teachers used chalk on a slate board, and the pace of lessons was slower.

Now, she is happy that the Indian government is reportedly planning to prevent children below 18 years from opening social media accounts under a new law, in line with a Supreme Court ruling that such accounts signed up by minors should be considered void.
item.content:encoded:
Digangana Mukherjee, a mother of a six-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, has banned television at her home in the Indian city of Mysore because she does not want her children to become addicted to watching content on screen.

A year ago, when her son’s school started using a smart classroom board that streamed online content, she and her husband decided to enrol him in a school where teachers used chalk on a slate board, and the pace of lessons was slower.

Now, she is happy that the Indian government is reportedly planning to prevent children below 18 years from opening social media accounts under a new law, in line with a Supreme Court ruling that such accounts signed up by minors should be considered void.

“I approve of it as a parent. My son is 10 and knows how to browse YouTube. It is already becoming scary for me. I don’t know what content is visible to him,” Mukherjee said.

While parents may welcome India’s proposed safeguards, enforcement could prove complicated in one of the world’s largest online markets.

Legal experts warn that policing underage accounts and preventing users from getting around restrictions and privacy rights would be the main stumbling blocks, while a blanket ban would deprive young people of valuable educational resources.

Other countries in the Asia-Pacific region have enacted such laws, with Australia setting the ball rolling last December when it banned social media access for children under 16 under its Online Safety Amendment Act.

Mukherjee, who runs a library at her home filled with old books and conducts storytelling sessions for children, said she could distinguish between those who have unrestricted access to online screens and those with limited exposure.

“I see a lot of children come in and out of my space. There is a stark difference between these children. The attention span is much less for those who have abundant access to screens. They are restless and are not able to sit still for long,” she said.

Children with unlimited screen access have many entertainment options, and they are not keen on books, according to Mukherjee.

“If there were fewer screens, people would read more books. Growing up, we had Sunday afternoons only to watch TV. The rest of the time, when I was really bored, I had to pick up a book,” she said.

Many social media users younger than 18 in India do not face online curbs.

Last month, India’s solicitor general Tushar Mehta concurred with the position of the Supreme Court, in response to a petition by the “Just Rights For Children Alliance” NGO, that social media accounts opened by minors should be voided. He said the federal government should step in to make such a ban mandatory.

Australia deactivated 4.7 million social media accounts opened by those below 16 in the first month of its ban. India’s Goa state has been considering an Australia-like social media ban for children, amid growing concerns over the impact of excessive use on their mental health.

Lawyers, however, warn that the proposed regulation to curb access for children in India is bound to face legal challenges.

“I understand the Supreme Court’s request to bring in safeguards and the government’s stance to bring in stronger regulation to combat the risks posed. What remains to be seen is the extent and severity of restrictions that ultimately take form,” said Ashima Chalia, founder and senior partner at Bengaluru-based Ayaam Legal.

The mother of a two-year-old baby said that she wished for such a legal curb to protect children from online risks such as sexual exploitation, cyberbullying and harmful content.

“As a parent, I would also wish to baby-proof the whole world against anything that may harm my kid,” Chalia said.

“No doubt there is a need for stricter legislation or rules, but the Indian government has a herculean task of balancing children’s access to education and beneficial digital resources,” she said.

These rules would have to address a user’s rights regarding personal information collection and storage as well as age-verification processes, she added.

While Chalia conceded that Indian regulators would face challenges from children in India lying about their age when opening social media accounts, she added: “An uphill battle surely, but absolutely attainable.”

Striking a balance

Ambareen Ali Shah, a New Delhi-based mother of a 14½-year-old boy, said she worried about how easy access to social media would affect children’s time management as they had to do online and offline school assignments.

“Once you have access to – say Instagram – the content is so interesting that it causes distraction,” she said.

Shah recalled that when she was a young girl, the only screen she had access to was the television, restricted to a few hours of viewing.

“We need to curb the time a child spends navigating the internet. On the other hand, social media is making kids smarter because they get access to a lot of information,” she said.

Amitraj Kaushal, a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India, said that there was a strong case for a statutory framework protecting children from risks associated with social media use.

Citing the need to limit their exposure to age-inappropriate material, Kaushal said: “Legislation can provide clarity by placing the primary compliance responsibility on platforms rather than criminalising children or their parents.”

Australia’s experience could be useful for India as its law requires social media platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent those below 16 years old from opening accounts, while children and parents are not penalised for non-compliance, according to Kaushal.

Debasree Basu, an adviser at G.M. International School in Mumbai, said, however, that a sweeping social media ban would be counter-productive.

“Restrictions do not work. We have already exposed today’s generation to so many things that to ban them now will only make them more rebellious,” she said.

“The message should be that we want to protect you, so please help us to do that. Then their whole attitude will change.”

item.title: [SCMP] A US scholar’s take on how shifts in US-China relations are felt in a Tsinghua classroom
item.description:
China and America are talking again. There are leaders’ meetings, phone calls and a new channel for discussing artificial intelligence. Officials are cautiously trying to keep the relationship from veering into crisis.

And yet some of the hardest questions remain untouched.

Neither side is giving much ground on advanced chips, export controls remain a battlefield and neither Washington nor Beijing appears ready to slow its race to develop increasingly powerful AI.
item.content:encoded:
China and America are talking again. There are leaders’ meetings, phone calls and a new channel for discussing artificial intelligence. Officials are cautiously trying to keep the relationship from veering into crisis.

And yet some of the hardest questions remain untouched.

Neither side is giving much ground on advanced chips, export controls remain a battlefield and neither Washington nor Beijing appears ready to slow its race to develop increasingly powerful AI.

So what, exactly, does it mean to “talk” when the two countries are still competing over the technologies that will shape the next decade?

It is a question Denis Simon is confronting in the classroom.

A veteran US-China technology and higher-education strategist and former executive vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University, Simon is now teaching at Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University.

The residential college and its Schwarzman Scholars programme were founded by Blackstone chief executive Stephen Schwarzman with the aim of bringing together future leaders from around the world.

The programme, which celebrated its 10th anniversary last year, is described by some observers as one of the crown jewels in the bilateral relationship.

Simon’s course focuses on China’s science and technology policy and innovation strategy, but the country’s relationship with the US will not stay in the background.

He was teaching the second seminar of the course in Beijing when US President Donald Trump went to China in May, and the third when Trump’s Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, went to Washington last month.

“That’s a kind of very interesting coincidence of time that gives the course a booster shot,” he said in an interview from Beijing. “The students are aware of both meetings. They’re much more informed about what’s going on.”

His students are studying a relationship that has become deeply contradictory: Washington and Beijing are rebuilding channels of communication even as they narrow the space for technological and scientific links.

The summits have not resolved that, but they have changed the atmosphere in the classroom.

“These leadership meetings really created a much more positive environment,” Simon said.

Before May, when the two sides were not talking, things were “topsy-turvy”, he said, adding that neither the Beijing visit nor the Washington trip was “a resounding big deal”. But what registered was simpler: the fact that the two leaders were talking and had met twice within six months.

However, Simon said the “biggest change” was that some students “have become seemingly somewhat more cautious about revealing where they actually stand”.

For example, an argument about export controls can sound like an argument about America, while a criticism of Chinese technology policy can become a political declaration. Even defending academic exchanges may raise questions about political loyalties.

“They have become much better at distinguishing what they think from what they believe they ought to say in terms of political correctness,” he said.

“That distinction matters enormously in a classroom. A good seminar depends upon intellectual risk-taking.”

Over the past three years, the discussions have, in several respects, become more sophisticated even as students have become a bit more restrained.

That is partly because while 40 per cent of students are American and 20 per cent Chinese, the others come from all over the world and are asking why they should have to choose between the two superpowers.

“They are not merely referees,” Simon said. “They have their own interests.”

He said they wanted American technology and capital, and they wanted Chinese markets, manufacturing capacity, infrastructure and technology.

But they did not necessarily see technological alignment with either Washington or Beijing as inevitable, or desirable.

In some ways, the students who are not American or Chinese are the ones who make the classroom genuinely international

Denis Simon, Schwarzman College

“In some ways, the students who are not American or Chinese are the ones who make the classroom genuinely international,” Simon said.

Their presence has also pushed Simon to modify the course, including replacing older readings with newer ones that reflect what has happened since the leaders’ meetings.

He no longer sees the technology relationship as a straightforward story of engagement followed by competition. Technology, economics, national security, industrial policy, scientific research and geopolitics have become too deeply entangled.

The old idea of separating economic and security issues has largely disappeared. But Simon is equally wary of the opposite assumption: that everything involving China and technology should now be treated as a security issue.

His students study semiconductors, export controls, AI, data governance, supply-chain resilience and industrial subsidies and are also asked some fundamental questions: where should the two countries compete, where should they put guardrails in place and where should they deliberately remain connected?

Simon uses a red-yellow-green framework to assess the security situation, with red – covering areas where national security is at stake – being relatively straightforward.

The same applies to low-risk green areas, including basic science and ordinary educational exchanges, but Simon added that yellow was the “really difficult category”, which meant proceeding with “conditions, transparency, safeguards or limits”.

His concern is that Washington increasingly has a tendency to turn yellow into red.

“Once that happens, the burden of proof shifts,” Simon said. “Instead of asking, ‘Why should this be restricted?’ we begin asking, ‘Can anyone prove that it is completely safe?’”

That, he added, was not a sustainable basis for technology policy.

The same tension is visible in the emerging AI channel between Washington and Beijing. Simon argued there was value in the new mechanisms for communication, but warned “communication” and “governance” were not the same thing.

A hotline can provide a way to communicate after an accident or during a crisis, while dialogue can make contact habitual, but neither of these things settles questions such as who gets access to advanced chips, how frontier AI should be developed or what happens when the two sides disagree about the rules.

He added: “Great-power relationships often advance in very small increments. The existence of a channel may look insignificant until the day you desperately need the channel.”

The question is whether those channels become durable institutions or remain dependent on the political mood of the moment.

Simon said that concern extended to the academic sphere, with universities are being increasingly being forced to “price geopolitical risk” into their calculations given the cost of being caught up in a political controversy.

His recent experience at Duke University in the US sharpened these concerns where a China science and technology graduate seminar he had taught for several years was dropped even though funding was available.

“What it told me is that the issue is no longer simply whether there is money to teach a course,” Simon said. “The institution is also asking: what is the reputational and political risk of teaching it?

“If American universities stop teaching about China’s innovation system because the China issue has become politically difficult, we will create an extraordinary paradox: we will become less capable of competing with a country precisely because we have become less willing to study it.”

Inside Schwarzman College, that question takes on another dimension. Students are watching China’s transformation from the “factory of the world” into an innovation power in electric vehicles, batteries, robotics, clean energy and AI.

To many observers, this change appears sudden, but Simon, who has followed China’s development for 40 years, sees something different.

“It really is part of a gestation period over time over the last 30-plus years in which China has steadily moved to make itself into an innovation-driven nation. So when people seem to be shocked, it’s that they haven’t been following this for 40 years, like I have.”

For Chinese students, he said, this was not simply a story of national technological achievement but the economy where they had to find jobs.

Many had assumed the factory era was behind them and that innovation was the next place to stand, but robotics and AI have complicated that assumption.

They may be headed back into the factory, but not the one their parents left.

Meanwhile, international students are confronting a different reality: China’s technological rise will shape the competitive environment in which they build their own careers.

The question, Simon said, was no longer simply whether China could innovate, but “how China’s innovation trajectory will alter international S&T [science and technology] affairs, including the once dominant role of the US”.

He said that ultimately that was what he wanted his students to understand, saying they should not expect a return to the US-China relationship of the 1990s or 2000s, while technological competition could not be wished away.

The objective, instead, was to build enough “connective tissue” around the new relationship that competition remained competition without becoming continuous conflict.

That is the wager behind institutions like Schwarzman College, NYU Shanghai and Duke Kunshan: not that they can eliminate strategic competition, but that they can continue putting people who might disagree in the same room, and teach them how to keep talking when agreement is no longer possible.

“Cooperation does not have to mean agreement, technological sharing, or slowing down,” he said. “Cooperation can mean simply agreeing on what happens when we disagree.”

item.title: [SCMP] Haze-hit Singapore parents call for Hong Kong-style school air con
item.description:
Salon manager Alice Pang says her 10-year-old daughter has likened the visibility inside her classroom in Singapore to Malaysia’s Genting Highlands, but while the mountain resort is often shrouded in fog caused by water particles, her child’s active imagination may have been triggered by worsening haze plaguing the city state.

Pang told This Week in Asia that her daughter, whose classroom did not have air conditioning, was already suffering from bad sinus, and the haze had made her eyes water.

While Pang would prefer her Primary 4 daughter to stay home as the pollutant standards index (PSI) climbs beyond 200 in some parts of the city state, the child is in the middle of exams.
item.content:encoded:
Salon manager Alice Pang says her 10-year-old daughter has likened the visibility inside her classroom in Singapore to Malaysia’s Genting Highlands, but while the mountain resort is often shrouded in fog caused by water particles, her child’s active imagination may have been triggered by worsening haze plaguing the city state.

Pang told This Week in Asia that her daughter, whose classroom did not have air conditioning, was already suffering from bad sinus, and the haze had made her eyes water.

While Pang would prefer her Primary 4 daughter to stay home as the pollutant standards index (PSI) climbs beyond 200 in some parts of the city state, the child is in the middle of exams.

Pang is among several parents who are increasingly worried about the open-air classroom environments in Singapore amid the transboundary haze fuelled by fires across Indonesia, particularly in Sumatra and Kalimantan.

“They have an air purifier in the classroom, but she says it isn’t working. It’s also too hot for the students. I think the government needs to step up and take action,” Pang said.

She argued that schools should roll out air-conditioning in classrooms to complement the air purifiers. Currently, her daughter’s school has air-conditioning only in certain facilities such as the music room.

On Wednesday afternoon, the PSI one-hour reading hit a high of 288 in the west of Singapore. The same day, Singapore began distributing N95 masks to vulnerable Singaporeans, including children aged between seven and 16, and providing air-conditioned rooms in shelters in community clubs and some residents’ committee centres.

On Saturday, Education Minister Desmond Lee said in a social media post that lessons and national examinations had continued in enclosed venues with air purifiers, and that his ministry might consider school closures if the next-day forecasts entered the hazardous range with a 24-hour PSI exceeding 300.

Across the 1km causeway in Malaysia, schools in several states have been shut until at least Friday. Under federal guidelines, educational institutions must close when the Air Pollutant Index (API) exceeds 180, or remains above 150 for three consecutive days. Both levels fall within the “unhealthy” range.

General practitioner Lawrence Ng said that common conditions triggered by haze included ⁠upper respiratory infections, bronchitis, ⁠conjunctivitis, allergic rhinitis, known as hay fever, and⁠ asthma.

“Children have smaller airways which are more susceptible to airway narrowing from pollutants,” Ng said.

Asked if implementing air-conditioning in classrooms was being considered to tackle the haze, Singapore’s Ministry of Education directed This Week in Asia to its haze management measures.

These include avoiding physical activities if the PSI is between 200 and 300, placing students in an enclosed indoor space with air purifiers and having those who are unwell temporarily placed in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier before they are brought to get medical attention.

Opposition MP Kenneth Tiong, who reiterated his call to provide air-conditioning in classrooms this week, told This Week in Asia he was not advocating for the air-conditioning to be on at all times but to have the option when needed.

In March, he advocated in parliament for air-conditioning in classrooms to help students and teachers handle the heat.

“The recent haze makes it more urgent. It has been very difficult for the kids: many are coughing, and I can see the toll it is taking on their health,” said Tiong, who is a Workers’ Party MP for the Aljunied constituency.

He noted that the National Environment Agency’s guideline said a purifier might not work as intended unless the doors and windows were closed, and that a closed, crowded room could build up heat.

“MOE’s haze plan says students who are unwell ‘will be temporarily accommodated in an air-conditioned room with an air purifier’. I believe a child should not have to fall ill first,” Tiong argued.

In March, then senior minister of state David Neo said Singapore had been careful not to rush into air conditioning, as the technology was not as energy efficient and instead relied on passive cooling solutions, such as cool paint, more breathable uniforms and school buildings designed for maximum natural ventilation.

Neo stressed there was a need to balance other considerations, such as long-term heat resilience, acclimatisation, energy consumption and impact on the environment.

Tiong told This Week in Asia that while sustainability was very important, air-conditioning in every classroom could be an insurance. “It has to be in place before the haze or the next heatwave arrives. Switched on only when needed, it uses far less power than air-conditioning left on all day,” he said.

He noted that in Hong Kong, the government had moved to air-conditioned classrooms for all public sector schools since 2017 for a more comfortable teaching and learning environment in hot weather.

A recurrent air-conditioning grant was provided from 2018 for Hong Kong schools to cover related daily expenses, including electricity charges and maintenance.

A mother of a six-year-old who previously lived in Hong Kong said she was shocked to learn that her child’s Primary 1 classroom in Singapore would not be air-conditioned.

Currently, her child’s kindergarten class is air-conditioned and has an air purifier, but she expressed concern about whether it had been serviced.

“I’m not asking them to have the air conditioning turned on every day,” she said, speaking on condition of anonymity. She questioned if some people underestimated the haze, given “this haze situation has been there for 20 years”.

Flynn Lee, a 50-year-old stay-at-home Singaporean mother of three children aged 11 to 16, however, said she trusted the government’s current measures. Only her daughter in Secondary 1 has air conditioning in her classroom.

“Air con is good to have, but I guess not all schools can afford it. It’s also not cheap to maintain, and this situation is not forever, so I guess we just have to get through this period,” Lee said, noting that her children’s schools had stopped all outdoor recess playing, moved co-curricular activities and physical education lessons indoors and reminded children to drink more water.

“It’s not really a fair statement to request for air con just because of the haze situation, which probably will last like weeks to a month and to have schools suddenly have to request to put up air conditioning.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s central bank insists it is independent. Investors want proof
item.description:
Indonesia has spent months trying to persuade investors that its economy is on the right course. A weakening rupiah, mounting budgetary pressures and a series of contentious policy decisions have made that task harder.

Doubts about the management of Southeast Asia’s largest economy have now coalesced around its central bank, whose independence has come under intense scrutiny recently as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to steer economic policy.

The appointment of Destry Damayanti – initially as acting governor of Bank Indonesia (BI) in late July before her formal appointment last month – was meant to reassure markets. But analysts say that confidence will only return if economic policymaking becomes more credible and decisions affecting the country’s financial health become more transparent.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia has spent months trying to persuade investors that its economy is on the right course. A weakening rupiah, mounting budgetary pressures and a series of contentious policy decisions have made that task harder.

Doubts about the management of Southeast Asia’s largest economy have now coalesced around its central bank, whose independence has come under intense scrutiny recently as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to steer economic policy.

The appointment of Destry Damayanti – initially as acting governor of Bank Indonesia (BI) in late July before her formal appointment last month – was meant to reassure markets. But analysts say that confidence will only return if economic policymaking becomes more credible and decisions affecting the country’s financial health become more transparent.

In an interview with Reuters on Monday, Destry insisted the central bank had “full autonomy” to set interest rates while maintaining “synergy” with the government.

“When we’re about to make a policy decision – whether to raise or lower interest rates or to ⁠use other incentives – we have full authority to make that decision,” she said.

Her assurances follow a turbulent few months for Indonesia’s economy. The rupiah hit record lows this year, with major credit rating agencies Moody’s and Fitch cutting their outlooks on the country’s sovereign rating from stable to negative.

Conflict in the Middle East has only compounded the challenges. Despite the soaring cost of oil globally, Jakarta has held subsidised fuel prices steady. State institutions have since had their budgets cut to pay for energy imports and Prabowo’s flagship welfare programmes.

On Friday, fears of foreign capital flight were further stoked after index compiler MSCI said in a statement that Indonesia no longer merited emerging-market status, citing “significant concerns” about market dysfunction, “including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement”.

The US firm said it was now proposing a downgrade to “standalone” status – worse than previously flagged – which would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by passive investment funds managing billions of US dollars. Indonesian stocks, already the world’s worst performers this year, plunged 11 per cent to multi-year lows on Friday in response – the steepest one-day drop since 1998.

Other developments that have unsettled markets in recent months include a new policy to centralise commodity exports, the abrupt dismissal of former finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa and his replacement by Suahasil Nazara, and the appointment of Prabowo’s nephew, Thomas Djiwandono, as a deputy governor of the central bank.

In June, parliament passed a revision to the financial sector law that now requires Bank Indonesia to support economic growth and job creation, in addition to its duties managing money supply, keeping inflation under control, issuing and circulating legal tender, regulating national payment systems and acting as a lender of last resort.

Asked how much the government was involved in monetary policy, Destry said officials had been invited to attend part of the bank’s monthly policy review, adding that she herself had attended meetings with Prabowo.

“In Indonesia, the president is the head of government and the head of state. BI is under the state of Indonesia, so automatically, if the president wants to know about developments, I think it’s normal,” she told Reuters.

The central bank held its benchmark rate at 5.75 per cent at its latest policy meeting in September, after raising it by a cumulative 100 basis points between May and June to stabilise and support the rupiah, which was trading at a near-record low of 18,070 per US dollar as of Friday afternoon.

Proof over promises

Economists who spoke to This Week in Asia agreed that the new governor’s message was welcome, but said investors would need to see Bank Indonesia demonstrate its independence.

“The governor’s reassurance is a constructive and necessary signal, but it is unlikely to restore investor confidence on its own,” said Josua Pardede, chief economist at Permata Bank.

“Restoring confidence requires a broader and sustained improvement in Indonesia’s economic policy credibility, not merely reassurance from the central bank.”

While Bank Indonesia “remains legally independent”, Pardede said the unexpected resignation of its previous governor and changes to its responsibilities had stoked speculation that its “institutional independence has weakened”.

Destry’s predecessor, Perry Warjiyo, resigned in July citing personal reasons.

Yusuf Rendy Manilet, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics Indonesia, called for government-central bank synergy to rest on “clear data”, saying that the bank should, for example, consult the government’s employment figures before setting the benchmark interest rate.

“When that happens, I think BI can be interpreted as still being relatively independent in implementing its policies,” he said.

Yusuf also wanted the bank to explain its purchases of government bonds. According to Reuters, Bank Indonesia bought nearly 300 trillion rupiah (US$16.7 billion) of them between January and September 30 to support economic growth.

“BI must convince investors that its bond purchasing policy has strong justification as a monetary policy and not because it is an extension of the government,” he said.

Deniey Purwanto, a senior researcher at the Institute for Development of Economics and Finance in Jakarta, said the central bank would be fully autonomous only when it could set rates “without considering its impact on government debt costs”.

Downgrade danger

Indonesia ran a deficit of 1.24 per cent of gross domestic product in the first nine months of this year, with the full-year target of 2.85 per cent coming in just under the statutory ceiling of 3 per cent.

Analysts like Pardede say government spending is outpacing tax revenue, citing investor concerns that include the expansion of state spending commitments despite a “relatively narrow tax base”, rising energy subsidies, repeated changes among senior economic officials and “uncertainty surrounding the roles of state-controlled investment and commodity institutions”.

MSCI’s Friday announcement about Indonesia’s market downgrade surprised officials, coming a month ahead of a scheduled review. In January, the index provider had warned about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as co-ordinated trading behaviour that affected price information. It suggested a possible downgrade to frontier-market status at the time.

Standalone status is reserved for markets that do not meet even this criteria. Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among the markets with the designation, with none in Asia, according to Bloomberg.

Uncertainty surrounding the roles of state-controlled investment and commodity institutions

Josua Pardede, Permata Bank economist

Meanwhile, higher oil prices could weigh further on both the rupiah and Indonesia’s finances. International benchmark Brent crude has been stubbornly trading above US$100 in recent days following fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, threatening oil supplies and raising fears of a widening Middle East conflict.

Yusuf expects little relief for Indonesia’s currency in the near term, forecasting that the rupiah will remain “quite volatile” against the US dollar through to the end of the year.

Pardede’s prescription for Indonesia’s US$1.3 trillion economy was directed at the government rather than the central bank.

“The government should prioritise disciplined budget execution, transparent public investment governance, regulatory certainty and policies that attract private capital rather than relying excessively on the state to drive growth,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China-led team hits 83% success rate anticipating earthquakes in ‘seismo-ripples’ study
item.description:
A China-led international team has reported a new pre-earthquake phenomenon that has shown strong predictive potential for major earthquakes since 2022 with minimal failures.

The anomalous seismic, magnetic and ionospheric resonance signals they observed – termed “seismo-ripples” by the researchers – are ringlike disturbance patterns triggered before earthquakes happen.

Their findings challenge the long-standing scientific belief that these events are unpredictable, opening up a promising new path to earthquake prediction.
item.content:encoded:
A China-led international team has reported a new pre-earthquake phenomenon that has shown strong predictive potential for major earthquakes since 2022 with minimal failures.

The anomalous seismic, magnetic and ionospheric resonance signals they observed – termed “seismo-ripples” by the researchers – are ringlike disturbance patterns triggered before earthquakes happen.

Their findings challenge the long-standing scientific belief that these events are unpredictable, opening up a promising new path to earthquake prediction.

“Historically, earthquake prediction has been considered nearly infeasible,” said the team from institutes in mainland China and Taiwan, along with Brazil and Japan, in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal NPJ Natural Hazards on Sunday.

Using data collected from seismometers, magnetometers and ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System receivers, the anomalous patterns were verified against 12 major earthquakes in China between 2022 and 2024.

“Since June 2022, prospective anomaly based on seismo-ripples has demonstrated a strong predictive capability for numerous earthquakes with a magnitude [greater than or equal to] six, with remarkably minimal to no failure,” the researchers wrote.

Of the 12 sites they proposed could be associated with future earthquakes, 83 per cent experienced a corresponding earthquake within three months of the seismo-ripple patterns emerging.

The average distance between predicted and actual epicentres was about 280km (174 miles) and the estimated magnitudes ran about 0.5 units larger than the final seismic readings.

“In essence, the core argument of our paper is that earthquakes are not inherently unpredictable,” said Chen Chieh-Hung, a lead author of the study and a professor at the Chengdu University of Technology.

Chen noted that prediction could mean different things to different people, with some expecting precision down to the exact minute or accuracy within a margin of a few kilometres, which he said would not be feasible at this stage.

“Nevertheless, we have opened a door. Earthquakes are not beyond the realm of prediction,” he said on Wednesday. “There is a possibility that they can be predicted. The next step is for the scientific community to work on refining this precision.”

Asia is one of the world’s most seismically active regions, with China experiencing roughly a third of all continental earthquakes despite having only about 7 per cent of the global land area.

Estimating long-term seismic probabilities – such as Japan’s assessment of a high probability for a major earthquake along the Nankai Trough in the next three decades – is an accepted scientific approach.

However, for decades, short-term earthquake prediction has been elusive and controversial.

According to the United States Geological Survey, a true earthquake prediction must specify three parameters: the date and time, the location and the magnitude of the incoming event.

This differs from earthquake forecasting, which calculates the probability of an earthquake occurring within a given area and time window.

Chen said the scientific consensus that earthquakes could not be predicted stemmed in part from papers published in the top journals Nature and Science in the 1990s. From then on, he said, this belief “effectively became an established rule”.

“Within the scientific community, the prevailing view is that earthquakes are unpredictable, and most researchers prefer not to wade into such controversial waters,” he added.

Chen pointed to other milestones once thought impossible, such as accurate weather forecasting and aircraft breaking the sound barrier.

“A more accurate way to frame it would be to say that we have yet to discover a sound, rationally valid or scientifically grounded method for predicting the occurrence of earthquakes,” he said.

Chen said that if the bar for prediction were set extremely high, then it would indeed be impossible. Instead, he argued that scientific efforts should focus on shifting from long-term forecasts to short-to-medium-term predictions.

Researchers from around the world have sought to identify earthquake precursors or signals occurring before seismic events that could be used for more reliable forecasting or even predictions.

In their paper, the China-led team explored a phenomenon of ringlike disturbances called seismo-circles or seismo-ripples that appear to propagate outwards from future earthquake epicentres.

“What’s particularly interesting about this phenomenon is that, initially, we did not know whether it was real or false,” Chen said.

To verify their findings, the team investigated past earthquake cases. They found that separate ripple-like anomalies had formed for two earthquakes that struck China within a day of each other in 2021.

Chen said this revelation gave the team the confidence to pursue the research further, and over the following two years they documented the anomalous occurrences and submitted formal reports.

In April 2022, after detecting anomalous ripple patterns in southwestern China, the researchers submitted a formal document to the China Earthquake Networks Centre – the country’s official body for earthquake monitoring and prediction evaluation – declaring a possible magnitude 6.3 event within two months.

On June 1, 2022, a magnitude 6.1 earthquake struck China’s southwestern Sichuan province, occurring 399km from the team’s predicted epicentre.

They then launched an effort between 2022 and 2024 to challenge the idea that earthquakes were inherently unpredictable, routinely monitoring seismo-ripples and submitting formal reports to authorities.

The team said its investigation highlighted a correlation between seismo-ripples and forthcoming seismic events, allowing for “reliable estimation of earthquake magnitude, location and timing”.

They noted there were still challenges to address, including ambiguous ripple signals that complicated exact estimates and the need for deeper understanding of the physics behind these anomalies.

In addition, seismo-ripple detection remains limited by instrument density and spatial network coverage.

To improve precision, an upgraded ground-based observation system is under construction in China. Looking ahead, the team plans to incorporate satellite data and artificial intelligence to enhance monitoring capabilities.

While their study focused on China’s North-South Seismic Belt, the researchers said the seismo-ripple phenomenon held potential for global application.

Chen said the main goal of their paper was not to claim that earthquakes could already be predicted but rather that they were not inherently unpredictable.

“At this stage, we are already able to distinguish between signals that are likely related to earthquakes and those that are not – a distinction we could not make previously,” he said.

“The next challenge is to improve precision, particularly regarding the location and timing of seismic events.”

Chen acknowledged that there was a long way to go before earthquake prediction would become a fully functional reality. But he said his team was committed to the task and invited other scientists to put their seismo-ripples model to the test.

item.title: [SCMP] From Abby Choi to the ‘Hello Kitty’ killing: Hong Kong’s most shocking crimes
item.description:
The alleged murder and dismemberment of Abby Choi Tin-fung in 2023, which prosecutors say was linked to a dispute over a luxury flat, has once again gripped Hong Kong as the trial over the 28-year-old socialite’s death entered its second week.

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of her body. Their father, Kwong Kau, 68, has pleaded not guilty to the same charge. All three men deny murdering Choi.

While Hong Kong has a reputation as one of the world’s safest cities, it has seen its share of sensational and gruesome crimes.
item.content:encoded:
The alleged murder and dismemberment of Abby Choi Tin-fung in 2023, which prosecutors say was linked to a dispute over a luxury flat, has once again gripped Hong Kong as the trial over the 28-year-old socialite’s death entered its second week.

Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, and his elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, have pleaded guilty to preventing the lawful burial of her body. Their father, Kwong Kau, 68, has pleaded not guilty to the same charge. All three men deny murdering Choi.

While Hong Kong has a reputation as one of the world’s safest cities, it has seen its share of sensational and gruesome crimes.

1. Plaza Hollywood stabbings (2023)

Just months after Choi’s alleged murder, two women were stabbed to death in a frenzied knife attack at the Plaza Hollywood shopping centre in Diamond Hill by a man suffering from severe mental illness.

News of the unprovoked attack, captured on CCTV, spread widely online and heightened safety concerns at a time when the city was still recovering from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Szeto Sing-kwong, 43, a former warehouse worker, wandered through the shopping centre with an unsheathed knife he had just bought before encountering Fong Hiu-tung, 26, and Lau Kai-hei, 22, outside a Sasa cosmetics shop.

CCTV footage showed Szeto repeatedly stabbing one of the women in an attack lasting nearly a minute. The second woman tried repeatedly to intervene but was herself slashed and stabbed.

Fong sustained 27 knife wounds and Lau eight, according to medical evidence. Both died from blood loss and respiratory failure.

Szeto later pleaded guilty to two counts of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility, after prosecutors accepted that an acute relapse of paranoid schizophrenia meant he should not be held liable for murder.

Last month, the High Court ordered him to receive indefinite mandatory psychiatric treatment and supervision at Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre in Tuen Mun, noting that he continued to show limited insight into his condition.

2. British banker turned double murderer (2014)

British banker Rurik Jutting tortured and killed two Indonesian women in his Wan Chai flat between October and November 2014.

Jutting tortured 23-year-old Sumarti Ningsih for three days, subjecting her to what the court described as increasingly cruel violence using a belt, sex toys, pliers and his fists, before slitting her throat on or about October 27. Her body was later found in a large black suitcase.

Five days later, he took 26-year-old Seneng Mujiasih, also known as Jesse Lorena Ruri, back to his flat and cut her throat.

It was reported that his murder spree was triggered by the break-up with his fiancée.

Jutting was sentenced to life imprisonment for two counts of murder in 2016. He later appealed to the Court of Final Appeal, which dismissed his final attempt after just eight minutes.

3. Son’s gruesome slaughter of parents (2013)

Henry Chau Hoi-leung, then 29, killed his parents in a rented flat in Tai Kok Tsui and placed their dismembered heads in a refrigerator.

Chau had planned to murder his father, Chau Wing-ki, 65, and mother, Siu Yuet-yee, 63, for six months. He told the court he hated his parents and blamed them for his failures in life and love.

He killed and dismembered the couple at a flat belonging to his friend, Angus Tse Chun-kei. Tse said Chau had threatened to harm his own mother, prompting him to help pack and dispose of some body parts at sea.

Chau was caught after sending text messages confessing to the killings, having earlier filed a missing persons report and made an online appeal for help finding his parents.

Forensic officers believed some of the couple’s body parts had been cooked, microwaved and salted. Others were decomposing when found.

In 2015, Chau was convicted of two counts of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. Tse was sentenced to one year in prison for preventing the lawful burial of bodies.

The case inspired the 2022 film The Sparring Partner.

4. The ‘Hello Kitty’ case (1999)

In one of Hong Kong’s most horrifying cases, 23-year-old nightclub hostess Fan Man-yee was kidnapped and tortured by three triad members before her death. Her head was later placed inside a Hello Kitty doll.

Fan was abducted and held in a flat in Granville Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, after the men accused her of stealing HK$4,000 (US$510) from one of their wallets.

She was held for nearly a month in the flat, which was filled with Hello Kitty toys. The attackers, believed to have been under the influence of drugs, were suspected of torturing her in the days before her death.

After she died, the men dismembered her body, boiled the flesh to conceal the smell of decomposition and discarded other remains. They kept her skull and sewed it into the head of a large Hello Kitty toy.

The case came to light when a 13-year-old girl told police she had been having nightmares and felt “haunted” by a ghost. She was the girlfriend of one of the three killers and had occasionally joined them in assaulting Fan.

In exchange for immunity, she testified against the men, who were convicted of manslaughter. Because only Fan’s skull, a tooth and some internal organs were recovered, the court heard there was insufficient evidence to determine whether she had been murdered or died from another cause, such as a drug overdose.

The three men were sentenced in 2000 to life imprisonment for manslaughter, false imprisonment and preventing Fan’s lawful burial. One had his sentence reduced to 18 years after a retrial.

5. The ‘Rainy Night Butcher’ serial killings (1982)

Perhaps Hong Kong’s most infamous serial killer, night-shift taxi driver Lam Kor-wan murdered four women in the 1980s after picking them up as passengers on rainy evenings.

He drove them to secluded locations, strangled them with wires, photographed their bodies, dismembered them and preserved body parts in containers at his home.

Lam was arrested in 1982 after attempting to develop photographs of his victims at a Kodak shop in Mong Kok. The shop manager alerted police, who ambushed Lam when he returned to collect the pictures.

Although the photographs suggested there may have been more victims, Lam was ultimately charged with the murders of four women police were able to identify.

The court heard that he had eaten part of one victim’s intestine and, according to evidence, including photographs and videos, engaged in necrophilia.

Lam was sentenced to death, but the sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment.

item.title: [SCMP] From kitchen waste to sky-high costs: inside Hong Kong’s quest for green jet fuel
item.description:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.
item.content:encoded:
China’s once-notorious “gutter oil”, recycled from kitchen and drainage waste, has almost vanished from dining tables in recent years and now carries the nickname liquid gold.

The substance has become a highly sought-after feedstock for producing clean energy, especially sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), with biofuel producers such as Hong Kong-based Ecoceres sourcing gutter oil across the Greater Bay Area.

EcoCeres’ co-chairman, Alan Chan Ying-lung, witnessed how the restaurant waste transformed from a nationwide food safety concern into a valuable commodity.

“I can recall that the gutter oil we collected was basically free 10 years ago, and authorities even offered subsidies [to collectors], but now the unit cost is even more expensive than fuel,” he said.

Gutter oil is among a selection of feedstocks, such as animal fat and agricultural waste, that can be used to produce renewable jet fuel, an alternative that will reduce life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel.

SAF, a “drop-in” substitute, can be safely blended with jet fuel and used in aircraft engines without modification, but the challenge is the price.

The Hong Kong government has set a 2030 target for the use of SAF, but has yet to clarify who will pay for it.

“Producers need confidence that demand will be there. Airlines need fuel that is available and affordable. Investors need clarity on the direction of policy. A well-designed policy can connect these needs,” the CEO of Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways, Ronald Lam Siu-por, said at a clean jet fuel conference in September.

A ‘cautious’ target

The city government initially set a goal for SAF to account for between 1 and 2 per cent of all fuel consumed by flights departing from Hong Kong International Airport by 2030.

But in the city’s first five-year plan released in September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu revised the target to 1 to 3 per cent. He also said the city would aim to develop an internationally competitive SAF value chain in the bay area.

Niki Wang Yangwen, Asia-Pacific associate director of biofuels at S&P Global Energy, said Hong Kong’s aim was considered achievable, with Asian economies generally setting targets of 1 to 5 per cent for 2030.

“From our conversations with the market, the general feeling is that 1 to 3 per cent is a fairly cautious target, and people do not have much concern about it,” she said of the city’s goal.

Some industry players expected the city to be a trial site for mainland China to gauge market reactions and, if things worked out, gradually roll out similar measures, she explained.

Hong Kong, like Singapore, is a key aviation hub in Asia, with a dominant home carrier and mostly international traffic, Wang said.

Hong Kong’s airport is one of the busiest in the world, last year recording 61 million passenger trips and a sector-leading 5.07 million tonnes of cargo throughput.

According to the Civil Aviation Department, the number of flights departing from Hong Kong, including cargo and passenger services, jumped by 8.6 per cent to 197,374 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the number in 2024 was 181,663, up by 31.6 per cent from 138,056 in 2023.

In addition, 197,325 flights arrived in 2025, representing an 8.7 per cent increase from the previous year.

Hong Kong is not alone in setting green fuel targets. Elsewhere, demand for SAF is being driven more by mandates than pledges by airlines.

The International Civil Aviation Organisation has adopted a collective goal to cut global aviation emissions by 5 per cent by 2030 on the path to net zero by 2050.

The European Union requires fuel suppliers at its airports to use SAF, starting at 2 per cent of overall fuel in 2025, rising to 6 per cent in 2030 and to 70 per cent by 2050.

Singapore has confirmed a goal of SAF accounting for 1 per cent of overall fuel by 2027 and 3 to 5 per cent by 2030, subject to global developments and SAF availability, while other Asian countries, including Thailand, Japan and South Korea, have also set targets.

How can Hong Kong achieve its goal?

In its latest policy address, the government committed to studying a mandatory consumption mechanism, and launching targeted publicity and educational campaigns by 2028. It will also develop a local blending facility to mix neat SAF with conventional jet fuel into a ready-to-use supply to support uptake.

Separately, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing’s Core Climate carbon marketplace will explore offering green energy and other environmental equity products to the market, including SAF certificates and green hydrogen certificates.

In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Transport and Logistics Bureau and the Environment and Ecology Bureau said the local blending facility was expected to begin operations by 2030.

“This will complete an end-to-end regional value chain, streamline logistics and enhance SAF price competitiveness,” the bureaus said.

As part of the broader value chain in the bay area, the government has also spearheaded the establishment of EcoCeres’ SAF production base in Dongguan, which will begin production by 2030, producing 450,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel per year at full capacity.

EcoCeres’ Chan said the company’s current production of about 770,000 to 800,000 tonnes, well above the 3 per cent requirement of around 200,000 tonnes, was manageable.

“I also believe we will not be the sole supplier. There will be other suppliers in a fair market, so I don’t think there will be any pressure on the overall supply, even at 3 per cent or up to 10 per cent,” he said.

EcoCeres, a clean energy unicorn backed by the family office of Henderson Land Development co-chairman Peter Lee Ka-kit, is the world’s second-biggest producer of SAF, after Finland’s Neste.

Chan said the supply chain was end-to-end, with Dongguan as its starting point. Used cooking oil is collected from nearby bay area cities and pre-processed in the area, while Hong Kong handles blending, research and development, and financing.

Who pays the extra cost?

Chan said the government should have a longer-term plan beyond 2030 and provide details of its mandatory mechanism, noting that the EU had set goals for 2050.

Merlin Lao Man-chi, the head of policy and research at the Business Environment Council, said the government’s mandatory mechanism was crucial, as it would determine market confidence and who would ultimately bear the cost.

“It is important to determine the cost allocation and who will be in charge of the cost as it could scale up the whole industry,” he said.

According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global SAF production is expected to reach 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, representing just 0.8 per cent of aviation fuel use, at a cost of US$4.3 billion to airlines.

The South China Morning Post contacted four Hong Kong-based airlines – Cathay, its budget arm HK Express, Hong Kong Airlines and Greater Bay Airlines – but none offered any comment.

Singapore introduced the world’s first green levy, with passengers bearing the cost, while the EU holds suppliers responsible through penalties.

Lao said the government should offer short-term subsidies, but it would also need to determine how to allocate costs in the longer run.

He said the levy mechanism in Singapore helped encourage acceptance among consumers, but such a move would be “a long shot” in Hong Kong and the government would need to work to garner broad public support.

Lao used Hong Kong’s ill-fated waste-charging scheme in 2024 as an example. Officials and lawmakers initially had good thoughts initially and all agreed on the proposal. But when it came to implementation, residents opposed the measure and the scheme was eventually scrapped.

Asked whether imposing a levy would threaten the city’s status as an international aviation hub, Lao said the fee could be imposed only on passengers or cargo departing from Hong Kong, not those in transit.

Hong Kong’s airport currently charges a HK$200 (US$25) departure tax. In the past few months, airlines have added fuel surcharges on the back of price hikes caused by the Middle East war.

“The mechanism will ensure that we do it first and decide the transshipment and transition later, as they are very price sensitive,” Lao said, noting that a green levy would also hedge against future price volatility.

Lawmaker Chan Siu-hung said he was not worried that the aviation industry would lose customers, as the city’s airport should fight for its own “target customers”.

“Everyone has to understand that protecting the environment comes at a cost. If we do not pay it today, our children and grandchildren will have to pay it in the future,” he said.

However, Chan argued that the government should not offer subsidies because Hong Kong relied on both local and international airlines. Subsidising local airlines could be regarded as unfair competition, while taxpayers’ money should not be used to fund foreign airlines, he said.

Alan Chan of EcoCeres said the extra cost of SAF should be seen as “green value” rather than a “green premium” as each tonne of its fuel would cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by up to 94.4 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel depending on feedstock composition. This was a benefit that everyone would enjoy, he argued.

“If you do not realise it is a value, the product itself will have no value,” he said. “Why would you pay more for the same thing?”

How to lower the price of SAF?

The IATA estimated that the price of SAF would surge to US$2,872 per tonne in 2026, about 2.5 times the price of jet fuel, while S&P Global Energy’s data showed that the SAF price in China was US$2,340 per tonne on October 6.

Lawmaker Chan said scaling operations was essential to bringing down SAF costs.

“Hong Kong is a small market without the scale or critical mass, but the Greater Bay Area has many airports, and their combined demand can reach critical mass,” he said.

If there was a clear demand for SAF, the region’s many facilities and suppliers would naturally be willing to invest in scaling, he added.

The legislator said the next step was developing a carbon trading market that could help bring down costs as the industry scaled up.

One example, he said, was the SAF certificate mentioned in the policy address: airlines could trade the certificates in the market, while companies short of carbon credits could buy them.

Samuel Wong, Asia-Pacific vice-president for sales at PAC LP, a technology supplier in the United States, said used cooking oil alone would not be sufficient to produce SAF on the scale the aviation industry would eventually require.

“Used cooking oil can be turned into SAF, but it can also be used to produce biodiesel and other renewable fuels, so different sectors are competing for the same limited supply,” Wong said. “That competition has pushed prices above US$1,000 per tonne in some markets.”

He said the supply of used cooking oil was inherently limited, meaning the industry would have to develop alternative feedstocks and production technologies as SAF demand increased.

“There are fundamental constraints on both supply and cost,” Wong said. “The amount of used cooking oil that can be sustainably collected is finite, so used cooking oil alone cannot provide all the feedstock needed to scale SAF globally.”

HEFA, or hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids, is currently the main commercial pathway used for producing SAF and uses feedstocks including used cooking oil, vegetable oils and animal fats.

But Wong said achieving much larger SAF volumes would require the industry to diversify beyond HEFA.

“HEFA is essential for scaling SAF today, but it cannot be the only solution,” he said. “The industry needs a portfolio of pathways.”

Lawmaker Chan said Hong Kong needed a detailed action plan beyond 2030.

“[The government] needs a mandatory target by 2030, and then have a clear direction in 2035 to raise the target along the way,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Is Philippines geared for El Nino? Critics say water-planning has run dry
item.description:
As the Philippines braces for months of drought and shortages in key resources due to the current El Nino season, questions are mounting over whether it could have prepared better to deal with a crisis that has been predicted well in advance.

The government’s haphazard response to El Nino reflects its persistent track record of failing to do adequate disaster and infrastructure planning, according to climate and risk specialists.

El Nino is a weather phenomenon that causes changes in winds and rainfall and erratic weather around the world due to warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. The 2026-2027 El Nino event was declared in June by the World Meteorological Organization and is expected to peak in November and December.
item.content:encoded:
As the Philippines braces for months of drought and shortages in key resources due to the current El Nino season, questions are mounting over whether it could have prepared better to deal with a crisis that has been predicted well in advance.

The government’s haphazard response to El Nino reflects its persistent track record of failing to do adequate disaster and infrastructure planning, according to climate and risk specialists.

El Nino is a weather phenomenon that causes changes in winds and rainfall and erratic weather around the world due to warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. The 2026-2027 El Nino event was declared in June by the World Meteorological Organization and is expected to peak in November and December.

On Thursday, Philippine Trade Secretary Cristina Roque told reporters that there was no need for residents to hoard bottled water and that supplies and prices of basic goods remained stable, following social media posts showing that Filipinos were buying water and other items in huge quantities at supermarkets.

“There is no need to panic, there is no need to hoard. We have enough to supply,” Roque said.

However, a suggestion on Wednesday by Rex Gatchalian, secretary of the Department of Social Welfare and Development, to buy buckets to collect rainwater and help prevent water shortages did little to assuage the public’s concerns.

The department said it would be distributing water treatment kits, with Gatchalian demonstrating that water filtered by one such kit was safe for drinking at a media briefing.

One social media user complained: “Telling citizens, many of whom are already struggling with rising living costs, to rely on buckets is a temporary band-aid.”

Analysts question Manila’s readiness to deal with a prolonged drought, amid reports that the government has cut Metro Manila’s water allocation in anticipation of El Nino peaking later this year.

Ven Paolo Valenzuela, a research fellow at Singapore Management University’s College of Integrative Studies, said the Philippines experienced one of its strongest El Nino events in 1997 and disaster planning had not improved almost 30 years later.

He said the problem was not the filtration technology, which he described as “very good” in helping communities hit by super typhoons and other natural disaster events. Rather, it was the absence of a broader plan to address an event with potentially far-reaching effects, he added.

“Thirty years later, you still haven’t solved these problems, still haven’t put [the infrastructure] in place.”

Patrick Manuel, country director of Waves for Water, a non-governmental organisation supplying the filtration kits to the government, said the devices alone could not address the challenges posed by El Nino.

His organisation first introduced the kits to remote communities whose access to clean drinking water was disrupted by the destruction caused by Typhoon Haiyan in 2013.

Manuel said addressing the impact of El Nino required a whole-of-society approach involving government agencies, local governments, the private sector, civil society organisations and communities to boost the country’s water infrastructure and promote responsible water use.

“Through our work with communities from all across the country, we’ve seen that there’s much more work to be done to provide Filipinos with the right tools and infrastructure to be able to have reliable access to clean and safe water,” Manuel said.

Pamela Cajilig, a Philippines-based disaster anthropologist and a fellow of the Atlantic Institute, said the government’s stopgap measures had fuelled distrust as they were seen as transferring responsibility for dealing with extreme weather to ordinary Filipinos.

While Filipinos should do their part, the government’s overemphasis on household measures without implementing a systematic national disaster plan appeared to show its preference for “romanticising resilience”, Cajilig said.

“There is also the practical question of how these filtration devices will work on a mass scale and for a prolonged period. A quick demo for the press does little to help us imagine actual scenarios,” she added.

Keith Paolo Landicho, a research associate of S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ humanitarian help and disaster relief programme, said Filipinos should be told how they would be protected by the state instead of being given another reminder on how to cope with the next disaster.

“Filipinos are tired of their resilience being celebrated while the systems that leave them exposed remain unfixed. Being told to collect rainwater in buckets is not a sustainable solution; it is a stopgap dressed up as preparedness,” Landicho said.

Compared with its neighbours, the Philippines appears to be lagging in preparation ahead of natural disasters, according to analysts.

Valenzuela cited Vietnam, which invested in infrastructure projects such as irrigation systems and sluice gates to regulate water flows from the Mekong River following the 2015–16 El Nino event.

Across the region, countries have been preparing for this season’s El Nino, such as Thailand’s enhancement of its climate databases and Indonesia’s establishment of a drought emergency mechanism in several districts, according to media reports.

The Philippine government’s move to limit Metro Manila’s water supply was a clear sign that it had planned poorly to deal with El Nino’s effects, Valenzuela said.

“We can’t even figure out how to put systems in place when it comes to decades of planning to prevent another major disaster that could happen in 10 or 20 years,” he added.

Landicho said, however, that the water supply situation in Metro Manila appeared to have improved compared with a few months ago, while the water levels in the nearby provinces of Bulacan and Pampanga had recovered from record lows in July.

Nonetheless, with the Philippine state weather bureau Pagasa having issued forecasts on El Nino as far back as March, the country was ill-prepared for “one of the most forecastable hazards”, Landicho added.

Cajilig said an El Nino-related disaster could ultimately have a devastating impact on the Philippines over the long term.

“Unlike rapid onset disasters in which we can immediately witness wide-scale loss of life, livelihood, and infrastructure, slow onset disasters like drought are less dramatic. Yet studies show that their economic impact can be greater across time – mostly because their effects go unaddressed and therefore linger,” she said.

Athea Penaloza, executive director of the Asia-Pacific Alliance for Disaster Management-Philippines, is concerned about a fall in food production and sustained price pressures faced by Filipinos as the agricultural sector could be the hardest hit if dry conditions were to persist, particularly in the first half of next year.

Calling on Manila to provide immediate support to agricultural communities, she said: “This is where the government needs to prepare more proactively. It is important to put concrete measures in place now to support farmers, protect agricultural production and minimise the impact on food security and the cost of living.”

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea’s cruise missile launches test regional defence as arms race intensifies
item.description:
North Korea’s apparent use of different launch methods to fire two types of cruise missiles from a tactical nuclear-capable submarine could complicate regional defence, while raising fresh questions about the operational readiness of its growing undersea arsenal, observers have said.

The North’s official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said on Thursday it had “test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles” off its eastern coast.

The tests “contributed to inspecting the regular mobilisation readiness of underwater combat systems and honing the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions”, KCNA said.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea’s apparent use of different launch methods to fire two types of cruise missiles from a tactical nuclear-capable submarine could complicate regional defence, while raising fresh questions about the operational readiness of its growing undersea arsenal, observers have said.

The North’s official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said on Thursday it had “test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles” off its eastern coast.

The tests “contributed to inspecting the regular mobilisation readiness of underwater combat systems and honing the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions”, KCNA said.

They also demonstrated “the high reliability, dependability and capabilities of the means of war deterrence”, it said, adding that the tests “had no negative impact whatsoever on the security of neighbouring countries”.

South Korea’s military did not publicly announce the launches, sparking speculation that it might have failed to detect them. The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said on Thursday, however, that it had tracked and monitored the launches throughout.

The JCS stressed that the military did not usually disclose North Korean cruise missile launches, limiting public announcements primarily to ballistic missile tests.

Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies said the projectiles were believed to include the Pulhwasal-3-31 (Fire Arrow Type 3-31), a strategic cruise missile with a potential range of about 2,000km that could carry small nuclear warheads.
